# Doubt and Faith: Questions That Actually Matter

Let me start with a confession that might surprise you coming from someone who's supposed to be talking about faith.

Last year, I went through a period where I genuinely wasn't sure if I believed in God. Not the dramatic, angry kind of doubt where you're shaking your fist at the sky. More like... waking up one morning and realizing the things I'd believed my whole life suddenly felt hollow. I'd say my prayers and wonder if anyone was listening. I'd read the Bible and think, "Is this just really old advice, or is it actually true?" I felt like I was supposed to have it figured out by now, and instead I was standing in the middle of this fog, unable to see clearly in any direction.

The worst part wasn't the doubt itself. It was thinking I wasn't allowed to have it.

I'm guessing some of you know what that feels like. Not necessarily about faith specifically, but that sense that you're supposed to have arrived at some kind of certainty—about what you believe, who you are, what matters—and you're still asking questions. And maybe you've felt like that's a failure on your part. Like doubt means you're not spiritual enough, or not smart enough, or not committed enough.

I want to tell you something that took me way too long to figure out: doubt isn't the opposite of faith. It's actually how faith grows.

## The Thing About Growing Up

Here's what's happening in your brains right now, literally. Your prefrontal cortex—the part that handles abstract thinking and questioning—is still developing. You're becoming capable of asking bigger, more complicated questions than you could ask at ten. You're developing the mental equipment to hold multiple perspectives at once, to notice contradictions, to wonder about things that adults sometimes just accept.

This is a feature, not a bug. Your doubt isn't a sign that something's wrong with you. It's a sign that you're thinking.

And here's the thing: if you're going to have a real faith—one that's actually yours and not just inherited from your parents or your church—it has to survive your questions. It has to be able to handle scrutiny. If your faith can't stand up to an honest question, then what you've got isn't really faith. It's just habit.

So when you doubt, when you ask hard questions, when you lie awake at night wondering if any of this is even true—that's not you falling away from faith. That's you potentially moving toward something deeper.

## Thomas and the Permission to Ask

You probably know the story of Thomas. He's the disciple who gets called "Doubting Thomas" in the worst way possible, like it's his permanent personality flaw. Jesus has risen from the dead, and everyone's telling Thomas about it, and he says something like, "Yeah, okay, but I need to see this myself."

And we've turned that into a cautionary tale. Poor Thomas. Didn't believe. Needed proof. How sad for him.

But let me ask you: what if Thomas was actually the most honest person in the room?

Everyone else is taking someone else's word for it. Thomas is saying, "I need to know this for myself. I need to see it." That's not faithlessness. That's integrity. That's refusing to pretend certainty he doesn't have.

And here's what actually happens: Jesus doesn't punish him for asking. He doesn't say, "Thomas, how dare you doubt me." He shows up, and he invites Thomas to touch him. He honors the question. He meets Thomas where he is.

And then—this is important—Jesus says something like, "Blessed are those who haven't seen and yet believe." Not "Blessed are those who never doubt." But "Blessed are those who believe without seeing." There's a difference. It's acknowledging that belief without seeing is hard. It's a real thing to do. And it's worth doing.

Thomas gets a bad rap, but what I see in that story is someone asking an honest question and being taken seriously by Jesus. I see doubt being treated not as a character flaw but as a legitimate part of how we come to know things.

## When the Questions Get Harder

But here's where it gets real: sometimes doubt isn't just a stepping stone to deeper faith. Sometimes it's genuinely painful. Sometimes you ask questions and the answers don't come. Sometimes you're dealing with suffering—your own or someone else's—and the faith you've been taught doesn't seem to account for it.

There's a whole book in the Bible basically dedicated to this. It's called Job. Job loses everything. His kids, his health, his wealth, his reputation. And his friends come around and basically tell him it's his fault. He must have done something wrong. God is just. Therefore, if something bad happened to you, you deserve it.

And Job says no. That's not true. I don't deserve this. And he demands answers from God.

For most of the book, God doesn't answer. Job keeps asking. His friends keep offering explanations that don't work. Job keeps saying those explanations are garbage. He's angry. He's confused. He's in pain. And he won't accept easy answers.

And you know what? God actually respects that. When God finally shows up, God doesn't explain suffering or justify what happened. God basically says, "I'm bigger than you understand, and you're asking the right questions even if I don't answer them the way you want." And that seems to be enough for Job. Not because his pain goes away, but because his doubt was taken seriously.

I'm telling you this because if you're going through something hard, and your doubt is real and painful, that's not a sign you're doing faith wrong. It might be a sign you're doing it the most honest way possible.

## The Next Part

So what do we do with all this? How do we live with doubt without it paralyzing us?

I think the answer is this: you don't resolve doubt by pretending it away. You move through it by staying in relationship with God, with your community, with the questions themselves.

Notice that Thomas doesn't resolve his doubt by thinking harder. He resolves it by encountering Jesus. Notice that Job doesn't get his questions answered; he gets God's presence. Notice that the Psalms are full of people crying out to God, asking why, expressing anger and confusion—and those prayers are in the Bible. They're part of the spiritual tradition. They're considered valid expressions of faith.

What if doubt is just the name we give to faith that's honest about what it doesn't know?

Here's what I've learned: I don't have to have everything figured out. I don't have to arrive at some final, permanent certainty about God. I can live in the questions. I can pray even when I'm not sure anyone's listening. I can read Scripture looking for truth even when I'm not sure what I believe. I can be part of a community of faith even when I'm in the middle of doubt.

And somehow, in that space—not resolved, not certain, but genuinely seeking—I've found something that feels like faith. Not faith in a set of propositions I've memorized. Faith in a presence I keep encountering, even when I can't fully explain it.

## The Actual Next Step

So here's what I want to leave you with. Not an answer, but a question. And maybe a practice.

The question is this: What's one thing you genuinely doubt? Not something you think you're supposed to doubt, but something real. Something that actually matters to you.

And here's the practice: Don't try to resolve it alone. Bring it to someone. Not to get it fixed, but to say it out loud. To a friend, to a mentor, to a pastor, to God in prayer. Just name it. Say the doubt out loud.

Because doubt that stays hidden festers. Doubt that gets spoken, that gets brought into relationship, that gets treated as something real and legitimate—that doubt can become the beginning of something deeper.

You're allowed to ask questions. You're allowed to not have it figured out. And that's not a failure of faith. That's where faith actually gets built.

# When Your Faith Feels Like a Question Mark

I want to start with a confession. Last month, I was sitting in my car in a parking lot—not for any dramatic reason, just waiting for someone—and I found myself genuinely angry at God. Not the kind of anger that feels righteous or productive. Just... frustrated. Confused. I remember thinking, *If you're real and you care, why is this so hard?* And then I sat there feeling guilty about being angry, which made me more frustrated, which made me feel worse about the whole thing.

The person I was waiting for got in the car, and I didn't say anything about it. But I've been thinking about that moment ever since, because I realized something: I was ashamed of my doubt. Not of the honest question itself, but of the fact that I was having it at all. Like doubt meant I was doing faith wrong.

I'm guessing some of you know that feeling.

## The Thing Nobody Tells You About Growing Up

Here's what I wish someone had told me when I was your age: doubt isn't the opposite of faith. It's not faith's enemy, waiting in the shadows to destroy it. Doubt is actually just what happens when you start thinking for yourself. It's what happens when you move from borrowed faith—the faith you inherited from your family or your church—to owned faith, the kind that's actually yours.

And that transition is uncomfortable. It has to be. Because if you never questioned anything, you'd never actually believe anything. You'd just be repeating words.

Think about it this way. When you were little, you probably believed what your parents told you about basically everything. The tooth fairy was real. Carrots helped you see in the dark. Your parents were basically infallible. But as you got older, you started noticing things didn't add up. You asked questions. You tested things. And yeah, some of those discoveries were disappointing. But the result is that now you actually *know* things. You don't just believe them because someone told you to.

Faith works the same way.

The problem is that we've created this weird culture where doubt is treated like a disease. You're supposed to have faith, and if you don't—if you have questions, if things don't make sense, if you're angry or confused or skeptical—then something is wrong with you. You're not spiritual enough. You're not trying hard enough. You're letting the world corrupt you.

But that's not true. And I think we need to name that clearly: **doubt doesn't mean you're failing at faith. It might actually mean you're beginning to understand it.**

## The Guy Nobody Talks About

Let me introduce you to Thomas. You probably know him as "Doubting Thomas," which is kind of a mean nickname when you think about it. Like his whole identity got reduced to the one time he asked a reasonable question.

Here's what happened: Jesus had been arrested, executed, and buried. Thomas's best friend—the person he'd given up everything to follow—was dead. And then the other disciples came to him saying, "We saw him. Jesus is alive. He's back."

And Thomas said, essentially, "I need to see this for myself."

Now, the church has spent two thousand years basically shaming Thomas for this. But let me ask you something: Is that actually unreasonable? His friend was dead. He watched it happen. And now people are telling him something that contradicts everything he knows about how the world works. And he says, "I'm going to need proof."

That's not faithlessness. That's actually pretty human.

But here's the thing that gets interesting. Thomas didn't just give up. He didn't say, "Well, I guess I'm out then." He stayed with the community. He stayed open. And when Jesus appeared to him directly, Thomas didn't say, "Oh, I guess I was wrong." He said something more profound: "My Lord and my God."

Thomas's doubt didn't disqualify him from faith. It led him deeper into it.

And here's what I think is important: Jesus didn't punish Thomas for his doubt. He didn't say, "Thomas, you should have just trusted the other disciples." He just... showed up. He made space for Thomas's real question.

## What Happens When You Actually Ask

I want to be honest about something, though. Sometimes when we bring our doubts to faith, we get brushed off. Someone tells us we just need to pray more, or read the Bible more, or have more faith. And that can feel really lonely. It can feel like your real question doesn't matter.

But I think there's something important to understand: the fact that a question is hard doesn't mean it's a bad question. Some of the biggest, most important questions in faith are hard. They're supposed to be.

Why do bad things happen? Where is God in suffering? Why does faith sometimes feel empty? Why do I have doubts when everyone around me seems so sure? These aren't questions you're supposed to get over. They're questions you're supposed to *live with*. They're the questions that actually shape who you become.

There's a whole book in the Bible—Job—that's basically just a guy asking God really hard questions about suffering and justice. And God's response isn't to answer all his questions. God basically says, "Job, you're asking good questions, but you're not seeing the whole picture." And Job has to sit with that. He has to learn to trust without having all the answers.

That's what faith actually looks like sometimes.

## The Weird Thing About Honest Questions

Here's what I've discovered: when you actually ask your questions—when you stop pretending to be sure and start being honest about what you actually think and feel—something unexpected happens. Your faith gets more real, not less real.

I'm not saying all your doubts will disappear. I'm saying that the faith that survives your questions is faith that actually belongs to you. It's not something you're performing for other people. It's not something you're white-knuckling your way through because you're supposed to.

It's real.

And real faith—the kind that's actually yours—is so much stronger than borrowed faith. It's the kind that can hold up when things get hard. It's the kind that can ask real questions and still show up. It's the kind that can say, "I don't have all the answers, and I'm going to keep seeking anyway."

## So What Now?

I don't want to end this by telling you to just "have faith" or "trust God" or whatever the nice Christian phrase is. You're smart enough to know when you're being handed a platitude.

Instead, here's what I'm going to suggest: **Get honest with someone.**

Not necessarily in a big, dramatic way. But find one person—a youth leader, a mentor, a friend, a parent, whoever—and tell them one real doubt you're carrying. One question that keeps you up at night. One thing about faith that doesn't make sense to you yet.

Just say it out loud.

Because doubt thrives in silence. It grows bigger and scarier when you're carrying it alone. But when you say it out loud to someone who won't judge you for it—someone who gets that faith and doubt aren't opposites—something shifts. You stop being ashamed of your own mind.

And that's where real faith begins.

Your questions matter. Your honesty matters. The fact that you're thinking about this stuff—that you're not just accepting everything on autopilot—that matters too.

You're not failing at faith because you doubt. You're actually doing something brave. You're figuring out what you actually believe.

And that's worth something.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

I want to start by telling you about something that happened to me a few years ago.

I was sitting in a church service—a perfectly normal Sunday—and the worship band was playing, and everyone around me had their eyes closed and their hands up, and I just... felt nothing. Absolutely nothing. And this thought crept in, quiet but clear: *What if none of this is real?*

And I didn't just mean the music or the atmosphere. I meant all of it. God. The resurrection. Prayer. The whole thing.

It wasn't dramatic. There was no lightning bolt of crisis. It was more like noticing a crack in a wall that might have been there for a while. And the scariest part wasn't the doubt itself—it was the feeling that I couldn't tell anyone. Because what would they think? That I was losing my faith? That I was a bad Christian? That something was wrong with me?

I'm telling you this because I have a suspicion that some of you know exactly what I'm talking about. Maybe not that specific moment, but something like it. A question you've been carrying around that you haven't said out loud. A prayer that felt like talking to the ceiling. A Bible passage that made you uncomfortable instead of comforted. A science class or a philosophy conversation or just a quiet Tuesday night where something shifted and you thought, *I'm not sure I believe this anymore.*

If that's you, I want to say something clearly before we go any further: **you are not broken.** You are not failing at faith. You are not disappointing God. You are doing something that every honest person who has ever taken faith seriously has done—you are thinking.

---

## Doubt Is Not the Opposite of Faith

We tend to treat doubt and faith like they're on opposite ends of a spectrum. More doubt means less faith. More faith means no doubt. But I don't think that's how it works. I think the opposite of faith isn't doubt—it's indifference. Doubt means you care enough to wrestle. Indifference means you've walked away from the ring entirely.

Think about it this way. You don't doubt things you don't care about. You've probably never lay awake at night wondering whether the capital of Mongolia is really Ulaanbaatar. You just don't care enough to doubt it. But the things that matter—whether you're loved, whether your life has meaning, whether God is real and whether God is good—those are the things worth losing sleep over. Doubt, in that sense, is a sign that something matters to you deeply.

And let's be honest about something else: you are at a stage of life where doubt is almost inevitable, and not because there's something deficient about being a teenager. It's because you're developing the capacity for abstract thought in ways you couldn't when you were eight. You're starting to own your beliefs instead of just inheriting them. That process is messy. It involves pulling things apart to see how they work. Sometimes things don't go back together the same way, and that's okay. That might even be the point.

A faith that has never been questioned is a faith that has never been tested. And untested faith is fragile in ways you might not discover until it's too late—until you're in a university lecture hall or a hospital waiting room or a moment of real suffering, and the whole thing collapses because it was never really yours. It was just something you were handed.

---

## A Guy Named Habakkuk

I want to introduce you to someone from the Bible you might not have heard much about. His name is Habakkuk, and he's a prophet, which means he's supposed to be one of the spiritual all-stars. And the very first thing he says—literally the opening lines of his book—is a complaint to God:

*"How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?"*

Read that again. This isn't a polite theological question. This is a man looking at the world—at violence and injustice and suffering—and saying to God, directly, *What are you doing? Why aren't you fixing this? Are you even paying attention?*

And here's what I find remarkable: God doesn't strike him down. God doesn't say, "How dare you question me." God actually responds. The response is complicated and not entirely satisfying—God basically says, "I'm doing something you wouldn't believe even if I told you," which, if we're honest, is kind of frustrating. But the conversation happens. The relationship holds. Habakkuk doubts loudly, and God doesn't flinch.

By the end of the book, Habakkuk lands somewhere interesting. He doesn't get all his questions answered. The injustice doesn't magically resolve. But he writes this:

*"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord."*

That's not naive optimism. That's not pretending everything is fine. That's a man who has looked at the worst of the world, screamed his questions at God, and somehow—on the other side of all that honesty—found something to hold onto. Not answers, exactly. More like trust. A bruised, hard-won trust that came *through* the doubt, not around it.

I think that kind of faith is worth more than the kind that never asks questions.

---

## What Honest Questions Actually Do

Here's what I've come to believe about doubt: it's not a pit you fall into. It's more like a tunnel you pass through. And on the other side, your faith might look different than it did before—probably simpler in some ways, more complex in others—but it will be *yours*. Not your parents' faith. Not your youth leader's faith. Yours.

But I want to be honest with you, because you deserve honesty: I can't promise you that every question has a neat answer. Some of the hardest questions—Why does God allow suffering? What happens to people who never hear the gospel? How do I reconcile what I read in certain parts of the Bible with what I know to be true and good?—these are questions that brilliant, faithful people have wrestled with for centuries without reaching total consensus. If someone gives you a thirty-second answer to one of those questions, be suspicious. The question deserves more respect than that.

What I *can* tell you is that asking those questions doesn't make you an outsider. It puts you in remarkably good company. David wrote psalms that are basically arguments with God. Job sat in ashes and demanded an explanation from the Almighty. The father of a sick child in Mark's gospel said to Jesus, with stunning honesty, "I believe; help my unbelief." That's maybe the most relatable prayer in the entire Bible. Faith and doubt, in the same breath, from the same mouth. And Jesus didn't turn him away.

I think God is less threatened by your questions than you think. I think God would rather have an honest wrestler than a polite pretender. The biblical word "Israel" literally means "wrestles with God." It's the name God gave to an entire people. Wrestling isn't a bug in the system. It might be a feature.

---

## So What Do You Do With This?

I'm not going to end with five easy steps, because this isn't a five-easy-steps kind of topic. But I want to leave you with one practice to try.

This week, I want you to write down the question. The one you've been carrying. The one you're afraid to say out loud. You don't have to show it to anyone. Just get it out of your head and onto paper—or into your phone, whatever. Give it actual words.

There's something that happens when you name a thing. It gets smaller. Not the question itself—the fear around it. The shame. The loneliness of carrying it alone.

And then, if you're ready—and only if you're ready—find one person you trust and say it out loud. Not someone who will panic. Not someone who will give you a bumper-sticker answer. Someone who will sit with you in it. A friend, a parent, a leader, a mentor. Someone who can say, "Yeah, I've wondered about that too," and mean it.

Because here's the last thing I want to say: doubt is lonely only when it's secret. The moment you share it, you'll almost certainly discover that you're not the only one. You never were.

Your questions are welcome here. Bring them.

I think the opposite of faith isn't doubt—it's indifference. Doubt means you care enough to wrestle. Indifference means you've walked away from the ring entirely.

Think about it this way. You don't doubt things you don't care about. You've probably never lain awake at night wondering whether the capital of Mongolia is really Ulaanbaatar. You just don't care enough to doubt it. But the things that matter—whether you're loved, whether your life has meaning, whether God is real and whether God is good—those are the things worth losing sleep over. Doubt, in that sense, is a sign that something matters to you deeply.

And let's be honest about something else: you are at a stage of life where doubt is almost inevitable, and not because there's something deficient about being a teenager. It's because you're developing the capacity for abstract thought in ways you couldn't when you were eight. You're starting to own your beliefs instead of just inheriting them. That process is messy. It involves pulling things apart to see how they work. Sometimes things don't go back together the same way, and that's okay. That might even be the point.

And doubt doesn't come from just one direction. Maybe yours is intellectual—things you're learning in school or reading online don't seem to fit with what you've been told in church. Maybe it's personal—you prayed for something that really mattered and nothing happened, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it's moral—you've seen things done or said in God's name that don't look anything like love, and you're wondering how the two can coexist. Whatever flavour your doubt takes, it's known. It's not new. And it doesn't disqualify you from anything.

A faith that has never been questioned is a faith that has never been tested. And untested faith is fragile in ways you might not discover until it's too late—until you're in a university lecture hall or a hospital waiting room or a moment of real suffering, and the whole thing collapses because it was never really yours. It was just something you were handed.

---

## A Guy Named Habakkuk

I want to introduce you to someone from the Bible you might not have heard much about. His name is Habakkuk, and he's a prophet, which means he's supposed to be one of the spiritual all-stars. And the very first thing he says—literally the opening lines of his book—is a complaint to God:

*"How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?"*

Read that again. This isn't a polite theological question. This is a man looking at the world—at violence and injustice and suffering—and saying to God, directly, *What are you doing? Why aren't you fixing this? Are you even paying attention?*

And here's what I find remarkable: God doesn't strike him down. God doesn't say, "How dare you question me." God actually responds. The response is complicated and not entirely satisfying—God basically says, "I'm doing something you wouldn't believe even if I told you," which, if we're honest, is kind of frustrating. But the conversation happens. The relationship holds. Habakkuk doubts loudly, and God doesn't flinch.

By the end of the book, Habakkuk lands somewhere interesting. He doesn't get all his questions answered. The injustice doesn't magically resolve. But he writes this:

*"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord."*

That's not naive optimism. That's not pretending everything is fine. That's a man who has looked at the worst of the world, screamed his questions at God, and somehow—on the other side of all that honesty—found something to hold onto. Not answers, exactly. More like trust. A bruised, hard-won trust that came *through* the doubt, not around it.

I think that kind of faith is worth more than the kind that never asks questions.

---

## What Honest Questions Actually Do

Here's what I've come to believe about doubt: it's not a pit you fall into. It's more like a tunnel you pass through. And on the other side, your faith might look different than it did before—probably simpler in some ways, more complex in others—but it will be *yours*. Not your parents' faith. Not your youth leader's faith. Yours.

But I want to be honest with you, because you deserve honesty: I can't promise you that every question has a neat answer. Some of the hardest questions—Why does God allow suffering? What happens to people who never hear the gospel? How do I reconcile what I read in certain parts of the Bible with what I know to be true and good?—these are questions that brilliant, faithful people have wrestled with for centuries without reaching total consensus. If someone gives you a thirty-second answer to one of those questions, be suspicious. The question deserves more respect than that.

What I *can* tell you is that asking those questions doesn't make you an outsider. It puts you in remarkably good company. David wrote psalms that are basically arguments with God. Job sat in ashes and demanded an explanation from the Almighty. The father of a sick child in Mark's gospel said to Jesus, with stunning honesty, "I believe; help my unbelief." That's maybe the most relatable prayer in the entire Bible. Faith and doubt, in the same breath, from the same mouth. And Jesus didn't turn him away.

I think God is less threatened by your questions than you think. I think God would rather have an honest wrestler than a polite pretender. The biblical word "Israel" literally means "wrestles with God." It's the name God gave to an entire people. Wrestling isn't a bug in the system. It might be a feature.

---

## So What Do You Do With This?

I'm not going to end with five easy steps, because this isn't a five-easy-steps kind of topic. But I want to leave you with something to try.

First, just ask yourself this—right now, even, sitting where you are: *What's one thing I used to be sure about that I now have questions about?* Or maybe: *Where's a gap between what I've been taught and what I actually see in the world?* You don't have to answer it fully. Just let yourself notice it. Give yourself permission to name it, even silently.

Then, sometime this week, write it down. The question you've been carrying. The one you're afraid to say out loud. You don't have to show it to anyone. Just get it out of your head and onto paper—or into your phone, whatever. Give it actual words.

There's something that happens when you name a thing. It gets smaller. Not the question itself—the fear around it. The shame. The loneliness of carrying it alone.

And then, if you're ready—and only if you're ready—find one person you trust and say it out loud. Not someone who will panic. Not someone who will give you a bumper-sticker answer. Someone who will sit with you in it. A friend, a parent, a leader, a mentor. Someone who can say, "Yeah, I've wondered about that too," and mean it.

Because here's the last thing I want to say: doubt is lonely only when it's secret. The moment you share it, you'll almost certainly discover that you're not the only one. You never were.

Your questions are welcome here. So please, bring them.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

So I want to start tonight by telling you about something that happened to me — and I'm telling you this because I think it matters, not because I have it all figured out.

There was a season in my life where I sat in church and felt absolutely nothing. The songs that used to move me just felt like words on a screen. Prayers felt like talking to a ceiling. And the worst part wasn't the emptiness itself — it was the fear that came with it. This creeping thought: *What if none of this is real? What if I've just been going along with something because everyone around me believes it?*

And I didn't tell anyone. For months. Because I thought if I said it out loud, people would panic. They'd pull me aside, give me a book, pray over me like I was broken. Or worse — they'd quietly decide I was a project, someone who needed to be fixed.

I'm telling you this because I have a suspicion that some of you are carrying something similar right now. Maybe not exactly that, but some version of it. A question you haven't said out loud. A doubt that sits in the back of your mind during worship, during small group, during those moments when everyone else seems so certain and you're thinking, *Am I the only one who isn't sure?*

You're not the only one.

And I want to be really clear about something before we go any further: **having doubts does not mean your faith is failing.** I know that might sound like something people just say, so let me try to explain why I actually believe it.

---

Think about any relationship in your life that matters to you — a close friendship, your relationship with a parent, whatever. Has it ever been easy the whole way through? Has there ever been a moment where you questioned whether they really cared, whether you could trust them, whether the whole thing was worth the effort?

Of course there has. That's what happens in real relationships. You hit friction. You misunderstand each other. You go through seasons where it doesn't feel the way it used to. And the relationships that survive those seasons — the ones where people are honest about the hard stuff instead of pretending everything is fine — those are the ones that actually become deep.

I think faith works the same way. Not because God needs us to doubt in order to grow, but because *we* are the kind of creatures who need to wrestle with things before we can truly hold onto them. The faith you inherited from your parents or your church — that faith carried you for a while, and that's good. But at some point, it has to become yours. And that process is rarely smooth.

---

I want to talk about someone in Scripture who gets a bad reputation, and I think it's unfair. You probably know where I'm going. Thomas.

Poor Thomas. Two thousand years of being called "Doubting Thomas," like that's his whole identity. Here's what actually happened.

Jesus has been crucified. Thomas watched it happen, or at least heard about it in devastating detail. The person he left everything to follow is dead. And then the other disciples come to him and say, "We've seen the Lord. He's alive."

Now put yourself in Thomas's position for a second. Not in the version where you already know the ending of the story, but in the real, raw moment. Your closest friend was publicly executed by the state. You're grieving. You're scared. You're probably questioning every decision that led you here. And now your friends are telling you something that sounds impossible.

Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

And honestly? I respect that. He's not being difficult. He's being human. He's saying, *I can't just take your word for this. The stakes are too high. I need to know for myself.*

Here's what I love about what happens next. Jesus shows up. And he doesn't scold Thomas. He doesn't say, "I'm really disappointed in you." He doesn't give him a lecture about faith. He walks straight to him and says, "Here. Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe."

Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is. He doesn't shame the question. He answers it.

And Thomas's response? "My Lord and my God." Which is, by the way, one of the most profound declarations of faith in the entire New Testament. It came *through* the doubt, not around it.

Yes, Jesus says, "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." That's true. But notice he doesn't say, "Cursed are those who needed to ask." He doesn't kick Thomas out of the group. Thomas goes on, according to tradition, to carry the gospel further than almost any other disciple — all the way to India. His doubt didn't disqualify him. It became part of his story.

---

Here's what I want you to hear, and I want you to hear it clearly: **there is a difference between doubt and unbelief.**

Unbelief is a settled decision. It's closing the door and walking away. Doubt is standing in the doorway, uncertain, but still *there*. Still looking. Still asking. The fact that your questions bother you — the fact that you care enough to feel unsettled — that tells me something important. People who don't care don't feel conflicted. Your doubt might actually be evidence that your faith is more alive than you think.

I'm not saying every question has a neat answer. Some of them don't. Why does God allow suffering? Why does prayer sometimes feel like nothing? Why does the Bible contain things that are genuinely hard to understand? These are real questions, and if anyone tells you they're simple, they're either not being honest or they haven't thought about them very hard.

But here's what I've found — and I'm not saying this as someone who has arrived, but as someone who's still walking. The people whose faith I admire most are not the people who never doubted. They're the people who doubted honestly and kept showing up. They brought their questions to God instead of just to their own heads. They stayed in the conversation.

There's a Psalm — Psalm 13 — where David literally opens with, "How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That's in the Bible. That's Scripture. A man after God's own heart, shouting into what feels like silence. And by the end of that same Psalm, he's singing again. Not because his circumstances changed, but because the act of being honest with God — brutally, painfully honest — brought him back to something real.

That's what I want for you. Not a faith that's never been tested. A faith that's been tested and survived. A faith with roots, not just leaves.

---

So here's what I'm not going to do. I'm not going to end this with five easy steps to overcome doubt. That would be dishonest, and you'd see right through it anyway.

Instead, I want to leave you with one practice. It's simple, but it's not easy.

**This week, tell God — out loud or on paper — the thing you're most afraid to say to him.**

The question you think is too dangerous. The frustration you've been swallowing. The thing you think might make you a "bad Christian" if you admitted it. Say it. Write it down. Don't dress it up in religious language. Just be honest.

You might feel nothing after you do it. That's okay. This isn't a magic formula. But I believe something shifts when we stop performing for God and start talking to him like he's actually there and actually listening. Because if he's real — and I believe he is — then he already knows what you're thinking. You're not protecting him from your doubts. You're only protecting yourself from the vulnerability of saying them out loud.

And if you need someone to say them to who has skin on — a leader, a friend, a parent — find that person. Not someone who will panic, but someone who will sit with you in the question. You deserve that.

Doubt is not the enemy of faith. Silence is. Pretending is. The willingness to ask hard questions and keep walking — that's not weakness. That might be the bravest kind of faith there is.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

So I want to start tonight by telling you about something that happened to me — and I'm telling you this because I think it matters, not because I have it all figured out.

There was a season in my life where I sat in church and felt absolutely nothing. I remember standing during worship, mouth moving, singing the lyrics, but feeling like I was reading a menu at a restaurant. Just text on a screen. The magic was gone. Prayers felt like talking to a ceiling. And the worst part wasn't the emptiness itself — it was the fear that came with it. This creeping thought: *What if none of this is real? What if I've just been going along with something because everyone around me believes it?*

And I didn't tell anyone. For months. Because I thought if I said it out loud, people would panic. They'd pull me aside, give me a book, pray over me like I was broken. Or worse — they'd quietly decide I was a project, someone who needed to be fixed.

I'm telling you this because I have a suspicion that some of you are carrying something similar right now. Maybe not exactly that, but some version of it. A question you haven't said out loud. A doubt that sits in the back of your mind during worship, during small group, during those moments when everyone else seems so certain and you're thinking, *Am I the only one who isn't sure?*

You're not the only one.

And I want to be really clear about something before we go any further: **having doubts does not mean your faith is failing.** I know that might sound like something people just say, so let me try to explain why I actually believe it.

---

Think about any relationship in your life that matters to you — a close friendship, your relationship with a parent, whatever. Has it ever been easy the whole way through? Has there ever been a moment where you questioned whether they really cared, whether you could trust them, whether the whole thing was worth the effort?

Of course there has. That's what happens in real relationships. You hit friction. You misunderstand each other. You go through seasons where it doesn't feel the way it used to. And the relationships that survive those seasons — the ones where people are honest about the hard stuff instead of pretending everything is fine — those are the ones that actually become deep.

I think faith works the same way. Not because God needs us to doubt in order to grow, but because *we* are the kind of creatures who need to wrestle with things before we can truly hold onto them. The faith you inherited from your parents or your church — that faith carried you for a while, and that's good. But at some point, it has to become yours. And that process is rarely smooth.

And here's the thing — it makes sense that this is happening *now*. Your world is getting bigger. You're learning about evolution in biology, reading about the Crusades in history, scrolling past footage of wars and famines and injustice every single day. Your childhood faith wasn't built to hold all of that. That doesn't mean it was wrong — it means you're outgrowing the container, and you need a faith that's big enough for the world you're actually living in. That friction you feel? It's not a sign that something is breaking. It might be a sign that something is expanding.

---

I want to talk about someone in Scripture who gets a bad reputation, and I think it's unfair. You probably know where I'm going. Thomas.

Poor Thomas. Two thousand years of being called "Doubting Thomas," like that's his whole identity. Here's what actually happened.

Jesus has been crucified. Thomas watched it happen, or at least heard about it in devastating detail. The person he left everything to follow is dead. And then the other disciples come to him and say, "We've seen the Lord. He's alive."

Now put yourself in Thomas's position for a second. Not in the version where you already know the ending of the story, but in the real, raw moment. Your closest friend was publicly executed by the state. You're grieving. You're scared. You're probably questioning every decision that led you here. And now your friends are telling you something that sounds impossible.

Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

And honestly? I respect that. He's not being difficult. He's being human. He's saying, *I can't just take your word for this. The stakes are too high. I need to know for myself.*

Here's what I love about what happens next. A week goes by. Imagine that week. Seven days of Thomas sitting with the other disciples, hearing their joy, feeling his own emptiness, wondering if he's the problem. Then Jesus walks into the room.

And there's this moment — I imagine a silence before Jesus speaks, and Thomas is bracing himself. He's expecting a rebuke. A lecture. *You should have believed them.* But that's not what happens. Jesus walks straight to him and says, "Here. Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."

Jesus doesn't scold the question. He *answers* it. And notice what he offers as evidence — his scars. The marks of his own suffering. He meets Thomas's pain with proof that he himself has suffered. That's not a lecture about faith. That's an invitation into intimacy.

And Thomas's response? "My Lord and my God." One of the most profound declarations of faith in the entire New Testament. It came *through* the doubt, not around it.

Yes, Jesus says, "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." That's true. But notice he doesn't say, "Cursed are those who needed to ask." He doesn't kick Thomas out of the group. Thomas goes on, according to tradition, to carry the gospel further than almost any other disciple — all the way to India. His doubt didn't disqualify him. It became part of his story.

---

Here's what I want you to hear, and I want you to hear it clearly: **the opposite of faith is not doubt. The opposite of faith is indifference.** Indifference doesn't care enough to ask. Indifference shrugs and moves on. But doubt? Doubt is standing in the doorway, frustrated, maybe even angry, but still *there*. Still looking. Still asking.

The fact that your questions bother you — the fact that you care enough to feel unsettled — that tells me something important. If you were truly done, you wouldn't feel conflicted. You'd feel nothing. Your doubt might actually be evidence that your faith is more alive than you think.

I'm not saying every question has a neat answer. Some of them don't. Why does God allow suffering? Why does prayer sometimes feel like nothing? How can science and Genesis both be true? Why does the church sometimes seem so judgmental when it's supposed to be the most loving place on earth? Why does the Bible contain things that are genuinely hard to understand?

These are real questions. I'm not going to pretend they aren't. And if anyone tells you they're simple, they're either not being honest or they haven't thought about them very hard.

But here's what I've found — and I'm not saying this as someone who has arrived, but as someone who's still walking. The people whose faith I admire most are not the people who never doubted. They're the people who doubted honestly and kept showing up. They brought their questions to God instead of just to their own heads. They stayed in the conversation.

There's a Psalm — Psalm 13 — where David literally opens with, "How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That's in the Bible. That's Scripture. A man after God's own heart, shouting into what feels like silence. And by the end of that same Psalm, he's singing again. Not because his circumstances changed, but because the act of being honest with God — brutally, painfully honest — brought him back to something real.

That's what I want for you. Not a faith that's never been tested. A faith that's been tested and survived. A faith with roots, not just leaves.

---

So here's what I'm not going to do. I'm not going to end this with five easy steps to overcome doubt. That would be dishonest, and you'd see right through it anyway.

Instead, I want to leave you with one practice. It's simple, but it's not easy.

**This week, tell God — out loud or on paper — the thing you're most afraid to say to him.**

The question you think is too dangerous. The frustration you've been swallowing. The thing you think might make you a "bad Christian" if you admitted it. Say it. Write it down. Don't dress it up in religious language. Just be honest.

You might feel nothing after you do it. That's okay. This isn't a magic formula. But I believe something shifts when we stop performing for God and start talking to him like he's actually there and actually listening. Because if he's real — and I believe he is — then he already knows what you're thinking. You're not protecting him from your doubts. You're only protecting yourself from the vulnerability of saying them out loud.

And if you need someone to say them to who has skin on — a leader, a friend, a parent — find that person. Here's how you'll know who the right person is: look for someone who listens more than they talk. Someone who admits when they don't know the answer instead of faking one. That's the person who can sit with you in the question without trying to rush you out of it. You deserve that.

Doubt is not the enemy of faith. Silence is. Pretending is. The willingness to ask hard questions and keep walking — that's not weakness.

God isn't intimidated by your questions. He's just waiting for you to ask them. So go ahead. Ask.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

I remember one Sunday morning specifically — the worship team was playing a song I used to love, and I looked around the room and everyone had their eyes closed, hands up, and I was just standing there with my mouth shut, holding a lukewarm coffee, thinking, *I feel nothing. I feel absolutely nothing.* And then on the drive home I turned the radio up loud so I wouldn't have to sit in the silence of what that meant.

The worst part wasn't the emptiness itself — it was the fear that came with it. This creeping thought: *What if none of this is real? What if I've just been going along with something because everyone around me believes it?*

And I didn't tell anyone. For months. Because I thought if I said it out loud, people would panic. They'd pull me aside, give me a book, pray over me like I was broken. Or worse — they'd quietly decide I was a project, someone who needed to be fixed.

I'm telling you this because I have a suspicion that some of you are carrying something similar right now. Maybe not exactly that, but some version of it. A question you haven't said out loud. A doubt that sits in the back of your mind during worship, during small group, during those moments when everyone else seems so certain and you're thinking, *Am I the only one who isn't sure?*

You're not the only one.

And I want to be really clear about something before we go any further: **having doubts does not mean your faith is failing.** I know that might sound like something people just say, so let me try to explain why I actually believe it.

---

Think about any relationship in your life that matters to you — a close friendship, your relationship with a parent. Has it ever been easy the whole way through? Has there ever been a moment where you questioned whether they really cared, whether you could trust them, whether the whole thing was worth the effort?

Of course there has. That's what happens in real relationships. You hit friction. You go through seasons where it doesn't feel the way it used to. And the relationships that survive those seasons — the ones where people are honest about the hard stuff instead of pretending everything is fine — those are the ones that actually become deep.

I think faith works the same way. Not because God needs us to doubt in order to grow, but because *we* are the kind of creatures who need to wrestle with things before we can truly hold onto them. The faith you inherited from your parents or your church — that faith carried you for a while, and that's good. But at some point, it has to become yours. And that process is rarely smooth.

---

I want to talk about someone in Scripture who gets a bad reputation, and I think it's unfair. You probably know where I'm going. Thomas.

Poor Thomas. Two thousand years of being called "Doubting Thomas," like that's his whole identity. Here's what actually happened.

Jesus has been crucified. Thomas watched it happen, or at least heard about it in devastating detail. The person he left everything to follow is dead. And then the other disciples come to him and say, "We've seen the Lord. He's alive."

Now put yourself in Thomas's position for a second. Not in the version where you already know the ending of the story, but in the real, raw moment. Your closest friend was publicly executed by the state. You're grieving. You're scared. You're probably questioning every decision that led you here. And now your friends are telling you something that sounds impossible.

Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

And honestly? I respect that. He's not being difficult. He's being human. He's saying, *I can't just take your word for this. The stakes are too high. I need to know for myself.*

Here's what I love about what happens next. Jesus shows up. And he doesn't scold Thomas. He doesn't say, "I'm really disappointed in you." He doesn't give him a lecture about faith. He walks straight to him and says, "Here. Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe."

Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is. He doesn't shame the question. He answers it.

And Thomas's response? "My Lord and my God." Which is, by the way, one of the most profound declarations of faith in the entire New Testament. It came *through* the doubt, not around it.

He doesn't say, "Cursed are those who needed to ask." He doesn't kick Thomas out of the group. Thomas goes on, according to tradition, to carry the gospel further than almost any other disciple — all the way to India. His doubt didn't disqualify him. It became part of his story.

---

Here's what I want you to hear, and I want you to hear it clearly: **there is a difference between doubt and unbelief.**

Unbelief is a settled decision. It's closing the door and walking away. Doubt is standing in the doorway, uncertain, but still *there*. Still looking. Still asking.

And I want to be honest — sometimes doubt doesn't even feel that hopeful. Sometimes it doesn't feel like standing in a doorway. It feels like being lost in the dark, not sure which direction the door even is. If that's where you are tonight, I'm not going to pretend that's a comfortable place. It's not. But I believe it's still a place where God meets people. Thomas was in a locked room when Jesus found him. You don't have to have your bearings for God to show up.

Why does the Bible contain things that are genuinely hard to understand? Why does the world your science teacher describes sometimes feel more solid than anything you've heard in a sermon? But here's what I've found — and I'm not saying this as someone who has arrived, but as someone who's still walking. The people whose faith I admire most are not the people who never doubted. They're the people who doubted honestly and kept showing up. They brought their questions to God instead of just to their own heads. They stayed in the conversation.

David — the one Scripture calls "a man after God's own heart" — opens with this: *"How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?"* That's not polite. That's not measured. That's a man shouting into what feels like silence, accusing God of looking away.

And then, by verse five — just four verses later — he writes, *"But I trust in your unfailing love; my heart rejoices in your salvation."* Not because his circumstances changed. Not because he got an answer. But because the act of being brutally honest with God — bringing the accusation, the pain, the fear — brought him back to something real. The psalm doesn't resolve the tension neatly. It holds the lament and the trust in the same breath. And that's what makes it true.

David did something in that psalm that I think we're often afraid to do. He told God exactly what he was feeling, without cleaning it up first. And that's actually what I want to invite you to try.

---

So here's what I'm not going to do. I'm not going to end this with five easy steps to overcome doubt. That would be dishonest, and you'd see right through it anyway.

Instead, I want to leave you with one practice. It's simple, but it's not easy.

**This week, say the thing you're most afraid to say — out loud, or on paper.**

The question you think is too dangerous. The frustration you've been swallowing. The thing you think might make you a "bad Christian" if you admitted it. Say it. Write it down. Don't dress it up in religious language. Just be honest.

If you believe God is listening, say it to him. If you're not sure anyone is listening — if that's the very doubt you're carrying — say it anyway. Write it in a journal, write it on your phone at midnight, say it into the silence of your room. The act of honesty matters even before you know who's hearing it.

You might feel nothing after you do it. That's okay. This isn't a magic formula. But I believe something shifts when we stop performing and start telling the truth. Because if God is real — and I believe he is — then he already knows what you're thinking. You're not protecting him from your doubts. You're only protecting yourself from the vulnerability of saying them out loud.

And if you need someone to say them to who has skin on — a leader, a friend, a parent — find that person. Not someone who will panic, but someone who will sit with you in the question. You deserve that.

Doubt is not the enemy of faith. Silence is. Pretending is. The willingness to ask hard questions and keep walking — that's not weakness. That might be the bravest kind of faith there is.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

So I want to start by telling you about something that happened to me that I don't talk about very often.

I was about sixteen, sitting in a service a lot like this one, and the worship music was playing, and everyone around me had their eyes closed and their hands up, and they all looked like they were feeling something real. And I remember standing there thinking: *I feel absolutely nothing.* Not sadness, not anger, not rebellion — just... nothing. Like I was standing on the outside of a window watching something I couldn't get into.

And then a worse thought came: *What if I've never actually felt anything? What if I've just been going along with this because it's what my family does, what my friends do, what I'm supposed to do?*

That thought scared me more than almost anything had up to that point in my life. Because if it was true, then who even was I?

I want to tell you that I went home and prayed and God spoke to me and everything was fine by Tuesday. That's not what happened. What actually happened is that I carried that feeling around for a long time — months — and I didn't tell anyone, because I thought something was wrong with me. Everyone else seemed so certain. I figured I was the only one who wasn't.

I wasn't. I know that now. But I didn't know it then, and the not-knowing made it so much lonelier than it needed to be.

So here's why I'm telling you this: if you have ever sat in a room like this and felt unsure — about God, about faith, about whether any of this is real — I want you to know that you are not broken. You're not failing some test. You're not disqualifying yourself from anything. You might actually be doing something braver than you realize.

---

## Doubt Isn't the Opposite of Faith

There's this idea floating around — sometimes spoken, sometimes just implied — that faith means certainty. That if you really believe, you won't have questions. That doubt is a defect, something to be fixed or prayed away as quickly as possible.

I think that idea has done enormous damage.

Here's what I've come to understand: doubt is not the opposite of faith. *Indifference* is the opposite of faith. If you didn't care at all, you wouldn't be wrestling with anything. The fact that you're asking hard questions — *Does God actually hear me? Why does suffering exist? How do I know this is true and not just cultural conditioning?* — that means something matters to you deeply enough to fight with it.

And you're in very, very good company.

---

## A Guy Who Needed to See for Himself

You've probably heard of Thomas. "Doubting Thomas." The guy who gets one of the worst nicknames in the history of the church for doing something incredibly human.

Here's what actually happened. Jesus had been crucified. Thomas had watched — or at least heard about — the most devastating thing imaginable: the person he'd given up his life to follow was dead. Gone. Everything they'd believed about who Jesus was and what he was going to do had apparently been wrong.

Then the other disciples tell Thomas they've seen Jesus alive. And Thomas says something that I think is one of the most honest sentences in the entire Bible: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I won't believe it."*

Now, we usually tell this story as a cautionary tale. Don't be like Thomas. Just believe. But slow down for a second. Think about what Thomas is actually saying. He's not being arrogant. He's not mocking anyone. He's saying: *This is too important for me to pretend. I can't just nod along with something this significant because other people tell me to. I need it to be real for me.*

And here's the part that always gets me: Jesus doesn't scold him. Not really. Jesus shows up, and he says to Thomas, *"Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand."* He meets Thomas exactly where Thomas is. He doesn't say, "You should have just trusted the others." He says, essentially, "You needed to see? Okay. Look."

Thomas responds with one of the most profound declarations of faith anywhere in Scripture: *"My Lord and my God."* Not "my teacher" or "my rabbi" — *my Lord and my God.* The guy with the most doubt makes the strongest statement of belief. That's not a coincidence.

His doubt didn't disqualify him. It led him somewhere deeper.

---

## Why This Matters Right Now

You're at an age where you're supposed to be questioning things. That's not me being condescending — I mean it literally. Your brains are doing this incredible work of moving from inherited beliefs to owned beliefs. You're figuring out what *you* think, not just what you've been told to think. That process is necessary, and it's often uncomfortable, and it almost always involves doubt.

Some of you grew up in church and you're starting to wonder if you believe this because it's true or because it's familiar. Some of you are dealing with things — grief, family stuff, mental health struggles — that make the idea of a loving God feel abstract at best and cruel at worst. Some of you have friends who aren't religious at all and they seem perfectly fine, and you're wondering what the point of all this is.

Those are real questions. They deserve real engagement, not bumper-sticker answers.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

I want to tell you about something I don't talk about much.

I was about sixteen, sitting in a service a lot like this one, and the worship music was playing, and everyone around me had their eyes closed and their hands up, and they all looked like they were feeling something real. And I remember standing there thinking: *I feel absolutely nothing.* Not sadness, not anger, not rebellion — just... nothing. Like I was standing on the outside of a window watching something I couldn't get into.

And then a worse thought came: *What if I've never actually felt anything? What if I've just been going along with this because it's what my family does, what my friends do, what I'm supposed to do?*

That thought scared me more than anything I'd felt before. Because if it was true, then who even was I?

I want to tell you that I went home and prayed and God spoke to me and everything was fine by Tuesday. That's not what happened. What actually happened is that I carried that feeling around for months. I cried in the car a couple of times. I argued with myself in my room. I kept showing up to things like this, half-curious, half-defiant, not sure why I bothered. And I didn't tell anyone, because I thought something was wrong with me. Everyone else seemed so certain. I figured I was the only one who wasn't.

I wasn't. I know that now. But I didn't know it then, and the not-knowing made it so much lonelier than it needed to be.

So here's why I'm telling you this: if you have ever sat in a room like this and felt unsure — about God, about faith, about whether any of this is real — you are not broken. You're not failing some test. You're not disqualifying yourself from anything. You might actually be doing something braver than you realize.

---

## Doubt Isn't the Opposite of Faith

There's this idea floating around — sometimes spoken, sometimes just implied — that faith means certainty. That if you really believe, you won't have questions. That doubt is a defect, something to be fixed or prayed away as quickly as possible.

I think that idea has done enormous damage.

Here's what I've come to understand: doubt is not the opposite of faith. *Indifference* is the opposite of faith. If you didn't care at all, you wouldn't be wrestling with anything. The fact that you're asking hard questions — *Does God actually hear me? Why does suffering exist? How do I know this is true and not just what I grew up with?* — that means something matters to you deeply enough to fight with it.

And you're in very, very good company.

---

## Thomas: The One Who Needed to See

You've probably heard of Thomas. "Doubting Thomas." The guy who gets one of the worst nicknames in the history of the church for doing something incredibly human.

Here's what actually happened. Jesus had been crucified. Thomas had watched — or at least heard about — the most devastating thing imaginable: the person he'd given up his life to follow was dead. Gone. Everything they'd believed about who Jesus was and what he was going to do had apparently been wrong.

Then the other disciples tell Thomas they've seen Jesus alive. And Thomas says something that I think is one of the most honest sentences in the entire Bible: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I won't believe it."*

We usually tell this story as a cautionary tale. Don't be like Thomas. Just believe. But slow down. Think about what Thomas is actually saying. He's not being arrogant. He's not mocking anyone. He's saying: *This is too important for me to pretend. I can't just nod along with something this significant because other people tell me to. I need it to be real for me.*

And here's the part that always gets me: Jesus doesn't scold him. Jesus shows up and says, *"Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand."* He meets Thomas exactly where Thomas is. He doesn't say, "You should have just trusted the others." He invites Thomas to look, to touch, to come closer — not to back away.

Thomas responds with one of the most profound declarations of faith anywhere in Scripture: *"My Lord and my God."* Not "my teacher" or "my rabbi" — *my Lord and my God.* The guy with the most doubt makes the strongest statement of belief. That's not a coincidence.

His doubt didn't disqualify him. It led him somewhere deeper.

If one person can be that honest about doubt, maybe we all can.

---

Thomas isn't alone. The Bible is full of people who brought their rawest, ugliest questions straight to God — and those words became Scripture. They became *holy.*

David, the man described as being after God's own heart, wrote things like *"Why, Lord, do you stand far off? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?"* and *"How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?"* That's not polished, confident faith. That's someone yelling into what feels like an empty sky.

The prophet Habakkuk opens his entire book with a complaint: *"How long, Lord, must I call for help, and you do not listen?"* He's watching violence and injustice tear his world apart, and he demands to know why God isn't doing anything about it. God doesn't strike him down for asking. Instead, there's a conversation — a real one, tense and unresolved in places — and Habakkuk lands somewhere surprising. Not on certainty, exactly, but on trust: *"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines... yet I will rejoice in the Lord."* He doesn't get all his answers. These writers show us that honest questions aren't the opposite of faith — they're one of its oldest languages. God didn't edit their doubts out of the story. He preserved them for people like us to find.

---

That doesn't mean every question has a neat answer. Some don't. And anyone who tells you they've got them all figured out is either lying or hasn't thought hard enough. But there's a difference between *"I have all the answers"* and *"I have enough to keep walking."* Faith isn't the absence of uncertainty. It's choosing to trust — honestly, with your eyes open — even when you can't see the whole picture.

---

## What to Do With This

Thomas brought his doubt into the room. He didn't leave. He didn't pretend. And Jesus met him there.

And I remember standing there thinking: *I feel absolutely nothing.* Not sadness, not anger, not rebellion — just... nothing. Like I was standing on the outside of a window watching something I couldn't get into.

And then a worse thought came: *What if I've never actually felt anything? What if I've just been going along with this because it's what my family does, what my friends do, what I'm supposed to do?*

That thought scared me more than almost anything had up to that point in my life. Because if it was true, then who even was I?

I want to tell you that I went home and prayed and God spoke to me and everything was fine by Tuesday. That's not what happened. What actually happened is that I carried that feeling around for a long time — months — and I didn't tell anyone, because I thought something was wrong with me. Everyone else seemed so certain. I figured I was the only one who wasn't.

I wasn't. I know that now. But I didn't know it then, and the not-knowing made it so much lonelier than it needed to be.

So here's why I'm telling you this: if you have ever sat in a room like this and felt unsure — about God, about faith, about whether any of this is real — I want you to know that you are not broken. You're not failing some test. You're not disqualifying yourself from anything. You might actually be doing something braver than you realize.

---

## Doubt Isn't the Opposite of Faith

There's this idea floating around — sometimes spoken, sometimes just implied — that faith means certainty. That if you really believe, you won't have questions. That doubt is a defect, something to be fixed or prayed away as quickly as possible.

I think that idea has done enormous damage.

Here's what I've come to understand: doubt is not the opposite of faith. *Indifference* is the opposite of faith. If you didn't care at all, you wouldn't be wrestling with anything. The fact that you're asking hard questions — *Does God actually hear me? Why does suffering exist? How do I know this is true and not just cultural conditioning?* — that means something matters to you deeply enough to fight with it.

And you're in very, very good company.

---

## A Guy Who Needed to See for Himself

You've probably heard of Thomas. "Doubting Thomas." The guy who gets one of the worst nicknames in the history of the church for doing something incredibly human.

Here's what actually happened. Jesus had been crucified. Thomas had lived through the aftermath of the most devastating thing imaginable: the person he'd given up his life to follow was dead. Gone. Everything they'd believed about who Jesus was and what he was going to do had apparently been wrong.

Then the other disciples tell Thomas they've seen Jesus alive. And Thomas says something that I think is one of the most honest sentences in the entire Bible: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I won't believe it"* (John 20:25).

Now, we usually tell this story as a cautionary tale. Don't be like Thomas. Just believe. But slow down for a second. Think about what Thomas is actually saying. He's not being arrogant. He's not mocking anyone. He's saying: *This is too important for me to pretend. I can't just nod along with something this significant because other people tell me to. I need it to be real for me.*

And here's the part that always gets me: Jesus doesn't scold him. Jesus shows up, and he says to Thomas, *"Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand."* He meets Thomas exactly where Thomas is. He doesn't say, "You should have just trusted the others." He says, essentially, "You needed to see? Okay. Look."

Thomas responds with one of the most profound declarations of faith anywhere in Scripture: *"My Lord and my God"* (John 20:28). Not "my teacher" or "my rabbi" — *my Lord and my God.* In fact, if you read John's Gospel as a whole, this is arguably *the* moment the entire book has been building toward — the climactic confession of who Jesus actually is. Which means John didn't include Thomas's doubt as a warning. He included it as the *culmination* of his argument. The guy with the most doubt makes the strongest statement of belief. That's not an accident.

His doubt didn't disqualify him. It led him somewhere deeper.

---

## Why This Matters Right Now

You're at an age where you're in the process of figuring out whether the things you were taught are things you actually believe. That process is necessary, and it's often uncomfortable, and it almost always involves doubt.

Some of you grew up in church and you're starting to wonder if you believe this because it's true or because it's familiar. Some of you are dealing with things — grief, family stuff, mental health struggles — that make the idea of a loving God feel abstract at best and cruel at worst. Some of you have friends who aren't religious at all and they seem perfectly fine, and you're wondering what the point of all this is.

Those are real questions. They deserve real engagement, not bumper-sticker answers.

I'm not going to stand up here and resolve all of that in the next few minutes. That would be dishonest. What I will say is this: the people I know who have the deepest, most resilient faith are not the people who never doubted. They're the people who doubted and stayed in the conversation. They didn't run from their questions, and they didn't let anyone shame them into silence. They brought their uncertainty to God — sometimes angrily, sometimes desperately — and they were honest about it.

The Psalms are full of this. David, the man described as being after God's own heart, wrote things like *"Why, Lord, do you stand far off? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?"* (Psalm 10:1) and *"How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?"* (Psalm 13:1). That's not polished, confident faith. That's someone yelling into what feels like an empty sky.

And it's Scripture. It's holy. God looked at those words — the anger, the confusion, the accusation — and said, *that belongs in my book.*

What's striking about many of those psalms is their shape. They often start in anguish and move, slowly, toward trust — but the movement isn't forced and it isn't instant. Sometimes it takes the whole poem. Sometimes it doesn't fully arrive. That's honest about how faith actually works. You don't skip from doubt to certainty in a single breath. You move through it, one hard sentence at a time.

---

## What Doubt Can Become

I want to offer you a different way to think about this. What if doubt isn't a pit you fall into but a doorway you walk through?

On this side of the door is faith that was handed to you — and maybe it's good, maybe it's real, but it's not fully yours yet. On the other side is something that belongs to you. Not your parents' faith, not your youth leader's faith, but yours — tested, questioned, and chosen with your eyes open. The doorway isn't comfortable. It's narrow and dark and you can't see what's on the other side while you're in it. But the people I trust most are the ones who walked through rather than turning back or pretending the door wasn't there.

That doesn't mean every question has a neat answer. Some don't. Some of the biggest ones — why innocent people suffer, what happens to people who've never heard the gospel, how a good God and a broken world coexist — these are questions that brilliant people have wrestled with for thousands of years. You're not going to solve them in the shower on a Wednesday night. And anyone who tells you they've got them all figured out is either lying or hasn't thought hard enough.

But there's a difference between *"I have all the answers"* and *"I have enough to keep walking."* Faith isn't the absence of uncertainty. It's choosing to trust — honestly, with your eyes open — even when you can't see the whole picture.

---

## One Thing to Try This Week

I'm not going to end with "just pray about it," because if you're in a season of doubt, prayer might feel like talking to a ceiling, and that's okay.

Here's what I want to suggest instead. Sometime this week — maybe tonight, maybe tomorrow — find a quiet moment and write down the one question about faith that bothers you the most. The one you've been afraid to say out loud. Don't censor it. Don't make it sound polite or spiritual. Just be honest.

Then do one of two things with it. Either bring it to someone you trust — a friend, a parent, a leader, me, whoever — and say, "Can I talk about this without being judged?" If that person's first instinct is to listen rather than fix, you've found the right person. Or, if you're not ready for that, bring it to God directly. Even if it feels weird. Even if it feels like talking to no one. You could literally say, "God, I'm not sure you're there, but if you are, here's what I'm struggling with." That's not a lack of faith. That's prayer in its rawest, most honest form.

Thomas brought his doubt into the room. He didn't leave. He didn't pretend. And Jesus met him there.

I won't promise you a timeline. Some people wait a long time, and the silence can feel unbearable. But I've never met anyone who regretted being honest with God, even when the honesty felt like it went nowhere. Honesty has a way of keeping the door open.

You're not broken for wondering. You might just be paying closer attention than you think.
