# When You're Not Sure Anymore

So I want to start by telling you about something that happened to me a few years ago.

I was sitting in a service — a perfectly normal service, nothing weird was happening — and the worship band was playing, and everyone around me had their eyes closed and their hands up, and I just... felt nothing. Absolutely nothing. And I remember standing there thinking, "What if I'm just going through the motions? What if I don't actually believe any of this? What if I've been pretending and I didn't even realize it?"

And that thought scared me so badly that I didn't tell anyone about it for months.

I want to talk tonight about that feeling. About doubt. About what happens when the questions get loud and the answers you used to have don't seem to fit anymore. And I want to say something right at the top, before we go any further:

If you have doubts, you are not broken.

I'm not going to stand up here and pretend I have all the answers wrapped up neatly, because I don't, and you'd see right through me if I tried. What I want to do instead is be honest with you about something the church doesn't always handle well — the reality that faith and doubt aren't opposites. They're more like neighbours. They live closer together than most people are comfortable admitting.

---

Here's the thing about being your age — and I don't mean that in a condescending way, I mean it as a genuine observation. You are at a point in your life where you're starting to think for yourself in ways you haven't before. You're developing the ability to question things, to see complexity, to notice when something doesn't add up. That's not a defect. That's your brain doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

And when that new capacity for critical thinking bumps up against the faith you were handed as a kid — the Sunday school version, the flannel-board version — it can feel like the whole thing is falling apart. You hear about suffering in the world and you think, "How does a good God let that happen?" You read something in the Bible that seems harsh or confusing and you think, "I don't know what to do with this." You pray and nothing seems to change and you wonder if anyone's listening.

Those aren't signs that your faith is dying. Those might actually be signs that your faith is trying to grow up. And growing up is almost always uncomfortable.

---

I want to talk about a guy in the Bible who gets a bad reputation. Thomas. You know him as "Doubting Thomas," which is honestly one of the most unfair nicknames in history. The man followed Jesus for three years, watched him heal people, listened to him teach, gave up his life to be a disciple — and he gets remembered for one moment of uncertainty. That's like being remembered for the one test you failed instead of the degree you earned.

Here's what actually happened. Jesus had been crucified. Thomas had watched the person he believed was the Messiah die a brutal, public death. Everything he'd built his life on for three years had, as far as he could tell, just been destroyed. And then his friends come to him and say, "We've seen him. He's alive."

And Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I'm not going to believe it."

Now — we usually read that as a failure. Poor Thomas, couldn't just take their word for it. But think about what he's actually doing. He's being honest. He's not pretending to believe something he doesn't. He's not faking it to keep the peace. He's saying, "This is too important for me to just nod along. I need to know it's real."

And here's the part that gets me every time: Jesus doesn't scold him. Not really. Jesus shows up, and the first thing he does is meet Thomas exactly where he is. He says, "Here. Put your hand here. Touch the wounds. Stop doubting and believe." He doesn't say, "How dare you question me." He doesn't say, "You should have just had faith." He walks right into the middle of Thomas's doubt and offers himself.

Thomas's response? "My Lord and my God." One of the most powerful declarations of faith in the entire New Testament. And it came *out of* his doubt, not in spite of it.

I think there's something massive in that story for us. Jesus didn't treat Thomas's doubt as betrayal. He treated it as an invitation.

---

What if we started thinking about doubt that way? Not as the enemy of faith, but as faith's growing edge?

I've come to believe that there are two kinds of faith. There's the kind you inherit — the faith you pick up because your parents believe it, because your community believes it, because it's just the water you swim in. And that faith is real. It matters. But at some point, if your faith is going to survive — if it's going to be *yours* — it has to go through the fire of honest questioning.

The Psalms are full of this. David, the man after God's own heart, wrote things like, "Why, Lord, do you stand far off? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?" and "How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?" These aren't polite prayers. These are someone shaking their fist at the sky and demanding answers. And they're in the Bible. They're *scripture*. God included them on purpose.

That tells me something important: God is not afraid of your questions. God is not threatened by your uncertainty. The tradition of wrestling with God — of arguing, of lamenting, of saying "I don't understand and I'm angry about it" — that tradition is as old as faith itself. The word "Israel" literally means "wrestles with God." It's in the name.

---

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't want to romanticize doubt either. Doubt can be genuinely painful. When you're lying in bed at 2 AM wondering if any of this is real, that's not fun. That's not some cool intellectual exercise. It can feel lonely and frightening, especially if you think you're the only one going through it.

You're not the only one. I promise you that. Look around this room. I guarantee you that most of the people here have had moments where they weren't sure. The difference is just that most of us have been taught to keep quiet about it.

And that silence is the real danger — not the doubt itself. When you can't talk about your questions, they don't go away. They just go underground. They fester. And eventually, people walk away from faith not because they had doubts, but because they had no one to be honest with about them.

So if I could ask one thing of this group, it would be this: let's be the kind of community where it's safe to say "I'm not sure." Where someone can raise their hand and say, "I don't know if I believe that," and the response isn't horror or a lecture, but, "Okay. Tell me more. Let's talk about it."

---

I want to leave you with something practical. Not a five-step plan to fix your doubt, because doubt isn't a problem to be solved. It's a conversation to be had.

Here's what I'd invite you to do this week. Find one person — a friend, a parent, a leader, whoever you trust — and tell them one honest thing about where you are with God right now. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It can be as simple as, "I've been struggling to pray lately," or "I read something that confused me," or "I'm not sure I believe the same things I believed two years ago."

Just say it out loud to someone. Because doubt festers in silence, but it often transforms in conversation.

And if you can't find a person yet, try telling God. I know that might sound strange — praying to a God you're not sure about. But I think there's something profoundly honest about a prayer that says, "God, I don't know if you're there. But if you are, I want to know you. Help me with my unbelief."

That's actually a prayer straight from the Bible, by the way. A father brings his sick son to Jesus and says, "I believe — help my unbelief." Faith and doubt, right there in the same sentence. In the same breath.

Maybe that's where most of us actually live. Not in certainty. Not in total disbelief. But somewhere in the middle, believing and doubting at the same time, and asking for help with both.

That's not failure. That might be the most honest faith there is.

# When You're Not Sure Anymore

So I want to start by telling you about something that happened to me — not because my experience is the point, but because I think it might sound familiar.

I was sitting in a service a few years ago, and everyone around me was singing. Eyes closed, hands up, the whole thing. And I remember standing there with my mouth barely moving, thinking: *I don't know if I believe any of this.* Not in a dramatic, angry way. It wasn't some crisis. It was more like I just… noticed. Like realizing you've been driving for twenty minutes and you can't remember a single turn. I looked around at everyone else and thought, "Do they all just *know*? Is something wrong with me?"

I want to start there because I think a lot of us have had some version of that moment. Maybe for you it was during a prayer that felt like it hit the ceiling and bounced back. Maybe it was when something terrible happened to someone you love and the things people said about God's plan made you feel sick instead of comforted. Maybe it was a science class, or a philosophy video on YouTube at 1 a.m., or just a slow, quiet feeling that the faith you inherited as a kid doesn't quite fit the person you're becoming.

And here's what I want to say right at the top, before we go any further: **that's not a sign that something is wrong with you.**

I know that might be hard to believe, because a lot of us have absorbed this idea — sometimes spoken, sometimes just in the air — that doubt is dangerous. That it's the opposite of faith. That if you're a good Christian, you're supposed to be certain all the time, and if you're not certain, you need to pray harder or read more or just stop asking so many questions.

I think that's one of the most damaging things we tell people. And I think it's wrong.

---

Let me take you to a scene you probably know. It's the week after Easter — the original Easter, I mean. Jesus has been crucified. Some of the disciples are saying he's alive again. And Thomas wasn't there when Jesus first showed up.

Now, we call him "Doubting Thomas," which has always struck me as unfair. We've turned his name into a label, like doubt was his whole identity. But think about what actually happened. Thomas had just watched his teacher and friend get executed by the state. He'd seen the nails. He'd watched him die. And now his friends are telling him, "He's back." 

What would you do? Honestly? If your friends told you something that impossible, would you just nod and go along with it?

Thomas said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I'm not going to believe it." And you know what? I respect that. He wasn't being rebellious. He wasn't trying to be difficult. He was being honest. He was saying, *I need more than secondhand reports. I need to experience this for myself.*

And here's the part that really matters: Jesus didn't reject him for it. Jesus showed up. He didn't say, "Thomas, you're out of the group." He didn't say, "Your faith is too weak." He said, "Here. Put your hands here. See for yourself."

Jesus met Thomas *in* the doubt. Not after he'd gotten over it. Not once he'd cleaned up his act and decided to believe. Right there, in the middle of the uncertainty.

I think that tells us something important about what God is actually like — and it's different from the version of God some of us are carrying around, the one who's keeping score of our confidence levels.

---

Thomas isn't the only one, either. The Bible is honestly full of people who wrestled with God and didn't get neat, tidy answers.

Look at the Psalms. David — the guy described as "a man after God's own heart" — wrote things like, "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That's Psalm 13. That's not polite. That's not a nice, composed prayer. That's someone who feels abandoned and is saying so out loud. 

Or look at Habakkuk, this minor prophet most people skip over. He opens his entire book by basically saying, "God, I've been crying out to you about the violence and injustice I see, and you're not doing anything. Why are you making me look at this? Why do you tolerate wrong?" He's not doubting that God exists — he's doubting that God is paying attention. He's doubting that God is good. And that, if we're being honest, is the doubt that really keeps people up at night.

What's remarkable is that these words are *in the Bible*. They weren't edited out. They weren't treated as embarrassing. They were preserved as Scripture — as sacred text — which means the tradition itself is telling us: this is part of it. Wrestling is part of it. Arguing with God is part of it. Feeling like the silence is unbearable is part of it.

Faith that has never been questioned is just… inherited assumption. It might be comfortable for a while, but it's brittle. It breaks when life gets heavy. The faith that actually holds — the kind that sustains people through real suffering, real complexity, real life — is almost always faith that has been through the fire of honest doubt and come out changed on the other side.

Not unchanged. Changed. That's important. The faith you might grow into won't look exactly like the faith you were handed as a kid, and that's okay. It might be less certain about some things and more certain about others. It might hold its beliefs with more humility and more depth. It might look less like a checklist and more like a relationship — which, if you think about it, is what it was always supposed to be.

---

Here's what I'm *not* saying. I'm not saying doubt is the goal. I'm not saying certainty is bad. I'm not saying all questions have answers or that if you just push through, everything will make sense. Some of it won't make sense. Some of the hardest questions — about suffering, about hell, about why God seems silent — don't have clean resolutions, and anyone who tells you they do is selling something.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me tell you about a conversation I had with someone a while back. She was seventeen, sharp as anything, and she'd been coming to church her whole life. And one day she pulled me aside and said, almost in a whisper, like she was confessing something terrible: *"I don't know if I actually believe any of this anymore. And I'm terrified to tell anyone."*

She wasn't angry. She wasn't trying to be edgy or provocative. She was just honest. And the thing that broke my heart a little wasn't the doubt itself — it was the *terror*. The sense that she'd somehow crossed a line. That doubt was the thing you kept hidden, because admitting it meant you were out. You'd failed. You were less.

So I want to start tonight by saying something clearly, and I want you to actually hear it:

**If you have doubts, you are not failing. You are thinking.**

And thinking is exactly what we want you to do.

---

## The Pressure to Perform Certainty

There's a particular kind of exhausting performance that happens in religious spaces sometimes. Everyone sings the songs with their eyes closed. Everyone says "amen" at the right moments. And somewhere along the way, doubt becomes the thing you don't say out loud, because you're not sure how it will land.

But here's what's actually happening in a lot of your heads — and I know this because I've talked to enough of you to know it's not just one or two people:

You're reading things that challenge what you were taught. You're noticing that good people suffer and bad people thrive, and you're not sure how that fits. You're asking whether you actually believe this, or whether you just believe it because your family does. You're wondering if prayer does anything. You're sitting with questions that don't have easy answers, and you're not sure if that's allowed.

It's allowed. It's more than allowed. It might actually be necessary.

---

## Thomas Wasn't the Villain

You've probably heard of Doubting Thomas. He's usually held up as a cautionary tale — the one who needed to see before he'd believe, the one who got it wrong. But I want to read the story again, because I think we've been a bit unfair to Thomas.

After Jesus died, the disciples were hiding. They were scared, confused, grief-stricken. And then — according to John's account — Jesus appeared to them in a locked room. But Thomas wasn't there. And when the others told him, "We've seen the Lord," Thomas said: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."*

Now, here's what I notice. Thomas doesn't run away. He doesn't leave the group. He stays. He keeps showing up, even while he's not sure. And a week later, Jesus appears again — and this time Thomas is there. And Jesus doesn't shame him. He doesn't say, "Well, Thomas, you really let me down." He says, *"Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe."*

Jesus meets him in the doubt. He shows up for the person who was honest about where he was.

Thomas's honesty didn't disqualify him. It's what made the encounter real.

---

## The Psalms Are Full of This

Thomas isn't alone. If you read the Psalms — actually read them, not just the nice bits they put on mugs — you'll find they're full of people shouting at God. Psalm 88 ends with the line "darkness is my closest friend." That's in the Bible. That's not a crisis of faith; that's a person being completely honest about their experience.

David, who wrote many of the Psalms, swings between "The Lord is my shepherd, I lack nothing" and "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — which, by the way, is also what Jesus says from the cross. The whole arc of Job is a man demanding answers from God, arguing with his friends who keep trying to give him tidy theological explanations, and eventually getting to speak directly with the divine — not because he had the right answers, but because he was relentlessly, stubbornly honest.

The Bible doesn't model a faith that's smooth and certain and never troubled. It models a faith that's in *conversation* — sometimes an argument, sometimes a lament, sometimes a desperate question hurled into the dark.

That's not the opposite of faith. That's what faith actually looks like when it's real.

---

## Doubt Is Not the Enemy of Faith — Pretending Is

Here's the thing about pretending to be certain when you're not: it doesn't make the doubt go away. It just makes it go underground, where it festers. And when something eventually shakes you — a loss, a hard question, a moment where the world doesn't behave the way you were told it would — you're not equipped for it, because you never learned to wrestle.

Doubt, when you actually engage with it, does something interesting. It forces you to figure out what you actually think, rather than just inheriting what everyone around you thinks. It separates the things that are real to you from the things you've just been performing. And sometimes — not always neatly, not always quickly — it leads you somewhere more solid than where you started.

I'm not promising that if you sit with your questions long enough, everything will resolve into a tidy answer. That's one of those things I'm not going to say, because it's not true, and you'd know it wasn't true. Some questions don't get answered in this life. Some things remain genuinely hard.

But there's a difference between doubt that you're running from and doubt that you're sitting with. One of them eats you alive in the dark. The other one, slowly, can become part of how you grow.

---

## What This Doesn't Mean

I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying doubt is automatically virtuous, or that uncertainty is the goal. I'm not saying "just keep questioning forever and never land anywhere." That's its own kind of avoidance.

What I'm saying is that honest questions, taken seriously, are the beginning of something — not the end. They're the start of a faith that actually belongs to you, rather than a faith you borrowed and never examined.

And I'm saying that you don't have to do this alone, in secret, terrified that someone will find out you're not sure. The people worth talking to about this stuff are the ones who won't panic when you say you're struggling. Find those people. They exist. They might even be in this room.

---

## A Practical Next Step

I don't want to end this with a nice bow on it, because that would kind of undercut everything I've just said.

So here's what I want to offer instead: one question, and one invitation.

**The question:** *What's the doubt or question you've been most afraid to say out loud?*

You don't have to say it to anyone right now. But I want you to name it to yourself. Write it down if that helps. Don't smooth it over with the answer you're supposed to have. Just sit with the actual question.

**The invitation:** Find one person — one — and tell them where you actually are. Not the version of you that's got it together. The version that's genuinely unsure about something. It might be a leader here, a friend you trust, a parent, someone older who's been through it. Just one person. And see what happens when you say the true thing instead of the safe thing.

Because here's what I believe — and I'm saying this not as a slogan but because I think it's real: a faith that's been questioned and wrestled with and dragged through doubt is more durable than one that's never been tested. It's more yours. It's more honest. And it might, in the end, be more alive.

You're not failing because you have questions.

You're just starting to take this seriously.

And that's worth something.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me tell you about a conversation I overheard once.

Two friends were sitting together after a church service — both around your age — and one of them leaned over to the other and said, very quietly, *"Do you actually believe any of this? Like, actually?"*

And the other one paused for a long time before saying: *"I don't know. I think so. Maybe. I don't know."*

And then they both kind of looked around to make sure no one had heard, and they sat up straight, and they sang the final song.

I think about that moment a lot. Because I think it happens more than we admit. People sitting in church, or youth group, or around a family dinner table, carrying a question they feel like they can't say out loud. Smiling at the right moments. Saying the right things. But underneath it, something that feels like a crack.

And I want to start tonight by saying: if that's you — if you're one of those people — you are in exactly the right place. And you are not broken.

---

## Doubt Isn't the Opposite of Faith

Here's something I think we get badly wrong: we treat doubt like it's the enemy of faith. Like faith is this fragile thing that will shatter if you ask the wrong question. So we learn not to ask. We learn to keep the questions small and quiet.

But that's not what faith actually is. And honestly? It's not even what faith looks like in the Bible.

Think about it. The Bible is full of people who were confused, angry, terrified, and completely unsure about what God was doing. The Psalms are basically a collection of people yelling at God. Job spends most of his book demanding answers and refusing to accept the tidy explanations his friends offer. Habakkuk opens with *"God, why aren't you listening?"* — and that's in the first verse. These aren't people on the fringes of faith. These are the people the Bible holds up as examples.

And then there's Thomas.

---

## Thomas Gets a Bad Deal

We call him "Doubting Thomas," and we say it like it's an insult — like he's the cautionary tale, the one who got it wrong. But read the story again carefully.

Jesus has died. The disciples have watched their friend and teacher be executed. They're hiding in a locked room, terrified that the same thing is going to happen to them. And then — somehow — Jesus appears. He's there, in the room, alive.

Thomas wasn't there. We don't know where he was. Maybe he was getting food. Maybe he needed to be alone. And when the others tell him what happened, he says: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe."*

That's not cynicism. That's grief. That's someone who loved Jesus so much that he cannot afford to hope unless he's sure. He's not being difficult — he's being honest. He's saying, *"This matters too much to me to pretend."*

And here's what gets me: Jesus doesn't punish him for it. Jesus comes back. He shows Thomas his hands. He says, *"Stop doubting and believe"* — but there's no anger in it. He came back for Thomas. He met him exactly where he was.

And Thomas's response? One of the most profound declarations in the whole New Testament: *"My Lord and my God."*

Thomas didn't arrive at faith despite his doubt. He arrived at faith through it.

---

## The Questions Are Allowed to Be Real

I want to be honest with you about something. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that if you just pray harder, or read your Bible more, all the questions will go away. They probably won't. And anyone who tells you otherwise is either not being straight with you, or they've stopped asking the questions that matter.

Some of the questions you might be carrying are genuinely hard. Why does God allow suffering? How can I believe in something I can't see or prove? What about people who've never heard of Jesus? Does prayer actually do anything? Is any of this real, or is it just something I was raised to believe?

Those aren't small questions. They're not questions you should be embarrassed about. They're the questions that philosophers and theologians have wrestled with for centuries, and the fact that you're asking them means you're taking this seriously. That's not a sign of weak faith. That might actually be a sign of growing faith.

Because here's what I've noticed: the people whose faith I find most compelling — most alive, most real — are not the people who never doubted. They're the people who doubted, and kept going anyway. Who sat with the uncomfortable questions instead of running from them. Who said, *"I don't have this all figured out, but I'm still here."*

Faith that has never been tested is like a muscle that has never been used. It might look fine, but you don't actually know what it can do.

---

## What Honest Questions Can Do

When you let yourself ask the real questions — not just the safe, Sunday-school ones — something interesting happens. You start to find out what you actually believe, rather than just what you've been told to believe. And that's a completely different thing.

Inherited faith can get you started. It's a gift. But at some point — and I think that point often happens around your age — you have to decide what you actually think. You have to make it your own, or let it go. And you can't do that if you're not allowed to ask the questions.

The Christian tradition, at its best, has always known this. Augustine wrestled. Luther wrestled. C.S. Lewis, who became one of the most well-known Christian writers of the twentieth century, spent years as an atheist. He didn't believe, and then he argued himself into belief — reluctantly, almost against his will. He described himself as "the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England."

Doubt was part of his story. It wasn't the end of his story.

---

## One Thing I'm Not Going to Say

I'm not going to say, "Just trust God and it'll all make sense." I don't think that's always true, and I don't think you'd believe me anyway.

What I will say is this: there's a difference between doubt that is a doorway and doubt that is a destination. Doubt as a doorway means you keep moving — you keep asking, keep reading, keep talking, keep showing up even when you're not sure why. Doubt as a destination means you park there, close the door, and decide you already know what you'll find if you look further.

The first kind of doubt is honest and alive. The second kind is just a different kind of certainty.

I'm not asking you to pretend you believe things you don't. I'm asking you not to pretend you've stopped searching when you haven't.

---

## Something to Take With You

Here's what I want to leave you with — not an answer, but a practice.

This week, I want you to write down one question you've never said out loud. One thing about faith, or God, or the church, or the Bible that you've wondered about but kept to yourself because it felt too risky to ask.

You don't have to show it to anyone. You don't have to post it or share it. Just write it down. Name it. Because there's something important about not letting the questions stay shapeless and vague in the back of your mind. When you write them down, they become real — and real questions can be explored.

And then — if you're brave enough — find one person you trust and show them what you wrote. A friend, a youth leader, a parent, anyone. Not because they'll have all the answers, but because the worst thing you can do with doubt is carry it alone in the dark.

Thomas didn't stay alone in his doubt. He stayed in the room with the other disciples. He kept showing up. And Jesus came back to find him there.

That's the invitation. Stay in the room. Keep asking. You're allowed to not have it figured out.

Nobody here does either.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me tell you about a conversation I overheard once.

Two friends were sitting together after a church service — both around your age — and one of them leaned over to the other and said, very quietly, *"Do you actually believe any of this? Like, actually?"*

And the other one paused for a long time before saying: *"I don't know. I think so. Maybe. I don't know."*

And then they both kind of looked around to make sure no one had heard, and they sat up straight, and they sang the final song.

I think about that moment a lot. Because I think it happens more than we admit. People sitting in church, or youth group, or around a family dinner table, carrying a question they feel like they can't say out loud. Smiling at the right moments. Saying the right things. But underneath it, something that feels like a crack.

And I want to start tonight by saying: if that's you — if you're one of those people — you are in exactly the right place. And you are not broken.

---

## Doubt Isn't the Opposite of Faith

Here's something I think we get badly wrong: we treat doubt like it's the enemy of faith. Like faith is this fragile thing that will shatter if you ask the wrong question. So we learn not to ask. We learn to keep the questions small and quiet.

But that's not what faith actually is. And honestly? It's not even what faith looks like in the Bible.

Think about it. The Bible is full of people who were confused, angry, terrified, and completely unsure about what God was doing. The Psalms are basically a collection of people yelling at God. Job spends most of his book demanding answers and refusing to accept the tidy explanations his friends offer. Habakkuk opens with *"God, why aren't you listening?"* — and that's in the first verse. These aren't people on the fringes of faith. These are the people the Bible holds up as examples.

And then there's Thomas.

---

## Thomas Gets a Bad Deal

We call him "Doubting Thomas," and we say it like it's an insult — like he's the cautionary tale, the one who got it wrong. But read the story again carefully.

Jesus has died. The disciples have watched their friend and teacher be executed. They're hiding in a locked room, terrified that the same thing is going to happen to them. And then — somehow — Jesus appears. He's there, in the room, alive.

Thomas wasn't there. We don't know where he was. Maybe he was getting food. Maybe he needed to be alone. And when the others tell him what happened, he says: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe."*

That's not cynicism. That's grief. That's someone who loved Jesus so much that he cannot afford to hope unless he's sure. He's not being difficult — he's being honest. He's saying, *"This matters too much to me to pretend."*

And here's what gets me: Jesus doesn't punish him for it. Jesus comes back. He shows Thomas his hands. He says, *"Stop doubting and believe"* — but the very fact that he came back for Thomas, that he showed up just for him, tells us there's no anger in it. He met him exactly where he was.

Thomas didn't arrive at faith despite his doubt. He arrived at faith through it.

And then they both kind of looked around to make sure no one had heard, and they sat up straight, and they sang the final song.

People sitting in church, or youth group, or around a family dinner table, carrying a question they feel like they can't say out loud. Smiling at the right moments. Saying the right things. # When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me start with something that actually happened to me.

I was sitting in a church service — not unlike this one — and everyone around me seemed completely fine. They were singing, hands raised, looking peaceful and certain. And I was sitting there thinking: *I don't know if any of this is real.* Not in an angry way. Just genuinely, quietly unsure. Like standing in a room where everyone else can see something you can't.

And the worst part wasn't the doubt itself. The worst part was thinking I was the only one. That everyone else had figured something out that I hadn't. That there was something wrong with me.

I want to start there because I suspect some of you know exactly what that feels like. And I want you to know, before we go any further: you're not broken. You're not failing. You might actually be paying attention.

---

## The Pressure to Perform Certainty

There's a particular kind of pressure that exists in religious spaces — and honestly, in lots of spaces — to have it all together. To know what you believe. To not ask questions that might make people uncomfortable.

And when you're 14, 15, 16, you're at this strange moment in life where you're starting to look at everything you were handed as a child and ask: *but is it actually true?* That's not rebellion. That's called growing up. That's your brain doing its job.

The problem is, faith communities don't always make it easy to ask those questions out loud. So the doubt goes underground. You smile and sing the songs and say the right things, and inside you're carrying this quiet uncertainty you're not sure you're allowed to voice.

I want to create a different kind of space today. A space where it's okay to say: *I'm not sure. I have questions. Some of this doesn't make sense to me.* Because I think that honesty is actually the beginning of something real, not the end of it.

---

## Thomas Gets a Bad Reputation

You've probably heard of Doubting Thomas. It's almost become an insult — like calling someone a pessimist or a cynic. But I think Thomas deserves a second look.

Here's what actually happened. Jesus had been crucified. The disciples were hiding behind locked doors, terrified. And then Jesus appeared to them — except Thomas wasn't there. So when the others told him, Thomas said: *Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe it.*

And you know what? That's a completely reasonable response. His closest friend had just been publicly executed. He'd watched it happen. And now people were telling him that friend had come back from the dead. Of course he needed more than second-hand reports. Of course he did.

What happens next is important. Jesus doesn't write Thomas off. He doesn't say, *Well, if you can't just believe, you're out.* He shows up. He stands in front of Thomas and says, *Here. Look. Touch.* He meets Thomas exactly where Thomas is.

And Thomas's response — "My Lord and my God" — is one of the most profound declarations of faith in the entire New Testament. It came through doubt, not despite it.

I think we've been reading this story wrong. Thomas didn't doubt his way out of faith. He doubted his way into a deeper encounter with it.

---

## What Doubt Actually Is

Here's a way of thinking about doubt that might help.

Doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Certainty is the opposite of faith. If you were absolutely certain about everything — if you could prove it all beyond question — you wouldn't need faith at all. Faith, by definition, involves not having all the answers. It involves trust in the presence of uncertainty.

So when you doubt, you're not stepping outside of faith. You're actually operating right in the territory where faith lives.

The question isn't whether you'll have doubts. You will. Everyone does, if they're being honest. The question is what you do with them.

There are basically two options. You can push the doubt down, perform certainty you don't feel, and hope it goes away. That might work for a while. But in my experience, unexplored doubt doesn't disappear — it just hardens. It becomes cynicism. It becomes the kind of exhausted, resentful unbelief that comes from never letting yourself ask the real questions.

Or you can take the doubt seriously. You can sit with it. You can ask it what it's actually about. And that's harder, and scarier, but it leads somewhere real.

---

## The Questions Worth Asking

Some doubts are about information. You've heard something about science and faith that seems contradictory. You've read something about the history of the church that disturbed you. You've noticed something in the Bible that doesn't seem to fit. Those are real questions and they deserve real engagement — not dismissal, not "just trust God." There are actually thoughtful people who have wrestled with those questions for centuries, and it's worth finding them.

But some doubts go deeper than information. Sometimes the doubt isn't really *does God exist* — it's *does God care about me specifically?* Or *if God is good, why did that happen?* Or *am I even the kind of person who belongs in this?*

Those aren't intellectual problems to be solved. They're wounds looking for a response. And they need something different — not an argument, but honesty. Maybe a conversation. Maybe prayer that sounds more like shouting than singing.

The Psalms are full of that, by the way. David — the man described as being after God's own heart — writes things like: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me?* That's not polished faith. That's raw, honest, desperate prayer. And it's in the Bible. Which suggests that maybe God can handle it when we're not okay.

---

## What I'm Not Saying

I want to be clear about something, because I don't want to give you a false comfort.

I'm not saying doubt always resolves neatly. I'm not saying if you ask the hard questions, you'll get satisfying answers to all of them. You probably won't. Some things remain genuinely uncertain. Some prayers feel unanswered. Some suffering doesn't make sense, and pretending it does is a lie.

What I am saying is that honest faith — faith that has looked at the hard stuff and kept going anyway — is more solid than faith that's never been tested. Not because the questions get answered, but because you find out whether there's something underneath them worth holding onto.

Some of you will wrestle with these questions for years. Some of you might walk away from faith for a while and come back. Some of you might land somewhere different from where you started. I can't promise you a specific destination. But I can tell you that the wrestling itself is not wasted. It matters. It shapes you.

---

## Something to Actually Do

I want to end with something practical, because I think it's easy to talk about doubt in the abstract and not know what to do with it on a Tuesday afternoon.

Here's what I want to invite you to try this week.

Write down — or just think clearly about — one question you've never felt safe asking out loud. Not a question you think you *should* have, but the one that's actually there when you're quiet. The one you've been carrying around.

Then do one of two things with it.

If it's an intellectual question — something about faith and science, or history, or something in the Bible — find one person you trust and ask them to help you find something worth reading about it. Don't google it at midnight and fall down a rabbit hole. Find a person. Start a conversation.

If it's a deeper question — something more like a wound than a puzzle — try praying it. Not the polished version. The real one. Say it out loud, or write it down, addressed to God. See what happens. You might feel nothing. That's okay. Do it anyway.

The point isn't to fix the doubt. The point is to stop carrying it alone.

---

Faith that has never asked a hard question is fragile. Faith that has asked the questions and kept going — even slowly, even limping — that's something that can last.

You're allowed to not have it all figured out. You're in good company.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me tell you about a moment that happened to someone I know.

She'd grown up in church her whole life. Sung the songs, learned the verses, gone to every camp and youth weekend. And then one night, when she was about sixteen, she was lying in bed and this thought just arrived, uninvited: *What if none of this is actually true?*

Not a gentle wondering. A cold, hollow feeling. Like the floor had dropped away.

And here's the part that stayed with her for years: she didn't tell anyone. Not her parents, not her youth leader, not her best friend who sat next to her every Sunday. Because she'd looked around at everyone else and they all seemed so *certain*. They raised their hands in worship, they said "God told me" with confidence, they cried at the right moments in the right talks. And she thought: if I say out loud that I'm not sure I believe any of this, they'll think something is wrong with me. They'll think I'm losing my faith. They'll try to fix me.

So she kept quiet. And the doubt sat in her chest like a stone for two years.

I want to start there tonight because I think some of you might know exactly what that feels like. And I want to say something clearly before we go any further:

**You are in the right room.**

---

Here's the truth: doubt is not the opposite of faith. Doubt is often what happens when faith starts to grow up.

When you're a kid, you believe things because the adults around you believe them. That's not a criticism — that's just how it works. You trust the people who feed you and look after you. But somewhere in your teenage years, something shifts. You start asking *why*. You start noticing the gaps. You start wondering if the things you've been handed actually hold up.

That process is not a spiritual problem. It's actually a sign that you're taking this seriously. You can't own something you've never questioned. The faith that survives your doubt is a much stronger thing than the faith that was never tested.

I'm not going to stand here and tell you that doubt is easy or that it doesn't hurt. Sometimes it really does. But I want to try and reframe what doubt actually is — not as a crack in the foundation, but as a sign that you're building something real.

---

Let me introduce you to someone from the Bible who I think gets unfairly treated.

Thomas. You've probably heard of him. "Doubting Thomas" — the guy who gets used as a cautionary tale, the one who didn't believe Jesus had risen until he could see the evidence for himself.

But look at the actual story for a second, because I think we miss something important.

The disciples are gathered together, and Jesus appears to them — but Thomas isn't there. And when they tell him later, "We've seen the Lord," Thomas says: *Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe.*

Now, that sounds shocking. But think about what Thomas is actually doing. He's not being cynical or dismissive. He's being honest. His friends are telling him the most extraordinary thing that has ever happened in human history, and he's saying: I need to see this for myself. I can't just take your word for it.

And here's what Jesus does when he appears to Thomas a week later. He doesn't lecture him. He doesn't say "shame on you for doubting." He says: *Here. Look. Touch. See for yourself.*

Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is. He doesn't demand that Thomas pretend to believe something he doesn't believe yet. He shows up and offers evidence.

And Thomas's response — "My Lord and my God" — is actually the most complete confession of faith in the entire Gospel of John. The man who doubted the most said the most.

That's not a coincidence.

---

Or think about the Psalms. If you've never really read them, you might assume they're all worship songs. Some of them are. But a lot of them are raw, desperate, almost angry conversations with God.

Psalm 88 ends with the word *darkness*. No resolution. No "but I know you're there." Just darkness. That's in the Bible. That's considered sacred text.

David writes again and again: *Where are you? Why have you hidden yourself? How long?* Job argues with God for thirty-five chapters. Habakkuk opens his book by basically saying, "God, I've been crying out to you and you're not listening — what is going on?"

These aren't people on the fringes of faith. These are the people the Bible holds up as examples. And they were not polite about their doubt. They brought it directly to God, loudly, honestly, with everything they had.

There's something in that worth noticing. The biblical tradition doesn't ask you to pretend. It actually seems to invite you to bring your real questions into the conversation rather than leaving them at the door.

---

So what do you do with doubt? I'm not going to give you a five-step plan, because doubt doesn't work like that. But I want to offer you a different way of thinking about it.

What if your questions aren't evidence that faith is failing — but evidence that you're actually engaging?

The person who never doubts has probably never really wrestled with what they believe. The person who doubts and keeps showing up, keeps asking, keeps looking — that person is doing something much harder and much more honest.

Doubt is not a destination. It's more like a corridor. You don't have to live there forever. But you do have to walk through it to get somewhere real.

And here's something I've found to be true: the questions that feel most dangerous — the ones you're most afraid to ask — are usually the ones most worth asking. Not because they'll all get neat answers. Some of them won't. But because the act of asking honestly, of refusing to settle for a faith that's just performance, is itself a kind of integrity.

You don't have to have it all figured out. Nobody does. Anyone who tells you otherwise is either lying or hasn't thought about it hard enough.

---

One more thing before I finish.

That girl I told you about at the start — the one who kept her doubt secret for two years? Eventually she told someone. A youth leader who didn't panic, didn't immediately try to fix her, just said: *Yeah. I've been there. Tell me what you're thinking.*

That conversation didn't resolve everything. But it broke something open. She realised she wasn't alone, that her questions weren't shameful, that she could keep walking even without certainty.

She's still in faith. Not a naive faith — a harder-won one. The kind that's been through something and came out the other side.

I'm not promising that's what happens for everyone. I'm not going to make promises I can't keep. But I do think that bringing your doubt into the light is almost always better than carrying it alone in the dark.

---

So here's where I want to leave you tonight.

Not with an answer. With a question.

**What's the thing you're most afraid to say out loud about your faith — or your doubt?**

You don't have to say it to anyone right now. But I want you to at least say it to yourself. Write it down if that helps. Sit with it. Don't rush past it.

And if you're ready to say it to someone — find one person you trust. Not someone who will panic or immediately try to fix you. Someone who will just listen. If you can't think of anyone, I'm here tonight, and so are the other leaders.

Your doubt is not the end of your story. For a lot of people, it's where the real story begins.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me start with something that actually happened to me.

A few years ago I was sitting in a church service — not as a teenager, as an adult who works with young people and talks about faith for a living — and the worship band started playing, and everyone around me had their eyes closed and their hands up, and I just... couldn't get there. I was standing there thinking: *is any of this real? Does any of this actually mean anything?* And then I felt this wave of something that wasn't quite guilt but was close to it. Like I was failing at something everyone else had figured out.

I looked around the room and I thought: does anyone else feel like this? Or is it just me?

I want to start there because I think that's where a lot of you might be, some of the time. And I want you to know, before we go any further: that's okay. That's actually more than okay. That's what we're going to talk about tonight.

---

## The thing nobody says out loud

Here's something that I think is true about a lot of Christian spaces, though nobody really announces it: there's an unspoken rule that doubt is something to be fixed quickly, apologised for, or kept quiet. You can have a question, as long as you also have the answer ready. You can go through a hard time, as long as it ends with a neat testimony about how your faith came out stronger.

And if you're sitting here tonight with questions you can't resolve, with things about God or the Bible or the church that genuinely don't make sense to you — it can feel like you're the only one. Like everyone else got the memo and you missed it.

You didn't miss it. There is no memo.

The reality is that almost everyone who has ever taken faith seriously has had moments — sometimes long stretches — of genuine uncertainty. The question isn't whether you'll doubt. The question is what you do when you do.

---

## Meet Thomas

You've probably heard of Doubting Thomas. It's almost become an insult, hasn't it? "Oh, don't be such a doubting Thomas." But I think Thomas gets a really unfair reputation, so let's actually look at what happened.

Jesus has been crucified. The disciples have scattered. And then, somehow, Jesus appears to them in a locked room — and Thomas isn't there. The others tell him: we've seen the Lord. He's alive.

And Thomas says: unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe.

Now. I want you to notice something. Thomas doesn't say this to Jesus. He says it to the other disciples. He's not being dramatic or theatrical — he's being honest with his friends about where he actually is. He's saying: I can't just take your word for it. I need something real.

A week later, Jesus appears again. And this time Thomas is there. And Jesus says to him — and this is the part that gets me — Jesus says: *Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.*

Jesus doesn't shame him. Jesus doesn't say, "I'm disappointed in you, Thomas." He shows up. He meets Thomas exactly where Thomas is. He offers him exactly what Thomas said he needed.

And Thomas responds with one of the most profound statements of faith in the whole New Testament: *My Lord and my God.*

Thomas went from "I will not believe" to "my Lord and my God" not by suppressing his doubt, but by bringing it into the open. His honesty was the path through, not the obstacle.

---

## The Psalms and the art of complaining to God

Thomas isn't alone. Open up the Psalms sometime — and I mean really read them, not just the nice ones — and you'll find David saying things like: *Where are you, God? Why have you forgotten me? Why do you hide your face?*

Psalm 88 ends with the word *darkness*. Just darkness. No resolution. No tidy bow. It's one of the most raw, honest pieces of writing in the entire Bible, and it's in the Bible. It's scripture. God kept it.

Or look at Job, who loses everything and spends most of the book demanding that God explain himself. His friends keep trying to get him to be more theologically correct, more polite, more careful. And at the end of the book, God says to Job's friends: you have not spoken what is right about me, as my servant Job has.

Job, who argued with God, got it more right than the people who were defending God.

That tells me something important: God is not fragile. He can handle your questions. He's not going to fall apart because you're honest about where you are.

---

## What doubt actually is

I want to offer you a different way of thinking about doubt.

Doubt is not the opposite of faith. The opposite of faith is certainty — or maybe indifference. Doubt is what happens when you care enough to keep asking. It's what happens when the easy answers stop being enough and you need something more real.

C.S. Lewis — who was an atheist before he became a Christian — said that his faith was shaped more by his honest questions than by anything else. He didn't talk himself out of doubt. He followed the questions to see where they led.

Your faith at 16 is not supposed to look like your faith at 40. It's not supposed to look like your parents' faith, or your youth leader's faith, or the faith of whoever seems most sorted in this room. It's supposed to be yours — and that means it has to go through you, including the parts of you that aren't sure.

A faith that's never been questioned is a faith that's never really been tested. And a faith that's never been tested is a fragile thing, built on the assumption that nothing will ever challenge it.

---

## What I'm not saying

I want to be clear about something, because I don't want to give you the wrong impression.

I'm not saying doubt is the destination. I'm not saying uncertainty is some kind of spiritual virtue you should aim for. I'm not saying "just keep questioning" as if questions are enough on their own.

What I'm saying is that the questions are worth taking seriously. That sitting with them honestly is better than pretending they don't exist. That the God who made you — including the part of you that asks hard questions — is not threatened by those questions.

And I'm saying: don't make a permanent decision based on a temporary feeling. There will be services where you feel nothing. There will be prayers that feel like they're going nowhere. There will be things you read or hear or experience that genuinely shake you. That's not the end of the story. That might be the beginning of a more honest one.

---

## Where to go from here

Here's your practical next step, and it's a simple one.

This week, I want you to write down — somewhere private, a notes app, a journal, the back of a notebook — one question about faith that you've never said out loud. The one you're almost embarrassed to admit you have. Not for anyone else to see. Just for you.

And then sit with it. Don't rush to Google an answer. Don't try to argue yourself out of it. Just let it be a real question, and notice what it feels like to finally acknowledge it.

If you want to go further: find one person you trust — a friend, a parent, a youth leader, someone — and say: *I've got a question I've been sitting with. Can I talk it through with you?* Not because they'll have the answer, but because questions are better when they're not carried alone.

Thomas didn't figure it out by himself. He was in the room with other people when Jesus showed up.

You don't have to have it all figured out. None of us do. But you do have to be honest about where you actually are.

And wherever that is tonight — that's a fine place to start.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me start with a scenario. See if any part of this sounds familiar.

You're sitting in church, or in a group like this one, and someone asks a question like, "How has God been speaking to you this week?" And around the room, people start sharing. And the answers sound so... certain. So full. And you're sitting there thinking: *I don't have an answer like that. I'm not sure I've heard anything. I'm not even sure I believe what I believed six months ago.*

So you say something vague. Something that sounds okay. And nobody knows.

Or maybe it's a different version. Maybe you're at school and someone makes a pretty decent argument against something you've always believed, and you don't have a comeback, and later that night you lie in bed thinking: *What if they're right? What if this whole thing is just... made up?*

And you don't tell anyone, because you're worried about what it means. About what it says about you.

I want to start tonight by saying: that experience — that gap between what you think you're supposed to feel and what you actually feel — is one of the most common experiences in faith. It just doesn't get talked about enough.

---

## Doubt Isn't the Opposite of Faith

There's this assumption that floats around, and it's never quite said out loud, but you can feel it: that good Christians are certain. That if your faith is real, it won't wobble. That doubt is something you either had before you believed, or something that means you're losing it.

That's not true. And I think deep down, a lot of you already know it's not true, because you're experiencing something more complicated than certainty — and you haven't stopped caring about God.

Doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Certainty is the opposite of faith. If you already knew, you wouldn't need faith. Faith, by definition, involves not having all the answers. The question isn't whether you'll ever doubt. The question is what you do with it.

And you're at an age where this is supposed to happen. You're not a child anymore, which means you can't just hold beliefs because your parents hold them or because you've always been told they're true. You're starting to own your life — your choices, your identity, your convictions. That process is supposed to involve some turbulence. That's not failure. That's growing up.

---

## Thomas Gets a Bad Deal

There's a character in the Bible who I think deserves a better reputation than he gets. His name is Thomas, and he's famous for one thing: doubting.

Here's the story. Jesus has been crucified. The disciples are terrified and hiding. And then Jesus appears to them — risen, alive. It's extraordinary. Except Thomas isn't there. He misses it. And when the others tell him what happened, Thomas says: "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

And we've been calling him "Doubting Thomas" ever since, like it's a character flaw.

But think about what Thomas is actually doing. He's not being cynical. He's not mocking. He's being honest. He's saying: *I want this to be true. I want it so much. But I can't just take your word for it. I need something real.*

That's not weak faith. That's integrity. That's someone who takes the truth seriously enough not to fake it.

And here's what happens next. A week later, Jesus appears again — and this time Thomas is there. And Jesus doesn't shame him. He doesn't say, "Well, if you'd been here last week like everyone else..." He walks straight over to Thomas and says: *Here. Look. Touch. See for yourself.*

Jesus meets Thomas in his doubt. He doesn't punish him for it. He shows up for it.

I find that really striking. Because it tells me something about the kind of God we're dealing with — one who isn't fragile, who isn't threatened by your questions, who doesn't need you to perform certainty you don't have.

---

## The Psalms Nobody Reads Aloud

Thomas isn't the only one. David — the guy described as a man after God's own heart — writes things in the Psalms that would make some church people uncomfortable. He writes: *"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me?"* He writes: *"How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?"* He writes prayers that are basically arguments with God.

Job does the same thing — takes his grief and his rage directly to God, refuses to pretend he's okay, refuses to say the safe religious things his friends keep suggesting. And at the end of the book, God says Job spoke what was right. Not his friends, who had all the tidy answers. Job, who kept showing up and kept being honest.

There's a pattern here. The people in Scripture who have the deepest, most enduring relationship with God are often the ones who argued with him, questioned him, sat in the dark and said, *I don't understand this.* Their faith wasn't smooth. It was real.

---

## What Honest Questions Actually Do

Here's what I've noticed about doubt, and what I think is worth sitting with.

When you push on a question — when you actually take it seriously instead of burying it — one of two things happens. Either you find something solid underneath, something that holds up under pressure, and your faith gets stronger for having tested it. Or you find that a particular belief you held was more fragile than you thought, and you have to revise it. And that's uncomfortable. But it's also how you stop carrying around beliefs that were never really yours to begin with.

Both of those outcomes are better than the third option, which is just pretending. Just smiling and saying the right things and slowly going hollow inside.

Honest questions are how you build a faith that's actually yours. Not your parents'. Not your youth group's. Yours.

And I'm not promising that every question gets answered. Some of them don't — not cleanly, not in the way you want. There are things about suffering and silence and unanswered prayer that I can't wrap up neatly, and I'm not going to try. But I've found that it's possible to live with open questions without them eating you alive — if you're willing to keep bringing them to God instead of just carrying them alone.

---

## A Few Things Worth Saying Plainly

I don't want to leave you with a list of steps, because faith isn't really like that. But I do want to say a few things plainly before we finish.

Your doubt does not disqualify you. It doesn't mean you're not a Christian, or that you're a bad one, or that you're on your way out. It might mean you're on your way in — into something more honest and more durable than what you had before.

You don't have to have this figured out. You're sixteen, or fifteen, or seventeen. You're not supposed to have it all figured out. Neither, honestly, are the adults in your life — most of us are just further along in learning to live with the mystery.

And the questions you're carrying? They're worth taking seriously. Not suppressing. Not performing your way around. Taking seriously.

---

## Something to Try This Week

Here's one practical thing I'd like to offer.

Sometime in the next few days, find a quiet moment — ten minutes, that's all — and write down the question about faith that you most don't want to say out loud. The one that feels most dangerous. The one you've been pushing down.

Just write it. You don't have to show it to anyone. You don't have to answer it. Just get it out of your head and onto paper, and then — and this is the important part — read it back as if you were praying it. Bring it to God directly. Say: *This is what I'm actually thinking. This is where I actually am.*

That's it. That's the whole thing.

Because the conversation has to start somewhere. And it might as well start with the truth.

# When You're Not Sure You Believe

---

Let me start with a scenario. Imagine you're sitting in church — or maybe you're here right now, in this room — and everyone around you seems totally fine. They're singing, they're nodding, they look like they've got it all figured out. And you're sitting there thinking: *I'm not sure I actually believe any of this.*

Maybe it's been happening for a while. You used to just accept what you were taught, and now you're older and you've started actually thinking about it, and the thinking has made things messier, not cleaner. Maybe something happened — something hard — and you found yourself wondering where God was. Maybe you just read something, or had a conversation, or watched a documentary, and now there's this uncomfortable gap between what you're supposed to believe and what you actually feel is true.

And here's the thing nobody says out loud: you feel like you're the only one.

You're not.

I'd be willing to bet that at least half the people in this room have had a version of that experience. The other half probably will. And I want to say something clearly before we go any further: having doubts does not mean your faith is broken. It might actually mean it's growing.

---

## Doubt Is Not the Opposite of Faith

We've got this idea in our heads — I don't know where it comes from exactly, maybe from the way we talk about faith in church, maybe from culture — that faith means certainty. That to believe in God is to have no questions, no wobbles, no 3am moments where you stare at the ceiling and think *what if none of this is real?*

But that's not what faith actually is. Certainty doesn't require faith. If I know for a fact that the chair I'm sitting on will hold my weight, I don't need faith to sit on it. Faith is what you exercise when you're not certain. When you act, when you trust, when you show up — even though you can't prove everything.

Doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Pretending is.

When you push your questions down, when you perform belief you don't feel, when you smile and nod because it seems easier — that's what actually hollows faith out. Honest doubt, on the other hand, is the beginning of something real.

---

## Thomas Didn't Get It Wrong

You've probably heard of Doubting Thomas. It's almost become an insult — like calling someone a Doubting Thomas means they're being difficult, stubborn, faithless.

But look at what actually happens in the story.

Jesus has died. The disciples are terrified, hiding behind locked doors. Then Jesus appears to them — and Thomas isn't there. He's missed it. And when the other disciples tell him what happened, Thomas says: "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

Now, honestly? That's a reasonable response. His best friend has just been publicly executed. He's grieving. And now people are telling him something that sounds impossible. Thomas isn't being awkward. He's being honest about where he actually is.

A week later, Jesus appears again — and this time Thomas is there. Jesus doesn't shame him. He doesn't say "I'm disappointed in you" or "you should have just trusted." He says: *Here. Look. Touch. See for yourself.*

And Thomas's response is the most complete confession of faith in the whole Gospel of John: "My Lord and my God."

The doubt didn't disqualify Thomas. It was part of the journey that got him there.

Jesus does say, "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" — and yes, that's us, that's our situation. But notice: he still showed up for Thomas. He still met him in the doubt. He didn't leave Thomas behind because Thomas needed more than the others.

That matters.

---

## The Psalms Are Full of This

Thomas isn't alone. The Bible is full of people who wrestle with God — and the wrestling isn't presented as a failure. It's presented as relationship.

The Psalms are extraordinary for this. Psalm 88 is basically 18 verses of someone telling God: *I feel like you've abandoned me, I'm in the darkest place, I've called out to you and heard nothing.* It ends with the word "darkness." That's it. No resolution. No tidy bow. Just honest, raw despair.

That's in the Bible. That's in the worship book of ancient Israel. Which means the community of faith looked at that kind of anguish and said: *yes, this belongs here. This is part of the story.*

Or look at Job — a man who loses everything and refuses to pretend he's okay with it. His friends keep trying to give him theological explanations for why this is happening. Job keeps saying: *I don't accept that. I want to talk to God directly.* And at the end of the book, God says that Job spoke rightly — more rightly than the friends who had all the answers.

The honest wrestler was closer to the truth than the people with the tidy explanations.

---

## Questions Can Be a Form of Seeking

Here's something worth sitting with: the questions you're asking might be the most serious spiritual thing you're doing.

When you look at the suffering in the world and ask *how can a good God allow this?* — that's not a faithless question. That's a question that takes both goodness and suffering seriously. When you wonder whether prayer actually does anything — that's a question that takes prayer seriously enough to ask whether it's real.

Shallow faith doesn't generate serious questions. Serious questions come from people who actually care about whether something is true.

I'm not going to stand here and give you five easy answers to the problem of evil or proof that prayer works. Anyone who does that is either selling something or hasn't thought about it hard enough. What I can tell you is that people have wrestled with these questions for thousands of years — brilliant, honest, serious people — and many of them have found that the wrestling itself brought them closer to something real, not further away.

That doesn't mean you'll end up believing everything you were taught as a child. Faith grows and changes. Some things you'll hold more loosely. Some things you'll hold more deeply. That's okay. That's what it looks like to actually own your faith rather than just inherit it.

---

## What Not to Do

Don't perform. If you don't believe something, don't pretend you do. It's exhausting, and it doesn't help anyone — least of all you.

Don't isolate. Doubt gets heavier when you carry it alone. The lie that you're the only one is powerful, and the only way to break it is to actually talk to someone.

Don't expect the questions to disappear. Some of them won't. Learning to live with uncertainty — to hold questions with curiosity rather than panic — is actually a sign of maturity, not weakness.

---

## Something to Try This Week

Here's a practical thing I want to leave you with.

Write down one question you've been afraid to ask. Not to show anyone — just for yourself. It might be a question about God, about suffering, about whether any of this is real, about something in the Bible that doesn't sit right with you.

Write it down and sit with it. Don't try to answer it immediately. Just acknowledge that it's real, that it's yours, and that you're allowed to have it.

Then, if you're brave enough — find one person you trust and tell them you've been wrestling with something. You don't have to share the question if you don't want to. Just say: *I've been having some doubts, and I'm trying to figure out what I actually believe.* See what happens.

Chances are, they'll say: *me too.*

Faith isn't a destination you arrive at and then you're done. It's more like a relationship — something you return to, argue with, sit in silence with, and slowly come to know more deeply over time.

You're allowed to be where you are.

The door is open. The questions are welcome.

And you're not as alone in this as you think.
