# When the Ground Shifts

## A talk on doubt and faith

---

Let me start with a scenario. See if any part of this sounds familiar.

You're sitting in church, or in a youth group, or maybe just in your bedroom at night, and a thought comes. Not a small thought. A big one. Something like: *What if none of this is actually true?* Or: *Why would God let that happen?* Or maybe just a quieter version — a kind of fog where the things you've always believed suddenly feel distant and uncertain, like trying to remember a dream.

And then — and this is the part I really want you to notice — you feel something else. You feel afraid of the thought. Maybe even ashamed of it. Like you've done something wrong just by thinking it. So you push it down. You sing the songs louder. You give the right answers in the group discussion. And you carry the question around in secret, wondering if you're the only one.

You're not the only one.

I want to say that clearly, at the start, so we can actually talk honestly for the next few minutes: doubt is not the opposite of faith. It is not a sign that you're failing, or drifting, or that God has given up on you. It is, in many cases, a sign that you're taking faith seriously enough to actually think about it.

---

Here's something worth knowing about growing up. Your brain — literally, neurologically — is going through a major renovation during your teenage years. The part of your brain that handles abstract thinking, questioning, and evaluating ideas is coming online. You are, for the first time, genuinely capable of looking at what you've been taught and asking: *but is it actually true?*

That's not a spiritual crisis. That's development. It's the same process that makes you question whether the career your parents planned for you is really what you want, or whether the friend group you've always been in still fits who you're becoming. You're supposed to ask questions. The tragedy would be if you never did.

Faith that has never been questioned is a bit like a muscle that's never been used. It might look fine, but it won't hold up under any real weight. The questions aren't the enemy. Refusing to ask them is.

---

I want to tell you about a man named Thomas.

You might know him as "Doubting Thomas," which is one of those nicknames that has followed someone around for two thousand years in a way that feels a bit unfair. Here's what actually happened.

Jesus has just been crucified. The disciples are hiding behind locked doors, terrified and grief-stricken. And then — according to John's Gospel — Jesus appears in the room. The disciples are overjoyed. But Thomas isn't there. He misses it.

When the others tell him what happened, Thomas says something remarkably honest. He says: *Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.*

Now, we often read that as Thomas being difficult. Stubborn. Faithless. But think about what he's actually saying. He's saying: *I need this to be real. I need it to actually be true, not just a story the others are telling me because they're desperate for it to be true.* He's not being cynical. He's being honest about what's at stake. If Jesus is alive, he needs to know it's really him — the same Jesus who died, with the wounds to prove it. He's not willing to settle for a comforting illusion.

A week later, Jesus comes back. And he goes straight to Thomas. He doesn't rebuke him. He doesn't say, *I'm disappointed in you.* He holds out his hands and says: *Put your finger here. See my hands. Stop doubting and believe.*

Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is. In his doubt. With his specific, named, honest questions.

And Thomas — who asked for proof, who refused to pretend — becomes the disciple who gives us one of the most profound statements of faith in the entire New Testament. He looks at Jesus and says: *My Lord and my God.* Not just "Lord." Not just a teacher or a prophet. God. The man who needed to touch the wounds ends up seeing more clearly than almost anyone.

His doubt didn't destroy his faith. It deepened it.

---

Thomas isn't alone in this. The Psalms are full of David essentially shouting at God — *Where are you? Why have you abandoned me? How long will this go on?* — and those cries are in the Bible. They're scripture. God didn't edit them out.

Job, who loses everything and demands that God explain himself, is described at the end of the book as having spoken what is right about God — more right than his friends, who spent the whole time giving neat theological answers and defending God's reputation. God wasn't impressed by the tidy answers. He honoured the raw, honest wrestling.

Habakkuk opens his whole book with: *How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen?* That's the first line. It's practically a complaint. And it's in the Bible.

There's a pattern here. The people in scripture who wrestle with God, who bring their real questions rather than their polished ones — they tend to encounter something deeper. Not easy answers. But something real.

---

I want to be straight with you about something. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that if you just pray more, or read your Bible more, or try harder, all your doubts will dissolve and you'll feel certain again. That's not true, and you'd know it wasn't true, and it wouldn't help you.

Some questions don't have clean answers. Some things about faith are genuinely hard. The existence of suffering. Why prayers sometimes seem to go unanswered. How to reconcile science and faith, or history and faith, or your own experience and faith. These are real questions that serious, intelligent people have wrestled with for centuries. You're not going to solve them on a Tuesday evening.

But here's what I've come to believe: there's a difference between a question that destroys and a question that digs. Some questions, when you sit with them honestly, when you bring them into the open and look at them — they take you deeper. They strip away the parts of your faith that were always a bit shallow, a bit secondhand, a bit inherited without being owned. And what's left, if you keep going, tends to be something more solid. More yours. More real.

Faith that has been through questions and survived them is different from faith that has never been tested. It's not more fragile. It's more honest. It knows what it's actually standing on.

---

So here's where I want to leave you.

Not with a neat conclusion, because this isn't that kind of talk. But with something practical.

In the next week, I want you to try this: write down one question you've been carrying but haven't said out loud. Just one. It doesn't have to be a big theological crisis — it might be something small, a nagging uncertainty, a thing that doesn't quite add up. Write it down somewhere private, where you don't have to perform anything for anyone.

And then — this is the harder part — find one person you trust enough to show it to. A friend. A parent. A youth leader. Someone who won't panic when they hear it and won't give you a canned answer. Just someone who will sit with you in the question.

You don't need to resolve it. You just need to stop carrying it alone.

Because here's the thing about doubt: it does its worst damage in the dark, when it's a secret. When it's out in the open, it becomes something you can actually look at. Something you can bring to God, the way Thomas did — honestly, with your hands open.

Jesus wasn't afraid of Thomas's doubt. He walked right into it.

He's not afraid of yours either.

---

*Take a moment to think: what's the question you haven't said out loud yet?*

d6UAlzkPbw-8KtlpplKES.text:
Okay. Let’s get settled. Can I be honest with you for a minute? Before I even start, I’m feeling a little nervous. Not just because talking in front of people is kinda terrifying, but because what I want to talk about today is… messy. It doesn’t fit in a neat box. And part of me wants to give you a talk that’s all clean answers and uplifting music, so we can all leave feeling fine. But I don’t think that’s what you need. I think you need something real.

So, I’m going to start with a story. Not from the Bible—at least, not yet—but from my own life, from when I was about your age.

I grew up going to church. I knew the stories, sang the songs, raised my hand during worship. My faith felt like a solid floor I was standing on. Then, in my junior year, my grandfather died. He was the kindest, most faithful man I knew. He prayed every day, served people quietly, loved his family fiercely. And he died slowly and painfully from cancer. I prayed—really prayed—for his healing. So did my whole church. And it didn’t come. At the funeral, everyone was saying things like, “He’s in a better place,” and “God’s plan is perfect.” And I nodded, because that’s what you’re supposed to do. But inside, my solid floor was cracking. A single, screaming question was echoing in my head: *“If God is good, and God is powerful… then what was that?”*

I felt guilty for even thinking it. I figured real Christians don’t have those thoughts. So I shoved it down. I faked it. I sang louder. I said “Amen” more forcefully. But the doubt didn’t go away; it just went underground, and it started poisoning everything. I felt like a fraud. I thought that maybe my faith was just too weak, or that I was somehow broken.

I’m telling you this for one reason: to normalise what you might be feeling. If you’ve ever sat in this room, or in your small group, or during a sermon, and thought:
*“Do I really believe this, or do I just believe it because my parents do?”*
*“Why does God feel so silent sometimes?”*
*“How can the Bible be true when science says…?”*
*“If God is love, why is there so much suffering in the world?”*
…Then you are not alone. You are not weird. You are not a faith-failure.

In fact, I’d be more worried if you *didn’t* have questions. It means you’re paying attention. You’re engaging. You’re thinking. Doubt isn’t the opposite of faith; *indifference* is. The opposite of love isn’t hate, it’s apathy. To doubt, to wrestle, to question—that means you care enough about something to want it to be real, to be true. It means your faith is alive enough to have growing pains.

Let’s get one thing clear: **Doubt is a normal part of growing up and growing in faith.** It is not a sin. It is not a sign of spiritual immaturity. Often, it’s a sign of spiritual deepening. You’re moving from a borrowed, handed-down faith to one you have to build and own for yourself. That process is messy. It involves taking things off the shelf, examining them, and deciding what you’re going to keep.

Maybe you think the Bible is full of people who never had a doubt in their lives. Let me introduce you to my man, Habakkuk. He’s a prophet, way back in the Old Testament. He’s not famous like David or Moses. He only gets three short chapters. But he’s the patron saint of the brutally honest doubters.

Habakkuk looks out at the world and what does he see? Injustice. Violence. Corruption. Good people suffering, bad people thriving. Sound familiar? And he turns to God and doesn’t offer a polite prayer. He launches a complaint. He basically says: *“God, what are you doing? Are you even paying attention? I cry out to you about violence and you don’t save? Why do you make me look at this garbage? Why are you silent?”* (That’s my paraphrase of Habakkuk 1:2-4).

This is not a Sunday school prayer. This is rage, confusion, and deep, theological doubt. “God, your management of the world seems deeply flawed. Explain yourself.”

And God *answers*. But God’s answer isn’t what Habakkuk wants to hear. God says, “I’m doing something, but you wouldn’t believe it if I told you. I’m raising up a brutal, pagan nation to come and judge my own people.” This, of course, makes no sense to Habakkuk. It leads to his *second* complaint: *“Um, God? You’re holy. How can you use people who are even *more* evil to punish people who are *sort of* evil? This makes you look bad!”* (See Habakkuk 1:12-17).

Here’s what I love about this. The Bible isn’t hiding this. It’s canonising it. It’s saying, “Here is a record of a faithful man who argued with God, who doubted God’s methods, who demanded an explanation.” God doesn’t strike him down. God engages him. The rest of the book is God laying out his bigger, longer, more mysterious plan—a plan Habakkuk can’t fully see from his tiny vantage point in history.

And Habakkuk’s conclusion is the most important part. He doesn’t get all his answers. The situation on the ground doesn’t change. The bad guys are still coming. But after wrestling, after yelling his doubts into the heavens, he comes to a place of staggering trust. He says:

> “Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, **yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.**” (Habakkuk 3:17-18)

His circumstances are a disaster. His questions aren’t all answered. But his faith has moved from a fragile belief in good circumstances to a rugged trust in a Person. His doubt led him to a deeper, more resilient faith. He moved from “God, why are you doing this?” to “God, I don’t understand you, but I trust you.”

That’s the vision I want to offer you. **Honest questions don’t have to destroy your faith; they can be the things that deepen it.** A faith that has never been questioned is a shallow faith. It’s like a muscle that’s never been stressed—it’s weak. Doubt is the stress that, if you lean into it, can make your faith muscles incredibly strong.

But here’s the crucial part: You have to bring your doubts *into* your faith, not let them pull you *out of* it. What poisoned me as a teenager wasn’t the doubt itself; it was the shame, the isolation, the feeling that I had to hide it. I treated my faith like a house of cards, terrified that one question would make the whole thing collapse. But what if faith isn’t a house of cards? What if it’s more like a tree? A question might shake a few leaves loose, it might even break a branch, but a healthy tree uses that storm to send its roots down deeper, searching for stronger ground.

So how do we do this practically? How do we wrestle well?

First, **change your conversation with yourself.** When a doubt pops up, don’t immediately think, “I’m a bad Christian.” Try thinking, “This is a sign my faith is growing. This is an invitation to go deeper.” Name the doubt. Write it down. “I doubt that God is good because of X.” “I doubt prayer works because of Y.” Just getting it out of the shadowy corners of your mind and into the light takes away half its power.

Second, **find your people.** You cannot do this alone. Is there one person—a youth leader, a friend in this group, a trusted mentor—with whom you can be brutally honest? Someone you can say to, “Hey, I’m really struggling to believe this right now,” without them freaking out, without them giving you a cheesy one-line answer? Find that person. If you can’t find one, be that person for someone else. Create a space where “I don’t know” is an acceptable thing to say.

Finally, and this is where I’ll end, I want to give you a very practical next step. It’s not a three-step fix. It’s a single practice.

I grew up going to church. I knew the stories, sang the songs, raised my hand during worship. My faith felt like a solid floor I was standing on. Then, in my junior year, my grandfather died. He was the kindest, most faithful man I knew. He prayed every day, served people quietly, loved his family fiercely. And he died slowly and painfully from cancer. I prayed—really prayed—for his healing. So did my whole church. And it didn’t come. At the funeral, everyone was saying things like, “He’s in a better place,” and “God’s plan is perfect.” And I nodded, because that’s what you’re supposed to do. But inside, my solid floor was cracking. A single, screaming question was echoing in my head: *“If God is good, and God is powerful… then what was that?”*

I felt guilty for even thinking it. I figured real Christians don’t have those thoughts. So I shoved it down. I faked it. I sang louder. I said “Amen” more forcefully. But the doubt didn’t go away; it just went underground, and it started poisoning everything. I felt like a fraud. I thought that maybe my faith was just too weak, or that I was somehow broken.

I’m telling you this for one reason: to normalise what you might be feeling. If you’ve ever sat in this room, or in your small group, or during a sermon, and thought:
*“Do I really believe this, or do I just believe it because my parents do?”*
*“Why does God feel so silent sometimes?”*
*“How can the Bible be true when science says…?”*
*“If God is love, why is there so much suffering in the world?”*
…Then you are not alone. You are not weird. You are not a faith-failure.

In fact, I’d be more worried if you *didn’t* have questions. It means you’re paying attention. You’re engaging. You’re thinking. Doubt isn’t the opposite of faith; *indifference* is. The opposite of love isn’t hate, it’s apathy. To doubt, to wrestle, to question—that means you care enough about something to want it to be real, to be true. It means your faith is alive enough to have growing pains.

Let’s get one thing clear: **Doubt is a normal part of growing up and growing in faith.** It is not a sin. It is not a sign of spiritual immaturity. Often, it’s a sign of spiritual deepening. You’re moving from a borrowed, handed-down faith to one you have to build and own for yourself. That process is messy. It involves taking things off the shelf, examining them, and deciding what you’re going to keep.

Maybe you think the Bible is full of people who never had a doubt in their lives. Let me introduce you to a guy named Habakkuk. He’s a prophet, way back in the Old Testament. He’s not famous like David or Moses. He only gets three short chapters. But he’s the patron saint of the brutally honest doubters.

Habakkuk looks out at the world and what does he see? Injustice. Violence. Corruption. Good people suffering, bad people thriving. Sound familiar? And he turns to God and doesn’t offer a polite prayer. He launches a complaint. He basically says: *“God, what are you doing? Are you even paying attention? I cry out to you about violence and you don’t save? Why do you make me look at this garbage? Why are you silent?”* (That’s my paraphrase of Habakkuk 1:2-4).

This is not a Sunday school prayer. This is rage, confusion, and deep, theological doubt. “God, your management of the world seems deeply flawed. Explain yourself.”

And God *answers*. But God’s answer isn’t what Habakkuk wants to hear. God says, “I’m doing something, but you wouldn’t believe it if I told you. I’m raising up a brutal, pagan nation to come and judge my own people.” If you’re thinking, *‘Wait, what? That sounds terrible,’* you are right there with Habakkuk. It made zero sense to him. It leads to his *second* complaint: *“Um, God? You’re holy. How can you use people who are even *more* evil to punish people who are *sort of* evil? This makes you look bad!”* (See Habakkuk 1:12-17).

God lays out his bigger, longer, more mysterious plan—a plan Habakkuk can’t fully see from his tiny vantage point in history. And Habakkuk doesn’t get all his answers for the future, but he decides to trust the character of the God he has known.

And Habakkuk’s conclusion is the most important part. He doesn’t get all his answers. The situation on the ground doesn’t change. The bad guys are still coming. But after wrestling, after yelling his doubts into the heavens, he comes to a place of staggering trust. He says:

> “Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, **yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.**” (Habakkuk 3:17-18)

His circumstances are a disaster. His questions aren’t all answered. But his faith has moved from a fragile belief in good circumstances to a rugged trust in a Person. His doubt led him to a deeper, more resilient faith. He moved from “God, why are you doing this?” to “God, I don’t understand you, but I trust you.”

This is an invitation to go deeper.” Name the doubt. Second, **find your people.** You cannot do this alone. Is there one person—a youth leader, a friend in this group, a trusted mentor—with whom you can be brutally honest? He’s been listening to that stuff since Habakkuk and before.

Option B: With someone else. Text that person you thought of. Having this conversation won’t magically resolve your doubt by next Tuesday. But it will break the silence. Your doubt is not a dead end. It can be a doorway. A doorway out of a second-hand, fragile faith and into a first-hand, resilient, deeply personal trust. You are not alone in this. The path you’re on—the path of asking, seeking, and knocking—is a well-worn path. It’s the path of Habakkuk, of Thomas, of David, of Job, of Mary who asked “How can this be?”, of Jesus himself who cried, “My God, why have you forsaken me?”

You are in good company. So let’s stop pretending, and start wrestling. And see if, on the other side of the struggle, we don’t find a God who is bigger, and a faith that is stronger, than we ever imagined.

Thanks for listening.

Good morning. Before we really get into this, I need you to do something for me. I want you to think of the biggest, most honest question you have about faith, God, church, the Bible, life… anything in that universe. Got it? Now, I want you to picture raising your hand right now and asking it out loud, in front of everyone here.

What happens in your gut? A little clench of anxiety? Do you imagine the room going silent? Do you worry someone might think you’re a bad Christian, or that you’re falling away, or that you’re just trying to cause trouble? If you felt any of that, you’re not alone. That feeling is why we need to talk about doubt.

Let me start with a story that isn’t from the Bible. It’s from my first year of university. I’d grown up in church, my faith felt pretty solid, and then I landed in a philosophy 101 class. The professor, a brilliant and kind man, wasn’t attacking anything. He was just asking questions. Really, really good questions. Questions like, “How do we know *anything* for certain?” and “If God is all-good and all-powerful, why does undeniable, random suffering exist?” I’d heard these before, but suddenly, in that lecture hall, they weren’t abstract. They were skeleton keys that seemed to unlock every door of certainty I had.

I’d walk back to my dorm, look at the Bible on my desk, and feel… nothing. Just a hollow, quiet static. My prayers hit the ceiling and evaporated. It wasn’t that I’d decided God didn’t exist; it was that the whole framework felt suddenly distant, like a story I’d been told but couldn’t quite believe anymore. And the worst part was the loneliness. At my campus Christian group, everyone seemed so sure. They talked about their “quiet times” and their conviction. I felt like an imposter in two worlds: too doubtful for the faithful, and too faithful for the doubters. I was stuck in the middle, thinking something must be broken in me.

Here’s what I wish someone had told me then, and what I’m telling you now: **Doubt is not your faith falling apart. It is often your faith growing up.**

Doubt isn’t the opposite of faith. Apathy is. Indifference is. Doubt is a sign of engagement. You don’t wrestle with something you don’t care about. That feeling of the ground shifting beneath your feet? It’s not necessarily a landslide. It might be the old, shaky floorboards of a faith you inherited being replaced, board by board, with something you can actually stand on for yourself. The transition is terrifying, but it’s necessary. If your faith never encounters a real question, it remains a childhood blanket—comforting, but not something you can build an adult life on.

So, let’s normalize this. Look around. I promise you, the person to your left and your right has a question they’re afraid to voice. The person up here talking has had seasons where it felt like walking through fog. It is a normal part of being a thinking human being on a spiritual journey. Full stop.

And because it’s normal, we see it all over the Bible, not in the neat Sunday school summaries, but in the raw, messy originals. We often talk about “Doubting Thomas” as if he’s the one bad example. But that’s incredibly unfair. Let’s reframe his story.

Jesus, Thomas’s best friend, teacher, and the man he believed was the Messiah, was brutally executed. Thomas’s world was obliterated by grief and trauma. Then, his friends come to him with the wildest, most impossible news: “We have seen the Lord!” And Thomas, in his raw, honest pain, says, “Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

He doesn’t say, “I’ll never believe.” He states what he needs. His doubt isn’t cynical dismissal; it’s a wounded heart’s cry for tangible proof. It’s the doubt of, “The world has hurt me too much to hope without something real.”

And how does Jesus respond? A week later, Jesus appears, walks right up to Thomas, and doesn’t say, “You faithless failure! How dare you!” He says, “Peace be with you.” Then he offers exactly what Thomas asked for: “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.”

Jesus meets Thomas *in* his doubt. He provides the evidence Thomas needed, not as a rebuke, but as a gift. And Thomas’s response is the most profound declaration of Christ’s identity in all the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!”

Thomas’s doubt wasn’t a roadblock to faith; it was the path to a faith that was entirely, unshakably his own. He didn’t get a second-hand, borrowed faith. He got a firsthand encounter because he was honest about what he needed. His doubt led him to a deeper, more personal confession than any of the other disciples had made at that point.

But maybe your doubt isn’t about evidence after a trauma. Maybe it’s the slow-burning kind. For that, I love the prophet Habakkuk. His book is basically a furious, frustrated prayer journal. He looks at the violence and injustice in his society and shouts at God: “How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?”

Habakkuk doesn’t quietly journal his concerns. He accuses God of being silent, of being inactive. And God doesn’t strike him down. God answers. Not with a simple explanation, but with a bigger perspective: “Look at the nations and watch—and be utterly amazed. For I am going to do something in your days that you would not believe, even if you were told.”

The conversation goes back and forth. Habakkuk pushes back again! And it ends not with all his questions answered, but with a profound statement of trust *in the midst* of the unanswered questions. He says, “Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.”

His faith isn’t based on everything going well. It’s a choice to trust the character of God even when the circumstances scream otherwise. His doubt led him to a faith that could survive famine.

This is the vision I want to offer you: **Honest questions don’t have to destroy faith; they can excavate it.** They dig away the loose soil of pat answers and clichés to hit the solid rock beneath. A faith that has never been questioned is a faith you don’t *know*—you’ve just never *not* had it. A faith that has been through the fire of doubt and come out the other side? That’s a faith you own. It’s resilient.

So, what do we do? How do we live in this space without getting lost?

First, **change the conversation in your own head.** When a big question arises, don’t immediately think, “Oh no, I’m losing my faith.” Try thinking, “This is a new frontier for my faith. This is where it gets to grow up.” Separate doubt from shame. They are not the same thing.

Second, **find a safe person.** This is crucial. You need at least one person—a youth leader, a wise friend, a parent, a mentor—with whom you can say the quiet part out loud. Someone who won’t gasp, quote a single Bible verse as a band-aid, or try to “fix” you, but who will say, “That is a massive question. Tell me more. Let’s sit in this together.” If you don’t have someone, start by being that person for others. Create a circle where “I don’t know” and “I’m struggling with this” are acceptable things to say.

Finally, I want to give you a very practical next step. It’s not a three-point answer. It’s a practice.

**For the next week, I want you to keep a “Doubt Journal.”**

Not a prayer journal where you feel you have to say the right things. A doubt journal. Get a notebook, or use a notes app. Every time a question pops into your head—whether it’s huge (“Is any of this real?”) or practical (“Why do we sing these same songs?”)—write it down. Don’t censor it. Don’t try to answer it immediately. Just honor it by writing it. At the end of the week, look at your list. You might be surprised. Some questions might look smaller on paper. Others will look huge and important. Pick one—just one—and take one step toward exploring it. That could mean:
*   Reading the story of a biblical character who asked something similar.
*   Finding a reputable book or article that tackles that topic.
*   Saying to your safe person, “So, I have this question about…”
*   Even praying the most honest prayer you can: “God, I am really hung up on this. I need your help to see you in it.”

The goal isn’t to have a tidy answer by Friday. The goal is to stop treating your doubts like enemies to be locked in the basement, and start treating them like guides, pointing you toward the parts of your faith that need to become stronger and more truly yours.

You are not alone in this. The path of faith isn’t a straight, well-lit highway. It’s more like a hike, with foggy patches, steep climbs, and breathtaking vistas. The doubt is just the fog. It doesn’t mean you’re off the path. It often means you’re right where you’re supposed to be, learning to walk by something deeper than sight.

Thanks for listening.

Okay, let’s get real for a minute.

I want you to think about the last time you were absolutely, 100% certain about something. Not just kind of sure, but deep-in-your-bones, no-questions-asked certain. Maybe it was that the answer on your math test was right. Or that your friend was telling you the truth. Or that you knew exactly what you wanted to do with your life.

Now, how long did that feeling last?

If you’re anything like me, those moments are pretty rare. Most of the time, life feels more… wobbly. We’re making decisions based on the best information we have, but there’s often a little voice in the back of our heads. A whisper that says, *“But what if…?”* *“Are you sure…?”* *“How do you really know…?”*

Let me tell you a story. When I was about 16, I went on a hiking trip with some friends. We had a map, we had a compass, and we were all convinced we knew the way to this amazing waterfall. For the first hour, everything was great. The trail was clear, the sun was out, we were laughing and talking. Then, the trail started to get fainter. The trees looked different than they did on the map. We came to a fork that wasn’t marked. We all stopped. The confident chatter died down. One friend was sure we went left. Another was adamant we went right. I just stood there, looking at the compass, then at the map, then at the trees, feeling this knot of confusion and anxiety in my stomach. I wasn’t just unsure of the path; for a second, I was unsure of the map itself. *What if it’s wrong? What if we’re totally lost?* That feeling—that’s doubt. It’s not just not knowing an answer. It’s the unsettling, sometimes scary, feeling that the things you were relying on to *find* the answers might be shaky.

Here’s my first point, and I need you to hear this: **If you have ever felt that wobble, that “what if,” in your faith—you are normal.** In fact, you’re in the best possible company. Doubt is not your faith’s failure. It is not a sign of weakness, or a one-way ticket to getting kicked off the team. Doubt is a normal part of being a thinking, feeling human being on a journey. And it is absolutely a normal part of growing up and growing in faith. Think about it: you’re asked to believe in a God you can’t see, in a world full of pain and chaos, with a brain that’s constantly developing and questioning everything from your parents’ rules to the meaning of life. Of course you’ll have questions! The faith you had when you were seven—simple, story-based, trusting—is not meant to fit the you who is 16. It has to grow up with you. And growing pains are real.

So let’s take the stigma away. Right now. Let’s agree that in this space, doubt isn’t a dirty word. It’s a real one. It’s the evidence that you’re taking this seriously, that you’re not just going through the motions. You’re engaging. And that is a good thing.

The Bible knows this. It’s not a book of plaster saints with perfect, unwavering faith. It’s full of people who argued with God, cried out in confusion, and flat-out said, “I’m not sure I believe this.”

I want to talk about one of my favourites: Habakkuk. He’s a minor prophet, which basically means he doesn’t get his own major motion picture, but he’s incredible. His whole short book is one long, angry, confused prayer. He looks at the world around him—full of violence, injustice, and corruption—and he basically marches up to God and says, “What are you doing? Are you even paying attention? I cry out to you about all this evil, and you do nothing! How can you just sit there and watch this?” (That’s my paraphrase of Habakkuk 1:2-4).

This isn’t a polite, “Dear God, I have a theological inquiry.” This is a shout of doubt. It’s doubt in God’s goodness. Doubt in God’s justice. Doubt that God is even *there* in the mess. Habakkuk is honest to the point of being rude.

And how does God respond? Does He strike Habakkuk down? Say, “How dare you question me!”? Nope. God answers. He says, “Look at the nations and watch—and be utterly amazed. For I am going to do something in your days that you would not believe, even if you were told” (Habakkuk 1:5). The answer isn’t a simple fix. It’s complex and involves a long, hard story. So Habakkuk doubts *again*. He comes back and says, “Hold on, that plan involves using people *worse* than us? That doesn’t seem right!”

The conversation goes back and forth. And here’s the miracle: through this raw, honest exchange of doubt and questioning, something shifts. Habakkuk doesn’t get all his answers. The circumstances don’t magically change. But by the end of the book, his faith has *transformed*. It’s moved from a faith based on everything going right, to a faith that can stand even when everything is going wrong. He ends with some of the most profound words of trust in the Bible: “Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior” (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

His doubt didn’t destroy his faith. His honesty led him to a deeper, tougher, more resilient kind of faith. He moved from wanting God to fix his circumstances, to trusting God in the midst of them. His questions were the fire that refined his belief, burning away the flimsy stuff until only the unshakeable core remained.

This is the vision I want to offer you: **Honest questions don’t have to be the enemy of faith. They can be its gym.** Faith isn’t a fragile glass sculpture that one question will shatter. Real faith is more like a muscle. It gets stronger when it’s tested, when it has to work, when it has to wrestle. A faith that has never been questioned is a faith you’ve never owned—it’s just something you’re borrowing from your parents, your friends, or your youth leader.

So, what do we do with the wobble? With the “what if”?

First, we have to name it. To ourselves, and to someone safe. Burying doubt because you’re scared of it is like ignoring that weird sound your car is making. It doesn’t make it go away; it usually means something worse happens later. Bring it into the light. Say it out loud: “I’m having a hard time believing God is good when I see…” or “The idea of a loving God doesn’t fit with…” or “I just don’t know if any of this is real.”

Second, we have to be okay with mystery. We live in a culture that demands instant answers. Google, YouTube tutorials, AI chatbots. But God is not a problem to be solved. He is a person to be known. And knowing a person takes time, patience, and living with some unanswered questions. Some of our “why” questions may not get answered this side of heaven. Can we be okay with that? Can we trust that not knowing the *answer* doesn’t mean we don’t know the *God* who holds the answers?

Finally, we engage. We follow Habakkuk’s model. We take our doubt to God Himself. We pray our questions, our anger, our confusion. We study. We read the parts of the Bible that deal with hard things—Job, Psalms of lament, Ecclesiastes, Jesus’ own cries of abandonment on the cross. We talk to wise people who aren’t scared of our questions. We don’t just sit in passive doubt; we use it as fuel for an active search.

So here’s your practical next step. I’m not going to give you a three-step prayer to make doubt vanish. That’s a cliché, and you’d see right through it.

Instead, I want you to try this **one thing** this week:

**Get a notebook, or open a notes app on your phone. At the top of a blank page, write this: “My Honest Questions.” And then, just write one. Don’t censor it. Don’t try to make it sound spiritual or neat. It could be huge: “How can a loving God allow suffering?” It could be personal: “Why do I feel so alone when I’m supposed to believe God is with me?” It could be practical: “Does prayer even do anything?” Just write one honest question.**

That’s it. That’s step one. You don’t have to answer it tonight. You don’t even have to show it to anyone. But by writing it down, you’re doing something powerful. You’re acknowledging it. You’re bringing it out of the shadows of your mind and saying, “This is a real thing I am carrying.”

And when you’re ready, maybe that page becomes the start of a conversation. With God. With a trusted friend. With me. But let it start with honesty.

You are not failing because you have questions. You are growing. You are on the path. And sometimes, the path gets faint. That doesn’t mean you’re lost. It often means you’re exactly where you’re supposed to be—learning to walk by faith, not by sight.

Thanks for listening.

Faith is similar. It evolves. It deepens. And sometimes, that means going through periods of doubt and questioning.

The Bible is full of people who wrestled with doubt. We tend to put these figures on pedestals, thinking they had it all figured out, but if you read their stories closely, you'll see that they were just as human as we are.

Take Thomas, for example. We call him "Doubting Thomas" for a reason. He refused to believe that Jesus had risen from the dead until he saw the wounds with his own eyes. Now, we could judge Thomas for his lack of faith. We could say he should have just trusted the other disciples. But Jesus didn’t shame him. He didn't dismiss him. He met Thomas where he was, showed him the evidence, and allowed him to come to his own understanding.

Or think about David. This is the guy who killed Goliath, who was called "a man after God's own heart." But David also committed adultery, had a man murdered to cover it up, and then wrote Psalms filled with anguish and self-doubt. He cried out to God, asking why he felt abandoned, why he was suffering. He didn't pretend to have all the answers. He was honest about his struggles.

And then there's Job. Poor Job. He lost everything – his family, his possessions, his health. And he spent the entire book of Job questioning God's justice. He wasn't afraid to be angry, to be confused, to demand answers. And in the end, God didn't give him easy answers. He didn't explain why Job had suffered. Instead, God revealed his own power and wisdom, reminding Job that there are things beyond human comprehension.

Even Habakkuk, the prophet, had questions. He saw injustice and violence all around him and asked God, "Why aren't you doing anything?" He felt like God wasn't listening, wasn't acting. And God responded to Habakkuk, not with a simple explanation, but with a promise that justice would eventually prevail, even if it wasn't in Habakkuk's lifetime.

These stories show us that doubt isn't the opposite of faith; it's often a part of it. It’s the wrestling match that can make us stronger. It's the digging that unearths deeper truths.

So, how do we navigate these periods of doubt? How do we turn our questions into opportunities for growth?

First, be honest with yourself. Acknowledge your doubts. Don't try to bury them or pretend they don't exist. They are there for a reason, trying to teach you something.

Second, find safe spaces to explore your questions. Talk to trusted friends, family members, or mentors who won't judge you or try to give you easy answers. Look for people who are willing to listen and engage with your doubts in a thoughtful way. That might be a youth pastor, a small group leader, or even a school counselor. The point is to find someone you trust and who creates a safe space for vulnerability.

Third, do your research. Read books, listen to podcasts, watch documentaries. Explore different perspectives. Don't be afraid to challenge your own assumptions. But be discerning about your sources. Not everything you read online is true. Look for credible sources and consider multiple viewpoints.

Fourth, don't be afraid to ask God your questions. He can handle it. He's not afraid of your doubts. In fact, He might be inviting you to a deeper conversation with Him. Prayer isn't just about reciting memorized words; it's about honest communication with God.

Fifth, remember that faith is a journey, not a destination. There will be times when you feel certain and times when you feel uncertain. That's okay. The important thing is to keep moving forward, to keep seeking truth, and to keep growing in your relationship with God.

Now, I know this is a lot to take in. And I don't have all the answers. But I hope this has given you permission to embrace your doubts, to see them not as a threat to your faith, but as an invitation to a deeper understanding.

I want to leave you with one practical next step. This week, I want you to sit with this question: **What is one question you have about your faith that you've been afraid to ask?**

Don't try to answer it right away. Just sit with it. Let it simmer. See where it leads you. Maybe it will lead you to a book, a conversation, or a prayer. Maybe it will lead you to a new understanding of God.

And if you feel comfortable, share that question with someone you trust. You might be surprised at what you discover.

Because ultimately, faith isn't about having all the answers. It's about trusting that even in the midst of our doubts and questions, God is still with us, guiding us, and leading us on a journey of discovery. Thanks for listening.

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here tonight. Seriously, it means a lot that you’ve shown up, especially on a [mention day of week, e.g., Tuesday] night.

I want to start tonight with a quick story, or maybe a scenario you can relate to. Imagine you’ve been working on something big. Maybe it’s trying out for the lead role in the school play, or you’re pushing yourself to make the varsity team in a sport you love, or you’re pouring hours into a really ambitious art project, or even a tough academic competition.

You start out feeling pretty good, right? You’re excited, you’re practicing, you’re studying, you’re putting in the work. You *believe* you can do it. You see yourself on that stage, or scoring that goal, or seeing your project come to life. There’s a confidence, a certainty, a kind of… faith, if you will, in your own abilities and in the outcome.

Then, inevitably, something happens. You mess up a line in rehearsal, badly. You miss a crucial shot in practice, over and over again. Your art piece isn't turning out the way you envisioned, or your code throws a hundred errors just before the deadline. Suddenly, that initial buzz, that confidence, that certainty? It starts to waver.

You start to think, "Maybe I’m not good enough. Maybe I don't have what it takes. Maybe this isn’t for me. Maybe I should just give up." That feeling? That knot in your stomach, that voice in your head questioning everything you thought you knew? That’s doubt.

And here’s the thing: that feeling of doubt, whether it’s about your ability to hit that note, or whether it’s about something much bigger, like your faith, it's not a sign of weakness. It's not a sign you're failing. It's actually a completely normal, and often necessary, part of growth.

### Doubt: Not a Bug, But a Feature

We often grow up thinking that faith is this perfectly smooth, unwavering thing. Like you sign up for it, and then you just believe, full stop, no questions asked. And if you *do* have questions, if you *do* feel uncertain, then maybe you’re doing it wrong. Maybe you’re not a "good enough" Christian. Maybe you just don’t have enough faith.

But I want to challenge that idea tonight. Because if you’re sitting here, or watching this, and you’ve ever felt a flicker of doubt about God, about the Bible, about your beliefs, about why bad things happen, about whether any of this is even real… I want you to know you are not alone. And more importantly, you are not failing. You are actually participating in a very human, very ancient, and very biblical process.

Doubt isn't the opposite of faith. It's often an essential element of it. Think of it like this: a tree with shallow roots might stand tall on a calm day, but the moment a storm hits, it’s the first to fall. A tree that has weathered winds and storms, that has had to push its roots deeper and wider to find stability – that tree is stronger. Its roots are more firmly established.

Your faith is the same. Faith that has never been questioned, never been challenged, never had to dig deep? It might be fragile. But faith that has wrestled with doubt, that has dared to ask the hard questions and search for answers, that faith becomes resilient, personal, and deeply rooted.

### A Prophet’s Honest Cry: Habakkuk

Let’s look at someone who really exemplifies this, someone from the Bible who didn’t just have quiet little doubts, but who *shouted* his questions at God. His name is Habakkuk.

Now, Habakkuk wasn't just some random guy. He was a prophet. Prophets were supposed to be the ones with the answers, the ones who heard directly from God, the ones who *spoke* for God. But Habakkuk wasn't speaking *for* God; he was speaking *to* God, and he was doing it with a lot of frustration.

He lived in a time of intense injustice and violence in Judah. He saw people being oppressed, corruption everywhere, and moral decay. And he couldn’t understand why God wasn’t doing anything about it.

So, he does something incredibly bold, something many of us might be afraid to do. He goes to God and he says, essentially, "How long, O Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, 'Violence!' but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrong? Destruction and violence are before me; there is strife, and conflict abounds. Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never prevails. The wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted." (Habakkuk 1:2-4)

Can you hear the raw honesty in that? He’s not whispering; he’s practically yelling at God. He’s looking at the world, seeing all the messed-up stuff, and he’s saying, "God, where are you?! Why aren’t you doing anything about this?! This isn't fair! This isn't right!"

And here’s the amazing part: God *answers* him. God doesn't shut him down for being insolent or lacking faith. God responds, and His response is, frankly, pretty wild. God says, "I *am* doing something, Habakkuk. I'm raising up the Babylonians—a ruthless and impetuous people—to march throughout the earth and seize dwellings not their own." (Habakkuk 1:5-6)

Now, imagine Habakkuk’s face when he hears that. The Babylonians were a terrifying, brutal empire. So, Habakkuk’s first thought is, "Wait, what?! You’re going to use *them*? The Babylonians are even worse than the people I'm complaining about! How can you, a holy God, use such evil to bring about justice? That doesn't make any sense!" (Habakkuk 1:12-17, paraphrased). He’s still wrestling. He’s still questioning God’s methods, God’s justice, God’s very character.

He then says, "I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what he will say to me, and what answer I will give to this complaint." (Habakkuk 2:1). He’s basically saying, "I’m going to wait here, and I expect an answer, God!"

And God answers him again. This time, God gives him a vision of the future, a promise that justice *will* ultimately prevail, that the wicked *will* be punished, and that His timing is perfect, even if it feels slow to Habakkuk. And then comes that incredibly famous line: "The righteous will live by faith." (Habakkuk 2:4).

Habakkuk didn't get immediate, easy answers. He got answers that were complex, that required him to trust God's long-term plan, even when the short-term looked bleak and confusing. He had to wait. He had to trust.

And what’s the result of all this wrestling? Habakkuk doesn't lose his faith. He deepens it. He ends his book with one of the most profound statements of trust in the entire Bible: "Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior." (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

He moved from "Why, God?" to "Even if everything falls apart, I will still trust you." His faith wasn't destroyed by his questions; it was forged in the fire of them.

### How Honest Questions Deepen Your Faith

So, what can we learn from Habakkuk, and from our own moments of doubt?

1.  **Doubt forces us to own our beliefs.** When you start asking "Why do I believe this?" or "Is this really true?", you're moving beyond simply inheriting your parents' or your church's faith. You're beginning to build *your own* faith. You're deciding for yourself what you believe and why. That makes your faith personal, authentic, and much more resilient.
2.  **Doubt is an invitation to seek.** Those questions, those uncertainties? They’re like signposts pointing you towards deeper understanding. They encourage you to read the Bible more closely, to research, to talk to wise people, to pray more earnestly, to truly grapple with what you believe. It's in the seeking that we often find God in new and profound ways.
3.  **Doubt builds resilience.** Just like that tree weathering the storm, a faith that has been tested and has come through on the other side is stronger. You learn that your faith isn't fragile, that it can handle your tough questions, and that God can handle them too. You develop a spiritual muscle that helps you navigate future uncertainties.
4.  **Doubt leads to a more authentic relationship with God.** If you can bring your raw, honest questions and frustrations to God, just like Habakkuk did, then you’re building a real relationship. You’re not pretending to have it all together. You’re being vulnerable, and God honors that. He’s not afraid of your questions, and He’s not intimidated by your doubts. He actually *invites* them, because they show you’re engaged, you’re thinking, you’re wrestling. That’s a relationship, not just a set of rules.

I’m not here tonight to give you pat answers. I can’t tell you *why* bad things happen, or *how* God always works, or *exactly* what you should believe. Because honestly, if someone tells you they have all the neat and tidy answers to every question about faith, they’re probably selling something. Faith is a journey, and sometimes, the answers don't come quickly, or they're not neat and tidy, or they lead to even more questions. And that’s okay.

What I *can* tell you is that the journey itself, the wrestling, the honest questioning – that's where true, vibrant faith is often found. It's where you stop living on borrowed faith and start living on your own, deeply rooted convictions.

### Your Next Step

So, here’s my challenge, my invitation to you this week.

Think about one question, one uncertainty, one doubt you have about God, about faith, about what you’ve been taught. Maybe it’s a big one, like "Why is there so much suffering?" Or maybe it’s a smaller, more personal one, like "Does God really care about my choices?"

Don’t try to answer it right now. Just identify it. Write it down if that helps you articulate it.

And then, here’s the brave part: find one person you trust – a youth leader, a parent, a mentor, a pastor, a really close friend – and share that question with them. Not for them to give you a pat answer, though they might have some helpful thoughts. But just to say it out loud. To acknowledge it. To bring it into the light.

And if you don't feel ready to share it with a person, then share it with God. Just be honest, like Habakkuk. Tell Him your question, your frustration, your uncertainty. He can handle it. He wants you to bring it to Him.

Because in that honest wrestling, in that brave questioning, you might just find that your faith isn't crumbling, but growing. You might find that God isn't distant or afraid of your doubts, but closer than you ever imagined, inviting you into a deeper, more authentic relationship.

Thanks for listening. And remember, it's okay to doubt. It's okay to question. It's often how we truly grow.

Alright everyone, grab a seat. We’re going to talk about something that I think is on a lot of our minds, maybe more than we admit, especially at this age. We’re going to talk about doubt.

Now, before anyone gets uncomfortable, let me start with a story. It’s not a deep, spiritual story, but it’s one that I think illustrates a feeling we’ve all had.

Imagine you’re in science class, maybe middle school or early high school. And the teacher is talking about, say, the solar system. You’ve been taught since you were tiny that there are nine planets. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto. Right? Pluto was always the little guy at the end, the underdog. You learned the mnemonic devices, you drew the diagrams. It was a fact. Solid. Unquestionable.

Then, one day, your teacher says, "Okay, so we're going to talk about the planets... and dwarf planets." And they proceed to explain that Pluto, your beloved ninth planet, has been reclassified. It’s not a planet anymore. It’s a dwarf planet.

Do you remember that feeling? For some of you, it might have been a "who cares?" For others, it might have been a genuine, "Wait, what?! Everything I thought I knew was wrong? Is anything real?" It’s a small thing, sure, but it’s that moment where a foundational ‘truth’ you’d always accepted suddenly gets shaken. You feel a little disoriented, maybe even a bit betrayed by the universe. And then you start asking questions: Why? Who decided this? What else have I been told that isn't quite right?

That feeling, that "wait, what?" – that moment of questioning something you’ve always held as true – that’s doubt. And it’s not just for Pluto. It happens in science, in history, in politics, in relationships, and yes, it absolutely happens in faith.

And here’s the most important thing I want you to hear tonight: **Doubt is not a sign of failure. It is not a weakness. It is not a sign that you are losing your faith.** In fact, it’s often a sign that your faith is actually *growing*.

Think about it. You guys are at an age where you’re questioning everything. You’re questioning your parents’ rules, your school’s policies, society’s expectations. You’re figuring out who *you* are, what *you* believe, not just what you’ve been told to believe. This is a critical developmental stage. Your brain is literally rewiring itself to think more critically, to process complex ideas, to form your own identity. It would be weirder if you *didn't* start asking hard questions about something as big and fundamental as faith.

A faith that has never been questioned is often a fragile faith. It’s like a house built on sand, or a borrowed coat. It looks good from the outside, but it might not withstand the first storm, or it might not truly fit you. When you start to doubt, you’re actually beginning the process of taking ownership of your faith, of moving from a childhood faith – where you believe because your parents believe, or because that’s what you were taught – to an adult faith, where you actively wrestle with the big questions and choose to believe for yourself.

And here’s another truth: You are not alone in this. Not by a long shot. Every single person who has ever had a deep and lasting faith has, at some point, wrestled with doubt. Even some of the biggest heroes of faith in the Bible.

Let’s talk about one of them: a prophet named Habakkuk. Now, Habakkuk isn’t as famous as, say, David or Moses or Peter. He’s a little book tucked away in the Old Testament, but his story is incredibly relevant to anyone wrestling with doubt.

Habakkuk lived in a really tough time for his people, Judah. The nation was steeped in injustice and violence. People were hurting each other, corruption was rampant, and it felt like God was nowhere to be found, or at least, wasn't doing anything about it.

So, Habakkuk does something pretty audacious. He doesn't just quietly wonder. He doesn't just shrug and give up. He goes directly to God, and he lays it all out. He basically says, "God, what gives?!"

Listen to his opening lines, from Habakkuk chapter 1, verses 2-4:
*“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing? Destruction and violence are before me; there is strife, and conflict abounds. Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never prevails. The wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted.”*

He’s not whispering this. He’s shouting it. He’s saying, "God, I see all this evil, and you’re just letting it happen! Where are you? Why aren’t you doing anything? You’re supposed to be just and powerful, but I’m seeing the opposite!" He’s expressing profound doubt about God’s character, God’s justice, God’s very involvement in the world.

And God *responds*. He doesn’t tell Habakkuk to shut up. He doesn’t scold him for his lack of faith. He doesn’t say, "Just trust me, it’ll be fine." Instead, God says, "Oh, you want to know what I’m doing? I’m doing something so wild, you wouldn’t believe it even if I told you. I’m raising up the Babylonians – a fierce and ruthless nation – to punish Judah."

Now, imagine Habakkuk’s face. He just complained about *injustice* and *violence* among his own people. And God’s answer is, "I’m going to bring an *even more* violent and unjust nation to destroy you!"

So, Habakkuk doesn't just accept it. He doubles down on his questions. He basically says, "Hold on a minute, God! That makes no sense! You are holy! You are pure! How can you use a nation that is even *more* wicked than us to punish us? How can you just stand by and watch them devour people more righteous than themselves? That violates everything I know about you!" (Habakkuk 1:12-17, paraphrased).

This is a man in deep, theological crisis. His understanding of God is being completely shattered. He’s looking at the world, looking at God’s stated character, and seeing a massive, painful disconnect.

But here’s what Habakkuk does next, and this is crucial. In Habakkuk 2:1, he says:
*“I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer when I am rebuked.”*

He doesn’t walk away. He doesn’t abandon his faith. He doesn’t throw his hands up and say, "This God makes no sense, I’m out." Instead, he takes a posture of *waiting and watching*. He positions himself to *listen* for God’s response. He’s saying, "I have these questions, I have these doubts, and I’m going to stay right here, in this place of tension, until I hear from you again."

And God *does* respond again. He tells Habakkuk that the vision of justice will come, in its own time. He reminds Habakkuk that even though it seems like evil is winning, God is still in control, and ultimately, "the righteous will live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4).

And what’s the result of all this wrestling? Habakkuk doesn’t get all his questions answered neatly. He doesn’t get a full explanation for why God does things the way He does. But he ends his book, after all his raw honesty and doubt, with one of the most powerful declarations of faith in the entire Bible. In Habakkuk 3:17-19, he says:
*“Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior. The Sovereign Lord is my strength; he makes my feet like the feet of a deer, he enables me to tread on the heights.”*

He’s saying, "Even if everything around me falls apart, even if the world makes no sense, even if I don’t understand God’s ways, I will still find my joy and my strength in Him."

That, friends, is a faith that has been forged in the fire of doubt. It’s not a borrowed coat anymore. It’s a custom-made suit, tailored through honest questioning and persistent seeking. Habakkuk’s questions didn’t destroy his faith; they deepened it. They took it from a theoretical understanding to a profound, lived experience of trusting God even when it didn't make sense.

So, what does this mean for you?

It means that your honest questions, your genuine uncertainties, your moments of "wait, what?" about God, about the Bible, about suffering, about why bad things happen to good people – these are not things to be ashamed of or to hide. They are opportunities. They are invitations to press in, to seek, to wrestle, just like Habakkuk did.

God is not afraid of your questions. He is not threatened by your doubt. He wants you to bring your authentic self, your real struggles, your deepest uncertainties to Him. He doesn't want you to pretend to have all the answers. He wants you to be honest.

I’m not here to give you pat answers. I can’t tell you that if you just read this one verse, all your doubts will vanish. Some questions might not have easy answers, or answers you’ll find immediately. But the journey of seeking, of wrestling, of honestly engaging with God and His word, that journey *itself* is what strengthens your faith. It’s how you build a faith that is truly yours, a faith that can withstand the storms of life.

So, as we wrap up tonight, I want to leave you with a practical next step. This isn't a homework assignment, but an invitation to engage with your own faith journey.

Here it is:
**What’s one question about faith that you’re genuinely wrestling with right now?**
Maybe it’s something you’ve always wondered but felt too silly or too scared to ask. Maybe it’s a contradiction you see in the world, or something in the Bible that doesn’t sit right. Maybe it’s about suffering, or injustice, or why God allows certain things.

Don't let that question fester in silence. Don't let it grow into a wall between you and God, or between you and your faith community.

Instead, I encourage you to do one of two things:
1.  **Find a safe person:** This could be a youth leader, a parent, a mentor, a trusted friend. Someone who you know will listen without judgment, who won't give you platitudes, but will genuinely engage with your question. Share your doubt with them. Start a conversation. You might be surprised to find they’ve wrestled with similar questions themselves.
2.  **Take a page from Habakkuk:** Find your "watchtower." Find a quiet space, maybe just for 10 or 15 minutes this week. And just like Habakkuk, lay out your question, your doubt, your confusion, honestly before God. Write it down in a journal. Say it out loud. Don't expect fireworks or an audible voice. Just present your heart, your mind, your struggle, and then take a posture of listening, of waiting. See what thoughts emerge, what scriptures come to mind, what sense of peace or direction you might find.

Doubt isn't the enemy of faith; it can be its training ground. Embrace your questions. Be honest with yourself, with others, and most importantly, with God. Because it's often in the wrestling that we find a deeper, more resilient, and more authentic faith than we ever thought possible.

Thanks for listening.

*“I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer when I am rebuked.”*

He doesn’t walk away or abandon his faith, or say, "This God makes no sense, I’m out." Instead, he takes a posture of *waiting and watching*. He positions himself to *listen* for God’s response. He’s saying, "I have these questions, I have these doubts, and I’m going to stay right here, in this place of tension, until I hear from you again."

And God *does* respond again. He tells Habakkuk that the vision of justice will come, in its own time. He reminds Habakkuk that even though it seems like evil is winning, God is still in control, and ultimately, "the righteous will live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). He’s not saying 'stop asking questions and just believe.' He’s saying the righteous *keep living*—they stay in the tension, keep showing up, keep asking. Faith isn't certainty, but commitment in the face of uncertainty.

And then God shows up, not with a 5-point answer, but with a vision of his overwhelming presence. Habakkuk sees God, and that’s what changes him—not getting all his questions solved.

And what’s the result of all this wrestling? Habakkuk doesn’t get all his questions answered neatly. He doesn’t get a full explanation for why God does things the way He does. But he ends his book, after all his raw honesty and doubt, with one of the most powerful declarations of faith in the entire Bible. In Habakkuk 3:17-19, he says:
*“Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior. The Sovereign Lord is my strength; he makes my feet like the feet of a deer, he enables me to tread on the heights.”*

He’s saying, "Even if everything around me falls apart, even if the world makes no sense, even if I don’t understand God’s ways, I will still find my joy and my strength in Him."

That, friends, is a faith forged in the fire of doubt. It’s not a borrowed coat; it’s a custom-made suit, tailored through honest questioning and persistent seeking. Habakkuk’s questions didn’t destroy his faith; they deepened it. They took it from a theoretical understanding to a profound, lived experience of trusting God even when it didn't make sense.

So, what does this mean for you?

It means your honest questions, your genuine uncertainties, your raw "where are you, God?" moments about suffering, injustice, or why bad things happen – these are not things to be ashamed of or to hide. They are opportunities. They are invitations to press in, to seek, to wrestle, just like Habakkuk did.

God is not afraid or threatened by your questions or doubt. He wants you to bring your authentic self, your real struggles, your deepest uncertainties to Him. He doesn't want you to pretend to have all the answers. He wants you to be honest.

I’m not here to give you pat answers. I can’t tell you one verse will make all your doubts vanish. Some questions might not have easy answers, or answers you’ll find immediately. But the journey of seeking, wrestling, and honestly engaging with God and His word *itself* is what strengthens your faith. It’s how you build a faith that is truly yours, a faith that can withstand the storms of life.

So, as we wrap up tonight, I want to leave you with a practical next step. This isn't homework, but an invitation to engage with your faith journey.

Here it is:
**What’s one question about faith that you’re genuinely wrestling with right now?**
Maybe it’s something you’ve always wondered but felt too silly or scared to ask. Maybe it’s a contradiction you see, or something in the Bible that doesn’t sit right.

Don't let that question fester in silence. Don't let it grow into a wall between you and God, or between you and your faith community.

Instead, I encourage you to do one of two things:
1.  **Find a safe person:** This could be a youth leader, a parent, a mentor, a trusted friend. Someone who you know will listen without judgment, who won't give you platitudes, but will genuinely engage with your question. If you’re not sure who that is, start with someone who’s admitted their own doubts before. That’s usually a good sign. If they try to 'fix' you or give easy answers, they’re probably not your person for this. If they say "That’s a great question, I’ve wondered that too," keep talking. Share your doubt with them. Start a conversation. You might be surprised to find they’ve wrestled with similar questions themselves.
2.  **Find your watchtower:** Take a page from Habakkuk. Find a quiet space, maybe just for 10 or 15 minutes this week. Your watchtower could be walking your dog without headphones for 15 minutes, sitting in your car after you park, or that one spot in your house where no one bothers you. Go there. Write the question at the top of a page in a journal. Then write everything that comes to mind—anger, confusion, whatever. Say it out loud. Don't expect fireworks or an audible voice. Just present your heart, mind, and struggle, then sit in silence for 5 minutes. Take a posture of listening, of waiting. See what thoughts emerge, what scriptures come to mind, what sense of peace or direction you might find. You’re not trying to hear a voice; you’re just making space for God in your struggle.

Doubt isn't the enemy of faith; it can be its training ground. Embrace your questions. Be honest with yourself, with others, and most importantly, with God. Because it's often in the wrestling that we find a deeper, more resilient, and more authentic faith than we ever thought possible.

If you want to see this kind of wrestling in action in the Bible, read Psalm 13 or Psalm 73. They’re short, and they’re basically ancient journal entries of doubt and honesty before God.

Thanks for listening.
