Alright everyone, settle in. Grab a seat. Take a deep breath. We’re going to talk about something that might feel a little uncomfortable, a little risky, but I promise you, it’s one of the most normal and important conversations we can have. We’re going to talk about doubt.

Now, I don't mean the kind of doubt you have when you're trying to decide between two equally tempting snacks. I mean the kind of doubt that makes your stomach clench a little, the kind that makes you question things you thought you knew, things you’ve been taught, things you *want* to believe.

Let me start with a story. When I was about your age, maybe a little older, I was pretty confident in my faith. I’d grown up in church, I knew all the Bible stories, I could answer most Sunday school questions. I figured I had a pretty good handle on things. I saw faith as a solid, unshakeable block of truth, and my job was just to hold onto it.

Then, life happened. Not one big, dramatic event, but a series of smaller, more insidious things. I had a science teacher who presented the universe in a way that seemed to leave no room for God. I had a friend who was incredibly smart and kind, but who saw no evidence for faith at all, and had some really tough questions I couldn't answer. And then there was just the sheer amount of suffering I started seeing in the world – stories on the news, things happening in my own community, people I knew going through really terrible times.

Suddenly, that solid block of truth I was holding onto started to feel less like granite and more like a sandcastle at high tide. Questions started bubbling up: *Is any of this actually real? How can a good God allow so much pain? Am I just believing this because I was raised to?*

And the worst part? I felt like I was doing something wrong by even having these thoughts. I felt guilty. I felt like a bad Christian. I was convinced that having doubts meant I was failing, that my faith wasn't strong enough, or worse, that it wasn't real. I tried to push those questions down, to ignore them, to pretend they weren't there. But they just kept coming back, usually when I was quiet, alone in my room, staring at the ceiling.

Have any of you ever felt like that? Like there’s a question tucked away in the back of your mind, a little voice of uncertainty, that you’re afraid to let out? Maybe it's about a specific part of the Bible, or why bad things happen to good people, or whether God really cares about *your* life.

If you have, I want you to know something incredibly important: **Doubt is not the enemy of faith. It’s often a necessary, even healthy, part of it.**

Think about it. You’re at an age where you’re constantly questioning. You’re questioning who you are, what you want to do, what you believe about the world. Your brain is literally wired to analyze, to probe, to challenge assumptions. This isn't a flaw; it's how you learn, how you grow, how you develop your own identity and your own convictions.

And that applies to faith too. A faith that has never been questioned is often a faith that hasn't truly been *owned*. It's like wearing clothes that someone else picked out for you; they might fit, but they don't necessarily feel like *you*. When you start to question, you’re actually beginning the process of making your faith your own, moving from what you were told to what you genuinely believe.

It’s not a sign of failure; it’s a sign that you’re engaging deeply. It’s a sign that you’re thinking critically. It’s a sign that you care enough to wrestle with these huge, profound questions. And guess what? You’re in excellent company.

The Bible, far from being a book of easy answers, is full of people who wrestled with deep, uncomfortable doubts. We often think of biblical heroes as these unwavering, perfectly faithful individuals, but that's rarely the full picture.

Take the prophet Habakkuk, for instance. Not one of the most famous guys, but his story is incredibly powerful for anyone who has ever looked at the world and thought, "What in the world is God doing?"

Habakkuk lived in a time of great injustice and violence. He saw corruption everywhere, people hurting each other, the powerful oppressing the weak. And he looked at God, and he just couldn't understand. So, he did something radical: he cried out to God, not with polite requests, but with an almost angry challenge.

He says, in Chapter 1, verses 2-4:
> "How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen?
> Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save?
> Why do you make me look at injustice?
> Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?
> Destruction and violence are before me;
> there is strife, and conflict abounds.
> Therefore the law is paralyzed,
> and justice never prevails.
> The wicked hem in the righteous,
> so that justice is perverted."

Can you hear the raw frustration in that? He’s basically saying, "God, are you even paying attention? Do you see what’s happening down here? Why aren't you doing anything? This isn’t right!" He's not whispering his doubt; he’s shouting it.

And God answers! But His answer isn't what Habakkuk expects. God says, "I *am* doing something. I’m raising up the Babylonians, a fierce and ruthless nation, to punish the people of Judah."

Now, imagine Habakkuk’s face. He just complained about injustice, and God’s solution is to bring in an even *worse*, more brutal empire? This doesn't solve his doubt; it intensifies it.

So Habakkuk goes back to God, even more perplexed. In verses 12-13, he says:
> "Lord, you are from everlasting!
> You are my God, my Holy One!
> We will not die.
> You, Lord, have appointed them to execute judgment;
> you, my Rock, have ordained them to punish.
> Your eyes are too pure to look on evil;
> you cannot tolerate wrongdoing.
> Why then do you tolerate the treacherous?
> Why are you silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?"

He's basically saying, "God, you’re supposed to be holy! You hate evil! So why are you using evil people to punish us, who are at least *less* evil than them? This makes no sense!"

But here’s the crucial part. After this second, even deeper complaint, Habakkuk doesn't walk away. He doesn't give up. He says, in Chapter 2, verse 1:
> "I will stand at my watchpost
> and station myself on the city wall;
> I will wait to see what he will say to me
> and what I will answer concerning my complaint."

He takes a posture of waiting, of listening. He brings his honest, angry, confused questions to God, and then he waits for God to speak. He doesn't get an immediate, perfect explanation that ties up all the loose ends. What he gets is a promise: "The righteous will live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). He gets a reminder that God is sovereign, that His timing and methods are not ours, but that ultimately, His justice will prevail.

And here’s the incredible result of Habakkuk’s wrestling. After all his complaints, his confusion, his challenges, he concludes his book with one of the most profound statements of faith in the Bible (Chapter 3, verses 17-18):
> "Though the fig tree does not bud
> and there are no grapes on the vines,
> though the olive crop fails
> and the fields produce no food,
> though there are no sheep in the pen
> and no cattle in the stalls,
> yet I will rejoice in the Lord,
> I will be joyful in God my Savior."

He didn't get all his questions answered. He didn't fully understand God's plan. But through his honest wrestling, his faith didn't evaporate. It deepened. He moved from understanding to *trusting*. He declared that even if everything around him fell apart, even if he didn't see God acting in the way he expected, he would still find his joy and salvation in God.

That, right there, is the power of honest questions. They don't destroy faith; they can actually make it stronger, more resilient, and more deeply personal. When you ask tough questions, you're not trying to tear down your faith; you’re digging deeper foundations. You’re making sure that what you believe isn't just a surface-level conviction based on what you’ve been told, but a truth that you have personally explored, grappled with, and ultimately chosen to stand on.

Think about any deep relationship you have – with a parent, a best friend, a mentor. The strongest relationships aren't ones where you never disagree or never ask hard questions. They're the ones where you *can* ask those hard questions, where you can be truly vulnerable and honest, and the relationship not only survives but grows stronger because of it. It's the same with God. He's not fragile. He can handle your toughest questions, your anger, your confusion. He invites it.

So, how do we do this? How do we lean into doubt in a way that builds faith instead of tearing it down? It’s not about finding all the answers – some questions simply don't have easy ones, and that's okay. Faith isn't the absence of doubt; it's trusting God *through* the doubt. It's about learning to live with the tension, to hold uncertainty with a posture of hope and continued seeking.

Here’s a practical step for you to consider this week:

1.  **Identify one honest question.** What’s one doubt, one uncertainty, one "why" about faith that has been sitting in your mind, maybe even bothering you, that you’ve been afraid to voice or explore? Don't censor yourself. Just acknowledge it.
2.  **Find a safe person.** This could be a trusted parent, a youth leader, a pastor, or a mentor – someone who you know will listen without judgment, who won't just give you pat answers, but will journey with you in the question. Share that question with them. You don't need a solution; you just need to voice it.
3.  **Bring it to God.** Even if it’s just in your own thoughts, or by writing it down in a journal. Tell God your question, your confusion, your frustration, just like Habakkuk did. Don't be afraid to be honest. He can handle it. And then, like Habakkuk, take a posture of waiting and listening, even if the answer doesn't come immediately or in the way you expect.

Doubt is not the end of your faith journey; it can be the beginning of a deeper, more authentic one. It’s an invitation to lean in, to explore, to wrestle, and ultimately, to discover a faith that is truly your own. So go ahead, ask the tough questions. You might be surprised by what you find.

> “Look at the nations and be astounded! For I am going to do something in your days that you would not believe, even if you were told. I am raising up the Babylonians—that ruthless and impetuous people—who will sweep across the whole earth to seize dwelling places not their own.”

Basically, God says, "I hear you, Habakkuk. And I'm going to act. I'm going to use an even worse, more violent nation – the Babylonians – to punish your people."

You're silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves!" (Habakkuk 1:13). He's wrestling with God's character, God's justice, God's plan. He’s saying, "God, your solution seems worse than the problem!" This is raw, honest doubt.

But here’s the crucial part. Habakkuk doesn't just walk away. He doesn't throw up his hands and say, "Forget it, I'm out." Instead, he says this in Habakkuk 2:1:

> “I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what he will say to me, and what answer I will give to this complaint.”

He takes his doubts, he lays them out before God, and then he *waits*. He positions himself to listen. He doesn’t get a neat, full explanation right away, but he gets a promise: "The righteous will live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). He's told that God's plan, though mysterious and painful now, will ultimately bring justice.

And in the end, after all that wrestling, all that questioning, Habakkuk comes to a place of profound faith, even *before* seeing the answers. Listen to his final prayer in chapter 3, verses 17-19:

> “Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior. It's like the difference between being given a house and building one yourself. The one you built, you know every beam, every nail, every creak. It's solid because you put in the work. When you wrestle with doubts, you're putting in the work to make your faith your own.

2.  **It leads to deeper understanding.** Sometimes the easy answers are shallow. When you push past them, you discover layers of truth you never knew existed. You might find new perspectives, new insights into God's character, new ways of reading scripture. You might realize God is bigger, more complex, and more loving than you ever imagined.

3.  **It builds resilience.** A faith that has wrestled with doubt and come through the other side is a strong faith. It's not easily shaken by new challenges or hard times because it's already faced some of its toughest questions. It knows how to lean into uncertainty. It knows God is still there, even when things don't make sense.

4.  **It fosters authenticity.** Trying to pretend you have it all figured out, or that you never struggle, is exhausting and inauthentic. Being honest about your doubts makes you real, relatable, and allows others to be real with you too. It creates a space for true community, where you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not.

God isn't looking for robots who just nod and agree. He's looking for people who are willing to engage with Him, even when it's messy, even when it's hard. He's big enough for your questions, your anger, your confusion. Doubt isn't the enemy of faith; often, it's the pathway to a more profound faith.

So, if you're sitting here today and you've got questions, if you've got doubts – welcome to the club. You're in good company. You're not failing. You're growing. You're following in the footsteps of prophets like Habakkuk, and countless others throughout history who have dared to wrestle with the big questions.

My challenge for you today, my practical next step, is this:

First, acknowledge it. What's one question, one doubt, one "I don't get this about God or faith" thought that's been quietly sitting in the back of your mind? Maybe you've been afraid to even let yourself think it, let alone say it out loud. Just identify it.

Second, do something with it. Don't just let it fester. You have a couple of options:

*   **Option A: Journal it.** Find a quiet moment this week. Write down that question, that doubt, those feelings, just like Habakkuk did. Write it as a letter to God. Be brutally honest. You don't need to censor yourself. Just get it out. Sometimes putting words to our doubts is the first step to processing them.
*   **Option B: Talk it out.** Find one trusted adult – a parent, a youth leader, a mentor, a pastor – someone you feel safe with. Tell them, "Hey, I've been wrestling with this question..." You don't need them to have all the answers. Sometimes just saying it out loud to another person, and having them listen without judgment, is incredibly powerful. And who knows, they might have wrestled with the exact same thing and can share their own journey.

Remember, God isn't fragile. Your faith isn't fragile. It's okay to ask, it's okay to wrestle. In fact, it's often in that wrestling that we find a deeper, truer, more resilient faith than we ever thought possible.

Don't be afraid of your doubts. They might just be God's invitation to go deeper.

**Title:** The Ghost in the Room
**Audience:** High School Youth Group (Ages 14–18)
**Tone:** Honest, conversational, warm

***

I want to start tonight by talking about a specific feeling. I’m guessing almost everyone in this room has felt it, but almost no one talks about it.

It happens during worship, or maybe during a small group discussion. Maybe it happens when you’re scrolling through Instagram and you see a post about how "God is good all the time," or you hear a story about a miraculous answer to prayer. Everyone around you is nodding. Everyone seems totally locked in. They have their hands raised, or they’re saying "Amen," and they look so... sure.

And you’re standing there, and you feel a tightening in your chest. Because you’re not sure.

Actually, maybe you’re thinking, *Really? Because that doesn't make sense to me.* Or maybe you’re thinking, *If God is so good, why is my family falling apart?* Or simply, *Is anyone else actually listening to this, or are we all just following a script?*

And then the second feeling hits: Panic. You think, *I’m in the wrong place. If I tell anyone what I’m actually thinking, I’m going to be the outcast. I’m the only one faking it.*

So, you put on the mask. You nod when you’re supposed to nod. You sing the lyrics even if they feel like ashes in your mouth. You bury the question deep down in the basement of your brain and lock the door.

I want to start tonight by telling you something that might surprise you coming from a stage like this: That feeling? That uncertainty? It doesn't mean you’re a bad Christian. It doesn't mean you’re failing.

It means you’re waking up.

We need to talk about doubt. Not as an enemy to be destroyed, but as a guest that shows up in the life of almost everyone who takes God seriously.

**The Myth of Certainty**

Somewhere along the line, a lot of us picked up a bad definition of the word "faith." We started thinking that Faith equals Certainty. We think that having faith means being 100% convinced, 100% of the time, with zero questions and zero hesitation.

If Faith = Certainty, then Doubt = Sin.

If that’s the equation, then the moment you have a hard question about science and the Bible, or the moment you wonder why God allows suffering, you feel like you’ve lost your faith. You feel like the floor is dropping out from under you.

But here is the honest truth: You are at an age where your brain is literally rewiring itself. You are moving from a child’s view of the world to an adult’s view. When you were six, you believed things because your parents told you they were true. That’s good; that’s how kids survive.

But now? You’re teenagers. You are biologically designed to question authority, to test boundaries, and to figure out what is true for *you*, not just for your parents. Why would your spiritual life be exempt from that?

If you never doubt, you never really own your faith. You’re just renting it from your parents or your youth pastor. Doubt is often the growing pain of a faith that is trying to become your own.

**The Patron Saint of "I Need Proof"**

I want to look at a guy in the Bible who gets a really bad rap. You know him. His nickname is literally an insult. We call him "Doubting Thomas."

Here’s the scene: It’s the days after Jesus has died. The disciples are terrified. They are hiding in a locked room because they think the people who killed Jesus are coming for them next. Their entire world has collapsed. The man they thought was the Messiah was executed.

Then, Jesus shows up. He walks through the walls, he eats with them, he shows them he’s alive. It’s the greatest moment in history.

But Thomas wasn't there. We don't know where he was—maybe getting food, maybe just taking a walk to clear his head because he was grieving. When he gets back, the other disciples are losing their minds with joy. They say, "We have seen the Lord!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s shoes. He has watched his best friend die. He is heartbroken. And now his friends are telling him something impossible.

Thomas doesn't say, "Oh, cool, sounds great."

He says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

We usually read that as Thomas being stubborn or lacking faith. But I see something else. I see a guy who is tired of getting his hopes up. I see a guy who refuses to settle for a rumor. He wants the truth. He’s basically saying, *I’m not going to pretend. This matters too much to me to fake it. I need to know it’s real.*

A week later, Jesus shows up again. Thomas is there this time.

Now, if doubt was a sin, if doubt made God angry, this is the part where Jesus should have blasted him. Jesus should have said, "Thomas, how dare you? Everyone else believed. Why are you so difficult? Get out."

Jesus doesn't do that.

He walks right up to Thomas. He holds out his hands. And he says, "Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."

Jesus doesn't shame Thomas for his questions. He meets Thomas inside of them. He offers Thomas his wounds.

This is crucial. The Bible is not a book about people who were always sure. It’s a book about people who wrestled with God.
*   David wrote the Psalms, and half of them are just him screaming, "God, where are you? Why have you forgotten me?"
*   Job lost everything and spent 30 chapters demanding an explanation from God.
*   Even Jesus, on the cross, cried out, "My God, why have you forsaken me?"

If Jesus is allowed to ask "Why," you are allowed to ask it too.

**The Danger of Pat Answers**

One of the reasons we struggle with doubt is that when we ask hard questions, well-meaning people sometimes give us terrible answers.

Maybe you’ve asked, "Why did my friend get cancer?" and someone said, "Well, God just needed another angel." (Which, by the way, is not bad theology, it’s just not in the Bible).
Or you ask about a contradiction in Scripture, and someone says, "You just need to pray more."

These are what we call "pat answers." They are band-aids over bullet holes. They are designed to shut down the conversation because the other person is uncomfortable with your doubt.

When we settle for clichés, our faith becomes fragile. It becomes like a glass ornament—it looks pretty, but if you drop it, it shatters.

We want a faith that is like a muscle. How does a muscle grow? You have to tear it. You put it under tension. You stress it. And when it heals, it grows back stronger.

Honest questions are the tension that makes faith strong.

**A Vision for Wrestling**

So, what do we do with our doubt? If we don't suppress it, do we just walk away?

There is a middle ground. It’s called *wrestling*.

In the Old Testament, there’s a story about Jacob literally wrestling with God all night long. He’s exhausted, he’s limping, he’s sweating. But he refuses to let go until God blesses him.

That is what a mature faith looks like. It’s not standing politely with your hands folded. It’s holding on to God and saying, *I don't understand this. This hurts. This doesn't make sense. But I’m staying in the room with You until we work this out.*

It is okay to deconstruct things. It is okay to take apart the things you were taught in Sunday School and look at them closely.
*   Is this actually what the Bible says, or is it just what my culture says?
*   Is God actually angry, or were my parents just angry?
*   Is science actually the enemy, or is it just discovering how God made the world?

When you ask these questions, you aren't destroying your faith. You are renovating it. You are stripping the wallpaper, tearing up the carpet, and checking the foundation. It’s messy. It looks like a disaster zone for a while. But eventually, you build something that you can actually live in. Something that can weather a storm.

The opposite of faith isn't doubt. The opposite of faith is *certainty*.

If you have proof, you don't need faith. I don't need "faith" that my chair will hold me up; I have evidence. Faith is reserved for the things we cannot fully see, the things we trust with our hearts even when our heads are still catching up.

**The Safe Place**

I want to close with this.

I know that admitting you have doubts is scary. You’re afraid that if you pull on the thread, the whole sweater will unravel. You’re afraid that if you ask "Is this real?" the answer might be "No."

But God is not intimidated by your questions. He is big enough to handle your anger, your confusion, and your skepticism. He handled Thomas. He handled David. He can handle you.

In fact, God would rather have your honest shouting than your polite, fake silence. He wants a relationship with *you*, not a relationship with a mask you’re wearing.

**A Practical Step**

So, I’m not going to end this talk by telling you to "just believe." I’m not going to tell you to stop doubting.

I’m going to give you a challenge.

Tonight, or maybe tomorrow morning, I want you to identify your "3:00 AM Question." You know the one. It’s the question that bothers you when everything is quiet. The one that makes you feel like a fake.

Maybe it’s about hell. Maybe it’s about LGBTQ+ issues. Maybe it’s about why God seems silent.

I want you to write it down. Actually put it on paper or in the notes app on your phone.

And then, I want you to do two things with it.

1.  **Bring it to God.** Literally pray: "God, I don't think I agree with you on this," or "God, I don't know if you’re there." That is a valid prayer. It’s an honest prayer.
2.  **Tell one safe person.** Do not keep it in the dark. Shame grows in the dark; it dies in the light. Find a leader here, a parent, or a friend who you respect—someone who won’t just give you a cliché—and say, "I’m having a hard time with this part of my faith."

You don't have to solve it today. You don't have to fix it by next week. You just have to be honest about it.

Let’s be a community where it’s safe to say "I don't know." Because it is usually in the "I don't know" that God finally has room to speak.

Let’s pray.

**Title:** The Elephant in the Sanctuary
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, vulnerable, honest.

***

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here tonight.

I want to start by describing a scenario. I want you to picture a typical Sunday morning or a Wednesday night youth service. The band is playing, and it’s a song everyone knows. The lights are dim, the volume is up, and the atmosphere feels electric.

You look to your left, and your friend has their eyes closed, hands raised, singing with their whole chest. You look to your right, and someone else is wiping away a tear, clearly having a profound spiritual moment.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you’re singing the words, but inside, you feel… nothing. Or maybe not nothing. Maybe you feel a sudden, cold spike of panic. You look at the lyrics on the screen—words about how God is good, how He’s always there, how He answers prayer—and a voice in the back of your head whispers: *Is that actually true?*

Or maybe the voice asks: *Do I even believe this? Or am I just singing because everyone else is singing?*

And then the guilt hits. You feel like a fraud. You feel like an imposter. You think, *If anyone here knew what was going on in my head right now, they wouldn’t let me back in the building.* So, you clap your hands, you smile, and you push that question down into the basement of your brain, lock the door, and hope it never comes back.

If that sounds familiar to you, I want you to know something very important tonight: You are not broken. You are not a "bad Christian." And you are definitely not alone.

Tonight, we’re going to talk about the elephant in the room. We’re going to talk about doubt.

### The Myth of Certainty

There is a weird pressure in religious circles, especially when you’re growing up, to have absolute certainty about everything all the time. We treat faith like it’s a house of cards—if you pull out one card, if you question one thing, the whole thing collapses. So we get terrified of questions.

But here is the reality: You are between the ages of 14 and 18. Your brain is changing faster than it ever will again. You are learning biology, physics, history, and philosophy. You are seeing tragedy in the news. You are experiencing heartbreak and loss for the first time. You are figuring out who you are.

It would be actually weird if your faith *didn't* have questions.

Think about it like this. When you were five years old, you probably wore shoes with Velcro straps. They were great. They fit you perfectly. But if you tried to squeeze your feet into those same Velcro shoes today, it would be painful. You wouldn’t be able to walk.

It’s the growing pains of moving from a "parent’s faith"—where you believe because Mom and Dad said so—to a faith that is actually yours. You are trading in the Velcro shoes for hiking boots that can actually handle the rough terrain of real life.

Jesus is out there doing ministry, healing people, and preaching, but He isn’t coming to break John out of jail.

*   "Why doesn't God answer my prayer?" implies you desire a connection with the Divine.

Put the question on the table. No filters.

**Title:** The Elephant in the Sanctuary
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, vulnerable, honest.

***

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here tonight.

I want to start by describing a scenario. I want you to picture a typical Sunday morning or a Wednesday night youth service. The band is playing, and it’s a song everyone knows. The lights are dim, the volume is up, and the atmosphere feels electric.

You look to your left, and your friend has their eyes closed, hands raised, singing with their whole chest. You look to your right, and someone else is wiping away a tear, clearly having a profound spiritual moment.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you’re singing the words, but inside, you feel… nothing. Or maybe not nothing. Maybe you feel a sudden, cold spike of panic. You look at the lyrics on the screen—words about how God is good, how He’s always there, how He answers prayer—and a voice in the back of your head whispers: *Is that actually true?*

Or maybe the voice asks: *Do I even believe this? Or am I just singing because everyone else is singing?*

And then the guilt hits. You feel like a fraud. You feel like an imposter. You think, *If anyone here knew what was going on in my head right now, they wouldn’t let me back in the building.* So, you clap your hands, you smile, and you push that question down into the basement of your brain, lock the door, and hope it never comes back.

If that sounds familiar to you, I want you to know something very important tonight: You are not broken. You are not a "bad Christian." And you are definitely not alone.

Tonight, we’re going to talk about the elephant in the room. We’re going to talk about doubt.

### The Myth of Certainty

There is a weird pressure in religious circles, especially when you’re growing up, to have absolute certainty about everything all the time. We treat faith like it’s a house of cards—if you pull out one card, if you question one thing, the whole thing collapses. So we get terrified of questions.

But here is the reality: You are between the ages of 14 and 18. Your brain is changing faster than it ever will again. You are learning biology, physics, history, and philosophy. You are seeing tragedy in the news. You are experiencing heartbreak and loss for the first time.

Maybe your doubt doesn't come from a worship service. Maybe it came from a biology class, or a conversation with a friend who belongs to a different religion, or a philosophy video on YouTube that made a point you couldn't answer. Maybe you looked at the world and thought, *If God is real, why is everything so messy?*

It would be weird if your faith *didn't* have questions.

Think about it like this. When you were five years old, you probably wore shoes with Velcro straps. They were great. They fit you perfectly. But if you tried to squeeze your feet into those same Velcro shoes today, it would be painful. You wouldn’t be able to walk.

Doubt is often just the feeling of your soul outgrowing your childhood understanding of God. It’s not a sign that you’re losing your faith; it’s a sign that your faith is trying to grow up. It’s the growing pains of moving from a "parent’s faith"—where you believe because Mom and Dad said so—to a faith that is actually yours.

### The Prisoner’s Question

I want to look at a story in the Bible that I think is one of the most important stories for anyone wrestling with doubt.

Usually, when people talk about doubt, they talk about "Doubting Thomas." Poor Thomas gets a bad rap. But I want to talk about someone else. I want to talk about John the Baptist.

Now, John was the ultimate hype man. He was the guy. He was Jesus’ cousin. He spent his life in the desert preparing the way for the Messiah. He baptized Jesus in the Jordan River. He saw the heavens open. He saw the Spirit descend like a dove. He heard the voice of God say, "This is my Son."

John had a front-row seat to something unmistakable. If anyone had proof, if anyone had "certainty," it was John.

But some time later, John isn't by the river anymore. He’s in a dungeon. He’s been arrested by King Herod, and he’s sitting in a cold, dark cell, awaiting execution. And Jesus? Jesus is out there doing ministry, but He isn’t coming to break John out of jail.

John is sitting in the dark, facing death, and the doubt creeps in. He calls two of his disciples and sends them to Jesus with a question. And the question is heartbreaking. He asks:

*"Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?"*

Do you feel the weight of that? This is the guy who introduced Jesus to the world! And now, when life has gone sideways, when the walls are closing in, he’s asking, *Did I get it wrong? Did I waste my life? Are you actually real?*

Now, watch how Jesus responds. This is crucial.

Jesus doesn't get angry. He doesn't say, "How dare you, John! After everything you saw? You of little faith!" He doesn't send a message back saying, "Just pray more, John," or "Stop being so negative."

Jesus says to the messengers: *"Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised..."*

Jesus meets John’s doubt with evidence. He meets John’s honest question with an honest answer. But then, Jesus adds one more thing. It’s a sentence we often skip, but it’s vital. He says:

*"Blessed is anyone who does not stumble on account of me."*

That isn't a threat. It’s an acknowledgment. Jesus is saying, *"John, I know this isn't what you expected. I know it’s hard to trust me when you’re sitting in a cell. I know you’re stumbling. But hang on."*

He doesn't shame him for asking. In fact, right after the messengers leave, Jesus turns to the crowd and calls John the greatest man who ever lived. He compliments John *in the middle of John’s doubt.*

That tells me that God is not intimidated by your questions. He is not fragile. If John the Baptist—the guy who saw the dove descend—can have days where he wonders if it’s all true, then you have permission to wonder too.

### The Danger of Silent Doubt

I need to be honest with you for a second. I’m not standing up here as someone who has it all figured out.

There are nights I pray and feel absolutely nothing but the ceiling fan spinning above me. There was a season a few years ago where I was reading the Old Testament, reading about God commanding wars and violence, and I thought, *I don't know what to do with this. This doesn't look like the Jesus I know.*

It scared me. I felt like if I pulled that thread, the whole sweater would unravel.

But here is what I learned: The most dangerous thing about doubt isn't the doubt itself. It’s the silence.

When we bury our questions because we’re afraid of being judged, those questions don’t die. They rot. They turn into cynicism. If you feel like you can’t ask "Why does God allow suffering?" or "Why does the Bible say this?" inside the church, you will eventually walk out the door to find answers somewhere else.

Faith is not the absence of doubt. Faith is courage in the face of doubt.

God wants a relationship with *you*, not a relationship with a fake version of you who pretends to agree with everything.

There is a long tradition in our faith called "lament." You see it in the Psalms. David, a man after God’s own heart, screams at God. He asks, "Where are you?" He says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

If you are angry at God, tell Him. If you are bored by God, tell Him. If you aren't sure He’s there, tell Him. That honesty is actually a form of prayer. It’s better to yell at God than to ignore Him. Yelling requires you to believe there’s someone on the other end listening.

### Deconstruction vs. Renovation

You might have heard the word "deconstruction" on TikTok or Instagram. It’s a buzzword right now for taking apart your faith.

I like to think of it more like a home renovation. Sometimes, you find out that there is mold in the drywall of your faith. Maybe you grew up with a view of God that was angry and mean, or a view of science that was fearful.

When you find that mold, you have to tear that wall down. That’s scary. It makes a mess. It looks like destruction.

But here is the thing: You aren’t tearing the house down just to live in the rubble. You’re tearing out the rot so you can build something stronger, something that can actually hold the weight of your adult life.

Now, I’m not saying your questions have easy answers. Some of them don't. You might tear down a wall and leave that space open for a long time. But I want you to notice that the fact you're asking these questions means something is alive in you. Apathy—not caring at all—is the enemy of faith. Struggle is just part of the journey.

### A Practical Step

I promised I wouldn't give you a pat answer. I’m not going to tell you that if you read three chapters of Romans tonight, your doubts will vanish. They might not. You might carry some questions for years.

But I have found that Jesus is worth sticking with, even in the mystery.

So, here is your challenge. It’s not a homework assignment, just a way to practice being honest.

**Step 1: The "One Percent More Honest" Prayer.**

Tonight, or tomorrow morning, find a quiet space. Don't try to pray the "right" way. Don't use the fancy words you hear pastors use.

I want you to tell God exactly what is on your mind, but be 1% more honest than you usually dare to be.

If you’re thinking, "This feels like talking to the ceiling," say: *"God, I feel like I’m talking to the ceiling right now."*
If you’re thinking, "I’m mad that my grandmother is sick," say: *"I’m furious that she’s sick and I don't understand why you aren't fixing it."*

Put the question on the table. And then, don't run away immediately. Sit in the silence for just two minutes.

**Step 2: Break the Silence.**

This week, find one person. Just one. A friend, a parent, a small group leader—someone you trust. And say the thing out loud.

"I'm having a hard time believing X."
"I don't understand why Y happened."

You might be surprised. They might not have the answer, but they might look at you and say, "Yeah. Me too."

You are safe to ask. You are safe to wonder. You are safe to struggle.

I can't promise the dark lifts on your schedule. But I can tell you that asking honest questions in the dark is not the same as being abandoned in it. God is big enough for your doubt, and He is right there in the questions with you.

Thanks, guys.

A strong relationship is one where you can say, "Hey, what you did hurt me," or "I don't understand why we’re doing this," and you stick around to work through it together.

God wants a relationship with *you*, not a relationship with a fake version of you who pretends to agree with everything.

There is a long tradition in our faith called "lament." You see it in the Psalms. David, a man after God’s own heart, screams at God. He asks, "Where are you?" He says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" He doesn't hold back.

If you are angry at God, tell Him. If you are bored by God, tell Him. If you aren't sure He’s there, tell Him. That honesty is actually a form of prayer. It’s better to yell at God than to ignore Him. Yelling requires you to believe there’s someone on the other end listening. The opposite of faith isn't doubt; the opposite of faith is apathy—not caring enough to even ask.

### Deconstruction vs. Demolition

You might have heard the word "deconstruction" on TikTok or Instagram. It’s a buzzword right now for taking apart your faith. It can feel really scary, like everything is falling apart.

I like to think of it more like a home renovation. Sometimes, you find out that there is mold in the drywall of your faith. Maybe you grew up with a view of God that was angry and mean, or a view of science that was fearful, or a belief that if you prayed the right words, bad things would never happen to you.

When you find that mold, you have to tear that wall down. That’s scary. It looks like destruction. It makes a mess. But you aren’t tearing the house down just to live in the rubble. You’re tearing out the rot so you can build something stronger, something that can actually hold the weight of your adult life.

Questions are the tools we use to do that renovation.

*   "Why is there evil in the world?" implies you believe there is such a thing as 'good' to compare it to.
*   "Why doesn't God answer my prayer?" implies you desire a connection with the Divine.

Your questions are actually proof that you care. Struggle is just part of the journey.

### A Practical Step

I promised I wouldn't give you a pat answer. I’m not going to tell you that if you read three chapters of Romans tonight, your doubts will vanish. They might not. You might carry some questions for years.

There are things in the Bible I still wrestle with. There are times I look at the news and think, *God, are you seeing this?*

But I have found that Jesus is worth sticking with, even in the mystery. I have found that the hiking boots are worth breaking in.

So, here is your challenge. It’s not a homework assignment, just a way to practice being honest.

I want you to try the **"One Percent More Honest"** prayer.

Tonight, or tomorrow morning, find a quiet space. Grab your phone and open the notes app, or grab a physical piece of paper.

Before you pray, I want you to write down the one question you are most afraid to ask God. The one that makes you feel like a "bad Christian."

Get it out of your head and onto the screen or the paper.

Then, pray it. Don't use the fancy words you hear pastors use. Tell God exactly what is on your mind, but be 1% more honest than you usually dare to be.

If you’re thinking, "This feels like talking to the ceiling," say: *"God, I feel like I’m talking to the ceiling right now."*
If you’re thinking, "I’m mad that my grandmother is sick," say: *"I’m furious that she’s sick and I don't understand why you aren't fixing it."*

Put the question on the table.

And then, here is the second part: **Don't run away immediately.**

Sit in the silence for just two minutes. We live in a noisy world. We are terrified of silence. But often, the reassurance doesn't come in a lightning bolt or a booming voice. It comes in a slow, quiet sense of presence. It comes in the realization that you threw your hardest questions at God, and He didn't strike you down. The floor didn't open up. He’s still there. He can handle it.

You are safe to ask. You are safe to wonder. You are safe to struggle.

God is big enough for your doubt. And He loves you way too much to let you stay in the dark forever.

Thanks, guys.

**Title:** The Elephant in the Sanctuary
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, vulnerable, honest.

***

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here tonight.

I want to start by describing a scenario. I want you to picture a typical Sunday morning or maybe a Wednesday night service like this one. The band is playing, it’s a song everyone knows, and the volume is up.

You look to your left, and your friend has their eyes closed, hands raised, singing with their whole chest. You look to your right, and someone else is wiping away a tear, clearly having a profound spiritual moment. It looks intense. It looks emotional.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you’re singing the words, but inside, you feel… nothing. Or maybe not nothing. Maybe you feel a sudden, cold spike of panic. You look at the lyrics on the screen—words about how God is good, how He’s always near, how He answers prayer—and a voice in the back of your head whispers: *Is that actually true?*

Or maybe the voice asks: *Do I even believe this? Or am I just singing because everyone else is singing?*

And then the guilt hits. You feel like a fraud. You feel like an imposter. You think, *If anyone here knew what was going on in my head right now, they wouldn’t let me back in the building.* So, you clap your hands, you smile, and you push that question down into the basement of your brain, lock the door, and hope it never comes back.

If that sounds familiar to you, I want you to know something very important tonight: You are not broken. You are not a "bad Christian." And you are definitely not alone.

Tonight, we’re going to talk about the elephant in the room. We’re going to talk about doubt.

### The Myth of Certainty

There is a weird pressure in religious circles, especially when you’re growing up, to have absolute certainty about everything all the time. We treat faith like it’s a Jenga tower—if you pull out one block, if you question one thing, the whole thing collapses. So we get terrified of questions. We think that to be faithful means never wondering "what if."

But here is the reality: You are between the ages of 14 and 18. Your brain is changing faster than it ever will again. You are learning biology, physics, history, and philosophy. You are seeing tragedy in the news. You are experiencing heartbreak and loss for the first time. You are figuring out who you actally are.

It would be weird if your faith *didn't* have questions.

Think about it like this. When you were five years old, you probably wore shoes with Velcro straps. They were great. They fit you perfectly. They were easy to put on. But if you tried to squeeze your feet into those same Velcro shoes today, it would be painful. You wouldn’t be able to walk. You’d be crippled.

Doubt is often just the feeling of your soul outgrowing your childhood understanding of God. It’s not necessarily a sign that you’re losing your faith; it’s a sign that your faith is trying to grow up. It’s the growing pains of moving from an "inherited faith"—where you believe because your parents or your culture said so—to a faith that is actually yours.

And let’s be honest: sometimes that transition isn't just growing pains. sometimes it feels like an amputation. But we have to go through it, or we’re stuck wearing shoes that don’t fit.

### The Prisoner’s Question

I want to look at a story in the Bible that I think is one of the most important stories for anyone wrestling with doubt.

Usually, when people talk about doubt, they talk about "Doubting Thomas." Poor Thomas gets a bad rap. But I want to talk about someone else. I want to talk about John the Baptist.

Now, John was the forerunner. He was the guy who spent his life in the desert preparing the way for the Messiah. He baptized Jesus in the Jordan River. He saw the heavens open. He saw the Spirit descend like a dove. He heard the voice of God say, "This is my Son."

If anyone had proof, if anyone had "certainty," it was John. He saw the special effects with his own eyes. He knew exactly who Jesus was.

But fast forward a few years. John isn't by the river anymore. He’s in a dungeon. He’s been arrested by King Herod, and he’s sitting in a cold, dark cell, awaiting execution. And Jesus? Jesus is out there doing ministry, healing people, and preaching. But here is the hard truth: Jesus isn’t coming to break John out of jail.

John is sitting in the dark, facing death, and the doubt creeps in. The walls are closing in, and the silence of God is deafening. So, he calls two of his disciples and sends them to Jesus with a question. And the question is heartbreaking. He asks:

*"Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?"*

Do you feel the weight of that? This is the man who introduced Jesus to the world! And now, when life has gone sideways, when he’s staring at the end of his life in a damp cell, he’s asking, *Did I get it wrong? Did I waste my life? Are you actually real?*

Now, watch how Jesus responds. This is crucial.

Jesus doesn't get angry. He doesn't say, "How dare you, John! After everything you saw? You of little faith!" He doesn't send a message back saying, "Just pray more, John," or "Stop being so negative."

Jesus says to the messengers: *"Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised..."*

Jesus meets John’s doubt with evidence. He meets John’s honest question with a gentle, honest answer. He points to the work He is doing.

But here is the part we often miss. Right after the messengers leave to take this answer back to the prison, Jesus turns to the crowd. He knows John is wavering. He knows John is struggling. And in that moment, Jesus calls John the greatest person ever born.

He compliments John’s character *in the middle of John’s doubt.*

That tells me that God is not intimidated by your questions. He is not fragile. He doesn't need you to pretend you’re okay when you’re not.

And there is a heavy footnote to this story. John never gets out of prison. He is executed there. He dies without ever seeing Jesus again in this life. He dies with the answer Jesus sent, but without the rescue he probably wanted.

That is a hard pill to swallow, but it’s also deeply comforting. It means you can have massive questions, you can face situations that don't make sense and don't get fixed, and you can still be called "great" by God. Your doubt doesn't disqualify you.

### The Danger of Silent Doubt

The most dangerous thing about doubt isn't the doubt itself. It’s the silence.

When we bury our questions because we’re afraid of being judged, those questions don’t die. They rot. They turn into cynicism. If you feel like you can’t ask "Why does God allow suffering?" or "Why does the Bible say this?" inside the church, you will eventually walk out the door to find answers somewhere else.

I want to offer you a different vision of what faith looks like.

Faith is not the absence of doubt. Faith is courage in the face of doubt.

Think about a close friendship or a relationship. If two people never, ever argue, never disagree, and never ask hard questions of each other, that’s not a strong relationship. That’s a polite distance. A strong relationship is one where you can say, "Hey, what you did hurt me," or "I don't understand why we’re doing this," and you stay in the room to work through it.

God wants a relationship with *you*, not a relationship with a fake version of you who pretends to agree with everything.

There is a long tradition in our faith called "lament." We see it all over the Psalms. We like the Psalms that say "The Lord is my Shepherd," but we skip the ones that sound like Psalm 77. In that chapter, the writer is up all night, too troubled to speak, and he asks:

*"Will the Lord reject forever? Will he never show his favor again? Has his unfailing love vanished forever? Has his promise failed for all time?"*

These aren't polite questions. This is a guy screaming at the ceiling.

But here’s the key: It’s in the Bible. God included the accusations against Him in His own book.

If you are angry at God, tell Him. If you are bored by God, tell Him. If you aren't sure He’s there, tell Him. That honesty is actually a form of prayer. It’s better to yell at God than to ignore Him. Yelling requires you to believe, even just a tiny bit, that there’s someone on the other end listening.

### Deconstruction vs. Demolition

You might have heard the word "deconstruction" on TikTok or Instagram. It’s a buzzword right now for taking apart your faith.

I like to think of it more like a home renovation. Sometimes, you find out that there is mold in the drywall of your faith. Maybe you grew up with a view of God that was angry and mean, or a view of science that was fearful, or a specific doctrine that just doesn't make sense to you anymore.

When you find that mold, you have to tear that wall down. That’s scary. It looks like destruction. It makes a mess.

And I won’t lie to you—sometimes you tear down the drywall and realize the foundation is cracked, too. Sometimes the renovation turns into a demolition. Sometimes you realize the house you grew up in just isn't safe to live in anymore, and you have to move. That is terrifying.

But you aren’t tearing the house down just to live in the rubble. You’re tearing out the rot so you can build something true. Something that can actually hold the weight of your adult life.

Questions are the tools we use to do that renovation.

*   "Why is there evil in the world?" implies you believe there is such a thing as 'good' to compare it to.
*   "Why doesn't God answer my prayer?" implies you desire a connection with the Divine.

Your questions are actually proof that you care. Apathy—not caring at all—is the enemy of faith. Struggle is just part of the journey.

### A Practical Step

I promised I wouldn't give you a pat answer. I’m not going to tell you that if you read three chapters of Romans tonight, your doubts will vanish. They might not. You might carry some questions for years. John the Baptist carried his until the end.

There are things in the Bible I still wrestle with. There are times I look at the news and think, *God, are you seeing this?*

But I have found that Jesus is worth sticking with, even in the mystery.

So, here is your challenge. It’s not a homework assignment, just a way to practice being honest.

I want you to try the **"One Percent More Honest"** prayer.

Tonight, or tomorrow morning, find a quiet space. Don't try to pray the "right" way. Don't use the fancy words you hear pastors use.

I want you to tell God exactly what is on your mind, but be 1% more honest than you usually dare to be.

If you’re thinking, "This feels like talking to the ceiling," say: *"God, I feel like I’m talking to the ceiling right now."*
If you’re thinking, "I’m mad that my grandmother is sick," say: *"I’m furious that she’s sick and I don't understand why you aren't fixing it."*

Put the question on the table.

And then, here is the second part: **Don't run away immediately.**

Sit in the silence for just two minutes. We live in a noisy world. We are terrified of silence.

I need to warn you: the clouds probably won't part. You might not feel a warm fuzzy presence. You might just feel like you're sitting in a quiet room. And that is okay.

The point isn't to force a feeling. The point is that you threw your hardest questions at God, and He didn't strike you down. You showed up authentically. You stopped pretending.

That silence isn't empty; it's a space where you can finally stop performing.

You are safe to ask. You are safe to wonder. You are safe to struggle.

God is big enough for your doubt. And He loves you—the real you, questions and all—way too much to let you stay in the dark forever.

Thanks, guys.

**Title:** The Elephant in the Sanctuary
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, honest, safe.

***

(Pause. Look around the room. Make eye contact, not in a creepy way, but in a way that says, *I see you.*)

I want to start tonight by describing a feeling that I’m guessing some of you know very well, but that almost none of us ever talk about out loud.

Here is the scenario: You are standing in the middle of a church service. Maybe it’s here, maybe it was at a summer camp, maybe it was a big conference. The music is swelling. The lights are dim. The person to your left has their eyes closed and their hands raised, tears streaming down their face. The person to your right is singing at the top of their lungs, looking like they are having the most spiritual moment of their life.

And you? You are standing there, looking at your shoes, and you feel… nothing.

Or maybe, it’s worse than nothing. Maybe you’re standing there and a thought creeps into your head that feels dangerous. A thought like: *Is this even real?* Or, *If God is so good, why is my life so messy?* Or simply, *I don’t think I believe this anymore.*

And immediately after that thought comes the panic. You look around at everyone else who seems so certain, so "on fire," and you come to the only conclusion that makes sense: *There is something wrong with me. I am a fake. I am an imposter. If they knew what was going on in my head, they’d ask me to leave.*

So, you sing the song. You nod your head during the sermon. You learn the language of faith, you learn when to say "Amen," but inside, you feel like you’re slowly drifting out to sea while everyone else is safe on the shore.

If that sounds familiar, I want you to take a deep breath. Because tonight, we are going to talk about the elephant in the room. We are going to talk about doubt.

And I want to start with a spoiler alert: **Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Doubt is often the growing pains of faith.**

See, when you were a kid, your world was very black and white. Your parents were superheroes who knew everything. Your teachers were always right. And God was the nice old man in the sky who made puppies and rainbows. That is a beautiful, necessary stage of life. It’s simple. It’s safe.

But you aren't kids anymore. You are teenagers. Your brains are literally rewiring themselves. You are waking up to the complexity of the world. You’re realizing that your parents are actually just people trying their best. You’re realizing that the world is full of injustice and pain. You’re learning algebra and chemistry and history.

You cannot navigate a complex, adult world with a simple, childhood faith. It doesn't fit anymore. It’s like trying to wear the shoes you wore in the third grade. They pinch. They hurt. They don’t work.

When you start to doubt, it doesn't mean you are losing your faith. It usually means your faith is trying to grow up. It means you are moving from a faith that you borrowed from your parents or your pastor, to a faith that is actually *yours*. But that transition is messy. It’s uncomfortable. And it usually starts with questions.

The problem is, we’ve created a culture where we think being a Christian means having zero questions. We think "faith" equals "certainty." But that’s not true. If you have absolute certainty, you don’t need faith. Faith is what happens in the gap between what we know and what we hope for.

I want to look at a guy in the Bible who gets a really bad rap. You know him. His name is Thomas.

History has given him a cruel nickname: "Doubting Thomas." We use him as a warning. *Don’t be like Thomas.* But I actually think Thomas is a hero. I think Thomas is the patron saint of honest questions.

Let’s look at the context. Jesus has been killed. The disciples are in hiding. They are traumatized, terrified, and grieving. Then, suddenly, people start saying Jesus is back. The other disciples tell Thomas, "We have seen the Lord!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s sandals. He watched his friend die. He is heartbroken. And now his friends are telling him something impossible.

Thomas doesn't fake it. He doesn't say, "Oh, cool, praise God," while secretly rolling his eyes. He respects the truth too much to pretend.

He says, famously: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."*

That is raw. That is aggressive. That is an ultimatum.

Now, here is the most important part of the story. A week later, Jesus shows up. Thomas is there.

Does Jesus look at Thomas and say, "How dare you? You terrible Christian. Get out. You didn't have enough faith"?

No.

Jesus walks right up to Thomas. He doesn't scold him for his questions. He answers them. He holds out his hands. He says, *"Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."*

Jesus wasn't intimidated by Thomas’s doubt. He didn't require Thomas to suppress his brain or his trauma in order to belong. Jesus met Thomas exactly where he was, questions and all.

In fact, notice that Thomas stayed in the room. Even when he didn't believe, he stayed with his community. And the community let him stay. They didn't kick him out for not being on the same page yet. That is what the church should be—a place where you can belong *before* you believe everything perfectly.

There is a difference, though, between doubt and cynicism.

Cynicism is when you ask a question looking for a fight. Cynicism is crossing your arms, leaning back, and deciding it’s all garbage before you even listen. Cynicism is lazy. It protects you from getting your hopes up.

Doubt is different. Doubt is wrestling. Doubt is leaning *in*. Doubt says, "I want to believe this is true, but I’m stuck on this part. God, if you’re real, you have to show me."

In the Old Testament, the name given to God’s people is *Israel*. Do you know what that word means? It doesn't mean "The People Who Always Agree." It doesn't mean "The People With All The Answers."

*Israel* means "He who wrestles with God."

That is your heritage. You are part of a thousands-year-old tradition of people who argued, wrestled, cried, screamed, and questioned God. Read the Psalms. Half of them are David shouting, "Where are you, God? Why have you forgotten me?"

If King David—the "man after God’s own heart"—could yell at God, you can too. God is big enough to handle your questions. He is not fragile. He is not sitting on his throne nervously biting his fingernails hoping you don't ask about evolution or suffering. He is the Truth, and if something is true, it can handle being questioned.

So, what does this look like for us? How do we actually do this?

First, we have to stop faking it.

When you bury your doubts, they don't die. They bury themselves alive. They rot. They turn into bitterness. If you ignore your questions because you're afraid of them, eventually the pressure will build up and your faith will explode.

Instead, I want to offer you a vision of what it looks like to let doubt do its work.

Imagine a forest. Sometimes, the underbrush gets too thick. It chokes out the light. So, nature has forest fires. They burn away the dead wood, the dry leaves, the stuff that isn't alive anymore. It looks scary. It looks destructive. But after the fire, the forest is healthier. The big, strong trees are still standing, and now there is room for new growth.

Doubt is a forest fire. It burns up the "dead wood" of your faith. Maybe it burns up the idea that God is a vending machine where you put in prayer and get out money. Maybe it burns up the idea that Christians are always perfect. Let that stuff burn. It wasn't true anyway.

What is left after the fire—the core of who Jesus is, his love, his resurrection—that is fireproof. And that is the faith that will last you for the rest of your life.

I am not saying this is easy. Sitting in the uncertainty is hard. It can feel lonely.

But I promise you, a faith that has been tested, a faith that has wrestled with the hard questions and come out the other side, is infinitely stronger than a faith that has never been challenged.

So, I’m not going to give you three easy steps to "fix" your doubt tonight. Because doubt isn't a sin to be fixed; it’s a journey to be walked.

Instead, I’m going to give you a challenge.

I want you to identify your "3 A.M. Question." You know the one. The one that keeps you up at night. The one you’re afraid to say out loud because you think it makes you a bad Christian.

Maybe it’s: *Why do bad things happen to good people?*
Maybe it’s: *Is the Bible really true?*
Maybe it’s: *Why don't I feel God like other people do?*

This week, I want you to write that question down. Get it out of your head and onto paper.

And then, I want you to do something brave. I want you to tell it to someone.

Not just anyone. Don't go to the person who always speaks in bumper-sticker slogans. Find a "Safe Person." Maybe it’s a leader here tonight. Maybe it’s a parent. Maybe it’s a mentor. Find someone who listens more than they talk.

Say to them: "I’m wrestling with this question. Can you help me carry it?"

You might be surprised to hear them say, "Me too. I’ve wondered that too."

God is not afraid of your honesty. In fact, honesty is the only thing he can work with. You can’t have a relationship with a fake version of yourself. God wants *you*—the real you, the confused you, the doubting you.

So bring your questions. Bring your skepticism. Bring your wounds. Just like Thomas did.

The doors are open. You are safe here.

Let’s pray.

*God, thank you that you are big enough for our questions. Thank you that we don’t have to pretend with you. For everyone in this room who feels like they are faking it, give them a sense of your peace. Help us to be brave enough to wrestle, and trust that you are holding on to us even when we have trouble holding on to you. Amen.*

*   Look at Job, who sat in the ashes of his life and demanded an explanation.

**Tone:** Conversational, honest, safe.

The person to your left has their eyes closed and their hands raised, tears streaming down their face. The person to your right is singing at the top of their lungs, looking like they are having the most spiritual moment of their life.

And you? You are standing there, looking at your shoes, and you feel… nothing.

Or maybe, it’s worse than nothing. Maybe you’re standing there and a thought creeps into your head that feels dangerous. A thought like: *Is this even real?* Or, *If God is so good, why is my life so messy?* Or simply, *I don’t think I believe this anymore.*

And immediately after that thought comes the panic. You look around at everyone else who seems so certain, so "on fire," and you come to the only conclusion that makes sense: *There is something wrong with me. I am a fake. I am an imposter. If they knew what was going on in my head, they’d ask me to leave.*

So, you sing the song. You nod your head during the sermon. You learn the language of faith, you learn when to say "Amen," but inside, you feel like you’re slowly drifting out to sea while everyone else is safe on the shore.

If that sounds familiar, I want you to take a deep breath. Because tonight, we are going to talk about the elephant in the room. We are going to talk about doubt.

And I want to start with a spoiler alert: **Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Doubt is often the growing pains of faith.**

See, when you were a kid, your world was very black and white. Your parents were superheroes who knew everything. Your teachers were always right. And God was the nice old man in the sky who made puppies and rainbows. That is a beautiful, necessary stage of life. It’s simple. It’s safe.

But you aren't kids anymore. You are teenagers. Your brains are literally rewiring themselves right now. That is a biological fact. It’s why you can feel on top of the world at 10:00 AM and absolutely hopeless by lunch. You are waking up to the complexity of the world. You’re realizing that your parents are actually just people trying their best. You’re realizing that the world is full of injustice and pain. You’re learning algebra and chemistry and history.

You cannot navigate a complex, adult world with a simple, childhood faith. It doesn't fit anymore. It’s like trying to wear the shoes you wore in the third grade. They pinch. They hurt. They don’t work.

When you start to doubt, it doesn't mean you are losing your faith. It usually means your faith is trying to grow up. It means you are moving from a faith that you borrowed from your parents or your pastor, to a faith that is actually *yours*. But that transition is messy. It’s uncomfortable. That is raw. That is aggressive. That is an ultimatum.

Now, here is the most important part of the story. A week later, Jesus shows up. Thomas is there.

Does Jesus look at Thomas and say, "How dare you? You terrible Christian. Get out. You didn't have enough faith"?

No.

Jesus walks right up to Thomas. He doesn't scold him for his questions. He answers them. He holds out his hands. He says, *"Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."*

Jesus wasn't intimidated by Thomas’s doubt. He didn't require Thomas to suppress his brain or his trauma in order to belong. Jesus met Thomas exactly where he was, questions and all.

The doors are open. You are safe here.

Let’s pray.

*God, thank you that you are big enough for our questions. Thank you that we don’t have to pretend with you. For everyone in this room who feels like they are faking it, give them a sense of your peace. Help us to be brave enough to wrestle, and trust that you are holding on to us even when we have trouble holding on to you. Amen.*

The problem is, we’ve created a culture where we think being a Christian means having zero questions. We think "faith" equals "certainty." But that’s not true. If you have absolute certainty, you don’t need faith. Faith is what happens in the gap between what we know and what we hope for.

I want to look at a guy in the Bible who gets a really bad rap. You know him. His name is Thomas.

History has given him a cruel nickname: "Doubting Thomas." We use him as a warning. *Don’t be like Thomas.* But I actually think Thomas is a hero. I think Thomas is the champion of honest questions.

Let’s look at the context. Jesus has been killed. The disciples are in hiding. They are traumatized, terrified, and grieving. Then, suddenly, people start saying Jesus is back. The other disciples tell Thomas, "We have seen the Lord!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s sandals. He watched his friend die. He is heartbroken. And now his friends are telling him something impossible.

Thomas doesn't fake it. He doesn't say, "Oh, cool, praise God," while secretly rolling his eyes. He respects the truth too much to pretend.

He says, famously: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."*

That is raw. That is aggressive. That is an ultimatum.

Now, I want to pause here, because there is a difference between what Thomas did and what we often see on the internet. There is a difference between doubt and cynicism.

Cynicism is when you ask a question looking for a fight. Cynicism is crossing your arms, leaning back, and deciding it’s all garbage before you even listen. Cynicism is lazy. It protects you from getting your hopes up.

Thomas wasn't being a cynic. He was wrestling. Doubt is leaning *in*. Doubt says, "I want to believe this is true, but I’m stuck on this part. God, if you’re real, you have to show me."

And here is the most important part of the story. A week later, Jesus shows up. Thomas is there.

Does Jesus look at Thomas and say, "How dare you? You terrible Christian. Get out. You didn't have enough faith"?

No.

Jesus walks right up to Thomas. He doesn't scold him for his questions. He answers them. He holds out his hands. He says, *"Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."*

Jesus wasn't intimidated by Thomas’s doubt. He didn't require Thomas to suppress his brain or his trauma in order to belong. Jesus met Thomas exactly where he was, questions and all.

In fact, notice that Thomas stayed in the room. Even when he didn't believe, he stayed with his community. And the community let him stay. They didn't kick him out for not being on the same page yet. That is what the church should be—a place where you can belong *before* you believe everything perfectly.

This idea of wrestling isn't new. In the Old Testament, after Jacob spends a whole night physically wrestling with God, God gives him a new name: *Israel*.

Do you know what that name means? It doesn't mean "He Who Always Agrees." It doesn't mean "The Guy With All The Answers."

*Israel* means "He who wrestles with God."

That is your heritage. You are part of a thousands-year-old tradition of people who argued, wrestled, cried, screamed, and questioned God. Read the Psalms. Half of them are King David shouting, "Where are you, God? Why have you forgotten me?"

If the "man after God’s own heart" could yell at God, you can too. God is big enough to handle your questions. He is not fragile. He is not sitting on his throne nervously biting his fingernails hoping you don't ask about evolution or suffering. He is the Truth, and if something is true, it can handle being questioned.

So, what does this look like for us? How do we actually do this?

First, we have to stop faking it. When you bury your doubts, they don't die. They bury themselves alive. They rot. They turn into bitterness. If you ignore your questions because you're afraid of them, eventually the pressure will build up and your faith will explode.

Instead, I want to offer you a vision of what it looks like to let doubt do its work.

Imagine a forest. Sometimes, the underbrush gets too thick. It chokes out the light. So, nature has forest fires. They burn away the dead wood, the invasive weeds, the stuff that isn't alive anymore. It looks scary. It looks destructive. But after the fire, the forest is healthier. The big, strong trees are still standing, and now there is room for new growth.

Doubt is a forest fire. It burns up the "dead wood" of your faith.

Maybe it burns up the idea that God is a vending machine where you put in a prayer coin and get out a blessing. Maybe it burns up the idea that Christians are always perfect. Let that stuff burn. It wasn't true anyway. It was dead wood.

What is left after the fire—the core of who Jesus is, his love, his resurrection—that is fireproof. And that is the faith that will last you for the rest of your life.

I am not saying this is easy. Sitting in the uncertainty is hard. It can feel lonely. But I promise you, a faith that has been tested, a faith that has wrestled with the hard questions and come out the other side, is infinitely stronger than a faith that has never been challenged.

So, I’m not going to give you three easy steps to "fix" your doubt tonight. Because doubt isn't a sin to be fixed; it’s a journey to be walked.

Instead, I’m going to give you a challenge.

I want you to identify your "3 A.M. Question." You know the one. The one that keeps you up at night. The one you’re afraid to say out loud because you think it makes you a bad Christian.

Maybe it’s: *Why do bad things happen to good people?*
Maybe it’s: *Is the Bible really true?*
Maybe it’s: *Why don't I feel God like other people do?*

This week, I want you to write that question down. Get it out of your head and onto paper.

And then, I want you to do something brave. I want you to tell it to a "Safe Person."

Now, you have to choose this person wisely. Don't go to the person who always speaks in bumper-sticker slogans. A Safe Person is someone who listens more than they talk. A Safe Person is someone who won't try to "fix" you immediately with a Bible verse, but who is willing to sit with you in the uncomfortable silence.

Maybe it’s a leader here tonight. Maybe it’s a parent. Maybe it’s a mentor.

Say to them: "I’m wrestling with this question. Can you help me carry it?"

You might be surprised to hear them say, "Me too. I’ve wondered that too."

God is not afraid of your honesty. In fact, honesty is the only thing he can work with. You can’t have a relationship with a fake version of yourself. God wants *you*—the real you, the confused you, the doubting you.

So bring your questions. Bring your skepticism. Bring your wounds. Just like Thomas did.

The doors are open. You are safe here.

Let’s pray.

*God, thank you that you are big enough for our questions. Thank you that we don’t have to pretend with you. For everyone in this room who feels like they are faking it, give them a sense of your peace. Help us to be brave enough to wrestle, and trust that you are holding on to us even when we have trouble holding on to you. Amen.*
