**Title:** The Ghost in the Room: Why Your Questions Don’t Scare God

**Intro: The "Imposter" Syndrome**

I want you to picture a scenario. Maybe you’ve lived it.

You’re in a room—maybe it’s a church service, maybe a camp meeting, maybe just a small group. The music is playing. The lights are dimmed. The person next to you has their hands raised, eyes closed, looking like they have a direct fiber-optic cable connection to heaven. The person on your other side is weeping, clearly moved by something profound. The speaker on stage is talking about how clearly God spoke to them this morning, like they were chatting over coffee.

And you’re standing there. And you feel… nothing.

Actually, that’s not true. You don’t feel nothing. You feel like a fraud.

You start running a mental checklist. You think, *“Do I actually believe this? Like, really? Because right now, the ceiling looks like a ceiling, the music just sounds like a G-chord, and I have about fifty questions that nobody seems to be talking about.”*

Maybe you’ve read something in biology class that doesn’t seem to mesh with Genesis. Maybe you looked at the news this week—saw a war, or a famine, or a tragedy—and thought, *“If God is good, why is that happening?”* Maybe you prayed for something really important, something good, and the answer was total silence.

So, you stand there. You maybe hum along to the song. You nod when the speaker makes a point. You put on the mask. Because the unspoken rule in many religious spaces feels like this: **Certainty equals Faith.** If you are a "good Christian," you are 100% sure, 100% of the time.

So, if you have questions, you bury them. You treat doubt like a crazy uncle at Thanksgiving—you hope he stays in the basement and doesn’t come upstairs to embarrass you in front of the guests.

I want to start tonight by telling you something that might feel like a relief, or might feel scary: The person with their hands raised? They have doubts too. The person crying? They have questions. The speaker on stage? If they are honest, they have nights where they stare at the ceiling and wonder.

You are not the only one. You are not a glitch in the system. You are a human being in the process of growing up, and tonight I want to suggest that your doubt isn’t the enemy of your faith. It might actually be the fuel for it.

**The House of Cards**

When we are kids, we tend to have what I call "House of Cards" faith.

A house of cards is structured, it’s neat, and it stands up as long as nothing shakes the table. In a child’s faith, everything is black and white. God is the good guy, the devil is the bad guy, if I do good things I get blessings, and the Bible is a simple rulebook.

But then, you become a teenager. Your brain changes. You start thinking critically—which, by the way, is a gift from God, not a sin. You start noticing nuance. You start experiencing real pain.

And suddenly, someone shakes the table.

Maybe a Christian you looked up to acts like a hypocrite. *Shake.*
Maybe you learn about the vastness of the universe and feel insignificant. *Shake.*
Maybe you lose a grandparent. *Shake.*

If your faith is a house of cards, one card slipping out brings the whole thing down. If you think, *“Well, I don’t understand this one weird verse in Leviticus, so I guess the resurrection didn’t happen,”* that is a fragile faith.

A lot of people panic when the shaking starts. They think the shaking means they are losing their faith. But what if the shaking is just the process of trading in a house of cards for a house of brick?

You cannot build a real, adult faith without deconstructing the simple, childish version you started with. You have to take it apart to see how it really works. That process—that wrestling, that questioning—is what we call doubt. And it is completely normal.

**The Patron Saint of "I'm Not Buying It"**

I want to look at a guy in the Bible who gets a really bad rap. You know him. His name is Thomas.

History has given him a cruel nickname: "Doubting Thomas." It’s like being known forever for your worst day. But I love Thomas, because Thomas is the patron saint of everyone who refuses to fake it.

Here’s the context: Jesus has been killed. It was brutal, public, and final. The disciples are in hiding, terrified that the Romans are coming for them next. Then, suddenly, rumors start flying. Mary Magdalene says the tomb is empty. Peter and John say they saw grave clothes. The other disciples say Jesus appeared to them in a locked room.

But Thomas wasn't there that night.

So, the disciples run up to Thomas, breathless, shouting, "We have seen the Lord! He’s alive!"

Now, pause. Put yourself in Thomas’s shoes. He watched his hope die on a Friday. He is heartbroken. He is traumatized. And now, his friends are telling him something that is medically, scientifically, and logically impossible.

If Thomas was a "people pleaser," he would have said, "Oh, wow! That’s great guys! Hallelujah!" He would have faked it to fit in.

But Thomas respects the truth too much to pretend.

He says, famously: *“Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”*

That is a heavy statement. He’s saying, *“I need evidence. I need to touch the wounds. I’m not settling for second-hand rumors.”*

Now, here is the most important part of the story.

A week later, they are in the house again. Thomas is there this time. The doors are locked. Jesus appears.

Does Jesus look at Thomas and say, *“Get out. Everyone else believed me, but you had to be difficult. You’re not cut out for this”*?

Does Jesus say, *“Thomas, you have too many questions, you’re ruining the vibe”*?

No.

Jesus walks straight to Thomas. He bypasses the guys who had it easy, and he goes to the guy who is struggling. And he holds out his hands.

He says, *“Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side.”*

Jesus doesn't shame Thomas for his doubt. He meets Thomas *in* his doubt. He offers himself to Thomas’s questions.

And because Thomas was honest about his doubt, he ends up making the strongest declaration of faith in the entire gospel. When he realizes it’s true, he falls down and says, "My Lord and my God!"

He wouldn’t have gotten to that depth of conviction if he hadn’t been honest about his depth of uncertainty.

**Doubt as a Muscle**

Here is the vision I want to offer you: **Faith is not the absence of doubt. Faith is courage in the face of doubt.**

If you are 100% certain that a chair will hold you, it takes no faith to sit in it. It’s just physics. Faith is when you aren’t sure, when the outcome is foggy, when the risk is real, and you choose to trust anyway.

Think about weightlifting. To build muscle, you actually have to tear the muscle fibers. You put the muscle under tension, it tears slightly, and when it heals, it heals back stronger and bigger.

Doubt is the tearing of the spiritual muscle. It hurts. It feels like weakness. It feels like you’re breaking. But if you stay in the gym—if you keep bringing those questions to God, if you keep wrestling—you heal back stronger.

A faith that has never been tested, never questioned, and never doubted is a fragile thing. But a faith that has looked into the dark, asked the hard questions, screamed "Why?" at the sky, and still chosen to follow Jesus? That is a faith that can survive a storm.

**The Difference Between Doubt and Cynicism**

Now, a quick warning. There is a difference between *honest doubt* and *cynicism*.

Honest doubt is looking for answers. It says, "I want to believe, but I’m stuck on this. Help me understand."

Cynicism is looking for an exit. It says, "This is all stupid, and I’m just looking for a reason to leave."

God can handle your anger. He can handle your confusion. Read the Psalms—David is constantly yelling at God, asking where He is, complaining that life isn’t fair. God put those complaints in the Bible! He’s not afraid of your questions.

But you have to actually *ask* them. You have to bring them to Him, rather than just using them as an excuse to walk away.

**Conclusion: The Safe Place**

I’m not going to give you a pat answer tonight. I’m not going to say, "Just pray more and the doubts will vanish." Sometimes, we carry certain questions for years. Sometimes, the answer is just, "I don't know yet."

But I want you to know that you don't have to leave your brain at the door to be a Christian. You don't have to fake certainty to be loved by God.

Jesus isn’t looking for robots who are programmed to agree. He’s looking for a relationship. And real relationships have conflict, questions, and hard conversations.

So, here is your challenge. Here is your next step.

I want you to identify the "Elephant in the Room." What is the one question, the one doubt, the one frustration with God that you have been afraid to say out loud because you think it makes you a "bad Christian"?

Write it down. Put it in the notes app on your phone.

And then, find **one person**. Not a peer who is just as confused as you, but maybe a leader here, a parent, a mentor, or a really solid friend. And say this: *“Hey, I’m wrestling with something, and I don’t want you to fix it, I just need to say it.”*

Bring the doubt into the light. Because when doubts stay in the dark, they turn into monsters. But when you bring them into the light, they just turn into questions. And questions have answers, even if we have to wait a while to find them.

You are safe to wrestle here. You are safe to ask. God is big enough for your questions.

Let’s pray.

**Title:** The Ghost in the Room
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14–18)
**Tone:** Conversational, honest, inviting

***

(Start by sitting on the edge of the stage or a stool. Don’t stand behind a podium if you can help it. Just be with them.)

I want to start tonight by talking about the ghost in the room.

No, I don’t mean the Holy Ghost. And I don’t mean a spooky, Halloween-movie ghost. I’m talking about a specific feeling that I’d bet almost every single one of you has felt, maybe even right now, but that nobody wants to admit to first.

Here’s the scenario: The music is playing. Maybe the band is really building it up, or maybe it’s a quiet, reflective song. The person next to you has their eyes closed and their hands raised. The person on your other side is crying a little bit, clearly having a moment. The leader up front is talking about how good God is, how close He feels.

And you are standing there, looking around, thinking: *“I don’t feel a thing.”*

Or maybe you’re in biology class, or watching the news, or scrolling through TikTok and seeing something terrible happening in the world, and a thought creeps into the back of your mind: *“Is any of this actually real? Is God actually there? Or are we just talking to the ceiling?”*

And immediately after that thought hits you, a second thought rushes in to crush it: *“What is wrong with me? I’m a Christian. I’m not supposed to think that. If I tell anyone, they’ll think I’m a bad person. I better just smile, nod, and sing the song.”*

That is the ghost in the room. It’s the pressure to pretend you are 100% certain about everything, 100% of the time.

So, before we go any further, I want to kill that ghost. I want to say something clearly, and I want you to hear me: **Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Silence is not the opposite of faith. Certainty is not the same thing as faith.**

If you have questions, if you have doubts, if you have moments where you feel like you’re losing your grip on what you believe—you are not failing. You are growing up.

Let’s be real for a second. When you were five years old, you probably believed whatever your parents told you. If they said the moon was made of cheese, you’d ask for a cracker. If they said Santa fits down the chimney, you didn’t ask about the physics of it. You wore the clothes they bought you, and you believed the things they taught you. It was a "hand-me-down" faith. It was comfortable, and it fit you then.

But you aren’t five anymore. You don’t wear the same shoes you wore in kindergarten because you grew out of them. If you tried to squeeze your feet into them now, it would hurt. You couldn’t walk.

The same thing happens with your soul. As you get older, your world gets bigger. You learn about science, and history, and suffering. You experience heartbreak. You see hypocrisy. The simple, kindergarten explanations don’t always fit the complex world you’re living in now.

When that happens, you have two choices. You can pretend the shoes still fit, squeezing your brain into a tiny box and ignoring your questions until your faith feels painful and fake. Or, you can admit that you need a bigger pair of shoes. You can admit that you need a faith that is big enough to handle your questions.

But that process—the process of trading the small shoes for the big ones—feels a lot like doubt. It feels scary. It feels like losing something. But actually, it’s the only way to find something real.

I think we do a bad job in the church of talking about this. We act like the Bible is full of people who never wavered, super-heroes of faith who walked around with halos, never questioning God.

But have you actually read this book? It is full of people freaking out.

David, the guy who wrote the Psalms, wrote songs that basically say, *“God, where are you? Why are you ignoring me? Why do the bad guys win?”* Jeremiah accused God of tricking him. Even Jesus, on the cross, cried out, *“My God, why have you forsaken me?”*

But I want to focus on one guy specifically. You know him. He’s got a nickname that has stuck to him for two thousand years, which I think is totally unfair.

Thomas. "Doubting Thomas."

Here’s the scene: It’s after the resurrection. Jesus has died. The disciples are terrified. They are locked in a room, hiding, afraid they’re going to be arrested next. Jesus shows up, walks through the wall, and proves he’s alive. It’s amazing.

But Thomas wasn’t there. We don’t know where he was. Maybe he was the only one brave enough to go out and get groceries. Maybe he was just taking a walk to clear his head because he was heartbroken.

So the other disciples run up to him later and say, "Thomas! We saw him! He’s alive!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s shoes. He watched his friend die. He saw the blood. He saw the tomb. He knows how the world works—dead people stay dead. And now his friends, who are exhausted and traumatized, are telling him a ghost story.

Thomas doesn’t say, "Oh, cool, I guess I’ll just go with the flow."

No. Thomas says, *“Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”*

We usually read that as Thomas being a cynic. We think he’s being stubborn. But I don’t think so. I think Thomas is being **honest**.

Thomas is saying, "I want to believe, but I can't just take your word for it. This matters too much to me. I need to know it’s real. I’m not going to fake it."

I respect that. I respect that way more than someone who just nods their head because everyone else is nodding.

A week later, they are all in the house again. This time, Thomas is there. Jesus shows up. And this is the most important part of the story. Watch what Jesus does.

Jesus doesn’t walk in and say, "Thomas, how dare you? Everyone else believed. Why are you such a failure? Get out of my group."

Jesus walks straight to Thomas. He looks him in the eye. And he holds out his hands.

He says, *“Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.”*

Jesus wasn’t offended by Thomas’s question. He answered it. He offered Thomas exactly what he needed. He invited Thomas to touch the wounds.

Here is the truth: **God is not intimidated by your questions.**

God isn’t sitting in heaven, nervously biting his nails, hoping you don’t read that one article or ask that one hard question that unravels the whole universe. If God is real, He is the source of all truth. That means honest questions will eventually lead you closer to Him, not further away.

The only thing that kills faith is silence. The only thing that kills faith is pretending.

If you suppress your doubts, if you shove them down into the basement of your heart and lock the door, they don’t die. They grow. They turn into resentment. They turn into cynicism. And eventually, the pressure gets too high, and the whole house blows up. That’s how we end up with people walking away from faith entirely—not because they had questions, but because they felt they weren’t allowed to ask them.

We need a faith that struggles.

Think about a relationship with a best friend or a boyfriend or girlfriend. If you are constantly polite, constantly agreeing, never arguing, never bringing up the things that bother you... do you have a real relationship? No. You have a polite acquaintance.

Real intimacy is messy. It involves conflict. It involves saying, "Hey, I didn't understand why you did that," or "That really hurt me." Working through that conflict is what makes the relationship strong.

It’s the same with God. Wrestling with God is a form of intimacy. It means you take Him seriously enough to demand an answer.

So, what does this look like for us, this week, in 2024?

It means we stop treating "doubt" as a dirty word. We start treating it as an invitation.

Maybe your doubt is intellectual. You have questions about evolution, or the reliability of the Bible, or other religions. That’s great. Go read. Go study. Don’t be afraid of what you’ll find. There are brilliant people—scientists, historians, philosophers—who love Jesus and have asked those same questions. You don’t have to check your brain at the door to be a Christian.

Maybe your doubt is emotional. You’ve prayed for something—for your grandma to get better, for your parents to stop fighting, for your anxiety to go away—and it feels like God left you on "read." That is a heavier kind of doubt. That’s the doubt of pain.

If that’s you, I want you to know that the Bible gives you language for that, too. It’s called "Lament." It’s a way of praying that is raw and unfiltered. It’s okay to tell God you’re angry. He can take it.

I want to offer you a vision of what your faith could look like in ten years.

I don’t want you to have a fragile faith that is protected by a glass case, where you never let anything touch it. I want you to have a faith that has been tested. A faith that has scars.

Because here is the beautiful thing about Thomas. After he touched the wounds, he fell to his knees and said, "My Lord and my God." His doubt didn't lead him to atheism; it led him to a deeper, more personal conviction than any of the other disciples. He didn't just believe because he was told to; he believed because he *knew*.

When you wrestle through your questions, the faith you find on the other side is yours. It’s not your parents’. It’s not your pastor’s. It is yours. And that is the kind of faith that can survive the storms of life.

So, I’m not going to end this talk by telling you to "just have faith" or "just pray more." That’s too easy, and it’s not helpful.

Instead, I’m going to give you a challenge.

I want you to be brave enough to articulate your question.

Maybe tonight, or when you get home, I want you to take a piece of paper, or the notes app on your phone. And I want you to write down the one question you are afraid to ask. The one that makes you feel like a "bad Christian."

Maybe it’s: *“Why do good people suffer?”*
Maybe it’s: *“How do we know Jesus is the only way?”*
Maybe it’s: *“God, do you even like me?”*

Write it down. Look at it. And then, I want you to do something radical. I want you to pray that question.

Don’t pray the polite version. Pray the raw version. Say, "God, I am struggling with this. I need you to show me something. I’m not leaving the room until we deal with this."

And then, find one person—a leader here, a parent, a mentor, a friend who you trust—and tell them. "Hey, I’m having a hard time with this."

You will be surprised by how many people will look back at you and say, "Me too. Let’s figure it out together."

You are safe here. Your questions are safe here. God is big enough for your doubt.

Let’s pray.

1NgUSOJjK7hc4Iw5Uh3OC.text:
**Title:** The Crumbling Wall and the Hand-Me-Down Jacket: Why Your Doubt Isn’t the End

**I. The Script**

I want to start by describing a scenario that I think a lot of you might recognize.

You’re sitting in a small group, or maybe a Sunday School class back when you were younger. The leader asks a question. It’s usually a question with a very obvious answer. Something like, "Why should we trust God?" or "What do we do when we’re scared?"

And everyone knows the script. You know the "Christian" answer. You raise your hand, you say, "Because He loves us," or "We pray," or the classic catch-all answer: "Jesus."

Everyone nods. The leader smiles. The moment passes.

But inside your head, there is a totally different conversation happening. Inside, you’re thinking, *Yeah, but what about when I prayed for my grandma to get better and she didn’t?* Or, *If God loves us, why is the world so messed up?* Or maybe, *Honestly, I’m not even sure I feel God right now. I feel like I’m talking to the ceiling.*

But you don’t say that. You stick to the script. Because you have this sinking feeling that if you actually said what you were thinking, the air would get sucked out of the room. You feel like admitting you have questions is the same thing as admitting you’re a bad Christian. You feel like doubt is a trapdoor, and if you step on it, you’re going to fall out of the faith entirely.

So, you fake it. You nod. You smile. And you start to feel like an imposter.

I want to start tonight by telling you something very clearly: If you have questions, if you have doubts, if you aren't sure about all of this... you are not failing. You are growing up.

**II. The Hand-Me-Down Jacket**

Here is the reality of being a teenager, specifically regarding faith.

When you are a kid, your faith is like a jacket that your parents or your church gave you. It’s a hand-me-down. It kept you warm. It served its purpose. You didn't pick it out; you just put it on because that’s what you were told to do. It was simple: God is good, be nice to people, Noah built an ark, Jonah got eaten by a fish.

But now, you are growing. You are learning about biology and history. You are seeing tragedy in the news. You are experiencing heartbreak. And suddenly, that little jacket doesn't fit anymore. It’s tight in the shoulders. The sleeves are too short. It’s uncomfortable.

When this happens, you have two choices.
Choice one: You keep trying to squeeze into a child’s faith, ignoring your questions, pretending everything fits, until the jacket eventually rips apart.
Choice two: You acknowledge that you need a bigger jacket. You acknowledge that the simple answers you got when you were seven don’t quite cover the complex questions you have now that you’re sixteen.

Doubt is often just the growing pains of your soul. It’s the friction of moving from a faith you were *told* to have, to a faith that is actually *yours*.

**III. The Prisoner in the Dungeon**

I think we do you a disservice in church sometimes. We talk about all these heroes of the Bible as if they were robots who never worried, never stressed, and never questioned. We give you the "Instagram highlight reel" of the Bible.

But if you actually read the book, it is full of people freaking out, asking God where He is, and wondering if they made a mistake.

I want to look at one guy specifically. John the Baptist.

Now, John is an intense guy. He’s the one who lived in the wilderness, ate locusts, and wore camel hair. He was the hype man for Jesus. He is the one who saw Jesus coming and literally shouted, "Behold! The Lamb of God!" He baptized Jesus. He saw the dove come down. He heard the voice from Heaven.

If anybody should have had zero doubts, it was John. He saw the miracles with his own eyes. He was 100% sure.

But then, things go wrong. John gets arrested for speaking out against the King. He gets thrown into a dungeon. And he sits there. Days turn into weeks. Weeks turn into months.

John probably thought, *Jesus is the Messiah. He’s here to set the captives free. I’m a captive. Surely, he’s going to bust me out of here any second.*

But Jesus doesn’t come. John sits in the dark, cold, damp silence. And the doubt starts to creep in. The walls start closing in. And John, the guy who was so sure, starts to wonder if he got it all wrong.

So, in Matthew 11, John does something incredible. He sends his friends to find Jesus and ask him a question. And the question isn't, "Hey, when are you breaking me out?"

The question is: *"Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?"*

Think about the weight of that. This is the guy who introduced Jesus to the world. And now, in his pain and confusion, he’s asking, "Did I make a mistake? Are you actually real?"

That is a heavy, dangerous question.

And here is the most important part: How does Jesus react?

If doubt was a sin, if questions were offensive to God, Jesus should have been angry. He should have said, "How dare John ask that? After everything I showed him? Tell John he needs to pray more and have more faith."

But Jesus doesn't do that. He doesn't shame him.

Jesus tells John’s friends, "Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk... the good news is proclaimed to the poor."

He gives John evidence. He reassures him. And then, after John’s friends leave, Jesus turns to the crowd and calls John the greatest man who ever lived.

He didn’t cancel John for doubting. He didn’t kick him out of the group. He loved him through the question.

**IV. Certainty vs. Trust**

We live in an information age. You guys have Google in your pockets. If you want to know the capital of Bolivia or the atomic weight of Gold, you can find out in three seconds with 100% certainty.

We are addicted to certainty. We want our faith to work like Google. We want to type in a prayer or a question and get an instant, verified result.

But faith isn’t a search engine. Faith is a relationship.

Think about a friendship or a dating relationship. Can you be 100% certain, scientifically prove, that your best friend won’t betray you? No. You can’t prove it. But you *trust* them because you have a history with them. You know their character.

The opposite of faith isn't doubt. The opposite of faith is *certainty*.

If you have absolute proof of something, you don't need faith. I don't need "faith" that this microphone is in my hand. I can see it. Faith is required exactly when we *don't* see, when we *don't* understand.

Paul Tillich, a famous theologian, once said that doubt isn’t the enemy of faith; it is an element of faith.

Think of it like working out. If you lift weights, you are actually tearing your muscle fibers. It hurts. It makes you sore. But that tearing is the only way the muscle grows back stronger.

Questions are the heavy lifting of the soul. When you ask, "Why is there suffering?" or "How do science and the Bible fit together?", you are tearing the muscle of that old, childhood faith. It hurts. It’s uncomfortable. But if you wrestle with it, rather than running away from it, you end up with a faith that is actually strong enough to handle the real world.

**V. The Danger of Silence**

The most dangerous thing you can do with your doubt is suppress it.

If you bury your questions because you’re afraid of what people will think, they don’t go away. They just rot. They turn into cynicism. You’ll eventually walk away from God, not because you found better answers, but because you got tired of pretending.

I know plenty of people who left the church, not because they learned some scientific fact that disproved God, but because they felt like they weren't allowed to be honest about their struggles. They thought they had to be perfect, and they knew they weren't, so they just quit.

God is big enough for your questions. He is not intimidated by your logic. He is not offended by your confusion. He is the Creator of the universe; He can handle a teenager asking "Why?"

In the Psalms, David—a man after God’s own heart—literally screams at God. He says, "Why have you forsaken me?" He says, "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?"

If David can talk to God like that, so can you.

**VI. A Practical Step**

So, where do we go from here? If you are sitting here tonight feeling like your faith is hanging by a thread, or if you just have that one nagging question you’ve been afraid to voice, I want to give you a vision for how to handle it.

Don’t do it alone. Doubt isolates us. It tells us, "You’re the only one thinking this." That is a lie.

I want you to try something this week. We often treat prayer as a time to tell God how great He is, or to ask for things we want. Those are good things.

But this week, I want you to try **The Prayer of Honest Anger.**

Find a quiet place. Put your phone in the other room. And talk to God with zero filter. Tell Him what you’re mad about. Tell Him what doesn't make sense. Tell Him you’re bored, or confused, or hurt.

Ask the hard question.

And then, don’t expect the sky to open up and a booming voice to answer you immediately. Just sit in the silence for a minute.

But take it a step further. Find one person—a leader here, a parent, a mentor, or a really solid friend—and say this sentence: *"I’m having a hard time believing [X]."*

Bring the monster out of the closet. Turn the lights on. You will find that once you say it out loud, it loses a lot of its power to scare you.

We are not looking for a blind faith that ignores reality. We are looking for a deep faith that has walked through the fire of questions and come out the other side—maybe a little scarred, maybe with a limp (like Jacob after he wrestled God), but real. Authentic. Yours.

It’s okay not to know. It’s okay to be in the dungeon like John for a season. Keep asking. Keep wrestling. God is right there in the mess with you.

Let’s pray.

**Title:** The Ghost in the Room
**Topic:** Navigating Doubt and Faith
**Audience:** Ages 14–18

***

**The Setup**

I want you to picture a scenario. It might feel familiar.

Imagine you’re in a room like this one. The music is playing—maybe it’s a song you’ve heard a hundred times. The lights are dimmed. The person to your left has their hands raised, eyes closed, looking like they are having a genuine, spiritual moment. The person to your right is singing along, looking totally locked in.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you’re trying to focus, but your brain won't shut up. You’re looking around thinking, *“Am I the only one who feels… nothing?”*

Or maybe it’s not during worship. maybe it’s in biology class, or watching the news, or scrolling through your feed and seeing something terrible happening in the world. And a thought creeps in: *“If God is real, why is this happening?”* Or, *“Is this stuff we talk about on Sundays actually true, or is it just a nice story we tell ourselves to feel better?”*

And immediately after that thought hits, a second feeling rushes in: Panic. Guilt.

You think, *“I shouldn’t be thinking this. I’m a Christian. I’m supposed to have faith. If I admit I have questions, everyone will think I’m a fake. If I admit I’m not sure, maybe the whole thing falls apart.”*

So, you do what most of us learn to do very early on. You bury it. You put on the "Church Face." You nod when the leader speaks, you sing the lyrics, and you hope that if you just act certain enough, the feelings of uncertainty will go away.

I want to start tonight by telling you something that we don’t say enough in church: **If you are wrestling with doubt, you are not failing.**

You aren’t a bad Christian. You aren’t "backsliding." You are a human being in the process of growing up. And here is the secret that most adults are terrified to tell you: We have those questions too.

**The GPS Metaphor**

Think about how a GPS works. When you’re driving and you miss a turn, what does it do? It says, "Recalculating."

It doesn’t scream at you. It doesn’t shut down the car. It doesn’t say, "Well, you missed the exit, so now you live on this highway forever. Good luck." It acknowledges that your position has changed, and it figures out a new route to the destination.

When you were a kid, your faith was simple. It was like a straight line. God made the world. Jesus loves me. Be nice to your sister. That is a beautiful, necessary starting point. It’s a child’s faith.

But you aren’t children anymore. You are entering a world that is complex, messy, and sometimes painful. You are learning about science, history, psychology, and suffering. You are seeing that good people sometimes get hurt and bad people sometimes get rich.

Your old map—that simple, straight line—might not account for the terrain you’re walking on now.

When you hit a question that your childhood faith can’t answer, that isn’t the end of your faith. It’s your soul saying, *"Recalculating."* It means you are ready for a bigger, deeper, more robust version of faith. But to get there, you have to be willing to ask the questions.

**The Patron Saint of "Wait a Minute"**

I want to look at a guy in the Bible who gets a really bad rap. His name is Thomas. You probably know him by his nickname: Doubting Thomas.

History has been really hard on Thomas. We treat him like the villain of the Easter story. But I actually think Thomas is the bravest guy in the room.

Here’s the context: Jesus has been killed. The disciples are hiding in a locked room, terrified that the Romans are coming for them next. Then, Jesus shows up—alive. It’s a miracle. Everyone is celebrating.

But Thomas wasn’t there that night. We don’t know where he was—maybe getting food, maybe just needing space to grieve. When he gets back, his friends are going crazy. They’re shouting, "We saw him! He’s alive!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s sandals. He watched his friend die. He is heartbroken. And now his friends are sounding delusional.

Thomas doesn't fake it. He doesn't say, "Oh, cool, praise the Lord," while secretly rolling his eyes. He respects the truth too much to pretend.

He says, essentially: *"Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe."*

That is a bold statement. He is drawing a line in the sand. He’s saying, *I want to believe, but I need this to be real. I can’t build my life on a rumor.*

A week goes by. This is the part we forget. For seven whole days, the other disciples are happy, and Thomas is sitting there in the tension. He’s the odd one out. That must have been a lonely week.

Then, Jesus shows up again.

And this is the most important part. Watch how Jesus treats Thomas.

Jesus doesn’t walk in and say, "Thomas, how dare you? Everyone else believed. Why do you have to be so difficult? You’re out of the group."

No. Jesus walks right up to him. He singles him out. And he doesn’t offer a lecture; he offers his wounds.

He says, *"Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."*

Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is. He answers the honest question with an honest presence. He wasn't intimidated by Thomas’s doubt. He didn't need Thomas to pretend. He wanted Thomas’s heart, and he knew that for Thomas, the path to the heart went through the head.

**Certainty vs. Trust**

We often think the opposite of faith is doubt. But I don’t think that’s true. I think the opposite of faith is **certainty**.

If you are 100% certain about something—if you can prove it like a math equation, if you have undeniable evidence sitting in front of you—you don’t need faith. You just have facts. I don’t have "faith" that this microphone is in my hand. I can see it.

Faith is what happens in the gap between what we know and what we hope for. Faith is choosing to trust even when we don't have 100% of the answers.

If you never doubt, it might mean you aren’t actually thinking about this stuff. It might mean you’re just repeating what you’ve been told.

Doubt is like the growing pains of the soul. When you lift weights, you actually tear your muscle fibers. It hurts. It makes you sore. But that tearing is the only way the muscle grows back stronger.

Your questions—about the Bible, about hell, about science, about why God seems silent—are those micro-tears. They hurt. They feel scary. But if you bring them to God, rather than hiding them from Him, they become the way your faith grows from a child’s faith into an adult’s faith.

**The Danger of Silence**

Now, there is a danger here. The danger isn't the doubt itself; the danger is isolation.

When we feel uncertain, the enemy wants us to isolate. He wants you to think, *“I’m the only one. I can’t tell my youth leader, they’ll be disappointed. I can’t tell my parents, they’ll freak out.”*

So you take your questions to the internet. And look, the internet has a lot of information, but it doesn’t have a lot of wisdom. Or you just bottle them up until one day you just walk away from God entirely because you think you aren't "allowed" to stay.

Please hear me: **God is not fragile.**

He is not up in heaven wringing his hands, worried that a 16-year-old in [Your City] has a question about evolution. He isn't offended by your confusion. He can handle your anger. He can handle your "Why?"

Read the Psalms. Half of them are David screaming at God, asking where He is, complaining that life isn't fair. And God called David a "man after His own heart."

God would rather have your honest shouting than your polite, fake silence.

**A New Vision**

So, what does this look like for us?

I want us to be a community where it is safe to say, "I don't know."

Imagine a faith that isn't a house of cards—where if you pull out one card, the whole thing collapses. Imagine a faith that is more like a hiking trail. Sometimes the view is clear and beautiful. Sometimes you’re in the fog and you can’t see five feet in front of you.

When you’re in the fog, you don’t run off a cliff. You slow down. You check your compass. You call out to the people hiking with you. You keep putting one foot in front of the other until the fog lifts. Because the fog *always* lifts eventually.

You can love Jesus and still have questions about the Old Testament.
You can trust God and still wonder why your prayer wasn't answered.
You can be a faithful Christian and admit that some days, you just aren't sure.

That isn't a failure of faith. That *is* faith. It’s the "recalculating."

**The Next Step**

I don’t want to wrap this up with a bow and pretend I just solved your doubt. That would be fake. But I do want to give you something to do.

I want you to identify your "Safe People."

Who is an adult in your life—maybe a leader here, a parent, a mentor—who you suspect is real? Someone who won’t freak out if you ask a hard question.

This week, I challenge you to start a conversation with them. It can be simple. You can say, *"Hey, I’ve been wondering about [X]..."* or *"Do you ever feel like God is far away?"*

Test the waters. Bring the ghost into the room.

And if you are sitting here tonight thinking, *“I don’t have any big questions right now, I feel good,”* that’s great! Your job is to be the friend who listens. When someone confesses they are struggling, don’t try to fix it. Don’t quote a Bible verse immediately to shut them up. Just say, *"Thanks for trusting me with that. I’m with you. Let’s figure it out together."*

Let’s be a generation that stops faking it. Let’s be like Thomas—brave enough to ask for what we need, and honest enough to wait for Jesus to show up. Because He always does.

Let's pray.

*God, thank You that You are big enough for our questions. Thank You that we don’t have to pretend with You. For anyone in this room feeling like they are faking it, or feeling like their questions disqualify them from Your love, please give them a sense of peace tonight. Remind us that You love us for who we are, not for how much we know. Help us to trust You in the fog. Amen.*

ylqaGb2_h4FVS7iAoMJXu.text:
**Title:** The Ghost in the Machine: Why Your Questions Don’t Scare God

**Intro: The Uncomfortable Silence**

I want to start by describing a specific feeling. I’m guessing most of you will recognize it, even if you’ve never said it out loud.

Imagine you are in a service, or at a camp, or maybe just in a small group. The music is playing, and the person next to you has their hands raised, eyes closed, looking like they are having a direct, high-speed connection with heaven. The person on your other side is taking furious notes during the sermon, nodding along like everything makes perfect sense.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you feel… nothing. Or maybe you don’t feel nothing; maybe you feel a friction in your brain. Someone says, "God is good," and your brain instantly flashes to a news headline about a war, or a friend who is sick, or a prayer you prayed that didn’t get answered. Someone talks about how the Bible is clear, and you’re thinking, "Is it? Because I read that one part about the bears mauling the kids, and it felt pretty confusing."

In that moment, a cold panic sets in. You look around and think, *"Everyone else gets it. Everyone else feels it. I am the only one faking it. If they knew what was actually going on in my head, they wouldn’t let me in the door."*

So, you do the only thing that feels safe: you learn to nod. You learn the right words to say in small group to get the leader to move on to the next person. You bury the questions deep down in the basement of your soul and lock the door.

I want to start tonight by telling you something that might sound counterintuitive: That feeling? That friction? That question mark rising up in your chest?

That is not the sound of your faith dying. That is the sound of your faith growing up.

**The Sweater That No Longer Fits**

When you are a kid, your parents or guardians buy your clothes. They pick them out, they put them on you, and for a long time, that works fine. But eventually, you hit a growth spurt. Suddenly, that favorite sweater is tight in the shoulders. The sleeves are halfway up your forearms. It’s uncomfortable. It restricts your movement.

You have two choices: You can keep squeezing into a child’s sweater and be miserable, or you can admit it doesn’t fit anymore and go find something that actually fits the person you are becoming.

Faith is very similar. When you are young, you often inherit a "child’s faith." It’s a faith given to you by your parents, your Sunday School teachers, or your pastors. It is usually simple. It sees the world in black and white. *Do good, get blessed. Pray, get answers. God is nice.*

But then you become a teenager. You start learning biology and physics. You start seeing the nuance of history. You experience your first real heartbreak or witness injustice. The black-and-white answers of childhood start to feel gray. The sweater doesn't fit.

This is the moment where doubt enters the room.

We are often taught that doubt is a sin. We treat it like a virus—if you catch it, you need to quarantine yourself so you don’t infect anyone else. But I want to suggest that doubt is actually an invitation. It is your mind and your soul demanding a faith that is big enough, rugged enough, and real enough to handle the actual world you live in.

If you never doubted, it would mean you aren't paying attention. The world is complicated. If your faith is going to survive the real world, it has to be able to handle complexity.

**The Guy with the Bad Nickname**

To prove to you that this isn't just some modern idea, I want to look at a guy who has been getting bad press for two thousand years. You know him as "Doubting Thomas."

Poor Thomas. He follows Jesus for three years. He leaves his job. He risks his life. At one point in the Gospel of John, when the other disciples are too scared to go to Judea because people want to kill Jesus, it’s Thomas who says, "Let us also go, that we may die with him." He was brave. He was loyal.

But he gets remembered for one bad week.

Here’s the scene: Jesus has been killed. The disciples are hiding in a locked room, terrified that the Roman soldiers are coming for them next. Thomas isn't there—we don't know why, maybe he was the only one brave enough to go out for supplies.

When he gets back, the other disciples are frantic with joy. They say, "We have seen the Lord! He’s alive!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s shoes. He saw Jesus die. He saw the brutality of the crucifixion. He is traumatized and heartbroken. And now, his friends are telling him something that sounds scientifically and logically impossible.

Thomas doesn’t say, "Oh, cool, thanks for the update." He says, essentially, *I need proof.*

He says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

This is a raw, gritty demand. Thomas isn't trying to be a jerk; he’s trying to protect his heart. He refuses to settle for a rumor. He refuses to pretend. He wants the truth, even if the truth is painful. He is saying, "I cannot build my life on something that might just be a ghost story."

A week goes by. I imagine that was a lonely week for Thomas. Everyone else is celebrating; he is still in the dark.

Then, Jesus shows up again. The doors are locked, but there He is.

And this is the part that matters most. Watch how Jesus reacts to Thomas.

Jesus does not say, "Thomas, how dare you? Everyone else believed. Why are you so difficult? You’re out of the group."

No. Jesus walks straight to Thomas. He looks him in the eye. And He holds out his hands.

He says, "Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."

Jesus doesn't shame Thomas for his questions. He meets Thomas *in* his questions. He offers Thomas his wounds.

Thomas’s doubt didn't drive Jesus away; it actually drew Jesus closer. Because Thomas was honest about what he needed, he ended up having a more intimate encounter with the risen Christ than almost anyone else. He is the one who falls to his knees and makes the strongest declaration of faith in the whole gospel: "My Lord and my God!"

He went from the deepest doubt to the highest praise. And he couldn't have gotten to that "high" without going through the "low."

**The Gym of the Soul**

Think about how muscles grow. If you go to the gym and lift a weight that is easy for you, nothing happens. To build muscle, you have to lift something heavy enough to create resistance. You actually have to create micro-tears in the muscle fibers. It hurts. It’s sore the next day. But when those fibers heal, they heal stronger and thicker than they were before.

Doubt is the resistance training of your faith.

When you ask, "Why does God allow suffering?" or "How do I know this is true?" or "Why does the church act like this sometimes?" you are lifting heavy weights. It feels like you are tearing apart. It feels like you are losing something.

But if you stay in the gym—if you keep wrestling, keep asking, keep seeking—your faith heals back stronger.

A faith that has never been questioned is a fragile faith. It’s like a porcelain vase—it looks pretty, but if life knocks it over, it shatters into a million pieces.

But a faith that has wrestled with doubt? That’s like a forged steel sword. It has been through the fire. It has been hammered. It isn't pretty and perfect; it has dents and scratches. But it is strong. It can handle the weight of tragedy. It can handle the confusion of adulthood.

I know plenty of people who have "deconstructed" their faith. And I know that word can be scary. But the goal isn't to tear the house down and live in the rubble. The goal is to tear down the rotten wood, the bad ideas, and the fear-based rules, so you can find the solid foundation underneath.

**The Trap of Pat Answers**

I want to apologize to you on behalf of the adults in your life. Because sometimes, when you come to us with your heavy questions, we get scared. We worry that if we don't have the answer, you’ll leave God.

So, we give you "pat answers." We say things like:
*   "Just have faith."
*   "God works in mysterious ways."
*   "You just need to pray more."
*   "Don't overthink it."

These answers are like putting a Band-Aid on a broken leg. They don't help, and they actually make you feel lonelier, because they make you feel like your problem is simple and you’re just too stupid to get it.

I want to give you permission to reject those answers.

"Just praying more" doesn't always solve an intellectual crisis. Sometimes you need to read a book. Sometimes you need to talk to a historian. Sometimes you need to sit in the silence and realize that God is big enough to handle the fact that we don't understand Him.

It is okay to say, "I don't know."
It is okay to say, "That doesn't make sense to me."
It is okay to say, "I am really angry at God right now."

God can handle your anger. Read the Psalms. David yells at God constantly. He asks, "Where are you? Why have you forgotten me?" If the guy who wrote the worship songs can yell at God, so can you.

**A Vision for the Future**

Here is what I hope for you.

I hope you don't settle for a shallow, borrowed faith. I hope you are brave enough to ask the hard questions.

But I also hope you don't let the questions turn into cynicism. Cynicism is easy; it’s just sitting on the sidelines making fun of the game. Wrestling is hard; it’s getting in the ring.

Don't walk away just because it gets complicated. Stay in the tension. Keep talking to Jesus, even if you’re just telling Him that you’re not sure He’s there.

Imagine a relationship with a best friend or a partner. If you never argued, never disagreed, and never expressed your true feelings, that wouldn't be a deep relationship; it would be a fake one. Intimacy comes from working *through* the hard stuff.

God wants intimacy with you. He doesn't want a robot that says "Amen" at the right times. He wants *you*. The messy, confused, questioning you.

**The Challenge: The 3 AM Question**

So, how do we land this?

I want you to think of the "3 AM Question." You know the one. It’s the question that keeps you up at night. The one you’re afraid to ask your small group leader because you think they’ll look at you funny. Maybe it’s about science, maybe it’s about sexuality, maybe it’s about hell, maybe it’s about why your grandmother died.

Here is your challenge for this week: **Bring it into the light.**

Doubt grows like mold—it thrives in the dark and damp. When you expose it to sunlight, it changes.

I want you to find one person this week—a leader, a parent, a mentor, or a friend who you respect—and ask them that question. But preface it like this:

*"Hey, I’m trying to figure out what I believe, and I’m stuck on something. Can I just be honest about a doubt I have, without you trying to fix it right away?"*

And if you are sitting here thinking, "I don't have anyone safe to ask," then write it down. Literally, get a piece of paper, write the question down, and pray this prayer: *"God, here is my question. I’m not going to hide it from You. I’m going to leave it here on the table. Show me the truth, even if it takes a while."*

You are not a bad Christian for having questions. You are a human being seeking the Divine. And the promise of Jesus is not that we will have all the answers. The promise is that when we seek, we will find—not always an explanation, but a Person. A Person who has wounds on his hands, and who says, "I know it’s hard. I’m here. Let’s walk through it together."

Let's pray.

**Title:** The ghost in the Room: Why Your Questions Don’t Scare God

**Intro: The Sunday Morning Mask**

Let’s be real for a second. I want to describe a scenario, and I want you to just nod internally if you’ve ever felt it.

It’s Sunday morning, or maybe a Friday night like this. The band is playing. The lights are dimmed. Everyone around you seems to be having a Moment. Maybe their hands are raised, or they have their eyes closed, and they look... peaceful. They look like they *know*. They look like they are connecting with something real and tangible.

And you’re standing there, and you feel absolutely nothing.

Actually, that’s not true. You don’t feel nothing. You feel like a fraud. You’re singing the lyrics—*“You make me brave,” “Good, Good Father”*—but in your head, there’s this nagging voice asking, “Is this even real? Am I just singing at the ceiling? Does anyone else feel like this is just emotional manipulation? If God is so good, why is the world so messed up?”

And then the fear hits. You think: *If I say this out loud, I’m out. If I admit I’m not sure about this whole Jesus thing, I’m a bad Christian. I’ve lost my faith.* So, you put on the mask. You smile, you sing the bridge, and you bury the question deep down where no one can see it.

If that’s you—if you’ve ever felt like the only imposter in the room—I want you to hear me clearly: You are not crazy. You are not a "bad Christian." And you are definitely not alone.

Tonight, we’re going to talk about the "D-word." Doubt.

**The Great Misunderstanding**

Somewhere along the line, a lot of us picked up a really bad definition of faith. We started thinking that faith is the same thing as certainty. We think faith means having zero questions, 100% confidence, and a brain that never argues with a sermon.

If faith is certainty, then doubt is the enemy. Doubt is the opposite of faith, right?

Wrong.

Certainty is the opposite of doubt. But faith? Faith actually *requires* doubt. Think about it. You don’t need "faith" that the sun will rise tomorrow; you have astronomical certainty. You don’t need "faith" that 2+2=4. You have proof.

Faith is what happens in the gap between what we know and what we hope for. If you knew everything for a fact, you wouldn’t need to trust God. You’d just have data.

The truth is, doubt isn’t a sign that your faith is dying. Usually, it’s a sign that your faith is growing up.

When you were five, your faith was simple. It was your parents’ faith. You believed because the people you trusted told you it was true. That’s a beautiful, childlike faith. But you aren't five anymore. You are seeing the world with your own eyes now. You’re seeing suffering. You’re learning biology and history. You’re experiencing heartbreak.

The faith that fit you when you were five won’t fit you when you’re fifteen. It’s like trying to wear your kindergarten t-shirt; it’s going to feel tight and uncomfortable. You have to stretch. And that stretching process? That feels like doubt. It feels like tearing. But it’s actually expansion.

**The Patron Saint of Honest Questions**

I want to look at a guy in the Bible who gets a really bad rap. You know him as "Doubting Thomas."

Poor Thomas. He follows Jesus for three years. He leaves his job, his family, his safety. At one point in the Gospel of John, when the other disciples are too scared to go to Judea because people want to kill Jesus, it’s Thomas who says, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”

Thomas was brave. He was loyal. But history remembers him for one bad week.

Here’s the scene: It’s the week after the resurrection. The disciples are hiding in a locked room, terrified. They tell Thomas, “We have seen the Lord! He’s alive!”

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s shoes. He watched Jesus die. He saw the brutality of the Roman Empire crush his best friend. His heart is broken. And now his friends are saying, “It’s okay! He’s back!”

Thomas isn't a cynic; he’s a realist. And more than that, he’s hurt. He is afraid to get his hopes up again just to have them crushed. So he says the famous line:

*“Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”*

We usually read that with a sneer, like Thomas is being stubborn. But I hear pain. I hear a guy saying, “I cannot build my life on a rumor. I need this to be real. I need to know.”

A week later, Jesus shows up.

Now, watch what Jesus *doesn't* do. He doesn't look at Thomas and say, “How dare you? After all I did for you? You have to question me? Get out.”

Jesus doesn't shame him. Jesus walks right up to Thomas—the one guy who couldn't just "take their word for it"—and he offers him his wounds. He says, “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side.”

Jesus meets Thomas in his doubt. He gives Thomas exactly what he needs to believe.

Here is the point: **God is not intimidated by your questions.**

God isn't up in heaven pacing the floor nervously because you read a science article that contradicts Genesis, or because you’re wondering why he allows suffering. He’s not fragile. He can handle your confusion. He can handle your anger. He can handle your "Why?"

In fact, I’d argue that until you ask the hard questions, your relationship with God is just polite. It’s surface level. It’s like being friends with someone but never talking about the thing that’s actually bothering you. Real intimacy happens when we get honest.

**The Difference Between Doubt and Cynicism**

Now, I do want to make a distinction. There is a difference between honest doubt and cynicism.

Cynicism is looking for an excuse to leave. It’s asking questions with your arms crossed, rolling your eyes, looking for a "gotcha" moment so you can walk away and do what you wanted to do anyway.

Honest doubt is different. Honest doubt is looking for a reason to stay. It’s saying, “God, I want to believe, but this doesn't make sense to me. Help me understand.”

It’s the difference between a heckler in the crowd and a student raising their hand in class. The heckler wants to destroy the speaker; the student wants to learn.

When you wrestle with God—when you bring him your raw, unfiltered questions—you aren't walking away from him. You are engaging with him.

There’s a concept in the gym called "muscle failure." To make a muscle grow, you have to lift weight until you literally can't anymore. You have to tear the fibers slightly so they rebuild stronger.

Doubt is spiritual muscle failure. You hit the limit of your current understanding. It hurts. It’s exhausting. But if you stay in the gym—if you keep bringing those questions to God and to safe community—you rebuild. And the faith you build on the other side is different.

It’s less "fluffy." It’s tougher. It’s gritty. It’s a faith that has been tested and survived. It’s a faith that knows that even when the lights go out, God is still there.

**No Pat Answers**

I know some of you have tried to ask questions before, and you got shut down. Maybe a parent, a pastor, or a leader gave you a bumper-sticker answer.
*“God works in mysterious ways.”*
*“You just need to pray more.”*
*“Don’t overthink it.”*

I’m sorry if that happened to you. Those answers are lazy, and they aren't helpful.

The Bible itself doesn't give pat answers. Have you read the Psalms? Half of them are David screaming at God. *“Where are you?” “Why do the wicked win?” “Have you forgotten me?”*

Have you read Job? It’s 35 chapters of a guy asking God why his life is falling apart, and God never actually gives him a clear reason. He just gives him His presence.

Sometimes, there isn't a neat answer. Sometimes the answer is, “We don’t know yet.” And that is a scary place to be. But it is also a holy place.

It is okay to sit in the tension. It is okay to say, “I love Jesus, but I don’t understand why hell exists.” It is okay to say, “I follow God, but I’m angry that my grandmother died.”

You don't have to resolve everything by the time the worship song ends. You can carry the question.

**A Vision for a Deep Faith**

Imagine if we stopped pretending.

Imagine if this youth group was a place where you didn't have to leave your brain at the door. Imagine if, when someone admitted they were struggling, we didn't panic and try to fix them, but instead said, “Yeah, that’s really hard. I don’t know either. Let’s look for the answer together.”

A faith that has been wrestled for is worth so much more than a faith that was just handed to you.

I know older people who have walked through fire. They’ve lost children, they’ve seen injustice, they’ve had their hearts broken. And yet, they still have a deep, quiet peace. Ask them about their faith. They won’t give you clichés. They will tell you that they yelled at God. They will tell you they doubted everything. But they will also tell you that in the middle of the darkness, when all the "religious" feelings stripped away, they found a Rock that didn't move.

That’s the goal. Not a faith that is blind, but a faith that sees the darkness clearly and trusts God anyway.

**The Practical Step**

So, how do we do this? How do we doubt *well*?

I want to challenge you to stop censoring your prayers. We often pray what we think we *should* say to God. "Dear Lord, thank you for this day, you are so good..." meanwhile, inside, you're anxious, angry, or numb.

God knows what you’re thinking anyway. You aren't fooling Him. So you might as well be honest.

Here is your challenge for this week. It’s a practice called **"The Box of Questions."**

I want you to take five minutes tonight or tomorrow morning. Get your phone, open the notes app, or grab a piece of paper.

I want you to write down the one question or doubt that you are most afraid to say out loud. The one that makes you feel like an atheist. The one that keeps you up at night.

Write it down. Look at it.

And then, I want you to talk to God about it. Not to ask for it to go away, but to acknowledge it. Pray something like this:

*“God, I don’t understand this. This [situation/verse/idea] really bothers me. I’m putting this in the box. I’m not walking away, but I need You to handle this, because I can’t right now. I’m going to keep following You, even while this question sits here.”*

And then, find one person—a leader here, a parent, a close friend—and tell them. "Hey, I’m struggling with [X]."

Don't carry it alone. Shadows get scary when you’re by yourself. When you turn the light on with a friend, the monsters tend to shrink.

You are loved. You are safe here. And your questions are welcome.

Let’s pray.

**Title:** The Ghost in the Room
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, honest, encouraging

***

(Pause. Look around the room. Don’t start with high energy; start with presence.)

I want to describe a scenario, and I want you to be honest with yourself about whether you’ve ever felt it.

Imagine you are in a room like this one. Maybe it’s at a summer camp, or a big youth rally, or just a Sunday morning service. The music is building. The lights are dim. The person next to you has their hands raised, tears streaming down their face, clearly having a significant spiritual moment. The person on your other side is singing with their eyes closed, looking totally at peace.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you feel… nothing. Or maybe not nothing. Maybe you feel like you’re watching a movie you don’t quite understand. You look at them, and then you look inside yourself, and you think, *“Am I missing the chip? Is my receiver broken? Why is this so real for them, but for me, it feels like I’m just standing in a room listening to a band?”*

And then the fear hits. The thought creeps in: *Maybe I’m faking it. Maybe I don’t actually believe this. Maybe I’m just here because my parents drove me, or because my friends are here.*

So, what do you do? Usually, you raise your hands anyway. You mouth the words. You learn the code. You learn how to nod during the sermon and say "Amen" at the right time. You construct a mask, because the alternative—admitting that you aren’t sure about any of this—feels terrifying. It feels like failure.

I want to talk about that feeling tonight. I want to talk about the ghost in the room that we’re all scared of: Doubt.

There is a massive misconception in Christian culture, one that I think does a lot of damage to people your age. It’s the idea that Faith and Doubt are enemies. We treat them like fire and water; if you have one, you can’t have the other. We think that if we are doubting, we are sinning, or we are backsliding, or we are losing our salvation.

But I want to offer you a different perspective tonight. I want to suggest that doubt is not the opposite of faith. Certainty is the opposite of faith. Doubt? Doubt is actually a symptom of growth. Doubt is the growing pains of a faith that is becoming your own.

Think about it this way. When you were five years old, you probably wore clothes that your parents picked out for you. You didn’t care about style or fit; you just wore the jacket because your mom handed it to you and said, "Put this on, it’s cold."

For a lot of us, that’s how our faith starts. It’s a "hand-me-down" faith. You believe because your parents believe, or because your pastor said so. It fits you because you’re small.

But then you hit 14, 15, 16. You start to grow. You start to see the world is complicated. You see suffering. You learn about science and history. You meet really kind, intelligent people who don’t believe what you believe. And suddenly, that hand-me-down jacket doesn’t fit anymore. It’s tight in the shoulders. The sleeves are too short. It’s uncomfortable.

When you feel that discomfort, you have two choices. You can keep squeezing yourself into a child’s jacket, pretending it fits, which makes you fake and miserable. Or, you can take the jacket off.

That moment—when you take off the childhood answers and you’re standing there shivering, waiting to find a faith that actually fits the adult you are becoming—that is doubt. It feels cold. It feels exposed. But it is the only way you get a faith that is actually yours.

We are not the first people to feel this. The Bible is actually full of people who wrestled with God, shouted at God, and questioned God.

Let’s talk about the guy who always gets a bad rap: Thomas.

You know him as "Doubting Thomas." History has given him this nickname like he’s the villain of the Easter story. But I love Thomas. I think Thomas is the patron saint of teenagers.

Here’s the context: Jesus has been killed. The disciples are hiding in a locked room, terrified that the Romans are coming for them next. They are traumatized. Their leader is dead. Their movement is over.

Then, the other disciples start saying, "We saw him! He’s alive!"

Now, put yourself in Thomas’s shoes. He wasn’t there when it happened. He’s hearing this impossible news. If Thomas was a fake, or if he just didn’t care, he would have just gone along with the group. He would have said, "Oh, cool, yeah, me too. Hallelujah." That’s the easy path. Groupthink is easy.

But Thomas respects the truth too much to fake it. He essentially says, *“I cannot believe this just because you tell me to. I saw him die. Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”*

That’s not a lack of faith; that is honesty. That is a man saying, *“I want this to be true, but I can’t risk my heart on a lie. I need to know.”*

A week later, the disciples are together again, and Thomas is there. Jesus shows up.

Now, watch what Jesus does *not* do.

Jesus does not look at Thomas and say, "How dare you? Everyone else believed. Why do you have to be so difficult? You’re a bad disciple. Get out."

Jesus doesn’t shame him. Jesus doesn’t give him a theology textbook. Jesus doesn’t tell him to just pray more and stop overthinking.

Jesus walks right up to Thomas, holds out his hands, and says, "Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side."

Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is. He gives Thomas the evidence he needs. He honors Thomas’s question with a presence.

This story tells me something vital: God is not intimidated by your questions. God is not fragile. You are not going to hurt God’s feelings by asking, "Are you really there?" or "Why do you allow suffering?" or "Why does the Bible say this weird thing?"

If God is real—if He is the creator of the universe, the architect of gravity and logic and the human brain—then He can handle your skepticism. In fact, I think He prefers your honest questions to your fake answers.

When you suppress your doubt, when you bury those questions because you think good Christians don’t ask them, those questions don’t die. They just rot. They turn into cynicism. They turn into bitterness. You end up leaving the faith not because you found answers that disproved God, but because you got tired of pretending you didn’t have questions.

Real faith is like a muscle. It only gets stronger when you tear it. When you lift a heavy weight, you are actually creating micro-tears in the muscle fibers. When they heal, they heal stronger.

Questions are the heavy weights. When you wrestle with a hard question—like "Why is there evil in the world?"—it tears at your childhood faith. It hurts. But if you stick with it, if you bring that question to God, to your leaders, to the text, what grows back is stronger. It’s a faith that has been tested. It’s a faith that understands nuance. It’s a faith that can survive the real world.

So, how do we do this? How do we doubt *well*?

First, stop looking for "pat answers." You know what I mean. The bumper-sticker slogans. "God works in mysterious ways." "Just let go and let God." "Everything happens for a reason."

Those phrases might be well-intentioned, but when you are in the middle of a crisis, they feel like a slap in the face. It is okay to reject clichés. It is okay to say, "That answer isn’t good enough for me right now."

Second, don’t doubt alone. This is the trap. The enemy wants you to isolate. He wants you to think you are the only one in the room who feels this way, because then you’ll feel shameful and keep your mouth shut.

If you talk to the leaders in this room—the adults who seem to have it all together—and you really ask them, "Have you ever wondered if this is all made up?", I guarantee you 90% of them will say, "Yes. Absolutely. Let me tell you about the time I almost walked away."

We are a community of people who are wrestling, not a club of people who have arrived.

And third, keep the conversation open with God. Even if the conversation is just you yelling at the ceiling.

There is a tradition in the Bible called "Lament." It’s basically complaining to God. The Psalms are full of it. David, the "man after God’s own heart," wrote songs that say, "God, where are you? Why have you forgotten me? Why do the bad guys win?"

God included those songs in the Bible. He put them in the playlist. That means He wants you to use them. You can pray your doubt. You can say, "God, I don’t feel you right now. I’m not sure I believe you’re listening. But I’m still talking. That’s all I’ve got."

That is a valid prayer. That is a faithful prayer.

I want to land this with a practical challenge.

I want you to think of the question you are most afraid to ask. The one that’s been sitting in the back of your mind, the one you think would get you kicked out of youth group if you said it out loud.

Maybe it’s about evolution. Maybe it’s about sexuality. Maybe it’s about hell. Maybe it’s just, "Why don’t I feel anything when I pray?"

I want you to go home tonight, take a piece of paper, or open the notes app on your phone, and write it down. Make it concrete.

Then, I want you to do something brave. I want you to bring that question into the light.

Maybe that means texting a leader here and saying, "Hey, can we grab coffee? I have a hard question." Maybe it means asking your parents. Maybe it means finding a book on the subject that isn’t afraid of the hard stuff.

But don’t let it stay in the dark. Monsters live in the dark. In the light, they just become things we have to deal with.

Your questions are not a sign that your faith is dying. They are a sign that your faith is trying to grow up. Don’t be afraid of the growing pains.

Let’s pray.

*God, thank you that you are big enough for our questions. Thank you that you didn’t turn Thomas away, and you won’t turn us away. For everyone in this room who feels like they are faking it, or feels like they are on the outside looking in, give them the courage to be honest. Help us to be a community where it is safe to struggle. We love you, even when we are confused by you. Amen.*

**Title:** The Ghost in the Room
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14–18)
**Tone:** Conversational, vulnerable, honest.

***

**(The speaker walks out, maybe sits on a stool rather than standing behind a podium. No notes, or just a single sheet. The vibe is low-pressure.)**

Hey everyone.

I want to start tonight by describing a specific feeling. I’m guessing a lot of you know it, but we rarely talk about it out loud because it feels dangerous.

Here’s the scene: You’re in a service, maybe here, maybe at a camp or a big conference. The music is building. The lights are low. The person leading worship is really into it, eyes closed, hands raised. You look to your left, and your friend is crying, clearly having a spiritual moment. You look to your right, and someone else is singing with their whole chest, looking totally connected to God.

And then there’s you.

You’re standing there, and you feel… nothing. Or maybe not nothing. Maybe you feel like a fraud. You’re singing the words—“I surrender all,” or “You are all I want”—but in your head, a little voice is whispering: *Do I really believe this? Is this even real? Or is this just emotional manipulation and lights and chords?*

You start thinking about that science documentary you watched last week, or the tragedy you saw on the news, or just the fact that your prayers lately have felt like they’re bouncing off the ceiling fan. And suddenly, you feel like there is a ghost in the room. That ghost is the thought: *Maybe I don’t believe any of this.*

And immediately, panic sets in. You think, *If I admit that, I’m out. If I admit I’m not sure, I’m a bad Christian. I’m failing.* So, you sing a little louder, you clap your hands a little harder, and you shove that ghost into the closet, hoping it suffocates.

I want to talk about that ghost tonight. I want to talk about doubt.

And I want to start by telling you something that might sound controversial, but I promise you it’s true: **Doubt is not the opposite of faith.** Unbelief is the opposite of faith. Cynicism is the opposite of faith. But doubt? Doubt is actually a part of faith. In fact, I’d argue that you can’t have a real, grown-up faith without it.

See, when you were five or six, the world was simple. Your parents were superheroes who could do no wrong. The moon followed your car home. God was a nice old man in the sky who gave you stuff if you were good. That’s "childhood faith." It’s beautiful, and it’s necessary for a kid. But you aren’t kids anymore.

You are teenagers. Your brains are literally rewiring themselves. You are waking up to the complexity of the world. You’re realizing your parents are human beings with flaws. You’re realizing the world is full of pain that doesn't make sense. If your faith doesn't struggle during this time, it means your faith isn't growing up with you. It means you’re trying to wear a toddler’s t-shirt on a teenage body. It’s going to feel tight. It’s going to feel uncomfortable. Eventually, it has to rip.

That ripping sound? That’s doubt. And it’s not a sign that you’re dying spiritually. It’s a sign that you’re growing.

I think the church has done you a disservice by making you feel like the goal of Christianity is "certainty." We act like the person with the strongest faith is the person who never has a question, who always smiles, and who has a Bible verse for every problem.

But when I open the Bible, I don’t see those people. I see people wrestling. I see people screaming at the sky.
