He’s the one who points at Jesus at the very beginning and says, "Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!"

John *knew*. He saw the dove come down. He heard the voice from heaven. If anyone should have had 100% certainty, it was John.

But fast forward a few years. John isn’t in the desert anymore; he’s in a dungeon. He got arrested for speaking truth to power. He’s sitting in a dark, damp cell, probably knowing he’s going to be executed. And Jesus? Jesus is out there healing people, sure, but he’s not overthrowing the government. He’s not getting John out of jail. He’s not acting like the conquering King John expected.

So, John—the guy who baptized Jesus—sends his friends to Jesus with a question. And the question is heartbreaking. He asks: *"Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?"*

Do you hear that? That is a crisis of faith. That is John saying, *Did I get this wrong? Did I waste my life? Are you actually who I thought you were?*

Now, pay very close attention to how Jesus responds.

If doubt was a sin, if questions were offensive to God, Jesus should have said, "Go tell John he should be ashamed of himself. Tell him to pray more and stop being so negative."

But he doesn’t do that.

He tells John’s friends to go back and report what they see—the blind seeing, the lame walking. He gives John evidence, but he doesn't give John a "Get Out of Jail Free" card. And then, after the messengers leave, Jesus turns to the crowd and calls John the Baptist the greatest man who ever lived.

*While John was doubting him,* Jesus was praising John.

Jesus wasn't offended by John’s question. He understood it. He understood that John’s circumstances didn't match his theology. And that’s where most of us live, isn't it? We read that God is good, but we see our friend get sick. We read that God provides, but we see our family struggle with money. We’re told God is close, but he feels a million miles away.

The gap between what we’re told and what we experience is where doubt lives.

So, what do we do with that?

Usually, we try two things that don't work.

Option one is **Suppression**. We fake it. We learn the Christian lingo. We nod during the sermon while making a grocery list in our heads. We treat faith like a fragile antique vase—if we touch it too hard or look at it too closely, it might shatter. So we put it on a shelf and never touch it. The problem is, a faith you can’t touch isn't real. It’s just decoration. And eventually, when a real crisis hits, that decorative faith will shatter anyway.

Option two is **Walking Away**. We decide that because we have *some* questions, the whole thing must be a lie. We throw the baby out with the bathwater. We think, *Well, I don't understand why God allows suffering, so God must not exist.* We trade the uncertainty of faith for the certainty of skepticism.

But I want to offer you a third option. **Wrestling.**

In the Old Testament, Jacob literally wrestles with God in the dirt all night long. He doesn't let go. He gets injured in the process—he walks with a limp for the rest of his life—but he also gets a blessing. He gets a new name: Israel. Do you know what Israel means? It means "He struggles with God."

God’s own people are named "The People Who Struggle with God."

God is not fragile. He is not intimidated by your questions. He is not up in heaven pacing back and forth nervously because you read a book about evolution or because you’re angry about a unanswered prayer. He’s big enough to handle your anger, your confusion, and your "Why?"

Actually, asking "Why?" is a form of prayer. Read the Psalms. Half of them are David complaining. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

If you are asking God where He is, you are still talking to Him. That is faith. It’s gritty, messy, unhappy faith, but it is faith. The only way to kill a relationship is silence. As long as you are bringing your doubt *to* God, rather than using your doubt to hide *from* God, you are in a relationship.

When you wrestle with these things, you move from a "Borrowed Faith" to an "Owned Faith."

Borrowed Faith is what you have from your parents or your youth pastor. It’s believing because someone told you to. Owned Faith is what happens on the other side of doubt. It’s saying, "Okay, I wrestled with this hard question. I didn't get a perfect answer, but I found enough Jesus to keep going. I trust Him, not because I have it all figured out, but because I know Him."

I’m not going to stand here and give you a three-step formula to fix your doubt. That would be insulting. Some of you are carrying heavy questions. Why did my parents get divorced? Why is the world burning? Why doesn't God speak to me like He seems to speak to others?

Those aren't questions that can be solved with a bumper sticker slogan.

But I will tell you this: The opposite of certainty isn't failure. It's trust.

Think about it. I don't need "faith" that the sun will rise tomorrow. I know it will. Physics dictates it. I need faith when I *don't* know the outcome. I need trust when I *can't* see the map.

If you are sitting here tonight feeling like an imposter because you have questions, I want you to take a breath. You are not a bad Christian. You are a human being in the process of knowing an infinite God. Of course you have questions. If you fully understood God, he wouldn't be God; he’d be something you invented.

So, here is how I want us to land this.

I want to invite you to stop running from the ghost in the room. Stop trying to fake it.

This week, I want you to try something scary. I want you to write a **"Raw Prayer."**

Find a quiet place. Get a notebook or the notes app on your phone. And I want you to write down everything you are afraid to say to God.

*   "God, I’m angry that..."
*   "God, I don't think you’re listening because..."
*   "God, this part of the Bible makes no sense to me..."
*   "God, are you even there?"

Write it all. Don't censor it. Don't try to make it sound "churchy." Don't add a "but I know you’re good" at the end if you don't feel it. Just write the raw, unfiltered truth.

And then, sit in the silence for a moment.

You won’t get struck by lightning. The floor won’t open up to swallow you.

What you might find, in that silence, is a strange sense of peace. Because you finally stopped pretending. You finally brought your whole self—shadows and all—into the light. And you will find that God is still there. He’s still looking at you with love. He’s not waiting for you to get your act together; He’s waiting for you to be honest.

You don't have to have it all figured out to belong here. This isn't a museum for perfect people. It’s a hospital for the hurting, and a laboratory for the curious.

Your questions are safe here. Your doubt is safe here. Keep wrestling. Keep asking. It’s how we grow.

Let's pray.

"God, thank you that you are big enough for our questions. Thank you that you didn't turn John away when he doubted, and you don't turn us away either. For the student here tonight who feels like they are faking it—give them the courage to be honest. Help us to trust you even when we can't trace you. We love you, even when we're confused by you. Amen."

I want you to imagine a scenario. Maybe you don’t have to imagine it because you’ve lived it. 

You’re sitting in a room much like this one. Maybe the band is playing, people have their eyes closed, and hands are raised. Or maybe you’re sitting in a circle in a small group, and everyone is nodding along to something the leader just said. Everyone around you seems so certain. They seem to just *get it*. 

And you are sitting there, looking around, and a quiet, terrifying thought creeps into your head: 

*“What if none of this is real?”*

Or maybe it’s not that broad. Maybe it’s more specific. Maybe it’s, *“How can a good God allow what happened to my family?”* Or, *“Why does the Bible say that one thing that seems so incredibly unfair?”* Or, *“Am I just believing this because my parents believe it, and I happen to live in a place where this is normal?”*

If you’ve ever had a moment like that, I want to guess what happened next. You probably panicked a little bit. You probably shoved the thought down as fast as you could, pasted a smile on your face, and hoped nobody could read your mind. Because in a lot of church cultures, we’ve been quietly taught that having questions means you are failing at faith. We’re taught that if you really loved God, you’d never have a shadow of a doubt. You’d just trust. 

So, when the questions come, we experience spiritual imposter syndrome. We think, *“If these people knew what was actually going on in my head, they’d ask me to leave.”*

I want to stop right here and tell you the most important thing you will hear tonight: Your doubt does not disqualify you. 

Doubt is not a sign that your faith is dying. More often than not, it’s a sign that your faith is trying to grow up. 

Think about it like this. When you are a kid, you wear the clothes your parents buy for you. You don’t think about it; you just put them on. Childhood faith is a lot like that. It’s an inherited faith. We believe what the adults around us tell us to believe. It’s simple, it’s neat, and it fits perfectly. 

But as you get older, your brain develops. You start paying attention to the world. You see real suffering. You encounter people who are brilliant and kind but who believe completely different things than you do. You experience heartbreak. 

Suddenly, that childhood faith feels like a pair of shoes you’ve outgrown. It pinches. It’s uncomfortable. It doesn’t fit the reality of the world you are actually living in. 

That discomfort? That’s doubt. And it is a completely normal, essential part of becoming an adult. You cannot develop a faith of your own without asking, *“Wait, do I actually believe this?”* 

We often treat doubt like it’s a sin. But the opposite of faith isn’t doubt. The opposite of faith is apathy—not caring at all. If you are doubting, it means you care enough about the truth to want to get it right. It means you are engaged. 

If you don’t believe me, I want to look at someone in the Bible. When we talk about doubt, people usually bring up Thomas. And Thomas is great, but I want to talk about someone else. I want to talk about John the Baptist. 

If anyone should have had zero doubts about Jesus, it was John. John was Jesus’ cousin. He was the ultimate insider. John’s entire life purpose, his whole career, was to prepare the way for Jesus. When Jesus finally showed up to start his ministry, John baptized him. John literally saw the heavens open; he saw the Spirit descend like a dove, and he heard the voice of God say, “This is my Son.” John pointed at Jesus in front of a crowd and yelled, “Look! The Lamb of God!”

He *knew*. He had the absolute, mountaintop, undeniable spiritual experience. 

But fast forward a little bit. Things don’t go the way John expected. John speaks truth to power, calling out a corrupt politician named King Herod. And for his trouble, John gets arrested and thrown into a dark, miserable dungeon. 

He’s sitting in a cell, facing execution. And meanwhile, he’s hearing rumors about what Jesus is doing. Jesus is healing people and preaching, sure. But Jesus isn’t overthrowing the Roman government. Jesus isn’t raining down fire on the corrupt politicians. Jesus isn’t breaking John out of prison. Jesus isn’t doing what John thought the Messiah was supposed to do.

So, sitting in the dark, John breaks. He sends his friends to track Jesus down and ask him a question. You can read this in Matthew chapter 11. John’s friends find Jesus and ask him, on John’s behalf: 

*“Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?”*

Just let the weight of that hit you. This is the guy who baptized Jesus. The guy who dedicated his entire life to announcing Jesus’ arrival. And now, he’s sitting in a cell, terrified, asking, *“Did I make a mistake? Was this all for nothing? Are you even who you say you are?”*

That is raw, agonizing doubt. It’s the doubt of someone who did everything right, and life still fell apart. 

Now, I want you to pay close attention to how Jesus reacts. Because how Jesus reacts to John is how God reacts to you. 

Jesus doesn’t get defensive. He doesn’t roll his eyes and say, “Oh my goodness, I literally had a dove land on me, what more does this guy want?” He doesn’t send a message back saying, “Tell John he needs to pray more and stop being so negative.” 

Instead, Jesus meets John’s doubt with deep compassion. He tells John’s friends, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised.” 

Jesus gives John evidence. He gently reminds John of the good work that is happening, even if it doesn’t look the way John expected it to. 

But here is the best part. After John’s friends leave to take the message back to the prison, Jesus turns to the crowd. The crowd just heard John’s moment of weakness. They just heard John question Jesus. And Jesus looks at the crowd and says, “Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist.”

In the exact moment of John’s deepest doubt, Jesus publicly defends his honor. He calls him the greatest. 

Jesus was not threatened by John’s questions. God is not threatened by yours. 

God is not insecure. He is not sitting up in heaven sweating because you watched a TikTok that made a really good point about evolution, or because you are angry that he didn’t heal your grandparent, or because you read a story in the Old Testament that makes you deeply uncomfortable. God is big enough to handle your questions. 

In fact, God invites them. Because a faith that cannot be questioned is a fragile faith. It’s a house of cards. If you never ask the hard questions, your faith will remain brittle. The moment a real storm hits—a tragedy, a betrayal, a massive failure—that brittle faith will shatter. 

But a faith that wrestles? A faith that says, *“God, I don’t understand this, and I’m angry, and I need you to show up”*? That is a robust faith. That’s a faith with deep roots. When you drag your doubts out into the light and wrestle with them, your faith stops being something you inherited from your parents, and it becomes something that belongs to *you*. 

So, what do we do with this? How do we handle the questions when they come?

The absolute worst thing you can do with doubt is hide it in the dark. When doubt is kept in isolation, it rots. It turns into cynicism. It turns into a cold, hard bitterness. 

Doubt needs air. It needs community. 

So, I want to give you a practical next step tonight. I want you to think of the biggest question you have right now. The one you’ve been afraid to say out loud. The “what if” or the “why” that lingers in the back of your mind when you’re trying to sleep. 

Your first step is simply to name it. You don’t have to solve it tonight. You just have to acknowledge it. Write it down on a piece of paper. Put it in the notes app on your phone. Just by articulating it, you take away some of its power to scare you. 

Your second step is to find someone safe to talk to. Not someone who will give you a cliché Christian bumper-sticker answer. Not someone who will just say, “Well, God works in mysterious ways, let’s pray about it.” Find someone who is a few steps ahead of you in life—a youth leader, a mentor, a parent, a pastor—someone whose faith you respect, but who you know is honest about their own struggles. 

Say to them, “I’m wrestling with this question, and I don’t expect you to have the perfect answer, but I just need to process it out loud.” 

A good leader won’t judge you. A good leader will probably say, “Yeah, I’ve wondered that too. Let’s look at it together.” 

You don’t have to have it all figured out. You are allowed to be a work in progress. You are allowed to have days where you believe with 100% certainty, and days where you are hanging on by a thread. 

Bring your questions. Bring your frustration. Bring your uncertainty. God is big enough for all of it, and there is a seat at the table for you, doubts and all.

But fast forward a little bit. Things don’t go the way John expected. John speaks truth to power, calling out a corrupt politician named King Herod. And for his trouble, John gets arrested and thrown into a dark, miserable dungeon. 

He’s sitting in a cell, facing execution. And meanwhile, he’s hearing rumors about what Jesus is doing. John was expecting a Messiah who would overthrow Rome and establish God's kingdom through power and judgment. But Jesus was doing something completely different—healing individuals, teaching about love, and seemingly ignoring the political corruption that John thought needed to be crushed. Jesus wasn’t breaking John out of prison. Jesus wasn’t doing what John thought the Messiah was supposed to do.

*“Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?”*

Jesus doesn’t get defensive. He doesn’t roll his eyes and say, “Oh my goodness, I literally had a dove land on me, what more does this guy want?” He doesn’t send a message back saying, “Tell John he needs to pray more and stop being so negative.”

Jesus gives John evidence. He gently reminds John of the good work that is happening, even if it doesn’t look the way John expected it to.

They just heard John question Jesus. And Jesus looks at the crowd and says, “Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist.”

God is big enough to handle your questions. 

In fact, God invites them. Because a faith that cannot be questioned is a fragile faith. It’s a house of cards. If you never ask the hard questions, your faith will remain brittle. And the moment a real storm hits—a tragedy, a betrayal, a massive failure—that brittle faith will shatter. 

But a robust faith? A faith that wrestles? A faith that says, *“God, I don’t understand this, and I’m angry, and I need you to show up”*? That is a faith with deep roots. When you drag your doubts out into the light and wrestle with them, your faith stops being something you inherited from your parents, and it becomes something that belongs to *you*. 

So, what do we do with this? How do we handle the questions when they come?

The absolute worst thing you can do with doubt is hide it in the dark. When doubt is kept in isolation, it rots. It turns into cynicism. It turns into a cold, hard bitterness. Doubt needs air. It needs community. 

So, I want to give you a practical next step tonight. I want you to think of the biggest question you have right now. The one you’ve been afraid to say out loud. The “what if” or the “why” that lingers in the back of your mind when you’re trying to sleep.

Someone who won't immediately try to "fix" your doubt with a Bible verse. Look for a person who will say, "That's a real question, and I've wondered that too," rather than "You just need to pray more." 

Say to them, “I’m wrestling with this question, and I don’t expect you to have the perfect answer, but I just need to process it out loud.” If you're not sure who that safe person is, I'm available after this talk, or you can text your small group leader this week. 

You might have that conversation and walk away with a clear answer. Or, you might walk away still uncertain, but just a little less alone with the uncertainty. Both are completely okay. Faith isn't about having all the answers perfectly lined up. It's about trusting God even when you don't.

You don’t have to have it all figured out. You are allowed to be a work in progress. You are allowed to have days where you believe with 100% certainty, and days where you are hanging on by a thread. 

Bring your questions. Bring your frustration. Bring your uncertainty. God is big enough for all of it, and there is a seat at the table for you, doubts and all.

I want you to imagine a scenario. It’s one you might be pretty familiar with. 

You’re standing in a room, maybe a room exactly like this one. The lights are turned low. The band is playing, the acoustic guitar is doing that slow, emotional strumming thing, and the people around you have their eyes closed. Some of them have their hands raised. They look peaceful. They look completely, one-hundred-percent certain. 

And you’re standing there, swaying a little bit so you don't look completely out of place, and a thought drops into your head out of nowhere: 

*What if I’m just making all of this up?*

Or maybe it’s a specific question: *If God is so good, why did my friend get sick?* Or, *How do I actually know any of this is real, and I wasn’t just born into the right family at the right time?*

If you’ve ever had a moment like that, I can guess what happened next. Your heart probably sped up. You might have felt a sudden rush of guilt, or a cold spike of panic. You looked around at the closed eyes and the raised hands, and you thought, *I am the only imposter in this room. Everyone else gets it. Everyone else has faith. I am broken.*

I want to stop right there and tell you the most important thing you will hear tonight: You are not an imposter. You are not broken. And you are definitely not the only person in the room wondering if the floor beneath you is solid.

In church culture, we have a really bad habit of treating doubt like a disease. We treat it like it’s highly contagious, and if we don’t quarantine the person asking the hard questions, they’re going to infect everyone else. We are often taught, directly or indirectly, that doubt is the opposite of faith. We are told that strong Christians don't question, they just trust.

But that is fundamentally untrue. It’s bad psychology, and it’s bad theology.

Let’s talk about the psychology first. You are teenagers. You are in a stage of life where your brain is literally rewiring itself. When you were a little kid, your brain was designed to accept whatever the adults around you told you. If your parents said the sky is blue, you believed them. If they said Noah put all the animals on a boat, you believed them. 

But right now, your brain is developing the capacity for abstract thought. You are biologically wired to start pulling apart the world you were handed, to look at the pieces, and to ask, *Does this actually make sense?* This is how you transition from an "inherited faith"—believing something because your parents or your youth pastor told you to—to an "owned faith"—believing something because you have wrestled with it and found it to be true for yourself. 

Doubt isn't a sign that your faith is dying. Doubt is a symptom of a growing mind. It means you are paying attention. It means you are taking this seriously enough to realize that it’s complicated.

But don't just take my word for it. Let’s look at the theology. Let’s look at how God actually responds to doubt in the Bible. 

Usually, when we talk about doubt, we talk about Thomas—the disciple who needed to touch the scars on Jesus’ hands before he believed. And we usually talk about him like he’s a cautionary tale: *Don't be a Doubting Thomas.* 

But I want to look at someone else tonight. I want to look at John the Baptist. 

If anyone should have had absolute, bulletproof certainty about Jesus, it was John. John was Jesus’ cousin. John was the guy who lived in the desert, eating locusts, yelling at the religious leaders, and preparing the way for the Messiah. John is the one who baptized Jesus. He literally saw the sky open up. He heard the voice of God say, "This is my beloved Son." John was there. He had the ultimate spiritual mountain-top experience.

But fast forward a bit, and John’s life has taken a dark turn. He has been arrested by a corrupt king named Herod. He is locked in a damp, dark dungeon. He is likely going to be executed. And Jesus—the guy John dedicated his entire life to, the guy John thought was going to overthrow the corrupt government and fix the world—is out in the countryside, preaching and going to dinner parties. He isn't overthrowing the government. And he certainly isn't breaking John out of prison.

Sitting in that dark cell, the mountain-top experience starts to fade. The reality of his suffering sets in. And John begins to doubt. *Did I get this all wrong? Did I waste my life for a fraud?*

So, John sends a few of his followers to find Jesus and ask him a question. It is the most brutally honest, heartbreaking question in the New Testament. They walk up to Jesus and say, "John wants to know: Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?"

Think about how offensive that question could have been. After everything they’d been through, John is questioning Jesus’ entire identity. 

If Jesus were like some modern Christians, he might have gotten defensive. He might have said, "Tell John he needs to pray more. Tell John to stop listening to secular music. Tell John he’s backsliding."

But Jesus doesn’t do that. He isn't threatened by John’s doubt. Jesus simply says to the messengers, "Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised." 

Jesus meets John’s doubt with evidence. He gently reminds John of what is true. 

But here is the best part of the story. It’s what happens *after* John’s messengers leave. Jesus turns to the crowd that has been watching this whole exchange. They’ve just heard John’s moment of weakness. And Jesus says to them, "Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist."

Do you see what just happened? In the very moment that John’s faith was at its absolute weakest, in the moment he was questioning everything, Jesus publicly defended him. Jesus called the doubting man the greatest man who ever lived. 

Jesus is not intimidated by your questions. He is not offended by your uncertainty. He does not love you less when you are standing in the dark, wondering if he is really there. 

We need to stop viewing doubt as a wrecking ball that destroys our faith, and start viewing it as a crucible that refines it. 

Think of a hermit crab. When a hermit crab grows, its shell gets too tight. It becomes uncomfortable. Eventually, the crab has to leave its shell and scurry across the ocean floor, completely naked and vulnerable, to find a bigger shell. 

That is what doubt is. It is the uncomfortable, vulnerable space between shells. 

You might be outgrowing the Sunday School version of God. When you were eight, it was enough to believe that God is a giant man in the sky who grants wishes if you’re good. But now you’re older. You’re seeing the pain in the world. You’re seeing hypocrisy. You’re reading science and history. And that old shell doesn't fit anymore. It’s cracking. 

That cracking feeling is doubt. And it is terrifying, because for a minute, you are out there in the open, and you feel like you're losing your faith. But you aren't losing your faith. You are just outgrowing a small version of God, so that you can step into a bigger, deeper, more mysterious version of God. A God who can handle your grief, your science, your logic, and your pain.

A faith that has never been tested is fragile. It’s made of glass. If you just smile and nod and pretend to believe everything perfectly, the minute real tragedy strikes your life, that glass faith will shatter. 

But a faith that has wrestled with doubt? A faith that has yelled at God in the dark? That faith is made of steel. It has been through the fire. It bends, but it doesn't break.

So, please, do not check your brain at the door when you walk into this building. Bring your intellect. Bring your skepticism. Bring your anger. God is big enough for all of it.

I want to leave you with a practical next step. Because it’s one thing to hear a talk about doubt; it’s another thing to actually face it. 

Sometime in the next couple of days, I want you to find a quiet place, pull out your phone or a piece of paper, and write down the one question you have been too afraid to ask out loud. What is the one thing about God, or the Bible, or church, that you are having the hardest time believing right now? Name it. Don't dress it up in nice religious language. Be as blunt as John the Baptist in that prison cell. 

Just sit with it for a minute. Notice that lightning doesn't strike you for writing it down. 

Then, I want to challenge you to find one safe person to share it with. Not someone who is going to panic. Not someone who is going to instantly quote a Bible verse at you and tell you to just "trust God." Find someone—a leader, a mentor, a parent, or a friend—who has lived a little life, who has a quiet, steady faith, and say to them: "I am struggling with this. Can we talk about it?"

You don't have to fake it here. You don't have to keep your eyes closed and your hands raised if your heart is full of questions. You are allowed to ask. You are allowed to seek. And I promise you, the God of the universe is not hiding from your search. 

Thanks, guys.

## The Uncomfortable Gift: Why Your Doubt Might Be the Healthiest Thing About Your Faith

**(Talk delivered to a youth group, ages 14-18)**

***

Hey everyone. Seriously, thanks for being here tonight.

I want to talk about something that we often treat like a spiritual disease—something we hide, confess in hushed tones, or pretend doesn’t exist, especially in a church setting.

I want to talk about doubt.

And I want to start by admitting that if you’re sitting here tonight feeling confused, skeptical, or even angry about what you believe, you are in the best possible place for growth.

### Part 1: The GPS Failure

Let’s start with a scenario. It’s happened to all of us.

You’re driving somewhere new, maybe it’s a college campus visit or a friend’s house deep in the suburbs. You’ve got the destination plugged into your phone. The voice is calm, confident: "In 500 feet, turn right." You follow it perfectly.

But then, the unthinkable happens. You’re on a road, but the little blue dot on the screen is spinning wildly. The voice starts looping the same instruction, or worse, it says, "Recalculating," and sends you down a dirt road leading to an abandoned warehouse.

In that moment, you have a physical, gut-level feeling of disorientation. The tool you trusted completely—the tool that promised clarity and direction—has failed you.

What do you do?

You don’t keep driving into the warehouse. You pull over. You turn the phone off and on again. You look at the paper map you keep in the glove box just in case. You start asking questions: *Where am I? Where was I trying to go? Is this map even accurate?*

That feeling of pulling over, of realizing the map you were handed isn't working for the terrain you’re actually driving on—*that* feeling is spiritual doubt.

And here’s the key: **Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Doubt is the moment you pull over and realize you need a better map.**

### Part 2: The Myth of The Perfect Christian

When we talk about faith, we are often shown a highly filtered, Instagram-ready version of it. We see the mountain-top moments: the instant healing, the sudden conversion, the person who always seems to know the perfect Bible verse for every situation.

We rarely see the middle part. We rarely see the messy, grinding, confusing middle where life doesn't make sense and God seems silent.

And because we only see the highlight reel, we develop the myth of the Perfect Christian. The Perfect Christian never questions the existence of God. The Perfect Christian never doubts the Bible. The Perfect Christian never gets angry at injustice.

When you, a normal, intelligent human being, start asking hard questions—*Does prayer actually work? Why do bad things happen to good people? Why does the church seem so hypocritical?*—you immediately assume you are failing. You assume you’ve lost your faith, or that you never had it in the first place.

I want to be absolutely clear tonight: **Doubt is not a sign of failure. It is a sign of intellectual and spiritual honesty.**

If your faith is real, it has to be able to withstand reality. If you are growing up—and you are—your understanding of the world is getting infinitely more complex. You’re learning about history, science, philosophy, and real human suffering.

If your faith stays the simple, black-and-white version you learned in Sunday School when you were eight, it will shatter when it hits the complexity of being eighteen.

Doubt is the necessary tool that forces you to upgrade your faith from the child’s version to the adult’s version. It means you are engaging, wrestling, and refusing to settle for easy answers.

### Part 3: The Prophet Who Argued with God

We often think of biblical heroes as people who had perfect, unwavering confidence. They didn't. They were often confused, terrified, and deeply doubtful.

Let’s look at a prophet named Habakkuk. He’s got a short book in the Old Testament, and he is perhaps the most honest skeptic in the entire Bible.

Habakkuk didn't doubt whether God existed. He doubted whether God was *good* or *fair*.

Habakkuk lived during a terrible time in Israel. There was violence, injustice, and corruption everywhere. He looked around and saw the wicked thriving and the righteous suffering.

So, what does he do? He goes to God and he shouts. Literally.

He opens his book with a complaint (Habakkuk 1:2-3):

> “How long, O Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?”

Read that again. Habakkuk is saying, "God, I see all this messed up stuff happening, and you are doing *nothing*. Why? If you are powerful and good, why is the world such a disaster?"

Now, imagine if we said that in church. We’d probably be told to pray harder or trust more.

But God doesn't zap Habakkuk. God doesn't tell him to shut up. God *answers* him.

God essentially says, "I hear you, Habakkuk. And I am doing something. I’m going to raise up the Babylonians—a terrible, violent nation—to destroy your people and bring judgment."

Wait. What?

Habakkuk is horrified. He was complaining about *small* injustice, and God responds by bringing *cataclysmic* injustice.

Habakkuk is basically like, "Whoa, whoa, whoa. That wasn’t what I meant! That’s a terrible plan! You are supposed to be holy! How can you use a nation even *more* wicked than us to punish us?"

He goes back to God, and this is the crucial part. Habakkuk 2:1 says:

> “I will stand at my watchpost and station myself on the tower; and I will look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint.”

He literally climbs up a tower, gets comfortable, and says, **"I have lodged my complaint. Now I am waiting for your response. I’m not leaving until I get an answer."**

Habakkuk models a faith that is not passive, but *engaged*. He treated God not as a fragile concept that couldn't handle his questions, but as a real being who could handle his anger, his skepticism, and his confusion.

His faith didn't deepen because God gave him an easy answer (God definitely didn't). His faith deepened because he was honest enough to ask the hardest questions and patient enough to wait in the confusion.

### Part 4: The Deepening

This is the central point: **Honest questions do not destroy faith; they deepen it.**

If you are afraid to ask a question because you fear the answer will wreck everything, you are operating under the assumption that the truth is the enemy of God. That’s a shaky foundation.

We have to move past the idea that faith is certainty. Certainty is easy. Certainty is knowing the answer before the question is even asked.

Faith, real faith, is trust in the midst of uncertainty. It's the decision to keep following the map even when the signal is weak and the road is dark.

When you encounter doubt, you have three choices:

1.  **Denial:** You stuff the question down, pretend it doesn't exist, and rely on platitudes. This leads to brittle faith that eventually snaps.

## When Faith Gets Complicated: Making Room for Doubt

**(Talk delivered to a youth group, ages 14-18)**

***

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here tonight.

I want to talk about the feeling that often makes us feel most alone in a room full of believers: doubt.

We often treat doubt like a spiritual failure—something we are supposed to hide, whisper about, or pray away immediately. But if you’re sitting here tonight feeling confused, skeptical, or even frustrated by questions you can’t answer, I want you to know something critical: you are not failing. You are engaging. This uncomfortable space you’re in can be a real turning point—painful, but deeply important for growth.

I know this feeling personally. I remember being your age, lying in bed after a youth retreat, and thinking: *What if I’m just repeating words into the air? What if prayer is just talking to the ceiling?* I didn’t tell anyone for months because I was terrified that admitting I was unsure meant I was abandoning my faith entirely.

But I learned that hiding that uncertainty didn't make it go away. It just made my faith brittle. Tonight, we’re going to talk about why bringing that doubt into the light is the healthiest thing you can do for your spiritual life.

### Part 1: Recalculating the Route

Let’s start with a scenario. It’s happened to all of us, even if you don't drive yet.

You’re navigating somewhere new—maybe it’s a big city using public transit, or you’re walking to a new friend’s house deep in the suburbs. You’ve got the destination plugged into your phone. The voice is calm, confident: "Turn left onto Maple Street." You follow it perfectly.

But then you hit a dead zone. The little blue dot on the screen starts spinning wildly. The voice says, "Recalculating," and then sends you down an alleyway that clearly leads nowhere.

In that moment, you get a physical feeling of disorientation. The tool you trusted completely—the tool that promised clarity and direction—has failed you.

What do you do?

You pull over. You stop walking. You look up from the screen and try to match the map to the actual terrain around you. You start asking questions: *Where am I, really? Where was I trying to go? Is the information I was given even accurate for this situation?*

That feeling of pulling over, of realizing the simple instructions you were given don't match the complex road you’re actually traveling—*that* feeling is spiritual doubt.

And here’s the key: **Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Doubt is the moment you pull over and realize you need to upgrade your navigation system.** It means you are demanding reality from your beliefs.

### Part 2: Faith is a Relationship, Not an Answer Key

When we talk about faith, we are often shown a highly filtered, highlight-reel version. We see the dramatic conversions, the instant healings, the people who always seem to have the perfect, confident answer for everything.

We rarely see the messy, grinding, confusing middle where life doesn't make sense and God seems silent.

We develop the myth of the Perfect Christian—the person who never questions the Bible, never doubts the existence of God, and never gets angry at the injustice in the world.

As you get older, your understanding of the world is getting infinitely more complex. You’re learning about history, science, philosophy, and real human suffering. If your faith stays the simple, black-and-white version you learned when you were eight, it will shatter when it hits the complexity of being eighteen.

Doubt is the necessary tool that forces you to upgrade your faith.

I want to offer a simple distinction:

**Faith is not certainty.** Certainty is knowing the answer before the question is even asked.
**Faith is trust in the midst of uncertainty.** It is the decision to keep showing up even when the signal is weak and the road is dark.

And here’s another helpful distinction: **Doubt versus Unbelief.**

*   **Unbelief** says, "I'm done listening. I've concluded this is false."
*   **Doubt** says, "I'm not sure. I don't understand, and this is painful, but I'm still here. I’m still listening."

If you are struggling with doubt, you are not failing. You are choosing to wrestle rather than walk away. You are choosing to maintain the relationship even when the relationship feels confusing.

### Part 3: The Prophet Who Demanded Honesty

We often picture biblical heroes as people with perfect, unwavering confidence. They weren't. They were often confused, terrified, and deeply doubtful.

Let’s look at a prophet named Habakkuk. He’s got a short book in the Old Testament, and he is perhaps the most honest skeptic in the entire Bible.

Habakkuk didn't doubt whether God existed. He doubted whether God was *operating justly* or *on time*.

Habakkuk lived during a terrible time in Israel. There was violence, corruption, and oppression. He looked around and saw the wicked thriving and the righteous suffering. He saw the injustice right in front of him.

So, he does something radical. He doesn't pray a polite prayer. He takes his complaint directly to God, and he shouts (Habakkuk 1:2-3):

> “How long, O Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?”

Habakkuk is essentially putting God on trial. He's saying, "If you are powerful and good, why is the world such a disaster? You are silent when I need you most."

Now, imagine if we said that in church. We’d probably be told to pray harder. But God doesn't zap Habakkuk. God *answers* him.

God essentially tells Habakkuk: "I hear you. And I am doing something. I’m going to use the Babylonians—a terrifying, violent nation—to bring judgment."

Habakkuk is horrified. He was complaining about the oppression of his own people, and God responds by bringing a confusing and terrifying judgment that involves an even more wicked nation.

Habakkuk is basically saying, "Wait, that’s not what I asked for! That’s a terrible plan! How can you use a nation even *more* wicked than us to discipline us? How does that prove you are holy?"

He goes back to God, and this is the crucial moment. Habakkuk 2:1 says:

> “I will stand at my watchpost and station myself on the tower; and I will look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint.”

He literally climbs up a tower, gets comfortable, and says, **"I have lodged my complaint. Now I am waiting for your response. I’m not leaving until I hear from you."**

Habakkuk models a faith that is not passive, but *engaged*. He treated God not as a fragile concept that couldn't handle his anger, but as a real being who could handle his deepest skepticism.

His faith didn't deepen because God gave him an easy answer. His faith deepened because he was honest enough to ask the hardest questions and patient enough to decide to trust *despite* the confusion.

### Part 4: The Path of Engagement

### Part 5: The Practice of Honesty

So, how do we move forward when the navigation system is spinning and we feel lost?

We stop hiding the doubt. We name it. We use doubt as a tool for spiritual inventory.

Right now, if you’re struggling, you probably have a cloud of vague skepticism hovering over you. We need to break that cloud down into specific, manageable questions.

Here is the practical step I want to offer you this week. It requires honesty, and maybe a pen and paper or a note on your phone.

#### Step 1: The Doubt Inventory (The Watchpost)

I want you to take 10 minutes this week, find a quiet spot, and write down the three most difficult, troubling, or confusing questions you have about faith right now.

Don’t filter them. Don’t worry if they sound blasphemous or dumb. Just capture them. They might be about suffering, science, the church, or the Bible.

Once you have your list of three, pick the one that feels the most urgent. And then, I want you to sit with this single question for a few days—not trying to answer it, but just acknowledging its presence.

I want you to try the Habakkuk approach. Take that question to God, or to a journal entry, and say: **"This is my confusion. This is my complaint. I am not walking away, but I am staying put until I find a deeper truth or learn how to trust while the answer is unclear."**

#### Step 2: The Conversation (The Relational Step)

Doubt thrives in isolation. It shrivels in community.

This week, I want you to choose one safe person—a trusted leader, a parent, a mentor, or even a close, wise friend.

You need to take your most urgent question and share it with them. But don’t just dump it on them. Give them a context so they don't feel pressured to give a pat answer.

Here is a simple script you can use:

> **“I’ve been wrestling with [insert your question]. I’m not trying to argue, and I don’t expect you to solve it right now. I just need to say it out loud to a safe person. Could you just listen to me for five minutes and tell me how you’ve handled questions that have no easy answers?”**

When you share your doubt in community, you realize you are not alone, and you gain access to the wisdom and experience of others who have wrestled through similar things.

#### Step 3: The Model Prayer

Finally, I encourage you to read the entire book of Habakkuk (it takes about 10 minutes). Read it not as a history lesson, but as a model for how to pray when you are angry and confused. Circle the sentences that sound like something you’ve wanted to say to God.

If you keep bringing your honest questions into the light, your faith has a chance to become resilient. It will be built on rock, not sand.

Don’t be afraid of the dark corners of your mind. God is already there. Let’s start talking honestly about what we really believe.

Thank you.

## The Engine of Growth: Why Your Questions Don’t Break Your Faith

**(Setting: The speaker is standing, perhaps leaning on a stool or table, looking relaxed and making direct eye contact with the group.)**

Hey everyone. Thanks for showing up tonight.

I want to talk about something that is often whispered about in these spaces, or sometimes ignored entirely, but which I guarantee every single one of you has experienced, probably this week.

I want to talk about doubt.

And before anyone mentally checks out because they think I’m about to give you five steps to *cure* doubt, I need you to know this: I’m not here to cure it. I’m here to normalize it, maybe even celebrate it.

Let’s be real for a minute. You are at an age where you are constantly being told what to believe. You’ve inherited traditions, rules, values, and yes, beliefs, from your parents, your teachers, your friends, and certainly from the people who run this youth group.

But you are also at an age where your brain is finally fully equipped to ask: *Wait, is that actually true?*

### The GPS on the Cliff Edge

Let me start with a scenario.

Imagine you are driving late at night—maybe you just got your license, maybe you’re borrowing your parents’ car—and you are following your GPS to a friend’s house deep in the countryside. It’s foggy, it’s dark, and you are totally dependent on that little electronic voice.

The voice says, “Turn right now.”

You look right. All you see is a sheer drop, a ravine, and a sign that clearly says, “Danger: Road Closed. Bridge Out.”

Now, what do you do?

The GPS has been right 99 times out of 100. It’s the trusted authority. It’s the voice you rely on. But your eyes, your gut, your actual immediate experience, is screaming: *If I turn right, I will drive off a cliff.*

Do you trust the authority, or do you trust your doubt?

You slam on the brakes. You stop. You check the map, you look for alternatives, you probably curse the technology. That moment of stopping—that is doubt. It is the intelligent refusal to follow instructions blindly when your internal sense of reality is screaming red alert.

In faith, we often treat doubt like that cliff. We think if we pause, if we question the instructions we’ve been given, we are rejecting God entirely. We believe that the opposite of faith is doubt.

But I want to challenge that.

**The opposite of faith isn't doubt. The opposite of faith is certainty.**

Certainty says, “I have all the answers, I don’t need to look any further.” Doubt says, “I need to know if this path is real, and I need to know why I’m taking it.”

### Doubt is Not Failure; It’s the Engine of Growth

If you are 14, 16, 18, and you are starting to question the stories you grew up with—if you are wondering why bad things happen, or why the rules seem arbitrary, or if the whole thing isn’t just a nice cultural tradition—that is not a sign that you are failing as a Christian.

**It is a sign that you are growing up.**

You are transitioning from *inherited belief* to *personal conviction*.

Inherited belief is like wearing clothes your parents bought you. They fit okay, they keep you warm, but they aren't *you*. Personal conviction is choosing your own style, tailoring the clothes, maybe even ripping them and sewing them back together until they perfectly match who you are becoming.

Inherited faith is comfortable, but it is fragile. The moment life hits you—a major illness, a crisis of injustice, a deep intellectual challenge in a college lecture hall—inherited faith shatters because it has no internal bracing.

Doubt is the process of building that internal bracing. It is the internal resistance training for your soul. You don’t get stronger muscles by lifting air; you get stronger by lifting heavy weights.

When you allow yourself to ask the hard, scary questions—the ones that feel too big or too disrespectful to say out loud—you are adding the necessary resistance that turns fragile belief into resilient conviction.

So, if you are wrestling right now with the existence of God, the goodness of God, or the relevance of God, please hear this: **That wrestling is the most honest prayer you can offer.**

### The Prophet Who Threw a Fit

We often look for examples of faith in the Bible that are neat and tidy—people who just said, "Yes, Lord," and everything worked out. But the Bible is actually filled with people who were deeply skeptical, profoundly angry, and totally confused.

Let’s talk about a prophet named **Habakkuk**.

Habakkuk is not famous like Moses or David. He’s a short book, tucked away in the Old Testament, but he is arguably the most relatable person in the entire Bible for a teenager wrestling with the world.

Habakkuk didn't doubt God's existence. He doubted God's *sense*.

He looked around his world and saw corruption, injustice, violence, and chaos. And he was furious. He didn’t whisper his concerns; he shouted them.

In Chapter 1, Habakkuk opens with a brutal complaint, essentially yelling at God:

> *“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?”*

He’s saying, "God, I see all this evil, and you’re just sitting there. You’re silent. You’re useless."

He is not being respectful. He is being brutally honest. He is doubting God's competence and God's care.

And here is the amazing thing: **God doesn't smite him.** God doesn't tell him to shut up and have more faith.

God responds.

God explains that He *is* working, but He’s working in a way Habakkuk cannot possibly understand yet. God tells Habakkuk that the answer is coming, but it’s going to be slow, messy, and totally unexpected.

Habakkuk’s response is not instant obedience. He goes to his watchtower—his place of observation—and says, essentially, "I’m going to wait here and see what you say, and then I’m going to see if I agree with it."

This is the process of faith. It’s the back-and-forth conversation. It’s the argument that leads to deeper understanding.

Habakkuk didn't get his easy answers. He didn't get a tidy solution to the world's injustice. But by the end of the book, after wrestling, arguing, waiting, and listening, he doesn’t have certainty, but he has **trust**.

You slow down, look right, and all you see is a sheer drop, a ravine, and a sign that clearly says, “Danger: Road Closed. Bridge Out.”

Now, what do you do?

The GPS has been right 99 times out of 100. It’s the trusted authority. But your eyes, your gut, your immediate experience, is screaming: *If I turn right, I will drive off a cliff.*

You slam on the brakes. You stop. That moment of stopping—that intelligent refusal to follow instructions blindly—that is doubt.

In faith, we often treat doubt like that cliff. We think if we pause, if we question the instructions we’ve been given, we are rejecting God entirely. We believe that the opposite of faith is doubt.

You are transitioning from *inherited belief* to *personal conviction*.

Inherited belief is like wearing clothes your parents bought you. They fit okay, but they aren't *you*. Personal conviction is choosing your own style, tailoring the clothes, and wearing them because you chose them.

Inherited faith is comfortable, but it is fragile. The moment life hits you—a crisis of injustice, a deep intellectual challenge in a college lecture hall—inherited faith shatters because it has no internal bracing.

Doubt is the process of building that internal bracing. It is the internal resistance training for your soul. You don’t get stronger muscles by lifting air; you get stronger by lifting heavy weights.

### The Prophet Who Threw a Fit

We often look for examples of faith in the Bible that are neat and tidy—people who just said, "Yes, Lord," and everything worked out. But the Bible is actually filled with people who were deeply skeptical, profoundly angry, and totally confused.

Let’s talk about a prophet named **Habakkuk**.

He’s saying, "God, I see all this evil, and you’re just sitting there. You’re silent. You’re useless."

He is not being respectful. He is being brutally honest. He is doubting God's competence and God's care.

God responds.

Habakkuk’s response is not instant obedience. He goes to his watchtower—his place of observation—and says, essentially, "I’m going to wait here and see what you say, and then I’m going to see if I agree with it."

This is the process of faith. It’s the back-and-forth conversation. It’s the argument that leads to deeper understanding.

### The Power of the Honest Question

In a world saturated with information, your greatest spiritual asset is your ability to ask intelligent, penetrating questions.

I know some of you are wrestling with things you learned in biology class, or maybe you read something online about historical criticism, or you’re seeing injustice in the world that seems to contradict everything we say about God’s goodness. Too many church environments try to treat faith like a fragile antique—something you can’t touch, can’t examine, and must only admire from a distance. If you touch it, it might break.

But real faith is not an antique. It’s a tool. It's a relationship.

If your faith is so fragile that one question about evolution, or suffering, or the historical accuracy of a text can destroy it, then you didn’t have faith; you had a pleasant assumption.

**Honest questions do not destroy faith; they destroy assumptions.**

And assumptions are what keep us stuck at the surface level.

When you encounter something difficult—a theological contradiction, a scientific finding that seems to conflict with Genesis, or a personal tragedy that makes you doubt God’s goodness—do not sweep it under the rug. Do not feel guilty for the confusion.

Instead, lean into it. Treat that doubt as a spiritual compass pointing you toward the next phase of your journey.

When you ask, "Why does God allow suffering?" you are not rejecting God. You are demanding a deeper theology of compassion.

When you ask, "Is the Bible really true?" you are not rejecting Scripture. You are seeking a more robust understanding of history, literature, and divine inspiration.

When you ask, "Do I really believe this?" you are taking ownership of your spiritual life.

### Avoiding the Pat Answers

### The Next Step

So, what do we do with this doubt? We use it. We honor it. We let it drive us.

If you have doubt, you are not broken. You are awake.

I want to offer you one practical next step. It’s an exercise in honesty, inspired by Habakkuk’s radical prayer.

Find a notebook, or open a blank document on your phone or laptop. Call it your **"Complaint Box"** or your **"Honest Questions"** file.

*   *Why did God let [Terrible Thing] happen?*
*   *If God is good, why are my prayers ignored?*
*   *Is this all just a comfort mechanism?*

Once you have written it down, you have done two things:

2. You have created a starting point for deeper investigation.

You have permission to be messy. You have permission to be angry. You have permission to doubt.

Don’t let your questions scare you. Let them guide you. Thank you.

But you are also at an age where your brain is finally fully equipped to ask: *Wait, is that actually true? Does this actually make sense?*

### The GPS on the Cliff Edge

Let me start with a scenario.

Imagine you are driving late at night—maybe you just got your license, maybe you’re borrowing your parents’ car—and you are following your GPS to a friend’s house deep in the countryside. It’s foggy, it’s dark, and you are totally dependent on that little electronic voice.

The voice says, “Turn right now.”

You look right. All you see is a sheer drop, a ravine, and a sign that clearly says, “Danger: Road Closed. Bridge Out.”

Now, what do you do?

The GPS has been right 99 times out of 100. It’s the trusted authority. It’s the voice you rely on. But your eyes, your gut, your actual immediate experience, is screaming: *If I turn right, I will drive off a cliff.*

Do you trust the authority, or do you trust your doubt?

You slam on the brakes. You stop. You check the map, you look for alternatives, you probably curse the technology. That moment of stopping—that is doubt. It is the intelligent refusal to follow instructions blindly when your internal sense of reality is screaming red alert.

In faith, we often treat doubt like that cliff. We think if we pause, if we question the instructions we’ve been given, we are rejecting God entirely. We believe that the opposite of faith is doubt.

But I want to challenge that.

**The opposite of faith isn't doubt. The opposite of faith is certainty.**

I know that sounds backwards. We usually think certainty is the goal. But certainty is what you have about a math equation: 2+2=4. You don't need faith for that; you have proof. Faith, however, is what you have in a relationship—and relationships require risk, trust, and vulnerability, not proof.

Certainty says, “I have all the answers, I don’t need to look any further.” Doubt says, “I need to know if this path is real, and I need to know why I’m taking it.” Doubt is the engine that moves you from blind obedience to conscious commitment.

### Doubt is Not Failure; It’s the Engine of Growth

If you are 14, 16, 18, and you are starting to question the stories you grew up with—if you are wondering why bad things happen, or why the rules seem arbitrary, or if the whole thing isn't just a nice cultural tradition—that is not a sign that you are failing as a person of faith.

**It is a sign that you are growing up.**

You are transitioning from *inherited belief* to *personal conviction*.

Inherited belief is like wearing clothes your parents bought you. They fit okay, they keep you warm, but they aren't *you*. Personal conviction is choosing your own style, tailoring the clothes, maybe even ripping them and sewing them back together until they perfectly match who you are becoming.

Inherited faith is comfortable, but it is fragile. The moment life hits you—a major illness, a crisis of injustice, a deep intellectual challenge in a college lecture hall—inherited faith shatters because it has no internal bracing.

And I want to be honest—that process can feel terrifying. It's not always a fun wardrobe refresh. Sometimes it feels like losing something you desperately needed. It feels like freefall. That fear is real, and it’s okay.

Doubt is the process of building that internal bracing. It is the internal resistance training for your soul. You don’t get stronger muscles by lifting air; you get stronger by lifting heavy weights.

When you allow yourself to ask the hard, scary questions—the ones that feel too big or too disrespectful to say out loud—you are adding the necessary resistance that turns fragile belief into resilient conviction.

So, if you are wrestling right now with the existence of God, the goodness of God, or the relevance of God, please hear this: **That wrestling is the most honest prayer you can offer.**

### The Prophet Who Threw a Fit

We often look for examples of faith in the Bible that are neat and tidy—people who just said, "Yes, Lord," and everything worked out. But the Bible is actually filled with people who were deeply skeptical, profoundly angry, and totally confused.

Let’s talk about a prophet named **Habakkuk**.

Habakkuk is not famous like Moses or David. He’s a short book, tucked away in the Old Testament, but he is arguably the most relatable person in the entire Bible for a teenager wrestling with the world.

Habakkuk didn't doubt God's existence. He doubted God's *sense* and God's *justice*.

He was watching his world fall apart—corruption at the top, violence in the streets, the powerful crushing the weak. He was furious that God was letting the injustice happen. He didn’t whisper his concerns; he shouted them.

In Chapter 1, Habakkuk opens with a brutal complaint, essentially yelling at God:

> *“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?”*

He’s saying, "God, I see all this evil, and you’re just sitting there. You’re silent. You’re useless."

He is not being respectful. He is being brutally honest. He is doubting God's competence and God's care.

And here is the amazing thing: **God doesn't smite him.** God doesn't tell him to shut up and have more faith.

God responds.

But here’s the critical detail: God’s answer isn't comforting. God tells Habakkuk, "I *am* doing something, but you won't believe it when I tell you." God explains that He is raising up the Babylonians—a terrifying, brutal, pagan empire—to bring judgment.

Habakkuk’s reaction is not peace. His reaction is horror. He says (and I’m paraphrasing): "Wait, that’s your answer? You’re going to use people even worse than the ones we have now? That doesn't solve the injustice; it makes it ten times worse! I asked for justice, and you gave me a nightmare."

The conversation got harder before it got better. God’s answer didn't clarify everything; it deepened the mystery.

Habakkuk’s next move is key. He goes to his watchtower—his place of observation—and says, essentially, "I’m going to wait here and see what you say, and then I’m going to see if I agree with it."

This is the process of faith. It’s the back-and-forth conversation. It’s the argument that leads not to easy answers, but to deeper understanding of the character of the one you are arguing with.

Habakkuk didn't get his tidy solution to the world's injustice. But by the end of the book, after wrestling, arguing, waiting, and listening, he doesn’t have certainty, but he has **trust**.

He says (in Chapter 3):

> *"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior."*

He moved from, "I believe in God because my life is good and makes sense," to, "Even if everything falls apart, even if I don't understand the plan, I still choose to trust the character of the one I’ve been talking to."

That is a faith forged in fire. That is conviction built on honest questioning.

### The Power of the Honest Question

In a world saturated with information, your greatest spiritual asset is your ability to ask intelligent, penetrating questions.

Too many church environments try to treat faith like a fragile antique—something you can’t touch, can’t examine, and must only admire from a distance. If you touch it, it might break.

But real faith is not an antique. It’s a tool. It's a relationship.

If your faith is so fragile that one question about evolution, or suffering, or the historical accuracy of a text can destroy it, then you didn't have faith; you had a pleasant assumption.

**Honest questions do not destroy faith; they destroy assumptions.**

And assumptions are what keep us stuck at the surface level.

When you encounter something difficult—a theological contradiction, a scientific finding that seems to conflict with Genesis, or a personal tragedy that makes you doubt God’s goodness—do not sweep it under the rug. Do not feel guilty for the confusion.

Instead, lean into it. Treat that doubt as a spiritual compass pointing you toward the next phase of your journey.

When you ask, "Why does God allow suffering?" you are not rejecting God. You are demanding a deeper theology of compassion.

When you ask, "Is the Bible really true?" you are not rejecting Scripture. You are seeking a more robust understanding of history, literature, and divine inspiration.

When you ask, "Do I really believe this?" you are taking ownership of your spiritual life.

I've sat with some of these questions for years. Some of them I still don't have answers to. And I've found that the sitting—the refusing to pretend I'm fine with something I'm not fine with—has done more for my faith than any easy answer I’ve ever received.

Sometimes, the best, most faithful answer we can give each other is vulnerability: **"That is a brutally honest question, and I don't have a satisfying answer. But let's look for one together."**

Spiritual maturity isn't having all the answers; it’s having the courage to live with the unanswered questions, holding them up to the light, and continuing to walk forward anyway.

### The Next Step

So, what do we do with this doubt? We use it. We honor it. We let it drive us.

If you have doubt, you are not broken. You are awake.

I want to offer you one practical next step. It’s an exercise in honesty, inspired by Habakkuk’s radical prayer.

Find a notebook, or open a blank document on your phone or laptop. Call it your **"Complaint Box"** or your **"Honest Questions"** file.

And I want you to write down, without filtering, without apologizing, every single doubt, frustration, or cynical thought you have about God, the church, or faith.

*   *Why does this rule feel stupid?*
*   *Why did God let my friend suffer like that?*
*   *What if none of this is real?*
*   *If God is good, why are my prayers ignored?*

Write your complaints like Habakkuk did—loudly, honestly, directly to God. Get it all out.

This is not a project to solve in one night. This is a practice of spiritual honesty.

Once you have written it down, you have acknowledged the truth of your current struggle.

Now, a second, equally important step: **Find one person you trust.** Maybe it's a leader, a parent, a mentor, or a friend who you know will listen without judgment. Don't ask them to solve your entire list. Just pick one item—one doubt, one complaint—and say it out loud to another human being.

Doubt is harder to carry alone. The moment you share it, you create a space for real faith to breathe.

You have permission to be messy. You have permission to be angry. You have permission to doubt.

The journey of faith is not a flat, smooth road to certainty. It is a rugged, winding path where the honest questions you ask today are the work itself. Some of those questions will find answers. Some won't—not for years, maybe not ever. But the asking is not wasted. The asking is the work.

Don’t let your questions scare you. Let them guide you. Thank you.

## The Engine of Growth: Why Your Questions Don’t Break Your Faith

**(Setting: The speaker is standing, perhaps leaning on a stool or table, looking relaxed and making direct eye contact with the group.)**

Hey everyone. Thanks for carving out time to be here tonight.

I want to start with a confession. I remember sitting in a youth group room, probably about where some of you are right now, and the leader was talking about how simple faith was. And all I could think was: *I don't believe any of this.*

I felt like an imposter. I felt guilty. I thought that if I admitted that huge, terrifying gap between what I was supposed to believe and what I actually felt, the whole spiritual infrastructure of my life would collapse.

I want to talk about that feeling. I want to talk about doubt.

And before anyone mentally checks out because they think I’m about to give you five steps to *cure* doubt, I need you to know this: I’m not here to cure it. I’m here to normalize it, maybe even celebrate it.

You are at an age where you are doing the most important work of your life: figuring out who you are and what you actually believe. You’ve inherited traditions, rules, values, and yes, beliefs, from the people who raised you.

But you are also at an age where your brain is finally fully equipped to ask: *Wait, is that actually true?* And more importantly: *Is it true for me?*

### The GPS on the Cliff Edge

Let me start with a scenario we can all relate to, even if you don't have your license yet.

Imagine you are driving late at night. You are completely dependent on your GPS to navigate a tricky, dark country road. It’s foggy, you can’t see the signs, and you are trusting that little electronic voice implicitly.

The voice says, “Turn right now.”

You look right. But instead of a road, all you see is a sheer drop, a ravine, and a sign that clearly says, “Danger: Road Closed. Bridge Out.”

Now, what do you do?

The GPS has been right 99 times out of 100. It’s the trusted authority. It’s the voice you rely on. But your eyes, your gut, your actual immediate experience, is screaming: *If I turn right, I will drive off a cliff.*

Do you trust the authority, or do you trust your doubt?

You slam on the brakes. You stop. You check the map, you look for alternatives, you probably curse the technology. That moment of stopping—that intelligent refusal to follow instructions blindly when your internal sense of reality screams red alert—that is doubt.

In faith, we often treat doubt like that cliff. We think if we pause, if we question the instructions we’ve been given, we are rejecting God entirely. We believe that the opposite of faith is doubt.

But I want to challenge that idea completely.

**The opposite of faith isn't doubt. The opposite of faith is certainty.**

Certainty says, “I have all the answers, I don’t need to look any further.” Certainty is stagnant. Doubt says, “I need to know if this path is real, and I need to know why I’m taking it.” Doubt is the engine that drives you forward.

### Doubt is Not Failure; It’s the Engine of Growth

If you are 14, 16, 18, and you are starting to question the stories you grew up with—if you are wondering why bad things happen, or why the rules seem arbitrary, or if the whole thing isn't just a nice cultural tradition—that is not a sign that you are failing as a person of faith.

**It is a sign that you are growing up.**

You are transitioning from *inherited belief* to *personal conviction*.

Inherited belief is like wearing clothes your parents bought you. They fit okay, they keep you warm, but they aren't *you*. They are fragile. The moment life hits you—a major illness, a crisis of injustice, a deep intellectual challenge in a college lecture hall—inherited faith shatters because it has no internal bracing.

Doubt is the process of building that internal bracing. It is the spiritual resistance training for your soul. You don’t get stronger muscles by lifting air; you get stronger by lifting heavy weights.

When you allow yourself to ask the hard, scary questions—the ones that feel too big or too disrespectful to say out loud—you are adding the necessary resistance that turns fragile belief into resilient conviction.

So, if you are wrestling right now with the existence of God, the goodness of God, or the relevance of God, please hear this: **That wrestling is the most honest prayer you can offer.**

### The Prophets Who Complained

We often think that people in the Bible just had perfect, clean faith. But if you actually read the Bible, it is filled with people who were deeply skeptical, profoundly angry, and totally confused.

Think about Thomas. We call him "Doubting Thomas." Why? Because when everyone else claimed Jesus was resurrected, Thomas said, "Show me the receipts. I need to put my fingers in the holes." He needed physical evidence. And Jesus didn't scold him; he showed up and invited Thomas to investigate. Thomas’s doubt led to one of the most powerful declarations in the New Testament: "My Lord and my God!"

But let’s talk about someone even angrier: a prophet named **Habakkuk**.

Habakkuk is tucked away in the Old Testament, but he is incredibly relatable for anyone wrestling with the world’s injustice. Habakkuk didn't doubt God's existence. He doubted God's *sense* and God's *timing*.

He was living in Judah, and things were bad. The rich were corrupt, the courts were rigged, and violence was everywhere. Habakkuk looked at the chaos, and he was furious. He didn’t whisper his concerns; he shouted them directly at God.

In Chapter 1, Habakkuk opens with a brutal complaint, essentially yelling:

> *“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save? Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?”*

He’s saying, "God, I see all this evil, and you’re just sitting there. You’re silent. You’re useless."

He is not being respectful. He is being brutally honest. He is doubting God's competence and God's care.

And here is the amazing thing: **God doesn't strike him down or tell him to shut up and have more faith.**

God responds. God explains that He *is* working, but He’s working in a way Habakkuk cannot possibly understand yet—by bringing the terrifying Babylonians to judge Judah.

Habakkuk’s response is not instant obedience. He goes to his watchtower—his place of observation—and says, essentially, "I’m going to wait here and see what you say, and then I’m going to see if I agree with it."

This is the process of faith. It’s the back-and-forth conversation. It’s the argument that leads to deeper understanding. It’s the Psalms, which are full of people screaming, "Where are you, God? Why have you abandoned me?"

Habakkuk didn't get his easy answers. He didn't get a tidy solution to the world's injustice. But by the end of the book, after wrestling, arguing, waiting, and listening, he doesn’t have certainty, but he has **trust**.

He says (in Chapter 3):

> *"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food... yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior."*

He moved from conditional faith ("I believe in God because my life is good and makes sense") to unconditional trust ("Even if everything falls apart, even if I don't understand the plan, I still choose to trust the character of the one I’ve been talking to"). That is conviction forged in fire.

### The Power of the Honest Question

In a world saturated with information, your greatest spiritual asset is your ability to ask intelligent, penetrating questions.

Too many church environments try to treat faith like a fragile antique—something you can’t touch, can’t examine, and must only admire from a distance. The fear is: if you touch it, it might break.

But real faith is not an antique. It’s a tool. It's a relationship.

If your faith is so fragile that one question about evolution, or suffering, or the historical accuracy of a text can destroy it, then you didn’t have faith; you had a pleasant assumption.

**Honest questions do not destroy faith; they destroy assumptions.**

When you encounter something difficult—a theological contradiction, a scientific finding, or a personal tragedy—do not sweep it under the rug. Do not feel guilty for the confusion. Instead, lean into it. Treat that doubt as a spiritual compass pointing you toward the next phase of your journey.

When you ask, "Why does God allow suffering?" you are not rejecting God. You are demanding a deeper theology of compassion. When you ask, "Do I really believe this?" you are taking ownership of your spiritual life. This process is messy, and it’s okay if you don't find the answers right away. Faith is trusting God even in the dark spaces where the answers aren't clear.

### Avoiding the Pat Answers

I know you guys are smart. You can spot inauthenticity from a mile away.

So, let me be clear: I am not going to stand here and offer you easy, bumper-sticker answers to your deepest doubts.

If you are struggling with the problem of evil, I won't tell you, "God works in mysterious ways." That’s a cliché that shuts down conversation. If you are struggling with scientific conflict, I won't tell you, "Just pray harder." That insults your intelligence.

Sometimes, the best, most faithful answer we can give each other is vulnerability: **"That is a brutally honest question, and I don't have a satisfying answer. But let's look for one together."**

True spiritual maturity isn't having all the answers; it’s having the courage to live with the unanswered questions, holding them up to the light, and continuing to walk forward anyway.

### The Next Step

So, what do we do with this doubt? We use it. We honor it. We let it drive us.

If you have doubt, you are not broken. You are awake.

Here’s what I want to invite you to do with that doubt. It’s an exercise in honesty, inspired by Habakkuk’s radical prayer.

Find a notebook, or open a blank document on your phone or laptop. Call it your **"Complaint Box"** or your **"Honest Questions"** file.

And I want you to write down, without filtering, without apologizing, every single doubt, frustration, or cynical thought you have about God, the church, or faith.

*   *Why does this rule feel stupid?*
*   *Why did God let [Terrible Thing] happen?*
*   *If God is good, why are my prayers ignored?*
*   *Is this all just a comfort mechanism?*

Write your complaints like Habakkuk did—loudly, honestly, directly to God. Get it all out.

This is not a project to solve in one night. This is a practice of spiritual honesty.

Once you have written it down, you have done two things:
1. You have acknowledged the truth of your current struggle.
2. You have created a starting point for deeper investigation.

You have permission to be messy. You have permission to be angry. You have permission to doubt.

Because the journey of faith is not a flat, smooth road to certainty. It is a rugged, winding path where the honest questions you ask today become the foundations of the deep, resilient conviction you will hold tomorrow.

Don’t let your questions scare you. Let them guide you. Go be honest. Go write your complaints. God can handle them. And I promise, your faith will be stronger for it.
