Good evening, everyone.

I want to start tonight by doing something that might feel a little uncomfortable. I want us to picture a specific moment.

Imagine it’s a Sunday night. You’re sitting right here, or maybe at church in the morning. The lights are dimmed, the music is swelling, the worship leader is singing that one song that everyone loves, and people around you are starting to raise their hands. You see the older kids, the leaders, maybe even your parents, and they all look… peaceful. They look like they have it together. They look certain.

And inside, you feel like you’re screaming.

Or maybe it’s quieter than a scream. Maybe it’s just a low-level hum of confusion. You’re looking at the lyrics on the screen about how God is good and how He is in control, and a voice in the back of your head whispers, *“Are you sure about that? Because the world looks like a mess, and my life feels chaotic, and I’m not actually sure if any of this is real.”*

If you’ve ever felt that, I want you to take a deep breath. Because I’m not going to tell you to stop feeling it. I’m not going to tell you that you’re broken. I’m not going to tell you that you need to just "try harder" to believe.

We’re going to talk about doubt tonight.

And the first thing I want to say—maybe the most important thing—is that if you are doubting, you are not doing it wrong. You are not failing at being a Christian. In fact, I would argue that you are right where you need to be.

Here is the lie we often believe: We think faith is the opposite of doubt. We think faith looks like a straight line of absolute certainty, where you never question and never waver. And if you dip below that line—if you ask a question, if you wonder why God allows pain, if you struggle with what the Bible says about a certain topic—we think we’ve lost the game.

But faith isn’t certainty. Faith is trust.

Think about it this way: You can know for a fact that a chair exists. You can see it. You can touch it. That’s certainty. But sitting in the chair? That’s trust. You don’t sit in a chair because you’ve studied the structural integrity of its legs. You sit in it because you believe it will hold you.

Right now, many of you are in a phase where you’re inspecting the chair. You’re kicking the legs. You’re wondering, “Is this thing going to collapse?” That can be terrifying. But it’s also necessary. Because a faith that hasn’t been inspected, a faith that hasn’t been wrestled with, isn’t really your faith. It’s just your parents’ faith. It’s borrowed luggage. You’re just carrying it around because you were told to.

Eventually, you have to open the bag and see what’s inside. You have to decide if you’re going to keep carrying it. And that process? That process involves doubt.

I think we need to look at the Bible for a minute, because we tend to sanitize the characters in it. We turn them into plastic action figures with perfect halos. But if you actually read the text, it’s full of people who are messed up, confused, and angry at God.

My favorite example of this is a guy named Jacob.

If you know Jacob’s story, you know he wasn’t exactly a saint. He was a twin, but he cheated his brother out of his birthright and his inheritance. He lied to his dad. He was a manipulator. He spent years running away from his mistakes.

Eventually, Jacob has to go home. He has to face his brother, Esau, who probably wants to kill him. The night before they meet, Jacob sends his family ahead and camps out by a river. The Bible says he is alone. And in the middle of the night, a “man” shows up. We understand this to be God or an angel representing God.

And they wrestle.

They wrestle all night long. It’s physical, it’s messy, it’s exhausting. It’s not a polite conversation. It’s a fight.

As the sun comes up, the man realizes he can’t overpower Jacob, so he touches Jacob’s hip and wrenches it out of its socket. But Jacob refuses to let go. The man says, “Let me go, it is daybreak.”

And Jacob says this incredible line. He says, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

Think about that. Jacob is wrestling with God. He is in pain, his hip is dislocated, he is exhausted, and he is holding onto the very being that is hurting him. Why? Because he is desperate. He knows that his only hope is in this relationship, even if he doesn’t understand it. Even if it hurts.

And God doesn't strike him down for asking questions. God doesn't say, "How dare you fight me." Instead, God blesses him. He changes Jacob’s name to Israel, which literally means “He struggles with God.”

The nation that God chose to represent Him on earth is named "The One Who Wrestles with God."

I love that. It means that doubt is not the opposite of faith. The opposite of faith is apathy. The opposite of faith is indifference. Doubt? Doubt is often a sign that you care deeply. Doubt means you are paying attention to the gap between what the world is and what it should be. Doubt means you are paying attention to the silence of God when you expected a shout.

So, how do we handle this? Because let’s be honest, doubt feels terrible. It feels like walking through a fog. You can’t see the path, you can’t see your hand in front of your face, and you feel lost.

We usually try to fix the fog in one of two ways. We either panic and try to manufacture fake certainty—pretending we believe things we don’t, which just leads to bitterness—or we walk away completely.

But there is a third option. And that is to walk through the fog.

I want to offer you a vision of doubt that is different than the one you might have been told. I want to suggest that honest questions don’t destroy your faith; they deepen it.

Think about your friendships. Who are your closest friends? Are they the people you only talk to about the weather? Or are they the people you’ve cried with? The people you’ve argued with? The people where you’ve said, “Hey, that really hurt me,” or “I don’t understand why you did that”?

Conflict and honesty usually deepen intimacy. When you stop pretending to be perfect, you actually connect.

It’s the same with God.

When you stop pretending you have it all figured out, you stop relating to a concept and start relating to a Person. You stop treating God like a formula to be solved and start treating Him like a Father who is big enough to handle your frustration.

Now, I have to be honest with you. I can’t give you a neat little formula where you ask your question and God gives you a PDF with the answer. That usually doesn’t happen. In fact, sometimes you ask the question and the answer is… silence.

That is the scariest part. When you say, “God, are you there?” and you hear nothing.

But even the silence is an answer. The silence forces you to decide: Do I trust God’s character when I can’t see His hand? Do I believe He is good even when my circumstances are not?

This is where the "limp" comes in. Remember Jacob? He walked away from that wrestling match with a permanent limp. He never walked the same way again.

I think that’s what doubt does to us. It changes the way we walk. It strips away the arrogant, cocky faith that says, “I know everything,” and it replaces it with a humble, quiet faith that says, “I don’t know everything, but I know Who I’m walking with.”

Maybe you’re here tonight and you’re struggling with the intellectual side of things. Maybe it’s science, or the problem of evil, or how the Bible fits with modern life.
Maybe you’re struggling with the emotional side. You’ve prayed for something—maybe a parent to get better, maybe a relationship to be restored, maybe for depression to lift—and it didn’t happen. And you’re thinking, “Why bother?”

I want to validate those questions. They are not disrespectful. They are human. And God is not scared of them.

So, what do we do with this? How do we move forward?

I want to give you a practical next step. It’s not about reading your Bible more, although that’s good. It’s not about praying harder, although that’s good too.

Tonight, I want to invite you to write a letter.

Not a letter to a friend. A letter to God.

I want you to be brutally, painfully honest. No church words. No “Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for this day.” I want you to write the raw stuff.

Write down your doubts. “God, I don’t think you’re listening.”
Write down your anger. “God, this isn’t fair.”
Write down your confusion. “God, I don’t understand why the Bible says this.”

Put it all on paper. And then, I want you to do something scary. I want you to ask Him one question at the end. Ask Him, “If you are real, and if you are good, can you help me trust you even with this question?”

Don’t expect an immediate lightning bolt. Just leave it there.

Because faith isn’t the absence of doubt. Faith is trusting God enough to bring your doubt to Him, rather than hiding it.

We are a people who wrestle. And if you’re wrestling tonight, you are in good company. You are walking in the footsteps of Jacob, and David, and Job, and Jesus himself, who cried out in the garden, “Is there another way?”

You are not alone. And the fog is not the end of the story. It is just the valley you walk through to get to the mountain. Keep walking. Keep asking. And don't let go until you are blessed.

And then, I want you to do something scary at the end of that letter. I want you to ask Him one question. Ask Him, “If you are real, and if you are good, can you help me trust you even with this question?”

Don’t expect an immediate lightning bolt. Just leave it there.

You are not alone. And the fog is not the end of the story. It is just the valley you walk through to get to the mountain. Keep walking. Keep asking. And don't let go until you are blessed.

Good evening, everyone.

I want to start tonight by doing something that might feel a little uncomfortable. I want us to picture a specific moment.

Imagine it’s a Sunday night. You’re sitting right here, or maybe you were at church this morning. The lights are dimmed, the music is swelling—the worship leader is playing that one song everyone knows, and people around you are starting to raise their hands. You look at the older kids, the leaders, maybe even your parents, and they all look… peaceful. They look like they have it together. They look certain.

And inside, you feel like you’re screaming.

Or maybe it’s not a scream. Maybe it’s quieter than that. Maybe it’s just a small, cold voice in the back of your head that says, *“I don’t think I believe this anymore.”*

You look at the lyrics on the screen about how God is good and how He is in control, and you look at the world—a world that feels messy, broken, and chaotic—and that voice whispers, *“Are you sure about that? Because this doesn’t look like a plan. This looks like a mess.”*

If you’ve ever felt that, I want you to take a deep breath. I’m not going to tell you to stop feeling it. I’m not going to tell you that you’re broken. I’m not going to tell you that you just need to "try harder" to believe.

We’re going to talk about doubt tonight.

And the first thing I want to say—maybe the most important thing—is that if you are doubting, you are not doing it wrong. You aren’t failing at being a Christian. In fact, if I’m being honest with you, I still have days where I kick the tires of my own faith. I still have moments where I look at the news or the pain in my own life and think, *“God, are you actually there?”*

I say that to let you know you aren’t alone. We often think that the people on stage or the adults in our lives have graduated from doubt. But they haven’t. We just get better at hiding it.

Here is the lie we often believe: We think faith is the opposite of doubt. We think faith looks like a straight line of absolute certainty where we never question and never waver. And if you dip below that line—if you ask a question, if you wonder why God allows pain, if you struggle with what the Bible says about a certain topic—we think we’ve lost the game.

But faith isn’t certainty. Faith is trust.

Think about your best friend. You don’t have a signed contract with them guaranteeing they’ll never hurt your feelings. You don’t have "certainty" that they won’t disappoint you eventually. Statistically speaking, they probably will let you down at some point. But you trust them. You show up at their house. You tell them secrets. You invest in the relationship.

Faith isn't about having a contract with God that explains every clause of the universe. Faith is showing up. It’s trusting that He knows what He’s doing, even when you don’t have the answers.

Right now, many of you are in a phase where you’re inspecting that relationship. You’re kicking the tires. You’re wondering, “Is this thing going to collapse?” That can be terrifying. But it’s also necessary. Because a faith that hasn’t been inspected, a faith that hasn’t been wrestled with, isn’t really your faith. It’s just your parents’ faith. It’s borrowed luggage. You’re just carrying it around because you were told to.

Eventually, you have to open the bag and see what’s inside. You have to decide if you’re going to keep carrying it. And that process? That process involves doubt.

I think we need to look at the Bible for a minute, because we tend to sanitize the characters in it. We turn them into plastic action figures with perfect halos who never mess up. But if you actually read the text, it’s full of people who are messed up, confused, and angry at God.

My favorite example of this is a guy named Jacob.

If you know Jacob’s story, you know he wasn’t exactly a saint. He was a twin, but he cheated his brother out of his birthright and his inheritance. He lied to his blind dad to get a blessing. He was a manipulator and a schemer. He spent years running away from his mistakes, living in exile.

Eventually, Jacob has to go home. He has to face his brother, Esau, who is coming to meet him with an army, and Jacob is terrified that Esau is going to kill him. The night before they meet, Jacob sends his family and everything he has ahead of him across a river, and he camps out alone on the other side.

The Bible says he is alone. And in the middle of the night, a “man” shows up. We understand this to be God, or an angel representing God.

And they wrestle.

They wrestle all night long. It’s physical, it’s messy, it’s exhausting. It’s not a polite theological discussion in a coffee shop. It’s a fight in the dirt.

As the sun comes up, the man realizes he can’t overpower Jacob, so he touches Jacob’s hip and wrenches it out of its socket. Imagine that pain. But Jacob refuses to let go. The man says, “Let me go, it is daybreak.”

And Jacob says this incredible line. He says, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

Think about that. Jacob is wrestling with God. He is in pain, his hip is dislocated, he is exhausted, and he is holding onto the very being that just hurt him. Why? Because he is desperate. He knows that his only hope is in this relationship, even if he doesn’t understand it. Even if it hurts.

And God doesn't strike him down for asking questions. God doesn't say, "How dare you fight me." Instead, God blesses him. He changes Jacob’s name to Israel, which literally means “He struggles with God.”

God didn't pick a people named "The Ones Who Had It All Figured Out." He picked "The Ones Who Wrestle." If your faith feels like a fight right now, you are actually acting more like the chosen people of God than the people who pretend everything is fine.

I love that. It means that doubt is not the opposite of faith. The opposite of faith is apathy. The opposite of faith is indifference. Doubt? Doubt is often a sign that you care deeply. Doubt means you are paying attention to the gap between what the world is and what it should be. Doubt means you are paying attention to the silence of God when you expected a shout.

So, how do we handle this? Because let’s be honest, doubt feels terrible. It feels like walking through a fog. You can’t see the path, you can’t see your hand in front of your face, and you feel lost.

For some of you, that doubt is in your head. You’re sitting in science class or history, and you’re thinking, “How does this match up with Genesis?” or “How can a good God allow natural disasters?”

For others of you, the doubt is in your gut. It’s emotional. You prayed for a parent to get better, and they didn’t. You prayed for a relationship to be fixed, and it fell apart. And the silence feels like a door slammed in your face.

We usually try to fix the fog in one of two ways. We either panic and try to manufacture fake certainty—pretending we believe things we don’t, which just leads to bitterness—or we walk away completely.

But there is a third option. And that is to walk through the fog.

I want to offer you a vision of doubt that is different than the one you might have been told. I want to suggest that honest questions don’t destroy your faith; they deepen it.

Think about your friendships again. Who are your closest friends? Are they the people you only talk to about the weather? Or are they the people you’ve cried with? The people you’ve argued with? The people where you’ve said, “Hey, that really hurt me,” or “I don’t understand why you did that”?

Conflict and honesty usually deepen intimacy. When you stop pretending to be perfect, you actually connect.

It’s the same with God.

When you stop pretending you have it all figured out, you stop relating to a concept and start relating to a Person. You stop treating God like a formula to be solved and start treating Him like a Father who is big enough to handle your frustration.

Now, I have to be honest with you. I can’t give you a neat little formula where you ask your question and God gives you a PDF with the answer. That usually doesn’t happen. In fact, sometimes you ask the question and the answer is… silence.

That is the scariest part. When you say, “God, are you there?” and you hear nothing.

But I want to suggest that even the silence is an answer. The silence isn't necessarily a "no." Sometimes, the silence is the space where God is teaching you to walk by touch rather than by sight. The silence forces you to decide: Do I trust God’s character when I can’t see His hand? Do I believe He is good even when my circumstances are not?

This is where the "limp" comes in. Remember Jacob? He walked away from that wrestling match with a permanent limp. He never walked the same way again.

I think that’s what doubt does to us. It changes the way we walk. It strips away the arrogant, cocky faith that says, “I know everything,” and it replaces it with a humble, quiet faith that says, “I don’t know everything, but I know Who I’m walking with.”

It changes you from someone who demands answers to someone who seeks a Person.

So, what do we do with this? How do we move forward when we feel like we’re in the fog?

I want to give you a practical next step. It’s not about reading your Bible more, although that’s good. It’s not about praying harder, although that’s good too.

Tonight, I want to invite you to write a letter.

Not a letter to a friend. A letter to God.

Write down your doubts. “God, I don’t think you’re listening. This feels like a waste of time.”
Write down your anger. “God, this isn’t fair. Why did you let this happen?”
Write down your confusion. “God, I don’t understand why the Bible says this, and it feels hateful.”

Put it all on paper. Don’t hold back. Give God the full file.

And then, I want you to do something scary. I want you to ask Him one question at the end. Ask Him, “If you are real, and if you are good, can you help me trust you even with this question?”

You could keep it in your Bible. Let it sit there next to the Psalms, which are full of these same kinds of angry, honest prayers. Let it be a reminder that you brought the ugly stuff to Him.
Or, maybe you need to burn it. Safely, of course. Burn it as a symbol that you are giving this weight to Him. You’re handing it over.
Or, if you’re brave enough, come find me or another leader you trust. Say, “I wrote this letter, and I want to read it to someone.”

The act of writing it? That is the act of faith. You are talking to Someone you aren't sure is there. That is what trust looks like.

Faith isn’t the absence of doubt. Faith is trusting God enough to bring your doubt to Him, rather than hiding it.

We are a people who wrestle. And if you’re wrestling tonight, you are in good company. You are walking in the footsteps of Jacob, and David, and Job, and Jesus himself, who cried out in the garden, “Is there another way?”

You are not alone. And the fog is not the end of the story. It is just the valley you walk through to get to the mountain. Keep walking. Keep asking. And don't let go until you are blessed.

You see the older kids, the leaders, maybe even your parents, and they all look… peaceful. They look like they have it together. They look certain.

And inside, you feel like you’re screaming.

Or maybe it’s quieter than a scream. Maybe it’s just a low-level hum of confusion. You’re looking at the lyrics on the screen about how God is good and how He is in control, and a voice in the back of your head whispers, *“Are you sure about that? Because the world looks like a mess, and my life feels chaotic, and I’m not actually sure if any of this is real.”*

I know that feeling. I remember being about sixteen, staring at the back of someone’s head during a service, and thinking, “If they knew what I was thinking right now, they’d think I was a fraud.” I felt like the only one in the room who was pretending.

If you’ve ever felt that way, I want you to take a deep breath. Because I’m not going to tell you to stop feeling it. I’m not going to tell you that you’re broken. I’m not going to tell you that you just need to "try harder" to believe.

We’re going to talk about doubt tonight.

You don’t sit in a chair because you’ve studied the structural integrity of its legs. You sit in it because you believe it will hold you.

Right now, many of you are in a phase where you’re inspecting the chair. You’re kicking the legs. You’re wondering, “Is this thing going to collapse?” That can be terrifying. But it’s also necessary. Because a faith that hasn’t been inspected, a faith that hasn’t been wrestled with, isn’t really your faith. It’s just your parents’ faith. It’s borrowed luggage. You’re just carrying it around because you were told to.

Eventually, you have to open the bag and see what’s inside. You have to decide if you’re going to keep carrying it. And that process? That process involves doubt.

If you want to know what it looks like to stop carrying borrowed luggage and start unpacking your own faith, we have to look at the people who did it first. We tend to sanitize the characters in the Bible. We turn them into plastic action figures with perfect halos. But if you actually read the text, it’s full of people who are messed up, confused, and angry at God.

My favorite example of this is a guy named Jacob.

If you know Jacob’s story, you know he wasn’t exactly a saint. He was a twin, but he cheated his brother out of his birthright and his inheritance. He lied to his dad. He was a manipulator and a grifter. He spent years running away from his mistakes because his brother, Esau, probably wanted to kill him.

Eventually, Jacob has to go home. He has to face the music. The night before they meet, Jacob sends his family ahead and camps out by a river. The Bible says he is alone. And in the middle of the night, a “man” shows up. We understand this to be God or an angel representing God.

And they wrestle.

They wrestle all night long. It’s physical, it’s messy, it’s exhausting. It’s not a polite conversation. It’s a fight. And this is the part that matters: God chooses to wrestle with Jacob. He doesn't pick a polished prophet. He picks the cheat, the liar, the guy on the run. God meets him right in the middle of his mess.

Write down your doubts. “God, I don’t think you’re listening.”
Write down your anger. “God, this isn’t fair.”
Write down your confusion. “God, I don’t understand why the Bible says this.”

Don’t expect an immediate DM back with the answer. Just leave it there.

One youth leader, one parent who gets it, one friend who won't panic. And say one true sentence: "I'm not sure I believe this right now." That's it. Doubt shared out loud loses some of its power to strangle you.

Because faith isn’t the absence of doubt. Faith is trusting God enough to bring your doubt to Him, rather than hiding it.

We are a people who wrestle. And if you’re wrestling tonight, you are in good company. You are walking in the footsteps of Jacob, and David, and Habakkuk, and Jesus himself, who cried out in the garden, “Is there another way?”

You are not alone. The valley feels low and dark, but it is just the path to the mountain. Keep walking. Keep asking. And don't let go until you are blessed.

I want to start tonight by telling you about a feeling I suspect many of you know, but we rarely talk about out loud. It usually happens about ten minutes after a really intense worship song or a really good sermon. You know, that moment when the lights are dim, the music is swelling, everyone around you has their eyes closed and hands raised, and they look… totally captured. They look like they have zero questions, zero hesitations, and like they have it all figured out.

And you’re standing there, clapping along, maybe singing the words, but inside, there’s this quiet, nagging voice. It’s saying something like: *“Is this actually real? Do I believe this? Or am I just going through the motions because everyone else is?”*

Maybe for you, it’s not even during the service. Maybe it’s on a Tuesday night when you’re lying in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking about the pain in the world, or the science class you sat through, or the bad thing that happened to a good person, and you think, “I’m not sure if God is actually there. I’m not sure if any of this holds up.”

If you have ever felt that, I have two things to tell you. First: me too. Second: you are not alone, and you are not doing it wrong.

We have this tendency in religious circles to treat doubt like a dangerous contaminant. Like it’s a virus. We think if we admit we’re struggling, we’re somehow being unfaithful. We think that certainty is the goal, and if you don’t have it, you’re failing at being a Christian. But tonight, I want to suggest something that might feel a little radical: I don’t think doubt is the opposite of faith. I think certainty is the opposite of faith.

Think about it. If you can see it, touch it, and prove it 100%, you don’t need faith. Faith only exists in the space between what you know and what you hope for. And that space? That space is where doubt lives.

You are at an age—14, 15, 16, 17, 18—where your brain is literally rewiring itself to think abstractly. You are moving from the faith of your childhood, which you accepted because your parents or your leaders told you to, to an adult faith. And adult faith has to survive the real world. It has to survive tragedy, science, history, and heartbreak. If you never question what you believe, you aren’t actually growing; you’re just memorizing.

So, let’s look at the Bible. Because if we look at the "heroes" of the faith, we don't see people who walked around with permanent, plastic smiles of certainty. We see people who wrestled.

I want to look at a guy named Habakkuk. He’s a minor prophet—you might have skipped over his book on the way to Psalms or Matthew—but he is arguably the most real person in the Old Testament.

Habakkuk lived in a time that feels surprisingly familiar. The world was chaotic. Violence was everywhere. The bad guys were winning, and the good guys were getting crushed. And Habakkuk looks at this mess and he basically yells at God. He doesn’t put his hands together and say, "Thank you for this lesson." He looks at heaven and says, "God, are you seeing this? Why are you letting this happen? This doesn't make sense. If you are good, why is the world so broken?"

Sound familiar?

Habakkuk chapter one, verse two: *"How long, O Lord, must I call for help? But you do not listen! I cry out to you, 'Violence!' but you do not save!"*

He accuses God. He questions God’s justice. He questions God’s existence. He is angry and confused. And here is the important part: God doesn’t strike him down. God doesn’t tell him to "just have more faith." God doesn't give him a cliché. God actually answers him.

God says, in essence, "I see it. I am working. I’m doing something that you wouldn’t believe even if I told you. It’s going to be hard, Habakkuk, but I am writing a story that is bigger than your current understanding."

And Habakkuk’s response is fascinating. He doesn’t get all the answers. He doesn't suddenly have a perfect explanation for why evil exists. But by the end of the book, he says, *"I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what he will say to me."*

He decides to wait. He decides to watch. He moves from yelling at God to watching for God.

This is the vision I want to offer you tonight: that honest, messy, yelling-at-the-ceiling questions can be the thing that actually deepens your faith.

Here’s why: when you stop pretending, you start seeking.

If you fake certainty, your faith stays on the surface. It’s like building a house on sand. It looks fine until the rain comes. But when you allow yourself to doubt, to ask the hard questions, to say, "I don't know," you are actually digging down to the bedrock. You are testing the foundation to see if it holds.

A faith that hasn't wrestled with doubt is fragile. It’s brittle. It breaks the first time you face a real crisis. But a faith that has survived the dark night of the soul? That is resilient. That is a faith that can actually help you navigate life.

Now, I need to be clear about something. I’m not saying you should doubt for the sake of doubting. And I’m not saying that every question has a neat, tidy answer. Sometimes, the answer is just mystery. And that is uncomfortable. We are used to Google. We are used to typing in a question and getting an answer in 0.5 seconds.

But God is not a search engine. You cannot just type in "Why did my parents get divorced?" or "Why am I struggling with my identity?" and get a PDF explanation. Sometimes, the answer isn't an explanation; the answer is a person. The answer is God sitting with you in the confusion.

A lot of you are afraid that if you ask the question, you’ll find out there’s nothing there. I get that. But what if asking the question is the only way to find out that there *is* something there? What if the reason you feel distant from God isn't because God isn't real, but because you've been relating to a version of God that is too small? Maybe the God you are doubting isn't the real God at all. Maybe it's a caricature, a straw man. And by tearing that down, you make room for the real God—the God who is big enough to handle your anger, your confusion, and your silence.

So, where do we go from here?

If you are sitting here tonight and you feel like a fraud because of your doubts, I want you to hear this clearly: You are welcome here. Your questions are welcome here. The church should not be a place for perfect people; it should be a hospital for the sick and a laboratory for the curious. If we aren't asking questions, we aren't learning.

I want to challenge you to stop treating your doubts like a dirty secret.

Here is your practical next step for this week. I want you to have an honest conversation with God. Not a polite, rehearsed prayer. I want you to write a letter to God—just you, a piece of paper, and a pen.

Write down exactly what you are thinking. If you are angry, write it down. If you think Christianity is stupid, write it down. If you are terrified that you are losing your faith, write that down. Ask the questions that keep you up at night. "God, where were you when I needed you?" "God, why is the Bible so hard to understand?" "God, do you even exist?"

Don’t hold back. You can burn it afterwards if you want. You don't have to show your youth leader. You don't have to show your parents. This is just between you and the Creator.

Do this because you need to know that the sky doesn't fall when you ask hard questions. You need to see that God doesn't run away from your honesty. In fact, I think God honors it.

Because here is the truth: Faith isn't about having all the answers. Faith is about trusting the One you do know, even when you don't understand the path you're on.

So, stop trying to manufacture a feeling you don't have. Stop acting. Give yourself permission to wrestle. Because the wrestling isn't a sign that you're losing your faith; it's a sign that your faith is becoming your own. And a faith that is truly yours, that has been tested and questioned and forged in the fires of doubt, is the only faith that will last.

Thanks for being here tonight.

Sometimes, the answer isn't an explanation; the answer is a person. The answer is God himself—specifically, Jesus—who shows up in the middle of the mess and says, "I’m not afraid of your questions. I’m not afraid of your anger. I’m here."

A lot of you are afraid that if you ask the question, you’ll find out there’s nothing there. I get that. But what if asking the question is the only way to find out that there *is* something there? What if the reason you feel distant from God isn't because God isn't real, but because you've been relating to a version of God that is too small? Maybe the God you are doubting isn't the real God at all. Maybe it's a caricature, a straw man. And by tearing that down, you make room for the real God—the God who is big enough to handle your anger, your confusion, and your silence.

So, where do we go from here?

If you are sitting here tonight and you feel like a fraud because of your doubts, I want you to hear this clearly: You are welcome here. Your questions are welcome here. The church should not be a place for perfect people; it should be a hospital for the sick and a laboratory for the curious. If we aren't asking questions, we aren't learning.

I want to challenge you to stop treating your doubts like a dirty secret.

Here is your practical next step for this week. I want you to have an honest conversation with God. Not a polite, rehearsed prayer. I want you to write a letter to God—just you, a piece of paper, and a pen.

Write down exactly what you are thinking. If you’re stuck, start with this: *"God, the thing I can’t say out loud is..."* or *"God, here is why I am mad at you..."*

If you are angry, write it down. If you think Christianity is stupid, write it down. If you are terrified that you are losing your faith, write that down. Ask the questions that keep you up at night. "God, where were you when I needed you?" "God, why is the Bible so hard to understand?" "God, do you even exist?"

Don’t hold back. You can burn it afterwards if you want. You don't have to show your youth leader. You don't have to show your parents. This is just between you and the Creator.

After you write it, I want you to read it aloud to yourself. You don't have to share it with anyone else, but you need to hear your own voice saying the words. Then, wait. Give it a week. See if anything shifts. Not because God will magically send a lightning bolt answer, but because you’ve stopped hiding.

Do this because you need to know that the sky doesn't fall when you ask hard questions. You need to see that God doesn't run away from your honesty. In fact, I think God honors it.

Because here is the truth: Faith isn't about having all the answers. Faith is about trusting the One you do know, even when you don't understand the path you're on.

So, stop trying to manufacture a feeling you don't have. Stop acting. Give yourself permission to wrestle. Build your watchtower. Write the letter. And see what God says when you stop pretending. Because the wrestling isn't a sign that you're losing your faith; it's a sign that your faith is becoming your own.

Thanks for listening.

Good evening. It’s good to see everyone.

I want to start tonight by telling you about a feeling I suspect many of you know, but we rarely talk about out loud. It usually happens about ten minutes after a really intense worship song or a really good sermon. You know, that moment when the lights are dim, the music is swelling, everyone around you has their eyes closed and hands raised, and they look… totally captured. They look like they have zero questions, zero hesitations, and like they have it all figured out.

And you’re standing there, clapping along, maybe singing the words, but inside, there’s this quiet, nagging voice. It’s saying something like: *“Is this actually real? Do I believe this? Or am I just going through the motions because everyone else is?”*

Maybe for you, it’s not even during the service. Maybe it’s on a Tuesday night when you’re lying in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking about the pain in the world, or the science class you sat through, or the bad thing that happened to a good person, and you think, “I’m not sure if God is actually there. I’m not sure if any of this holds up.”

I want to be honest with you: I know that feeling.

When I was seventeen, my grandmother died of cancer. It was slow and painful, and I watched a woman I loved waste away in front of me. Our whole church had been praying for her healing. We believed. We really did. And when she died, I sat in the back row at her funeral and thought, “If God is real, he’s either not good or he’s not paying attention.” I didn’t tell anyone for three months. I thought that if I admitted I was angry, or that I was doubting the logic of everything I’d been taught, it meant I was failing at being a Christian. I thought youth group was for people who had their act together, not for people who were yelling at the ceiling.

If you have ever felt that way, I have two things to tell you. First: you are not alone. Second: you are not doing it wrong.

We have this tendency in religious circles to treat doubt like a dangerous contaminant. Like it’s a virus. We think if we admit we’re struggling, we’re being unfaithful. We think that certainty is the goal, and if you don’t have it, you’re failing. But tonight, I want to suggest something that might feel a little radical.

I’m not saying certainty is bad. It’s nice to be sure. But when certainty becomes a wall that keeps out new information or hard questions, it stops being faith and starts being a defense mechanism. Real faith—the kind the Bible talks about—isn't about having zero questions. Faith only exists in the space between what you know and what you hope for. And that space? That space is where doubt lives.

You are at an age—14, 15, 16, 17, 18—where your brain is literally remodeling itself. You are developing the ability for abstract thought. You are moving from the faith of your childhood, which you accepted because your parents or your leaders told you to, to an adult faith. Adult faith has to survive the real world. It has to survive tragedy, science, history, and heartbreak. If you never question what you believe, you aren’t actually growing; you’re just memorizing.

This doubt you’re feeling? It’s not a sign that you’re breaking. It’s a sign that you are growing up. It’s developmental. You are becoming capable of owning your beliefs instead of just borrowing them.

So, let’s look at the Bible. Because if we look at the "heroes" of the faith, we don't see people who walked around with permanent, plastic smiles of certainty. We see people who wrestled.

I want to look at a guy named Habakkuk. He’s a minor prophet—you might have skipped over his book on the way to Psalms or Matthew—but he is arguably the most real person in the Old Testament.

Habakkuk lived in a time that feels surprisingly familiar. The world was chaotic. Violence was everywhere. The bad guys were winning, and the good guys were getting crushed. And Habakkuk looks at this mess and he basically yells at God. He doesn’t put his hands together and say, "Thank you for this lesson." He looks at heaven and says, "God, are you seeing this? Why are you letting this happen? This doesn't make sense."

Now, Habakkuk didn't question if God existed. He knew God was there. He questioned God’s character. He questioned God’s justice. He was angry and confused. And here is the important part: God doesn’t strike him down. God doesn’t tell him to "just have more faith." God doesn't give him a cliché. God actually answers him.

God says, in essence, "I see it. I am working. I’m doing something that you wouldn’t believe even if I told you. It’s going to be hard, Habakkuk, but I am writing a story that is bigger than your current understanding."

And Habakkuk’s response is fascinating. He doesn’t get all the answers. He doesn't suddenly have a perfect explanation for why evil exists. But by the end of the book, he says, *"I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what he will say to me."*

He decides to wait. He decides to watch. He moves from yelling at God to watching for God.

There is a really important distinction here I want you to catch. There is a difference between asking "God, where are you?" and refusing to look for an answer. Habakkuk didn’t stop at yelling—he climbed the rampart to *watch* for God’s response. Honest doubt is open-handed; it asks because it wants to find. Cynicism is closed-fisted; it asks to prove there’s nothing there. Tonight, I’m inviting you to the first kind.

This is the vision I want to offer you: that honest, messy, yelling-at-the-ceiling questions can be the thing that actually deepens your faith.

Here’s why: when you stop pretending, you start seeking.

If you fake certainty, your faith stays on the surface. It’s like building a house on sand. It looks fine until the rain comes. But when you allow yourself to doubt, to ask the hard questions, to say, "I don't know," you are actually digging down to the bedrock. You are testing the foundation to see if it holds.

A faith that hasn't wrestled with doubt is fragile. It’s brittle. It breaks the first time you face a real crisis. But a faith that has survived the dark night of the soul? That is resilient. That is a faith that can actually help you navigate life.

Now, I need to be clear about something. I’m not saying you should doubt for the sake of doubting. And I’m not saying that every question has a neat, tidy answer. Sometimes, the answer is just mystery.

We are used to Google. We are used to typing in a question and getting an answer in 0.5 seconds. But God is not a search engine. You cannot just type in "Why did my parents get divorced?" or "Why am I struggling with my identity?" and get a PDF explanation. Sometimes, the answer isn't an explanation; the answer is a person. The answer is God sitting with you in the confusion.

In fact, Jesus actually met a guy who felt exactly this way. In Mark chapter 9, a father brings his son who is sick to Jesus and begs for help. Jesus tells him, "Everything is possible for one who believes." And the father, with tears in his eyes, looks at Jesus and says, *"I do believe; help me overcome my unbelief!"*

Did you catch that? He didn't pretend. He didn't hide his doubt. He brought his doubt *to* Jesus. And Jesus didn't scold him. Jesus healed the boy. Jesus honored that honest, messy, half-faith.

A lot of you are afraid that if you ask the question, you’ll find out there’s nothing there. I get that. But what if asking the question is the only way to find out that there *is* something there? What if the reason you feel distant from God isn't because God isn't real, but because you've been relating to a version of God that is too small? Maybe the God you are doubting isn't the real God at all. Maybe it's a fake version, an imposter. And by tearing that down, you make room for the real God—the God who is big enough to handle your anger, your confusion, and your silence.

By the end of his book, Habakkuk comes to this place. He writes, *"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior."*

He’s saying: Even if everything goes wrong. Even if I don't get the explanation. Even if the world is still broken. I’m going to trust God’s character. He moved from demanding answers to choosing trust. That’s not settling for less—that’s finding something deeper.

So, where do we go from here?

If you are sitting here tonight and you feel like a fraud because of your doubts, I want you to hear this clearly: You are welcome here. Your questions are welcome here. The church should not be a place for perfect people; it should be a hospital for the sick and a laboratory for the curious. If we aren't asking questions, we aren't learning.

I want to challenge you to stop treating your doubts like a dirty secret.

Here is your practical next step for this week. I want you to have an honest conversation with God. But I want you to do it in two parts.

First, the writing. I want you to write a letter to God—just you, a piece of paper, and a pen. Write down exactly what you are thinking. If you are angry, write it down. If you think Christianity is stupid, write it down. If you are terrified that you are losing your faith, write that down. Ask the questions that keep you up at night. "God, where were you when I needed you?" "God, why is the Bible so hard to understand?" "God, do you even exist?"

Don’t hold back. You can burn it afterwards if you want. You don't have to show your youth leader. You don't have to show your parents. This is just between you and the Creator.

But then—here’s the hard part—I want you to climb your own rampart. Habakkuk didn't just write a complaint; he watched for a response.

This week, after you pour your heart out on paper, try to watch for God's answer. It might not come as a booming voice. It might come as a friend saying exactly what you needed to hear, or a verse you’ve read a hundred times suddenly hitting different, or just a strange sense of peace that doesn't make sense. Keep a simple "watch log" for one week. Write down where you might have seen God moving, even if you’re not sure.

We’re not just looking for proof; we’re practicing the posture of Habakkuk—standing ready to be surprised.

Do this because you need to know that the sky doesn't fall when you ask hard questions. You need to see that God doesn't run away from your honesty. In fact, I think God honors it.

Because here is the truth: Faith isn't about having all the answers. Faith is about trusting the One you do know, even when you don't understand the path you're on.

So, stop trying to manufacture a feeling you don't have. Stop acting. Give yourself permission to wrestle. Because the wrestling isn't a sign that you're losing your faith; it's a sign that your faith is becoming your own. And a faith that is truly yours, that has been tested and questioned and forged in the fires of doubt, is the only faith that will last.

Thanks for listening tonight.

Hi everyone. I want to start with a situation that I think feels familiar to a lot of us, even if we don’t talk about it.

Imagine it’s a Sunday morning. Or maybe a Wednesday night at small group. The lights are dimmed, the music is playing—that kind of atmospheric swell where the bass is just humming in your chest—and everyone around you is closing their eyes. Hands are going up. People are whispering, "Yes, Lord," and "I feel you, God."

And you are standing there.

Inside, you feel… nothing. Or maybe worse, you feel panic. You look around and think, "Is this real for them? Am I the only one who feels like I’m acting? Is this just a psychological trick we’re all playing on ourselves to feel better about life?"

You start asking the questions that terrify you in the quiet moments of the night. *What if I’m wrong? What if this is just a story we tell ourselves? What if God is actually silent?*

And then comes the shame. Because you think, "If I were a 'good' Christian, I wouldn’t be thinking this. If I really had faith, I wouldn’t be standing here analyzing the acoustics. I’d be feeling the Spirit. There must be something wrong with me."

If that has ever been you, or if it’s you right now, I have really good news for you. You aren’t broken. You aren’t failing. You are just awake.

Tonight, I want to talk about doubt. And I want to start by saying something clearly: Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Certainty is the opposite of faith.

We often treat doubt like it’s a virus. Like if you catch it, you need to be quarantined so you don’t infect everyone else. We treat questions like they are dangerous. But if you are 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 years old, and you aren’t asking questions, I’m actually worried about you. Because you are in a phase of life where you are supposed to deconstruct everything. You are figuring out who you are, what the world is, and what you believe.

You can’t just wear your parents’ faith anymore. It doesn’t fit. It’s like trying to put on a toddler’s t-shirt. You’re growing, and growing pains hurt. Doubt is that pain. It’s the feeling of your faith getting bigger, stretching out, moving from something you borrowed to something that is actually yours.

Let’s look at the Bible. We love to polish up the characters in Scripture and make them look like stained-glass saints who never questioned anything. But if you actually read the text, it’s full of people who were wrestling with God in the mud.

Take the guy we all know: Thomas. We call him "Doubting Thomas" like it’s an insult. It’s a label he’s been stuck with for 2,000 years. But let’s look at his story for a second.

Jesus has just been killed. It’s a catastrophe. Thomas’s world is over. His leader is dead. His friends are hiding in a locked room, terrified they’re next. Then, the other disciples tell Thomas, "Hey, we saw him. He’s alive."

Now, stop and think about what Thomas is feeling. He’s grieving. He’s probably angry. And his friends are telling him a story that sounds physically impossible. Dead people don’t just walk out of tombs.

So Thomas says, "Look, unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

People often paint Thomas as being stubborn or negative. I think Thomas was being incredibly brave. He was refusing to pretend. He refused to say "I believe" when he didn't. He was the only one in the room who was honest enough to say, "This doesn't make sense to me."

He didn't want a feeling. He didn't want a hallucination. He wanted truth. He wanted reality.

And here is the beautiful part. How does Jesus respond to Thomas? Does Jesus strike him down with lightning? Does Jesus kick him out of the group? Does Jesus say, "You just have to have more faith"?

No.

A week later, Jesus shows up. He walks right up to Thomas and says, "Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe."

Jesus meets Thomas in the middle of his doubt. He doesn’t scold him for asking questions; he provides evidence. He honors Thomas’s desire for truth.

This changes how we view doubt. Doubt isn’t a sign that you are far from God. Sometimes, doubt is the very place where God is closest, because you are actually looking for him. You are engaging your brain. You are engaging your heart. You aren't just going through the motions.

There is a massive difference between doubting *and* questioning, and doubting *in order to* walk away.

There is a kind of cynicism that is just a wall. It says, "I’m not going to believe anything because I don’t want to be hurt." That’s fear. But there is another kind of doubt. It’s the doubt that says, "I want to believe this, but I need to understand it. I need to know it’s real." That is a seeking doubt. That is the kind of doubt that leads to a deeper faith.

Think about it like a muscle. If you never lift a weight, your muscles stay weak. It’s only when you put them under tension, when you push against resistance, that they grow. Doubt is the resistance. If you never have any doubts, your faith never gets strong. It just stays fragile.

When you ask, "Why does God allow suffering?" or "Is the Bible actually true?" or "Why do Christians act like hypocrites?"—those questions are scary, but they are also the doorway to a faith that can actually withstand the real world.

Because here is the reality: You are going to graduate high school. You are going to go to college or get a job. You are going to meet people who think this whole "God thing" is a joke. You are going to face tragedy. You are going to have days where life hits you like a truck.

If your faith is just a bunch of songs you sang on a Wednesday night and a list of rules you followed because your parents said so, that faith is going to shatter. It’s not going to survive.

But if your faith has been tested? If you have wrestled with the hard questions and said, "God, I don't get this, but I’m sticking around to find out"—that faith is solid. That is a faith that is yours.

So, how do we do this? How do we doubt well?

First, we have to stop pretending. We have to kill the "Christianese" mask. You know what I’m talking about. Someone asks, "How are you doing?" and you say, "Blessed! Just living the dream!" even though you’re depressed or angry or confused.

God can handle your anger. God can handle your confusion. He is big enough. You don’t need to protect him. The Psalms are full of people yelling at God. David, who was called a man after God’s own heart, wrote things like, "God, where are you? Why are you hiding from me? Why are the wicked winning?"

If the Bible contains those questions, surely we can ask them too.

Second, we need to stop looking for quick fixes. We live in a Google society. We want an answer in 0.5 seconds. We want the algorithm to solve our theology. But faith isn’t a math problem you solve. It’s a relationship you navigate.

Sometimes, the answer isn't a sentence. Sometimes the answer is a Person. You might not get the explanation for *why* something happened, but you might get the presence of God to walk through it with you. That is harder, but it is better.

I want to challenge you to reframe how you see your doubts. Don't see them as enemies. See them as indicators. They are telling you what you care about. If you doubt because of suffering, it means you care about justice. If you doubt because of science, it means you care about truth. Those are good things. Bring those things to God.

I’m not saying you should just doubt forever. Doubt is a room you walk through, not a place you build a house and live in. You don't want to stay in the "I don't know" forever. You want to keep moving toward "I trust." But you have to walk through the room to get to the other side.

So, I want to give you a practical step for this week. This isn't about reading five chapters of the Bible or praying for an hour. This is about honesty.

I want you to write down your one biggest doubt. The one question that keeps you up at night. The one that makes you feel guilty for even thinking it.

Write it on a piece of paper. Be specific. Don't write "I doubt God." Write, "God, I don't understand why you let my parents get divorced." Or, "God, I feel like you are silent when I pray, and it makes me feel like an idiot for talking to the ceiling."

Once you write it down, I want you to do one of two things.

Option A: If you have a leader here, or a parent, or a mentor you trust, and you feel safe, go to them this week and say, "Can I share something with you? I’m wrestling with this." Just say it out loud. Shame thrives in secrecy. The moment you say it out loud to a safe person, it loses a lot of its power.

Option B: If you aren't ready to say it to a person yet, that is totally okay. I want you to pray that doubt. Just talk to God. Say, "God, here is the thing. I’m scared to ask this, but I’m asking it."

Don't try to solve it. Don't go to Google for an apologetics answer. Just tell God.

Here is the promise we have: "Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you." That doesn't say "Draw near to God only when you have it all figured out." It just says draw near.

You are loved in your questioning. You are held in your uncertainty. Faith isn't about having all the answers; faith is about trusting the One who does.

Let’s stop being afraid of the questions. Let’s be a people who are brave enough to ask them, and trust that God is big enough to handle them.
