Imagine this: it’s late at night, you’re scrolling, and you land on a video of someone confidently explaining why faith is pointless. Or why the Bible is unreliable. Or why science has “disproved” God. The comments are a warzone. Part of you wants to slam your phone down and never think about it again. Another part of you can’t look away, because… what if they’re right?

Or maybe it’s not a video. Maybe it’s quieter than that. Maybe it’s sitting in a room like this and singing words like *“I believe”* while a different voice in your head is saying, “Do I?” Maybe it’s praying and feeling nothing. Maybe it’s watching someone you love suffer and thinking, *If God is good, what is this?* Maybe it’s hearing Christians speak with total certainty about something you’re not sure anyone can be totally certain about—and you feel like you’re the only one who didn’t get the memo.

If any of that sounds familiar, I want you to hear this clearly: you are not broken. You are not a bad Christian. You are not the only one. Doubt is not a sign that your faith is dead. It might be a sign that your faith is growing up.

Because growing up—really growing up—includes learning that the world is more complicated than you thought when you were nine. You start noticing contradictions. You meet people who don’t believe what you believe, and they’re not villains—they’re smart, kind, thoughtful. You experience disappointment. You realize adults don’t always know what they’re doing. You discover that some church people can be hypocritical. You start forming your own opinions instead of borrowing someone else’s.

And faith, if it’s real, has to be able to survive reality.

So let’s just make this a safe statement in this room: **doubt is allowed here. Questions are allowed here. Uncertainty is allowed here.**

Not because we don’t care about truth. Actually, the opposite. Because people who care about truth ask questions.

### Doubt isn’t the enemy of faith—pretending is

There’s a kind of doubt that’s really just avoidance: “I don’t want to deal with this, so I’ll dismiss everything.” That’s not what I’m talking about tonight.

I’m talking about the kind of doubt that shows up when you’re honest. The kind that says: “I want to believe, but this part is hard.” Or: “I believe… and I’m scared I’m fooling myself.” Or: “I need more than slogans.”

That kind of doubt isn’t a failure. It’s a sign you’re awake.

Sometimes people treat faith like it’s confidence with religious vocabulary. Like if you ever hesitate, you’ve lost. But that version of faith is fragile. It depends on never being challenged, never being hurt, never being confused.

Real faith is not fragile. Real faith can handle questions, because it’s not built on pretending.

And the Bible—if you actually read it—does not hide human struggle. It includes prayers that sound like arguments. It includes people who are angry at God, confused by God, and disappointed in God. Not as villains. As people of faith.

### Thomas: the disciple who said what others only thought

Let’s talk about Thomas.

Thomas has a reputation problem. You’ve probably heard him called “Doubting Thomas.” Like his name is basically a warning label. But it’s worth noticing something: Thomas is the one who says out loud what a lot of people keep inside.

In John 20, after Jesus has been crucified, the disciples are devastated and terrified. Then something unbelievable happens: Jesus appears to them alive. But Thomas isn’t there when it happens.

So the others tell him, “We have seen the Lord.”

And Thomas basically says, “I’m not going to pretend I’m okay with this. Unless I see it, unless I can touch the wounds, I’m not going to believe.”

Now, you can read that as stubborn. Or you can read it as honest.

Think about it. Thomas watched Jesus die. He’s not doubting a small thing. He’s doubting the most outrageous claim in Christianity: that death didn’t win.

And here’s what I love: when Jesus appears again, he doesn’t humiliate Thomas. He doesn’t say, “Wow, you’re the worst disciple.” He doesn’t kick him out. He doesn’t punish him for not being easy to convince.

Jesus walks straight into Thomas’s doubt and says, in effect, “Okay. Here. Look. Touch. Bring your questions into the light.”

Jesus meets him.

And Thomas responds with one of the clearest confessions of faith in the whole gospel: “My Lord and my God!”

Thomas doesn’t end up with smaller faith because he asked for evidence. He ends up with a deep, personal faith because he brought his doubt to Jesus instead of hiding it.

That’s important: **Thomas didn’t let his doubt make him disappear. He stayed close enough to encounter Jesus.**

If you’re in a season of doubt, one of the biggest dangers isn’t the questions themselves. It’s isolation. It’s deciding, “I can’t say this out loud,” and slowly pulling away until you’re alone with your thoughts and your algorithm and your anxiety.

### Doubt can be a doorway, not a dead end

Here’s a picture that helps me.

Sometimes faith you inherit as a kid is like a house you grew up in. It’s familiar. It’s where your family lives. You didn’t build it. You just lived there.

But then you grow older, and you start noticing things. A crack in the wall. A door that doesn’t close. A weird smell in one room. And at some point you have a choice. You can pretend you don’t see it because you’re scared the whole house will collapse. Or you can start asking, “What’s actually going on here?”

Doubt is often the moment you stop living in someone else’s faith and start building your own.

That doesn’t mean you throw everything away. It means you learn what’s solid and what needs repair. You learn the difference between the core and the extras. You learn what you actually believe and why.

And yes—sometimes doubt hurts. Sometimes it feels like losing something. If you’ve ever had a belief that used to comfort you stop working, that can feel like grief. So I’m not going to pretend doubt is fun.

But I will say this: **a faith that has never been tested might not be faith. It might be familiarity.**

Honest questions don’t have to destroy faith. They can refine it. They can strip away the versions of Christianity that are more about control than love. They can expose the idea that God is only present when you feel spiritual. They can push you toward a faith that can survive real life.

### What if God isn’t threatened by your questions?

One of the quiet fears people have is: “If I ask the wrong question, will God be angry?” Or: “If I admit I’m not sure, will God leave?”

But look at Jesus with Thomas. Jesus doesn’t act threatened. He doesn’t act fragile. He doesn’t say, “How dare you.”

He moves toward Thomas.

If God is real, then God is not insecure.

God doesn’t need you to protect him from your thoughts. He already knows them.

And here’s something else: doubt and faith are not always opposites. Sometimes the opposite of faith isn’t doubt—it’s certainty without humility. The kind of certainty that refuses to listen, refuses to learn, refuses to admit complexity. That kind of certainty can become a way of staying in control.

But faith, at its core, is trust. And trust can exist even when you don’t have all the answers.

You can say, “God, I don’t get this, but I’m still talking to you.” That’s faith.

You can say, “I’m not sure what I believe right now, but I’m open.” That’s faith.

You can say, “If you’re real, meet me.” That’s faith.

### A more honest definition of faith

Sometimes people define faith as never questioning. But that’s not how relationships work.

If you’ve ever been close to someone—really close—you know that questions don’t kill relationships. Silence does. Pretending does. Performing does.

A strong relationship can handle hard conversations. “Why did you do that?” “Do you really care about me?” “I’m struggling to trust you.” Those are risky things to say. But they can actually deepen the relationship—because they’re real.

Faith is not a performance for God. It’s a relationship with God.

And relationships grow through honesty.

So if you’re doubting, maybe the question isn’t, “How do I get rid of doubt as fast as possible?” Maybe it’s, “How do I be honest in this season without walking away from the possibility of God?”

### The danger of quick answers

Let me say something that might be relieving: not every question has an immediate answer. And not every Christian who speaks confidently actually knows what they’re talking about.

Sometimes people offer quick answers because they’re uncomfortable with mystery, or they’ve never sat with the pain of the question. Sometimes they want to protect you from discomfort. Sometimes they want to protect themselves.

But quick answers can feel like betrayal when your question comes from something real—like grief, or anxiety, or disappointment, or trauma.

If you’ve been handed pat answers and it made you feel unseen, that makes sense. You’re not wrong for wanting something more honest.

In the Bible, there are whole books that basically say, “Life is confusing, suffering is real, and God is still worth talking to.” Job doesn’t get a neat explanation. Habakkuk asks why God seems silent and unfair. David writes psalms that start with, “How long, Lord?” Scripture doesn’t rush people through their questions.

So don’t rush yourself.

### What to do with doubt: bring it into the light

Here’s a vision I want you to consider: what if doubt isn’t something you’re supposed to hide from God and others, but something you can bring into the light—carefully, wisely—and let it become a place where God meets you?

Not every environment is safe. Not every person will respond well. But you need at least one place where you can be honest.

Because doubt grows in the dark. It either grows into cynicism, or it grows into curiosity. And which direction it goes often depends on whether you have space to talk and think and pray without being shamed.

### A practical next step

I want to end with something simple and real you can do this week. Not a dramatic promise, not a perfect solution. Just a step.

**Choose one honest question you have right now and write it down.** Not ten questions. One. The question that keeps resurfacing.

It might be:
- “God, are you actually there?”
- “Why does prayer feel pointless?”
- “Why would a good God allow this?”
- “What do I do with parts of the Bible that confuse or bother me?”
- “How do I know I’m not just believing what I was taught?”

Write it down. Then do two things:

1) **Talk to someone wise and safe.** Not someone who will panic, not someone who will shut you down, not someone who will use your question as a debate trophy. A youth leader, a mentor, a thoughtful friend, a parent—someone who can handle honesty. Your goal isn’t to “win” the question. Your goal is to bring it into the open.

2) **Pray one sentence a day for a week—using your real question.** Something like:  
“God, if you’re there, help me be honest and help me find what’s true.”  
Or: “Jesus, meet me like you met Thomas.”  
Or even: “God, I don’t know how to pray, but I’m here.”

That’s it. One question. One conversation. One sentence a day.

Because faith doesn’t usually grow through pretending you’re certain. It grows through choosing honesty and staying close enough to be met.

And if you’re sitting here thinking, “I’m not even sure I belong in a place like this because I have doubts,” I’ll say it again: you’re not disqualified. You might actually be exactly the kind of person God can work with—someone who cares enough about truth to ask, and brave enough to be real.

Job doesn’t get a neat explanation for his suffering. Habakkuk basically argues with God about injustice. David writes psalms that start with, “How long, Lord?” Scripture doesn’t sanitize faith into constant confidence. It shows faith as something that can sound like grief, protest, confusion—and still be faith.

So don’t rush yourself.

---

## **What if God isn’t threatened by your questions?**

One of the quiet fears people have is: “If I ask the wrong question, will God be angry?” Or: “If I admit I’m not sure, will God leave?”

But look at Jesus with Thomas. Jesus doesn’t act threatened. He doesn’t act fragile. He doesn’t say, “How dare you.”

He moves toward Thomas.

If God is real, then God is not insecure.

God doesn’t need you to protect him from your thoughts. He already knows them.

And here’s something else: doubt and faith are not always opposites. Sometimes the opposite of faith isn’t doubt—it’s certainty without humility. The kind of certainty that refuses to listen, refuses to learn, refuses to admit complexity. That kind of certainty can become a way of staying in control.

But faith, at its core, is trust.

And trust can exist even when you don’t have all the answers.

You can say, “God, I don’t get this, but I’m still talking to you.” That’s faith.

You can say, “I’m not sure what I believe right now, but I’m open.” That’s faith.

You can say, “If you’re real, meet me.” That’s faith.

---

## **A more honest definition of faith**

Sometimes people define faith as never questioning. But that’s not how relationships work.

If you’ve ever been close to someone—really close—you know that questions don’t kill relationships. Silence does. Pretending does. Performing does.

A strong relationship can handle hard conversations:
“Why did you do that?”
“Do you really care about me?”
“I’m struggling to trust you.”

Those are risky things to say. But they can actually deepen the relationship—because they’re real.

Faith is not a performance for God. It’s a relationship with God.

And relationships grow through honesty.

So if you’re doubting, maybe the question isn’t, “How do I get rid of doubt as fast as possible?” Maybe it’s, “How do I be honest in this season without walking away from the possibility of God?”

---

## **Bring your doubt into the light (carefully, wisely)**

Here’s a vision I want you to consider: what if doubt isn’t something you’re supposed to hide from God and others, but something you can bring into the light—carefully, wisely—and let it become a place where God meets you?

Not every environment is safe. Not every person will respond well. That’s real.

But you need at least one place where you can be honest.

Because doubt grows in the dark. It either grows into cynicism, or it grows into curiosity. And which direction it goes often depends on whether you have space to talk and think and pray without being shamed.

And remember Thomas: he came back to the table. He didn’t have it all figured out. He wasn’t sure. But he stayed close enough to be met.

---

## **A practical next step**

I want to end with something simple and real you can do this week. Not a dramatic promise. Not a perfect solution. Just a step.

**Choose one honest question you have right now and write it down.** Not ten questions. One. The one that keeps resurfacing.

It might be:
- “God, are you actually there?”
- “Why does prayer feel pointless?”
- “Why would a good God allow this?”
- “What do I do with parts of the Bible that confuse or bother me?”
- “How do I know I’m not just believing what I was taught?”

Write it down. Then do two things:

### 1) Talk to someone wise and safe
Not someone who will panic. Not someone who will shut you down. Not someone who will use your question as a debate trophy. A youth leader, a mentor, a thoughtful friend, a parent—someone who can handle honesty.

And if initiating that conversation feels terrifying—and for a lot of people, it does—here are words you can literally copy and paste:

**“Hey, I heard a talk at youth group about asking hard questions, and I have one I’m wrestling with. Could we grab a drink or go for a walk this week and talk?”**

That’s enough. You don’t have to write an essay. You don’t have to prove you’re “serious.” Just open the door.

### 2) Pray one sentence a day for a week—using your real question
Something like:
- “God, if you’re there, help me be honest and help me find what’s true.”
- “Jesus, meet me like you met Thomas.”
- “God, I don’t know how to pray, but I’m here.”

One sentence. Once a day. For seven days.

**One question. One conversation. One sentence a day.**

Because faith doesn’t usually grow through pretending you’re certain. It grows through choosing honesty and staying close enough to be met.

And if you’re sitting here thinking, “I’m not even sure I belong in a place like this because I have doubts,” I’ll say it again: you’re not disqualified.

You might actually be exactly the kind of person God can work with—someone who cares enough about truth to ask, and brave enough to be real.

Hey—before we dive in, let me tell you what happened last Tuesday.

I was babysitting my neighbour’s kid, Sam. He’s seven. We’d just finished a jigsaw puzzle of the solar system—Saturn’s rings were slightly crooked, but we were proud. As I tucked him in he asked, “How do we know space isn’t just a big black blanket with holes poked in it?” I started to give the textbook answer about stars and fusion and light-years, then stopped. Because honestly, I’ve never touched a star. I’ve only seen tiny dots. I told him, “We don’t fully know. People smarter than me trust the math, but yeah—it could feel like a blanket.” He nodded, satisfied that an adult admitted the mystery, and rolled over.

I drove home thinking: if a seven-year-old can spot the holes in our certainty, no wonder fourteen-to-eighteen-year-olds do it faster. And no wonder it feels risky to say out loud, “God, I’m not sure You’re there, or good, or listening.” So tonight let’s treat the room like Sam’s bedroom—safe enough to name the holes in the blanket.

1. Doubt is not the enemy; it’s the itinerary.

Brains between 14-18 are literally rewiring. Neural highways are being asphalted; others are closed for construction. You’re tasting independence, absorbing injustice, scrolling global suffering before breakfast. Doubt isn’t a detour from faith; it’s often the only road that reaches an adult-sized faith. Little-kid Sunday-school answers can’t hold the weight of real life. If you never question them, they simply shatter later.

So first, permission granted: it’s normal. Biologists call it cognitive differentiation; youth workers call it “Wednesday.” You’re not defective; you’re developing.

2. The Bible is full of people airing their suspicions out loud.

Pick a page, you’ll find complaints. I’ll spotlight three.

Thomas. We nickname him “Doubting Thomas,” but John simply calls him Thomas. One week earlier he’d been ready to die with Jesus in Jerusalem. Then his mentor was executed. When the friends say, “We saw Him alive,” Thomas doesn’t swing to atheism; he demands the same experience: “Unless I touch the wounds, I won’t believe.” That’s integrity, not smart-aleckry. Jesus shows up, offers His scars, and Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God.” Notice Jesus doesn’t scold him for the prior doubt; He meets him in it. The result isn’t a weaker Thomas but a thicker, embodied faith that can carry the church to India (tradition says he sails east and starts communities that still exist).

David. Psalm 13: “How long, O Lord? Will You forget me forever?” Fourteen-year-old David probably sang shiny shepherd songs about green pastures. King-in-exile David writes angsty slam poetry. Faith isn’t the absence of complaint; it’s complaining in the right direction—toward God, not away.

Job. Forty-two chapters of argument. God finally shows up in a whirlwind and, instead of giving reasons, gives Job a universe-sized tour: “Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundation?” That sounds harsh until you realise God is treating Job like an adult conversation partner, not a toddler. The answer to suffering isn’t a tidy slogan; it’s a relationship big enough to hold the questions.

3. Honest questions deepen the roots.

Imagine faith like a tree. Clichés are plastic leaves—green all year, but crack under pressure. Real leaves grow, die, rot, feed the soil, and new ones sprout. Questions are the winter season: looks dead, but sap is descending, widening the trunk. A faith that has never doubted is brittle; one that has wintered can flex in a storm.

Neuroscience back-up: memories encoded with emotion and struggle stick better than rote repetition. Wrestling with doubt literally imprints faith on your brain’s long-term storage. God doesn’t want fan-girls and boys; God wants partners. You can’t get to “my Lord and my God” without passing through “I won’t believe unless.”

4. What this doesn’t mean.

I’m not saying every question feels good. Doubt can be terrifying, like stepping onto black ice. Some nights you’ll scroll TikTok till 2 a.m. because the silence is loud. Some of you carry church-hurt, or your parents’ divorce, or a friend’s suicide—questions that ache. I’m not handing you a permission slip for apathy. I’m saying: bring the ache to the centre. The Psalms do.

5. How to doubt faithfully—three habits.

a. Name it precisely.  
Instead of “I don’t know if I believe any of this,” try: “I can’t reconcile a good God with my friend’s depression.” Specific questions get specific conversations. Vague ones get vague guilt.

b. Choose your companions.  
Find two people—one older, one peer—who won’t Instagram your struggle. Ask them, “Can I show you the raw version?” If they answer with “You just need to read Leviticus,” keep shopping. If they say, “Tell me more,” you’ve found gold.

c. Keep the appointment.  
Even if you sit in the back row and mouth the creeds like they’re foreign subtitles, show up. Faith is formed in habits before it’s felt in fireworks. Thomas was in the room when Jesus arrived. If he’d bailed on the community, he’d have missed the scars.

6. A practice for the next seven days.

Tonight, write your top three doubts on paper—yes, paper, so the pixels don’t judge you. One per line, leave space. Fold it small, seal it in an envelope. Each evening this week, open Psalm 13 (only six verses—tweet-length). Read it slowly, then under one doubt write a sentence: a feeling, a question, a random word. By next Friday you’ll have a conversation partner: David. Bring the envelope to youth group or a trusted adult and say, “Let’s talk.” That’s it. No altar call, no lightning. Just a map of where you are.

7. Close with the blanket again.

Remember Sam’s space blanket? Astronomers now know the “holes” are galaxies, burning balls of gas, bigger than his imagination. The mystery didn’t shrink; it enlarged. Doubt poked holes in his picture—and let more light in.

Same for you. The stars you’ll discover on the other side of your questions won’t be the cute felt ones from preschool. They’ll be gigantic, nuclear, terrifyingly beautiful. Bring your telescope. Bring your doubt. The One who flung those stars can handle both.

See you next week—and if you’re early, I’ll save you a seat, back row or front, wherever you need to land.

Hey—before we dive in, let me tell you what happened last Tuesday.

I was babysitting my neighbour’s kid, Sam. He’s seven. We’d just finished a jigsaw puzzle of the solar system—Saturn’s rings were slightly crooked, but we were proud. As I tucked him in he asked, “How do we know space isn’t just a big black blanket with holes poked in it?” I started to give the textbook answer about stars and fusion and light-years, then stopped. Because honestly, I’ve never touched a star. I’ve only seen tiny dots. I told him, “We don’t fully know. People smarter than me trust the math, but yeah—it could feel like a blanket.” He nodded, satisfied that an adult admitted the mystery, and rolled over.

I drove home thinking: if a seven-year-old can spot the holes in our certainty, no wonder fourteen-to-eighteen-year-olds do it faster. And no wonder it feels risky to say out loud, “God, I’m not sure You’re there, or good, or listening.” So tonight let’s treat the room like Sam’s bedroom—safe enough to name the holes in the blanket.

1. Doubt is not the enemy; it’s the itinerary.

Brains between 14-18 are literally rewiring. Neural highways are being asphalted; others are closed for construction. You’re tasting independence, absorbing injustice, scrolling global suffering before breakfast. Doubt isn’t a detour from faith; it’s often the only road that reaches an adult-sized faith. Little-kid Sunday-school answers can’t hold the weight of real life. If you never question them, they simply shatter later.

So first, permission granted: it’s normal. Biologists call it cognitive differentiation; youth workers call it “Wednesday” (a fancy way of saying “the day the wheels come off”). You’re not defective; you’re developing.

2. The Bible is full of people airing their suspicions out loud.

Pick a page, you’ll find complaints. I’ll spotlight three.

Thomas. We nickname him “Doubting Thomas,” but John simply calls him Thomas. One week earlier he’d been ready to die with Jesus in Jerusalem (John 11:16). Then his mentor was executed. When the friends say, “We saw Him alive,” Thomas doesn’t swing to atheism; he demands the same experience: “Unless I touch the wounds, I won’t believe.” That’s integrity, not smart-aleckry. Jesus shows up, offers His scars, and Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God.” Notice Jesus doesn’t scold him for the prior doubt; He meets him in it. The result isn’t a weaker Thomas but a thicker, embodied faith that can carry the church to India (tradition says he sails east and starts communities that still exist).

David. Psalm 13: “How long, O Lord? Will You forget me forever?” David isn’t humming “Kumbaya”; he’s screaming into the dark. He feels erased, unseen, like the kid who checks their phone at 2 a.m. and nobody’s texted. Faith isn’t the absence of complaint; it’s complaining in the right direction—toward God, not away. By the end of the psalm David still doesn’t have answers, but he has a direction: “I trust in Your unfailing love.” The ache doesn’t vanish; it moves.

Job. Forty-two chapters of argument. God finally shows up in a whirlwind and, instead of giving reasons, gives Job a universe-sized tour: “Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundation?” That sounds harsh until you realise God is treating Job like an adult conversation partner, not a toddler. The answer to suffering isn’t a tidy slogan; it’s a relationship big enough to hold the questions. It doesn’t solve the pain, but it re-frames who’s carrying it.

3. Honest questions deepen the roots.

Imagine faith like a tree. Clichés are plastic leaves—green all year, but crack under pressure. Real leaves grow, die, rot, feed the soil, and new ones sprout. Questions are the winter season: looks dead, but sap is descending, widening the trunk. A faith that has never doubted is brittle; one that has wintered can flex in a storm.

Neuroscience back-up: memories encoded with emotion and struggle stick better than rote repetition. Wrestling with doubt literally imprints faith on your brain’s long-term storage. God doesn’t want fan-girls and boys; God wants partners. You can’t get to “my Lord and my God” without passing through “I won’t believe unless.” And—because I promised honesty—some mornings I still wake up on the “unless” side of that sentence. I’m learning that’s okay too.

4. What this doesn’t mean.

I’m not saying every question feels good. Doubt can be terrifying, like stepping onto black ice. Some nights you’ll scroll TikTok till 2 a.m. because the silence is loud. Some of you carry church-hurt, or your parents’ divorce, or a friend’s suicide—questions that ache. I’m not handing you a permission slip for apathy. I’m saying: bring the ache to the centre. The Psalms do.

5. How to doubt faithfully—three habits that might help

a. Name it precisely.  
Instead of “I don’t know if I believe any of this,” try: “I can’t reconcile a good God with my friend’s depression.” Specific questions get specific conversations. Vague ones get vague guilt.

b. Choose your companions.  
Find two people—one older, one peer—who won’t Instagram your struggle. Ask them, “Can I show you the raw version?” If they answer with “You just need to read Leviticus,” keep shopping. If they say, “Tell me more,” you’ve found gold.

c. Keep the appointment.  
Even if you sit in the back row and mouth the creeds like they’re foreign subtitles, show up. Faith is formed in habits before it’s felt in fireworks. Thomas was in the room when Jesus arrived. If he’d bailed on the community, he’d have missed the scars.

Tonight, write your top three doubts on paper—yes, paper, so the pixels don’t judge you. One per line, leave space. Fold it small, seal it in an envelope. Each evening this week, open Psalm 13 (only six verses—tweet-length). Read it slowly, then under one doubt write a sentence: a feeling, a question, a random word. By next Friday you’ll have a conversation partner: David. Bring the envelope to youth group or a trusted adult and say, “Let’s talk.” If you end up with more questions than sentences, that’s not failure—that’s the tree widening.

No pressure, no performance—just a map of where you are.

7. Close with the blanket again.

Remember Sam’s space blanket? Astronomers now know the “holes” are galaxies, burning balls of gas, bigger than his imagination. The mystery didn’t shrink; it enlarged. Doubt poked holes in his picture—and let more light in.

Same for you. The stars you’ll discover on the other side of your questions won’t be the cute felt ones from preschool. They’ll be gigantic, nuclear, terrifyingly beautiful. Bring your telescope. Bring your doubt. The One who flung those stars can handle both.

See you next week—and if you’re early, I’ll save you a seat, back row or front, wherever you need to land.

Hey everyone, thanks for scooting in close—yes, even the kid in the hoodie who’s already counting the minutes until snack time. I want to tell you about last Tuesday night. I was driving my little sister home from her piano recital. She’s 12, wears the same Converse every day, and had just completely botched the middle section of “Let It Go.” (I know, still.) As we pulled out of the parking lot she stared out the window and said, “I’m not sure I believe any of the God stuff Mom tells me.” No pre-amble, no tears—just a quiet confession to the glass. I felt the steering wheel get hot under my hands, because honestly, I’d been carrying the same sentence in my chest for weeks and hadn’t dared say it out loud.

So that’s where we’re starting tonight: with the moment the song falls apart and the questions slip out. If you’ve ever whispered, “What if this whole thing is made up?”—congratulations, you’re alive. Doubt isn’t an alien parasite that hops aboard when your faith immune system is weak; it’s standard equipment in the human package, like hip bones and the ability to binge three episodes when you swore you’d stop at one.

Growing Pains, Not Failure Pains  
Let’s name the pressure you feel. At school you’re told to question everything—except, apparently, the youth-group statement of faith. Meanwhile your Instagram feed is full of sunset captions: “Just so thankful to Jesus!!!” which can make you feel like the only person whose spiritual life isn’t a constant filter of golden hour. Add youth-group shorthand where “I’ll pray for you” sometimes sounds like “I’ve got my life together and you don’t,” and it’s no wonder you fake certainty.

But here’s neurobiology for you: between ages 14-18 your brain is literally re-wiring abstract-reasoning highways. Teenagers don’t just accept inherited maps; they need to draw their own. Doubt is the GPS recalculating. If you never asked, “Does the route I was handed actually go anywhere?” you’d be psychologically stuck in toddler mode. Faith that never outgrows the toddler seat isn’t mature; it’s arrested.

Biblical Hall of Doubters  
Let’s tour the spiritual zoo where every cage card reads, “Yes, this one too.”

Job: poster-child for cosmic complaint. Loses family, skin, 401(k) of camels. His friends try to solve him like a math problem; Job keeps saying, “I will speak to the Almighty, I want answers, not your memes.” God finally shows up—not with a spreadsheet of reasons but with  chapters of rhetorical questions about galaxies and mountain goats. Conclusion? It’s okay to demand an audience with the Divine; just brace yourself for an answer bigger than your question.

David: the shepherd-turned-king who writes psalms that swing from “Why have you forsaken me?” to “My heart is steadfast.” Spotify would call that bipolar; theology calls it honest. David never edits out the dissonance, and God never edits David out of the lineage of Jesus.

Thomas: the guy who missed Easter Sunday. While other disciples are busy hashtagging #HeIsRisen, Thomas says, “I won’t believe until I poke the holes.” A week later Jesus shows up: “Here, poke.” No shame, no lecture on having more faith—just an invitation to touch. Thomas’s doubt becomes the canvas for the most explicit confession of Jesus’s divinity in John’s gospel: “My Lord and my God.” Turns out skepticism can climb higher than naïve belief ever could.

I picked Thomas because teenagers feel pressure to pretend they were in the room the first time. You weren’t. You’re in the upper school of faith, and Jesus offers the same deal: bring your finger, bring your questions.

When Questions Dig Down Rather Than Tear Down  
Imagine faith as a tent you inherited from parents. It’s bright, holds up in mild weather, but you’re taller now; the canvas grazes your head. You can either (A) stay inside complaining it’s cramped, (B) pack it in and declare tents obsolete, or (C) pound new stakes, expand the perimeter, maybe sew on a patched section. Option C is hard work; doubt is the mallet. Each question you hammer can either stake the tent deeper or smash it flat—depends on the swing.

The deepest roots in the forest aren’t the saplings that never faced wind; they’re the ones clenched around storms. Likewise, a faith you’ve questioned, re-examined, and chosen again develops tensile strength. You’ll meet 40-year-olds who still believe because they were “raised that way,” and the slightest crisis snaps them. But you’ll also meet people who walked through the crater and came out with a quiet, unshakable core—because they let the questions burn off everything that shouldn’t stick.

Avoiding Cliché Quick-Sand  
“Everything happens for a reason.” Insert eye-roll. Some things happen because of physics, bullies, or bad theology.  
“God works in mysterious ways.” Translation: I don’t know, please stop talking.  
“Just pray more.” Sometimes prayer feels like texting a satellite phone that never buzzes back.

David never edits out the dissonance, and God never edits David out of the family tree. The lineage of Jesus isn’t a hall of heroes; it’s a string of broken people who kept showing up. If doubt disqualified you, the whole story would end in Genesis.

Thomas: the guy who missed Easter Sunday. While the rest are hashtagging #HeIsRisen, Thomas says, “I won’t believe until I poke the holes.” A week later Jesus shows up: “Here, poke.” No shame, no lecture on having stronger faith—just an invitation to touch. Thomas’s skepticism becomes the canvas for the clearest confession of Jesus’s divinity in John: “My Lord and my God.” Turns out the longest step up the ladder of faith can be the one you take with a question in your hand.

When Questions Dig Down Rather Than Tear Down  
Imagine faith as a tent you inherited from your parents. Bright colors, holds up in mild weather, but you’re taller now and the canvas grazes your head. You can (A) stay inside complaining it’s cramped, (B) chuck it and declare tents obsolete, or (C) pound new stakes, sew on extra canvas. Option C is sweaty; doubt is the mallet. Each swing can either anchor the tent deeper or smash the poles—depends on the heart behind the hammer.

I’ve spent a season pounding. Three years ago my mom got cancer and the chemo prayers didn’t work the way the prayer chain promised. I sat in the ICU hallway writing angry journal fragments: “If you’re sovereign, I don’t like your steering.” I still don’t have a tidy answer. What I do have is the night a nurse slipped me a cold Coke, the moment a friend wordlessly sat cross-legged on the linoleum, and the realization that something—or Someone—was still in the hallway after I ran out of sentences. The questions didn’t dissolve; they became the ground the tent got staked into.

Avoiding Cliché Quick-Sand  
“Everything happens for a reason.” Insert eye-roll. Some things happen because of physics, bullies, or toxic theology.  
“God just needed another angel.” As if death is a staffing issue.  
“Just pray more.” Sometimes prayer feels like texting a satellite phone that never buzzes back.

Clichés are microwave burritos: they look like food, but they’re hollow calories. Real faith language admits mystery without hoarding it. It can say, “This sucks, I don’t see it, and I’m still here.”

Practical Next Step: The 3-Week Thomas Experiment  
1. Name it: Grab a notes app or an actual dead-tree journal. Write one sentence a day that starts with “I’m unsure about…” No filter, no emoji. After three weeks you’ll have a map of your honest soul.  
2. Voice it: Pick one adult safe-zone (youth leader, coach, aunt) and read three of those sentences out loud. Ask them to respond with story, not solution. If they start fixing, gently say, “I just need to be heard first.”  
3. Touch it: Thomas needed flesh. Translate that: go serve somewhere that makes you touch pain—soup kitchen, animal shelter, anti-trafficking org. Sometimes doubt is abstract until you rub up against reality. Ask God to meet you in the concrete. Then add one more nightly sentence: “Today I saw…”

You won’t walk out with a theological Swiss Army knife. You will walk out with better questions—and maybe a bruise on your finger where the divine poked through.

Close  
When my sister finally looked over at me in the car I didn’t have a 5-point apologetic. I said, “Yeah, me too. Let’s keep the window down for air, and keep driving.” That’s all I’m suggesting tonight: keep driving. You’re not disqualified from the pilgrimage because you asked for a bathroom break. The ones who stop, look around, double-check the map—those travelers actually know where they’re going.

So may your doubt be the kind that digs stakes, not graves. May the questions burn off everything that shouldn’t stick until you’re left with a quiet, unshakable core: not a faith that owns all the answers, but a faith that knows the One who holds the questions—and keeps holding you.

Alright, snacks are waiting. Bring your uncertainty; it’s welcome here.

qHSbDqOKcJxIxzHePjfCU.text:
When I was sixteen, I sat in a youth group exactly like this one, singing a worship song I’d heard a hundred times, and suddenly—between the second chorus and the bridge—something inside me whispered, *What if none of this is real?*

Not a dramatic, movie-style crisis. Just a quiet, terrifying thought that landed like a stone in my stomach. I looked around at everyone else with their eyes closed, hands raised, and I thought: *Am I the only one faking this?*

I didn’t tell anyone for two years. I kept showing up, kept singing, kept nodding along in small group because I thought that’s what you’re supposed to do. I thought doubt was like spiritual termites—if you admit they’re there, the whole house collapses. So I locked the door and pretended the foundation was solid.

Here’s what I wish someone had told me that night: **Doubt isn’t the opposite of faith. It’s part of it.**

If you’re sitting here tonight and some part of you is wondering whether prayer is just talking to yourself, or if the Bible stories are just ancient myths, or if God is really there when everything feels dark and silent—you’re not broken. You’re not failing. You’re being honest. And honesty is where actual faith begins.

---

Let’s talk about Thomas for a second. You probably know him as “Doubting Thomas,” like it’s his main personality trait, like he’s the disciple who just couldn’t get it together. But that’s not fair, and it’s not the whole story.

Thomas had been through trauma. He watched his mentor, his rabbi, his friend get executed by the state. He saw the hope of a movement die. Then his friends start showing up saying, “He’s alive! We saw him!” And Thomas says what any rational person would say: “Unless I see the nail marks, unless I can touch the wounds—I’m not buying it.”

He’s not being difficult. He’s being *devastated*. He’s protecting himself from false hope. He’s saying, “I need something real, not just your excited feelings.”

And here’s the part that changed everything for me: **Jesus shows up.** Not to shame him, not to say, “Wow, Thomas, way to kill the vibe.” He shows up and says, “Put your finger here. Touch my hands. Touch my side. Stop doubting and believe.”

But the Greek word there isn’t “stop doubting” like you’d scold a kid. It’s more like, “Don’t stay stuck in unbelief. Move through it.” Jesus doesn’t erase Thomas’s questions. He *enters* them. He offers his wounded body as evidence. He meets Thomas in the exact place of his doubt.

And Thomas? He becomes the first person in the entire gospel to look at Jesus and say, “My Lord and my God.” Not Peter. Not John. Thomas—the doubter, the skeptic, the one who needed proof—makes the most profound confession of identity in the whole story.

His doubt didn’t destroy his faith. It became the doorway to a deeper one.

---

Here’s why this matters for you: Your brain right now is literally wired to question everything. It’s not a bug; it’s a feature. The same developmental stage that makes you question your parents’ rules or your school’s policies or why society is the way it is—that same impulse is what makes you question faith. And that’s not a crisis. That’s you taking faith seriously instead of swallowing it whole.

There’s a difference between *doubt* and *unbelief*. Doubt is questioning *within* a relationship. It’s saying, “God, I don’t understand you, and I’m angry, and I need answers.” Unbelief is walking away from the relationship altogether. Doubt is Jacob wrestling the angel all night long, refusing to let go until he gets a blessing. Unbelief is just going to bed.

The Bible is full of people who wrestle. David writes psalms that say, “Why have you forsaken me?” and “How long, O Lord?” Job sits in ashes and demands God explain himself. Habakkuk looks at the violence in his world and says, “God, why are you letting this happen?” These aren’t side characters. These are the heroes of the story. They’re the ones who show us that faith isn’t about having all the answers—it’s about bringing your whole self, questions and all, into the presence of God.

---

So why are we so afraid of doubt? I think it’s because we’ve been sold a version of faith that looks like certainty. Like if you really believe, you’ll never wonder, never waver, never wake up at 3 AM wondering if you’re delusional. But that’s not faith—that’s fundamentalism. That’s pretending.

Real faith is more like trust than certainty. It’s the difference between saying “I’m 100% sure this bridge won’t collapse” and saying “I’m scared, but I’m going to walk across anyway.” Trust is what you do *despite* the doubt, not in the absence of it.

And here’s the wild part: **Doubt can actually make your faith stronger.** Not because it feels good—it doesn’t. But because when you doubt, you’re pressure-testing the foundation. You’re checking to see what’s real and what’s just inherited tradition, what’s actually yours and what’s just performance.

Think about it like this: When you’re a kid, you believe what your parents believe because they believe it. That’s fine for a kid. But you’re not a kid anymore. And faith that’s just inherited is fragile. It’ll break the first time it gets challenged. But faith that you’ve questioned, wrestled with, doubted, and still chosen? That’s yours. It’s been through fire. It can bend without breaking.

---

I want to be clear: I’m not giving you a three-step plan to eliminate doubt. I’m not going to say “just read your Bible more” or “just pray harder,” because that’s not how this works. Those are good things, but they’re not magic spells that make uncertainty disappear.

What I’m offering is permission. Permission to stop performing. Permission to be honest. Permission to ask the scary questions without thinking you’re betraying God.

Because here’s what I believe: **God is not threatened by your questions.** The Creator of the universe can handle your doubt. The God who knit your brain together knows how it works. The Jesus who showed Thomas his scars isn’t going to ghost you for being honest.

In fact, I think God prefers your honest doubt over your fake certainty. The father in Mark 9 who says to Jesus, “I believe; help my unbelief”—that’s the prayer that gets answered. That’s the prayer that moves Jesus. Not perfect faith, but honest, messy, mixed-up faith.

---

So here’s one practical thing you can try this week. I want you to write your own psalm of doubt. Not a prayer that sounds good. Not something you’d post on Instagram with a sunset background. I want you to get a piece of paper and write the most honest, unfiltered questions you have.

Write things like:
- God, why does prayer feel like talking to a wall?
- If you’re good, why is there so much suffering?
- Why do the people who claim to follow you act like that?
- I don’t feel you. Are you even there?

Write it like a letter you’re not sure you’ll send. Be specific. Be angry if you’re angry. Be confused if you’re confused. Don’t tidy it up.

Then—this is the important part—don’t throw it away. Keep it. Put it in a drawer. Come back to it in a month, in six months, in a year. See what’s changed and what hasn’t. Notice if God met you in any of those questions, even if the answer wasn’t what you expected.

This isn’t about getting to the other side of doubt. It’s about learning to live with it, to let it be part of your story, to see it as a sign that your faith is alive and breathing—not a museum piece, but something that moves and grows and sometimes bleeds.

---

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here. I want to start with a story about a guy named Alex.

Alex grew up in church. He knew the songs, the Bible stories, the right answers. When he was twelve, his youth leader told him faith was like a shield that could block anything life threw at him, and Alex believed it. But then at fourteen, his parents got divorced, and the shield cracked. At fifteen, his best friend was hit by a car, and the shield shattered completely. He sat in the back row during the funeral, listening to people say “God’s will” and “everything happens for a reason,” and all he could think was: *If that’s true, I don’t think I want anything to do with this God.*

Alex stopped praying. Stopped singing. When youth group started, he’d find excuses to leave early or just not show up. He felt like a fraud—like everyone else had this solid, unshakeable faith, and he was the only one falling apart. The doubt felt like a disease he needed to hide.

Here’s the thing: Alex is real. I know him because Alex is me. And maybe, in some way, Alex is you too.

If you’re sitting here tonight and there’s a voice in your head saying, “I don’t know if I believe any of this,” or “I’m not sure God is good,” or even “What if it’s all made up?”—I want you to know something. That doesn’t make you broken. That makes you human.

We don’t talk about this enough in church, but doubt isn’t the opposite of faith. It’s part of it. It’s the questions that keep you up at night. The anger you feel when prayers go unanswered. The moment you read something in the Bible and think, “That can’t be right.” All of that? It’s normal. It’s healthy. It’s what happens when your faith is growing up.

When you’re a kid, faith is simple. You believe what you’re told. But when you hit fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, your brain changes. You start thinking abstractly. You see hypocrisy. You experience pain that doesn’t have easy explanations. And suddenly, the faith that fit you at ten doesn’t fit anymore. You’re not failing—you’re outgrowing your old faith. And that’s terrifying because it feels like losing it.

But here’s what I wish someone had told Alex back then: **Questions are not the enemy of faith. They are the refining fire.**

Let me tell you about Thomas.

You’ve probably heard him called “Doubting Thomas,” like it’s his permanent nickname. But that’s branding, not biography. Thomas was one of Jesus’s twelve closest friends. When Jesus decided to go to Jerusalem knowing it would get him killed, Thomas was the one who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” That’s not doubt—that’s devotion so fierce he’s ready to die for it.

But then Jesus does die. And Thomas watches everything collapse. The movement, the miracles, the hope—it all ends in a cross. So when the other disciples tell him, “We’ve seen the risen Jesus,” Thomas doesn’t buy it. He says, “Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe.”

We treat that like a sin, but it’s actually one of the most honest moments in the Bible. Thomas isn’t being difficult. He’s grieving. He’s protecting himself from false hope. He’s saying, “If Jesus is alive, I need to know it’s really him—not a ghost, not wishful thinking, not my friends seeing what they want to see. I need the real thing.”

And here’s the wild part: Jesus gives it to him. A week later, Jesus shows up and says, “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.” But that translation is weak. The original Greek isn’t “stop doubting.” It’s closer to “Don’t become faithless—become faithful.” It’s not a rebuke. It’s an invitation. Jesus doesn’t shame Thomas for needing proof. He meets him in it.

Thomas’s doubt didn’t destroy his faith. It forged it. After that moment, Thomas becomes the first person in the Bible to call Jesus “God” outright. His tested faith is stronger than the easy belief he had before.

That’s the pattern. Look at David in the Psalms: “How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?” Look at Job, who spends 35 chapters demanding answers before God shows up. Look at Habakkuk, who straight-up argues with God about injustice. The Bible isn’t full of people who never questioned. It’s full of people who brought their questions *to* God.

Because here’s what nobody tells you: **Certainty is brittle. Tested faith is flexible.**

Think about it like this. When you work out, you’re actually tearing your muscles. That’s what makes them grow back stronger. Doubt is the workout for your faith. It tears down the easy answers, the inherited beliefs, the stuff you never really examined. And if you sit with it—if you don’t run from it—what grows back is stronger. Not because you have more answers, but because you have a deeper relationship with the questions.

The problem isn’t that we doubt. The problem is that we’re terrified to admit it. So we perform faith instead of living it. We nod along in small group while thinking, *None of this makes sense.* We sing songs about God’s goodness while privately raging that he didn’t show up when we needed him. And that gap between what we say and what we feel? That’s what destroys faith. Not the doubt itself, but the loneliness of carrying it alone.

So what do we do with this?

First, give yourself permission to not have it figured out. If faith is a journey, doubt is the part where you’re actually walking instead of being carried. It’s active. It’s engaged. It means you care enough to wrestle.

Second, find someone you can be honest with. Not someone who will give you three Bible verses and a pat on the back. Someone who will sit with you in the questions. Maybe that’s a friend, a youth leader, a parent who gets it. The goal isn’t to get answers immediately. The goal is to stop feeling alone.

Third, get curious instead of defensive. When you hit something in the Bible that bothers you, don’t slam the book shut. Ask: Why does this bother me? What does this reveal about God, or about people, or about the world they lived in? When you pray and feel nothing, don’t quit. Ask: What is silence teaching me? The questions themselves become a form of prayer.

And finally, hold onto this: **Faith is not the absence of doubt. It’s the decision to stay even when you’re not sure.**

It’s showing up to youth group when you’re not sure you believe. It’s praying “I believe; help my unbelief” like the guy in the Gospels did. It’s choosing to live as if love matters, as if justice matters, as if there’s something bigger than you, even on the days you can’t feel it.

I want to end with something practical. Tonight, before you go to sleep, I want you to do one thing. Grab your phone, open a notes app, or find a piece of paper, and write down one honest question you have about God, faith, or life. Just one. Not a performance question—not “How can I share the gospel more effectively?” I mean the real one. The one that keeps you up. The one that makes you angry. The one you’re scared to say out loud.

Write it down. And then, for the next week, just sit with it. Don’t try to answer it. Don’t try to make it go away. Just let it be there. Carry it with you like Thomas carried his grief. And see what happens.

If you want to talk about it, find me or one of the leaders after. Not because we have all the answers—we don’t. But because we’ve learned that questions are better when they’re shared. And because we believe that God is big enough to handle your honesty.

You’re not failing. You’re just becoming the kind of person who has a faith that can survive the real world. And that’s not a small thing. That’s everything.

Alex grew up in church. He knew the songs, the Bible stories, the right answers. When he was twelve, his youth leader told him faith was like a shield that could block anything life threw at him, and Alex believed it. But then at fourteen, his parents got divorced, and the shield cracked. At fifteen, his best friend was hit by a car, and the shield shattered completely. He sat in the back row during the funeral, listening to people say “God’s will” and “everything happens for a reason,” and all he could think was: *If that’s true, I don’t think I want anything to do with this God.*

Alex stopped praying. Stopped singing. When youth group started, he’d find excuses to leave early or just not show up. He felt like a fraud—like everyone else had this solid, unshakeable faith, and he was the only one falling apart. The doubt felt like a disease he needed to hide.

Here’s the thing: Alex is real. I know him because Alex is me. And maybe, in some way, Alex is you too.

If you’re sitting here tonight and there’s a voice in your head saying, “I don’t know if I believe any of this,” or “I’m not sure God is good,” or even “What if it’s all made up?”—I want you to know something. That doesn’t make you broken. It means you’re paying attention. It means you’re thinking.

We don’t talk about this enough in church, but doubt isn’t the opposite of faith. It’s part of it. It’s the questions that keep you up at night. The anger you feel when prayers go unanswered. The moment you read something in the Bible and think, “That can’t be right.” All of that? It’s normal. It’s healthy. It’s what happens when your faith is growing up.

When you’re a kid, faith is simple. You believe what you’re told. But when you hit fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, your brain changes. You start thinking abstractly. You see hypocrisy. You experience pain that doesn’t have easy explanations. And suddenly, the faith that fit you at ten doesn’t fit anymore. You’re not failing—you’re outgrowing your old faith. And that’s terrifying because it feels like losing it.

But here’s what I wish someone had told Alex back then: **Questions are not the enemy of faith. They are the refining fire.**

Let me tell you about Thomas.

You’ve probably heard him called “Doubting Thomas,” like it’s his permanent nickname. But that’s branding, not biography. Thomas was one of Jesus’s twelve closest friends. When Jesus decided to go to Jerusalem knowing it would get him killed, Thomas was the one who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” That’s not doubt—that’s devotion so fierce he’s ready to die for it.

But then Jesus does die. And Thomas watches everything collapse. The movement, the miracles, the hope—it all ends in a cross. So when the other disciples tell him, “We’ve seen the risen Jesus,” Thomas doesn’t buy it. He says, “Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe.”

We treat that like a sin, but it’s actually one of the most honest moments in the Bible. Thomas isn’t being difficult. He’s grieving. He’s protecting himself from false hope. He’s saying, “If Jesus is alive, I need to know it’s really him—not a ghost, not wishful thinking, not my friends seeing what they want to see. I need the real thing.”

And here’s the wild part: Jesus gives it to him. A week later, Jesus shows up and says, “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.” But that translation is weak. The original Greek isn’t “stop doubting.” It’s closer to “Don’t become faithless—become faithful.” It’s not a rebuke. It’s an invitation. Jesus doesn’t shame Thomas for needing proof. He meets him in it.

Thomas’s doubt didn’t destroy his faith. It forged it. After that moment, Thomas becomes the first person in the Bible to call Jesus “God” outright. That’s not a small detail—it means his tested, questioned, doubted faith was the first to truly see who Jesus was. His questions led him deeper, not further away.

And that’s the pattern. Look at David in the Psalms: “How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?” Look at Job, who spends 35 chapters demanding answers before God shows up. And when God finally does show up, he doesn’t actually answer Job’s questions—he asks his own. That’s a more honest picture of how God deals with doubt: not always with explanations, but with presence. Look at Habakkuk, who straight-up argues with God about injustice, asking why God would use wicked people to punish the slightly less wicked. The Bible isn’t full of people who never questioned. It’s full of people who brought their questions *to* God.

Because here’s what nobody tells you: **Certainty is brittle. Tested faith is resilient.**

Think about it like this. When you work out, you’re actually tearing your muscles. That’s what makes them grow back stronger. Doubt is the workout for your faith. It tears down the easy answers, the inherited beliefs, the stuff you never really examined. And if you sit with it—if you don’t run from it—what grows back is stronger. Not because you have more answers, but because you have a deeper relationship with the questions.

The problem isn’t that we doubt. The problem is that we’re terrified to admit it. So we perform faith instead of living it. We nod along in small group while thinking, *None of this makes sense.* We sing songs about God’s goodness while privately raging that he didn’t show up when we needed him. And that gap between what we say and what we feel? That’s what destroys faith. Not the doubt itself, but the loneliness of carrying it alone.

I should probably say this, too: I’m not here to talk you into staying. If you’re at the point where you’re done, where you’ve walked away or you’re about to, I’m not going to pretend I can argue you back. This isn’t a sales pitch. It’s just an honest conversation about what faith can look like when you stop pretending.

So what do we do with this?

First, give yourself permission to not have it figured out. If faith is a journey, doubt is the part where you’re actually walking instead of being carried. It’s active. It’s engaged. It means you care enough to wrestle.

Second, find someone you can be honest with. Not someone who will give you three Bible verses and a pat on the back. Someone who will sit with you in the questions. Maybe that’s a friend, a youth leader, a parent who gets it. The goal isn’t to get answers immediately. The goal is to stop feeling alone.

Don’t quit praying—ask what the silence might be teaching you. The questions themselves become a form of prayer. Even that father in the Gospels who cried out to Jesus, “I believe; help my unbelief”—he was bringing his doubt right to the source.

Which brings me to this: **Faith is not the absence of doubt. It’s the decision to stay even when you’re not sure.**

It’s showing up to youth group when you’re not sure you believe. It’s praying that honest prayer. It’s choosing to live as if love matters, as if justice matters, as if there’s something bigger than you, even on the days you can’t feel it.

I want to end with something practical. Tonight, before you go to sleep, I want you to do one thing. Grab your phone, open a notes app, or find a piece of paper, and write down one honest question you have about God, faith, or life. Just one. Not a performance question—not “How can I share the gospel more effectively?” I mean the real one. The one that keeps you up. The one that makes you angry. The one you’re scared to say out loud.

If you want to talk about it, find me or one of the leaders after. Not because we have all the answers—we don’t. But because we’ve learned that questions are better when they’re shared. And because we believe that God is big enough to handle your honesty.

You’re not failing. You’re just becoming the kind of person who has a faith that can survive the real world. And that’s not a small thing. That’s everything.

Not a performance question—not “How can I share the gospel more effectively?” I mean the real one. The one that keeps you up. The one that makes you angry. The one you’re scared to say out loud.

You experience pain that doesn’t have easy explanations. And suddenly, the faith that fit you at ten doesn’t fit anymore. You’re not failing—you’re outgrowing your old faith. So when the other disciples tell him, “We’ve seen the risen Jesus,” Thomas doesn’t buy it. He says, “Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe.”

He’s saying, “If Jesus is alive, I need to know it’s really him—not a ghost, not wishful thinking, not my friends seeing what they want to see. I need the real thing.”

And here’s the wild part: Jesus gives it to him. A week later, Jesus shows up and says, “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.” But that translation is weak. The original Greek isn’t “stop doubting.” It’s closer to “Don’t become faithless—become faithful.” It’s not a rebuke. It’s an invitation. Jesus doesn’t shame Thomas for needing proof. He meets him in it.

Thomas’s doubt didn’t destroy his faith. It forged it. After that moment, Thomas becomes the first person in the Bible to call Jesus “God” outright. His tested faith is stronger than the easy belief he had before.

That’s the pattern. Look at David in the Psalms: “How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?” Look at Job, who spends 35 chapters demanding answers before God shows up. Look at Habakkuk, this minor prophet who looks at the violence in his world and says to God, “Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?” He doesn’t get a satisfying answer—just God’s presence. Even Jesus, in the garden and on the cross, asked questions that didn’t get immediate answers. The Bible isn’t full of people who never questioned. It’s full of people who brought their questions *to* God.

Because here’s what nobody tells you: **Certainty is brittle. Tested faith is flexible.**

It tears down the easy answers, the inherited beliefs, the stuff you never really examined. And if you sit with it—if you don’t run from it—what grows back is stronger. Not because you have more answers, but because you have a deeper relationship with the questions.

The problem isn’t that we doubt. The problem is that we’re terrified to admit it. So we perform faith instead of living it. We nod along in small group while thinking, *None of this makes sense.* We sing songs about God’s goodness while privately raging that he didn’t show up when we needed him. And that gap between what we say and what we feel? That’s what destroys faith. Not the doubt itself, but the loneliness of carrying it alone.

So what do we do with this?

First, give yourself permission to not have it figured out. If faith is a journey, doubt is the part where you’re actually walking instead of being carried. It’s active. It’s engaged. It means you care enough to wrestle.

Second, find someone you can be honest with. Not someone who will give you three Bible verses and a pat on the back. Someone who will sit with you in the questions. Maybe that’s a friend, a youth leader, a parent who gets it. Find the adult here who looks like they’ve been through something—usually it’s the one who doesn’t rush to fill silences. Or find that one friend who doesn’t panic when you say scary things out loud. The goal isn’t to get answers immediately. The goal is to stop feeling alone.

Third, get curious instead of defensive. When you hit something in the Bible that bothers you, don’t slam the book shut. Ask: Why does this bother me? What does this reveal about God, or about people, or about the world they lived in? When you pray and feel nothing, don’t quit. Ask: What is silence teaching me? The questions themselves become a form of prayer.

It’s showing up to youth group when you’re not sure you believe. Even if you’re here tonight thinking, “I’m probably going to walk away from all of this eventually”—you’re still welcome here. Doubt that stays in community is different than doubt that isolates. You don’t have to believe to belong.

It’s praying “I believe; help my unbelief” like the guy in the Gospels did. It’s choosing to live as if love matters, as if justice matters, as if there’s something bigger than you, even on the days you can’t feel it.

I still don’t know why my friend died. I still have days when the silence feels louder than God. But I’ve learned that questions are better when they’re shared, and that God is big enough to handle your honesty.

Grab your phone, open a notes app, or find a piece of paper, and write down one honest question you have about God, faith, or life. Just one. You’re not failing. You’re just becoming the kind of person who has a faith that can survive the real world. And that’s not a small thing. That’s everything.

The 2 AM Questions

You’re lying in bed, phone dark, everyone else asleep. And suddenly your brain decides it’s the perfect time for a full-scale audit of everything you’ve ever believed.

What if this is all made up? What if God’s just a story we tell ourselves because the universe is too terrifying without a plot? What if when I pray, I’m just talking to my own anxiety in a really elaborate way?

You don’t get up and turn on the lights because that would make it too real. You just lie there, feeling the questions press down like a weighted blanket you never asked for. And somewhere in that space, a second question shows up: *What’s wrong with me?*

Let me answer that one first: Nothing. Nothing is wrong with you.

The Doubt Tax

Here’s what nobody tells you: doubt isn’t a bug in the system of faith. It’s a feature of having a functioning brain. You’re at an age where you’re supposed to start questioning everything. That’s literally your job right now. Your brain is finally powerful enough to spot contradictions, to imagine alternatives, to ask “why” fifty times in a row until the adults around you want to scream. This is what growing up looks like.

If you’re not doubting anything, you’re either asleep or you’ve accidentally joined a cult. Questions are how we sort out what’s real from what’s just inherited. The fact that you’re wrestling with this stuff doesn’t mean your faith is weak. It means you’re taking it seriously enough to examine it.

I know that’s not always how it feels. Sometimes it feels like you’re the only one in your youth group who’s faking it. Like everyone else has this warm, certain glow while you’re stuck with a stomach full of spiritual acid reflux. You hear people talk about their “quiet time with God” and you think: *I tried that. Felt like I was journaling into a void.*

Can I tell you something? Some of the most honest, grounded adults you know—people with deep, resilient faith—went through exactly what you’re going through. The difference is they stopped pretending. They stopped performing certainty and started living with the questions.

The Guy Who Missed the Big Moment

Let me introduce you to someone who would absolutely get your 2 AM questions.

His name is Thomas. You’ve probably heard him called “Doubting Thomas,” which is kind of a raw deal—like calling Peter “Denying Peter” for the rest of eternity. But Thomas isn’t a cautionary tale. He’s the most relatable person in the whole New Testament.

Here’s the scene: Jesus has risen from the dead. He’s appeared to the other disciples. They’re all buzzing with this impossible, world-shaking news. And Thomas? He missed it. He was out—maybe grabbing groceries, maybe taking a walk because his entire world had just imploded and he needed air. When he gets back, his friends are saying: “We saw him! He’s alive!”

And Thomas, bless him, doesn’t fake the enthusiasm. He doesn’t plaster on a smile and say, “Oh, awesome, cool, yeah.” He says: “Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

That’s not polite doubt. That’s not a gentle question. That’s a demand for evidence. That’s a man saying: *My grief is too real for your easy answers. My hope is too shattered for your neat little resurrection story. If God is real, God is going to have to show up for me.*

And here’s the part that changes everything: a week later, Jesus does. He appears again. He looks straight at Thomas—Thomas, the one who asked the inconvenient questions—and says, “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.”

Notice what Jesus doesn’t do. He doesn’t scold him. He doesn’t say, “Wow, your faith is so weak.” He doesn’t tell him to pray more, read more, try harder. He just shows up. He gives Thomas what he needs: presence, not platitudes. Touch, not theology.

Thomas’s doubt didn’t disqualify him. It became the doorway to a deeper, more honest kind of faith. The kind that can say, “My Lord and my God,” because it’s touched the wounds, not just heard the stories.

The Psalms Are Just Emo Songs

If Thomas doesn’t convince you, flip open the middle of the Bible. The book of Psalms is basically an ancient playlist of every human emotion, and honestly, some of these tracks are pretty dark.

David, the guy who wrote most of them, spends a lot of time basically saying: “God, where are you? Why are my enemies winning? Why do the wicked prosper? I’m crying my eyes out and you feel farther away than ever.”

Psalm 22 starts with: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” That’s not a polite spiritual question. That’s a scream into the void. And it’s in the Bible. On purpose.

The Bible isn’t a book of answers. It’s a book of people who refused to let go of God even when they were furious with God. They argued. They complained. They demanded explanations. And somehow, in the middle of all that wrestling, they found a relationship that was real enough to survive the questions.

Because here’s the thing: a faith that can’t survive being questioned is a faith that isn’t worth holding onto. It’s a paper faith, not a living one. Real faith is more like a muscle. It gets stronger when you work it, when you test it, when you use it to carry the weight of your actual life.

The Difference Between Cynicism and Honest Doubt

Let me make a distinction, because this matters. There’s a difference between honest doubt and performative cynicism.

Cynicism is when you decide you already know the answer, and the answer is *nothing means anything and everyone’s a hypocrite.* It’s a shield you put up to avoid being disappointed again. It’s safe, but it’s also dead.

Honest doubt is different. Honest doubt is when you say, “I don’t know, but I want to know. This doesn’t make sense to me, but I’m still here. I have questions, but I’m not walking away.”

Honest doubt is what happens when your faith is alive enough to be uncomfortable. It’s the growing pains of a soul that’s trying to make what you were taught fit what you’re actually experiencing. That’s not weakness. That’s integrity.

The poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote: “Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.” That’s the move. Not rushing to answers. Not pretending you’re fine. Just learning to live with the questions, letting them shape you, trusting that the God who can handle the universe can handle your honesty.

When Certainty Breaks

I want to warn you about something. There’s a version of faith that’s all about certainty. It feels good for a while. You get all the right answers, you learn the Christianese, you know what you’re supposed to say. But that kind of faith is brittle. It doesn’t bend; it snaps.

And it usually snaps in your first year of college, or when someone you love gets sick, or when you read a book that asks questions your youth group never touched. And when it snaps, people tend to think the whole thing was a lie. They walk away.

But what if the certainty was the lie? What if real faith has room for mystery? What if the goal isn’t to believe harder, but to believe more honestly?

I’ve met people whose faith survived the worst things imaginable—not because they had perfect answers, but because they had a relationship that was honest enough to include the screaming and the silence. They built their faith on bedrock, not on a house of cards made of easy answers.

Your Next Move

So what do you do with the 2 AM questions? You don’t have to solve them tonight. You don’t have to have a neat conclusion by next Sunday. But here’s one practical thing you can try:

Pick one question. Just one. Not the biggest one, not the one that feels like it could unravel everything. The one that’s most personal. The one that keeps showing up.

Write it down. Actually write it. “God, why does prayer feel so empty?” “If you’re good, why is there so much suffering?” “How do I know you’re real and not just a habit?”

Then, for the next week, carry that question with you like a stone in your pocket. Don’t try to answer it. Just notice when it bumps against things. Notice what makes it heavier, what makes it lighter. Notice where you see it reflected—in a conversation, in a song, in a moment of quiet.

At the end of the week, find one person you trust and read it to them. Not to get an answer. Just to say it out loud. To let it exist in the space between you.

If you can’t think of anyone, find me after. I’ll listen. Not to fix you. Just to be there.

Because here’s what I believe: God isn’t scared of your questions. God is in the questions. The doubt isn’t a detour from the path of faith. It *is* the path, for a while. And you’re not walking it alone.

The 2 AM questions are a sign that your soul is awake. That’s not failure. That’s you, coming alive.

Here’s the scene: Jesus has risen from the dead. He’s appeared to the other disciples. They’re all buzzing with this impossible, world-shaking news. And Thomas? He missed it. He was out—maybe grabbing groceries, maybe taking a walk because his entire world had just imploded and he needed air. When he gets back, his friends are saying: “We saw him! He’s alive!”

That’s not polite doubt. That’s not a gentle question. That’s a demand for evidence. That’s a man saying: *My grief is too real for your easy answers. My hope is too shattered for your neat little resurrection story. If God is real, God is going to have to show up for me.*

The 2 AM questions are a sign that your soul is awake. That’s not failure. That’s you, coming alive.
