I want to tell you about a night I remember from when I was sixteen. 

Youth group had just ended. Everyone else was in the parking lot, laughing, planning where to get food, and I was sitting in the back row, staring at the cross on the wall, feeling like a complete fraud. That night’s talk had been about “radical faith,” about trusting God no matter what. And everyone around me seemed so sure—nodding along, singing every word of the closing song like they meant it. But I kept thinking about my friend whose dad had just died, about the news headlines that made no sense, about how when I prayed lately, it felt like I was talking to my ceiling. 

I remember thinking: *Is everyone else just faking it, or am I the only one broken?*

That’s the story I wish someone had told me was normal. Because here’s the truth: if you’ve got questions you’re scared to say out loud, if some part of the Christian story feels like it’s not quite fitting right now, if you’ve ever sat in church thinking *I’m not sure I believe any of this*—you’re not broken. You’re growing. And you’re in shockingly good company.

Let’s just name it: doubt feels like failure, especially here. It feels like you’re letting down your parents, your youth pastor, maybe even God. We’ve absorbed this idea that faith means certainty, that good Christians have it all figured out, that questions are something to outgrow, like acne or boy bands. But that’s a lie. Doubt isn’t the opposite of faith. It’s the doorway to a deeper one.

Your brain right now is literally built to question. Between fourteen and eighteen, your mind is developing the ability to think abstractly, to imagine different realities, to spot contradictions. You’re not just being difficult—you’re becoming more fully human. The same mental wiring that makes you ask “What if God doesn’t exist?” is what lets you ask “What if we could end poverty?” or “What if I’m not who everyone thinks I am?” This is what growing up looks like. And faith that can’t hold up to your honest questions isn’t faith worth having. It’s a house of cards.

So let’s talk about someone who gets that.

You’ve probably heard of “Doubting Thomas,” right? It’s become a nickname, almost an insult—like he’s the disciple who flunked the faith test. But I want you to hear his actual story, because it’s way more interesting.

Thomas had been following Jesus for years. He’d left everything—his job, his family, his safety. He’d watched Jesus heal people, challenge the powerful, speak with this authority that felt like lightning. And then he watched Jesus die. Not just die, but be publicly executed as a criminal. Can you imagine what that did to Thomas? This wasn’t a theoretical disappointment. This was his entire world collapsing.

So when the other disciples tell him, “We’ve seen the risen Jesus,” Thomas doesn’t fake a smile and pretend he’s fine. He says, “Unless I see the nail marks and put my finger where the nails were, I’m not buying it.” That’s not weakness. That’s brutal, gut-wrenching honesty. He’s saying, *The pain is too real for easy answers. If God is alive, I need something real enough to touch.*

Here’s what gets me: Thomas stays. He doesn’t leave the community of believers. He tells them his doubt, right there in the room. And a week later, when Jesus shows up, he doesn’t shame Thomas. He holds out his hands and says, “Touch me. Put your finger here. See for yourself.” Jesus gives Thomas exactly what he needs—not a lecture, not a verse to memorize, but his wounded, physical presence.

The story doesn’t end with Thomas getting scolded. It ends with Jesus saying, “You believe because you’ve seen. Blessed are those who believe without seeing.” And we usually hear that as a dig at Thomas, but what if it’s not? What if Jesus is saying: *Thomas, your need for evidence was honest, and I met you there. And for everyone who comes after, who won’t get to touch my scars—your honest wrestling will be the thing that makes faith possible for them.*

Thomas’s doubt didn’t disqualify him. It deepened his faith into something he could actually live with. After that, tradition tells us Thomas took the story of Jesus all the way to India, where he was eventually killed for his belief. The man who needed to touch the wounds became the one who gave his life for the truth. That’s not a flimsy faith. That’s a faith that’s been through the fire and come out stronger.

So what if doubt isn’t the enemy of faith, but the thing that saves it from being shallow? Think about it: the relationships that last aren’t the ones where you pretend everything’s fine. They’re the ones where you can say “I’m not okay,” or “I don’t understand you right now,” and the other person doesn’t leave. They stay, and you work through it. Why would your relationship with God be any different?

A faith that’s never been questioned is like a muscle that’s never been used. It might look fine, but it can’t hold weight. The questions you’re carrying—the ones about suffering, about science, about why the Bible says what it says, about whether any of this matters—they’re not sin. They’re you, trying to build a faith that can survive the real world. And that’s holy work.

But here’s the thing: you can’t do that work alone. Thomas stayed in the community. He told his friends the truth. And that’s the practical, terrifying next step I want to offer you.

**Tonight, I want you to write down one question you’re actually carrying.** Not a safe question. A real one. The one that keeps you up at night. Write it on a piece of paper. Keep it in your pocket for the next week. Treat it like a stone you’re turning over in your hand—not to solve it, but to live with it honestly. See what happens when you stop pretending.

**Then, find one person you can be real with.** Maybe it’s a friend in this room. Maybe it’s a leader who’s earned your trust. Maybe it’s a parent who can handle complexity. Tell them your question. Not to get an answer, but to practice staying in community with your doubt. Because the worst thing you can do is isolate yourself with your questions. That’s how doubt curdles into cynicism. But shared doubt? That’s the beginning of wisdom.

I’m not going to give you a three-point plan to fix your faith. I’m not going to tell you to just pray more or read your Bible harder, because if you’re anything like I was at sixteen, that sounds like telling someone to just stop being sad. Instead, I want you to hear this: God is big enough for your questions. The Jesus who met Thomas in his doubt is the same Jesus who can meet you in yours. He’s not threatened by your honesty. He’s present in it.

A few years after that night when I was sixteen, I found myself in another room, with different people, and I finally said out loud: “I don’t know if I believe any of this.” And instead of telling me to try harder, they said, “Yeah, me too sometimes. Let’s figure it out together.” That’s when faith started to feel real again.

Carry your question. Find your person. And trust that the God who made your curious, questioning mind can handle whatever you need to ask.

# The Questions We Don't Say Out Loud

There's a moment I keep thinking about. A student named Marcus came up to me after a talk like this one, looked at his shoes, and said: "I don't know if I believe any of this anymore. But I can't tell my parents. They'd lose it."

We walked around the block. He talked about the science classes that made Genesis feel like a fairy tale, about prayers that seemed to vanish into ceiling tiles, about a youth pastor who once told him that "real Christians don't doubt." By the time we got back, he was crying—not from sadness, exactly, but from relief. Someone finally knew.

Here's what I want you to hear before I say anything else: that conversation is sacred. The questions you're carrying, the ones you haven't said out loud, the ones that wake you up at 3 AM—they belong here. They don't make you a bad Christian. They make you human.

---

I think we need to start by being honest about how weird it is that doubt feels so dangerous in church. Most of you are in a season where you're supposed to be questioning everything. Your teachers want you to think critically. Your coaches want you to analyze your performance. Your friends are debating politics and ethics and whether pineapple belongs on pizza. Questioning is how you grow.

But somehow, when it comes to faith, we get this message that questions are dangerous. That faith means having all the answers locked down. That if you're not 100% certain, you're doing it wrong.

Let me tell you something I've learned from sitting with hundreds of people your age: the ones who struggle most with faith aren't the ones asking hard questions. They're the ones pretending they don't have them. The performance of certainty is exhausting. And it's brittle. It breaks.

Real faith—robust, lasting, honest faith—has room for "I don't know." It has to. Because you're not the first person to wonder, and you won't be the last.

---

There's a story I want to tell you about a man named Habakkuk. He's not as famous as David or as quotable as Paul, but he's maybe the most honest person in the whole Bible.

Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah, probably around 600 BC. And he was furious with God. Not in a abstract, theological way. In a *where are you* way.

He looks around his country and sees violence, corruption, injustice. The powerful crush the weak. The legal system is rigged. And God seems to be doing nothing. So Habakkuk does something remarkable: he complains. Directly. To God's face.

"How long, LORD, must I call for help, but you do not listen?" That's how his book opens. No preamble. No "I know you're probably busy." Just raw frustration.

God answers. It's not a great answer—basically, "I'm going to send the Babylonians to punish Judah." Which raises even worse questions, because the Babylonians are *worse* than the people they're punishing. Habakkuk's second complaint is basically: "Are you seeing what I'm seeing? You're using *them*?"

Here's what gets me: God doesn't strike him down. Doesn't say "how dare you question me." The conversation continues. God invites Habakkuk to keep watching, to keep waiting. And the book ends with one of the most beautiful, strange passages in Scripture—a declaration of trust that doesn't pretend everything is fine.

"Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls..." Do you hear what's happening? He's imagining total devastation. Total loss. Everything that makes life good, gone.

And then: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior."

This is not someone who got all his questions answered. This is someone who kept showing up to the conversation. Who chose—deliberately, in the absence of certainty—to trust the character of the God he'd been arguing with.

Habakkuk's doubt didn't destroy his faith. It deepened it. Because it was *engaged* doubt, not detached cynicism. He cared enough to fight.

---

I want to name something that I think happens a lot. There's a difference between intellectual doubt—"Does this make sense?"—and what I'd call relational doubt: "Can I really trust God?" They're related, but they're not the same.

You might have questions about the historical reliability of Scripture, or about how to reconcile faith and science, or about why a good God allows suffering. Those are real and important. But often, underneath them, there's something more personal. A prayer that wasn't answered the way you hoped. A loss that doesn't fit any theological framework. A sense that God, if God is there, feels distant.

Both kinds of doubt deserve attention. But I think we sometimes try to solve the intellectual questions while ignoring the relational ones. We want the right argument, the knock-down proof, as if faith were primarily about winning debates. But faith, at its core, is trust in a person. And trust is built through relationship, not just information.

This means that your doubt might need different things at different times. Sometimes it needs better thinking—resources, conversations, patient study. Sometimes it needs lament—permission to grieve what you thought you knew, or what you hoped would be true. Sometimes it just needs time. The pressure to resolve everything immediately is not from God. God is patient. God waits.

---

I want to push back on one more thing. Sometimes you'll hear that doubt is the opposite of faith, so you just need to suppress it and believe harder. But that's not how trust works anywhere else in your life.

If you're uncertain whether a friend has your back, you don't just decide to stop wondering. You watch them. You test the relationship, maybe in small ways at first. You see if they're trustworthy. And if they are, your trust grows—not because you forced it, but because it was earned.

Faith is similar. It's not blind. It's *earned* trust, built through experience, through the slow accumulation of moments where God proved faithful even when you weren't sure. The Psalms are full of this—"I waited patiently for the LORD; he turned to me and heard my cry." Waiting comes first. The hearing comes after.

Your doubt, honestly examined, can actually become part of your testimony. Not something to hide, but something that shaped you. The questions that drove you deeper. The darkness that made you desperate for light.

---

So what do you do with this? I don't want to give you a three-step plan that pretends to solve everything. But I do want to offer something concrete.

Here's my suggestion: find one person you can tell the truth to. Not performative doubt, the kind that's really just cynicism or an excuse to disengage. Your real questions. The ones that scare you.

Maybe that's a parent, though I know for some of you that feels impossible. Maybe it's a youth leader, a teacher, a counselor, a friend who's a little further along. Someone who won't panic, who won't give you easy answers, who can sit with you in the not-knowing.

And here's the second part: keep showing up. However you can. Prayer, even when it feels like talking to yourself. Scripture, even when it confuses you. Community, even when you're not sure you belong. These practices don't prove anything. But they keep the relationship alive while you figure out what you believe.

There's a phrase from the philosopher Søren Kierkegaard that I come back to: "Faith is the highest passion in a human being." Not the easiest. Not the most comfortable. The highest—meaning it costs something, it risks something, it demands everything.

You're in the middle of that risk right now. It doesn't feel like faith, maybe. It feels like confusion, or exhaustion, or loneliness. But if you're still asking, still seeking, still hoping against hope that there might be something true and good to build your life on—that *is* faith. Small, stubborn, honest faith.

The God who met Habakkuk in his complaint is not afraid of your questions. The God who let Thomas touch the wounds is not threatened by your need for evidence. The God who became human and cried out "why have you forsaken me" knows what it is to feel abandoned.

You are not alone in this. And you don't have to pretend to be further along than you are.

So here's what I'm asking you to carry with you: one true thing you can say about where you are right now. Not where you think you should be. Where you are. And one person you might say it to.

The conversation matters. The honesty matters. You matter—questions, doubts, and all.

**The 3 AM Search History**

I want to start with a confession about what happens at three in the morning.

You know the drill. You’re supposed to be asleep, but your brain has other plans. You’re staring at the ceiling, or at the blue light of your phone under the covers, and you’re Googling things like “how do we know God is real” or “contradictions in the Bible” or “why do bad things happen to good people if God is all-powerful.” Maybe you’re not typing it into a search bar—maybe you’re just lying there with the question burning a hole in your chest, wondering if you’re the only one in your youth group who feels like they’re faking it.

Here’s what I need you to hear first: **you are not broken.** That 3 AM feeling isn’t a spiritual emergency. It’s not a failure of faith. It’s actually a sign that your brain is doing exactly what it’s supposed to do at your age.

Between fourteen and eighteen, something shifts neurologically. You start developing what psychologists call “metacognition”—you start thinking about your thinking. You stop accepting things just because an adult said them, and you start asking, *“But is it actually true? Do I actually believe this, or do I just believe that I should believe it?”* That’s not rebellion. That’s intellectual integrity. That’s growing up.

And here’s the wild part: the Bible is actually full of people who had the spiritual equivalent of a 3 AM spiral.

**The Prophet Who Wouldn’t Stop Complaining**

Let me tell you about Habakkuk. He’s a minor prophet, which just means his book is short, not that he’s unimportant. Habakkuk is basically the patron saint of unanswered questions.

The book opens with him straight-up yelling at God. No polite prayer language. No “Dear Heavenly Father.” Just: *“How long, LORD, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save?”* He’s looking around at a world that’s falling apart—violence, injustice, suffering—and he’s saying, “God, where are you? And if you’re here, why are you doing such a terrible job?”

God answers. Which seems good, except God’s answer is essentially: *“Oh, you think things are bad now? Wait until you see what I’m planning. I’m sending the Babylonians to destroy everything.”*

This is not comforting. This is not “God has a plan, sweetie.” This is God saying the plan involves something worse.

So Habakkuk complains *again*. He’s like, “Wait, hold up. You’re holy. You can’t look on evil. So why are you using people who are *more* evil to fix the evil? That doesn’t make mathematical sense.” He’s arguing theology with the Creator of the universe. He’s not afraid that God will smite him for asking. He just needs to know.

And here’s where it gets interesting. God doesn’t give him a satisfying answer. God doesn’t explain theodicy or provide a chart of the divine master plan. God basically says, *“The righteous will live by faith.”* Which is… cryptic? Helpful, but not in the way Habakkuk probably wanted.

But then Habakkuk writes one of the most beautiful poems in the Bible. He says: *“Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior.”*

Notice what he’s saying. He’s not saying, “Now I understand everything and it all makes sense.” He’s saying, “I still don’t see the fruit. I still don’t have the evidence I asked for. The questions are still there. But I’m choosing to stay. I’m choosing to rejoice—not because the doubt is gone, but because the dialogue continues.”

**Excavation, Not Demolition**

We often think doubt works like a wrecking ball. One question swings in, and the whole building of faith collapses. But what if it’s more like archaeology?

When archaeologists find an ancient city, they don’t just accept the topsoil. They dig. They remove layers of dirt, debris, and later additions that don’t belong to the original structure. Sometimes the digging is uncomfortable. Sometimes they hit bedrock and realize some of what they thought was ancient was actually just garbage dumped there in the 1950s.

Doubt works like that. When you ask, “Do I actually believe this?” or “Is this consistent with a loving God?” you’re not destroying your faith. You’re excavating it. You’re finding out what’s bedrock and what was just cultural topsoil—things you inherited from your parents, or from a youth group culture, or from a fear of hell, rather than from your own encounter with whatever is true.

The faith that survives honest questioning is different from the faith that never asks. It’s thinner in some places—yes, you lose some certainties—but it’s denser. It has texture. It’s connected to your actual brain, your actual experience, not just a script you’re performing.

And here’s something nobody tells you: the people you admire most in the Christian tradition—the writers, the saints, the theologians—nearly all of them have journals or letters where they’re screaming into the void like Habakkuk. C.S. Lewis wrote about his grief after his wife died in terms that would get him kicked out of some churches today. Mother Teresa’s private letters reveal decades of feeling nothing but silence from God. They didn’t publish these doubts to be edgy. They wrote them because faith that can’t accommodate darkness isn’t faith—it’s denial.

**What to Do With the Questions**

So what do you do when you’re in it? When the 3 AM questions show up and won’t leave?

I’m not going to tell you to “just pray more” or “read your Bible until you feel better.” That’s like telling someone with a broken leg to just run faster. Instead, I want to give you one specific practice. I’m going to call it the **Habakkuk Journal**.

Here’s how it works:

Get a notebook or open a notes app that no one else has access to—not because it’s shameful, but because it needs to be private enough that you won’t censor yourself. Once this week, set a timer for ten minutes and write a letter to God that begins exactly like Habakkuk’s: *“How long, LORD…”* or *“I don’t understand why…”* or even *“I’m angry at you because…”*

Write the thing you’re most afraid to say out loud. The doubt about whether prayer actually works. The suspicion that maybe the universe is just random. The anger at a specific loss that doesn’t fit with the “God is good” slogan.

Then—and this is the hard part—don’t try to resolve it. Don’t end the entry with “but I know God has a plan.” Just let it sit there. Close the notebook. Come back to it in three days. Read what you wrote. And then write a second entry—not an answer, not a theological correction, just an update on where you are now. Is the question sharper? Has it shifted? Are you still in the dark?

Do this for a month. You’re not looking for the moment when the doubt disappears. You’re looking for the moment when you realize you’re still showing up to the conversation—even angry, even confused, even silent. That’s the Habakkuk moment. That’s faith with calluses on its hands.

If you’re not a journal person, find one adult—maybe not even your pastor, maybe a teacher, a counselor, an older cousin—who has eyes that don’t panic when you ask scary questions. Ask them: *“Did you ever think about leaving? What kept you here?”* Listen for the hesitation in their voice. The real answer is usually in the pause before they speak.

**The Permission to Be Unfinished**

I’ll close with this: you are allowed to be unfinished. You are allowed to sit in the back row during worship because the lyrics feel too heavy to sing right now. You are allowed to read the Bible with a pen in your hand, underlining the parts that trouble you instead of the parts that comfort you. You are allowed to say, “I don’t know,” when someone asks what you believe.

The goal was never to achieve a state of perfect certainty. The goal is to become someone who can hold complexity without letting go of hope. Habakkuk never got his explanation. But he got something better: he got to keep talking. He got to keep wrestling. And in the wrestling, he found that God could handle his weight.

Your questions are not a detour from the path of faith. Right now, they *are* the path. Keep walking. Keep asking. The dark room at 3 AM is not empty. You’re just learning to see in the dark.

And if you’re here, why are you doing such a terrible job?”

God answers. Which seems good, except God’s answer is essentially: *“Oh, you think things are bad now? Wait until you see what I’m planning. I’m sending the Babylonians to destroy everything.”*

This is not the cross-stitched pillow version of “God has a plan.” This is God saying the plan involves walking through fire before you get to the other side.

So Habakkuk complains *again*. He’s like, “Wait, hold up. You’re holy. You can’t look on evil. So why are you using people who are *more* evil to fix the evil? And here’s where it gets interesting. God doesn’t give him a satisfying answer. God doesn’t explain theodicy or provide a chart of the divine master plan. God basically says, *“The righteous will live by faith.”* Which is… cryptic? Helpful, but not in the way Habakkuk probably wanted.

Habakkuk is terrified by this answer. He says his heart pounds, his lips quiver, his bones literally shake. He’s not immediately signing up for this plan. But he decides that if the world is falling apart, he’s going to hold onto the one thing that isn’t. He writes one of the most beautiful poems in the Bible: *“Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior.”*

The faith that survives honest questioning is different from the faith that never asks. It’s thinner in some places—yes, you lose some certainties—but it’s denser. It has texture. It’s connected to your actual brain, your actual experience, not just a script you’re performing.

Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save?”* He’s looking around at a world that’s falling apart—violence, injustice, suffering—and he’s saying, “God, where are you? And if you’re here, why are you doing such a terrible job?”

God answers. Which seems good, except God’s answer is essentially: *“Oh, you think things are bad now? Wait until you see what I’m planning. I’m sending the Babylonians to destroy everything.”*

This is not comforting. This is not “God has a plan.” This is God saying the plan involves something worse.

So Habakkuk complains *again*. He’s like, “Wait, hold up. You’re holy. You can’t look on evil. So why are you using people who are *more* evil to fix the evil? That doesn’t make mathematical sense.” He’s essentially asking the hardest question: how can a good God allow evil? That question has a fancy name—theodicy—but Habakkuk just calls it “what the heck.” He’s arguing theology with the Creator of the universe. He’s not afraid that God will smite him for asking. He just needs to know.

And here’s where it gets interesting. God doesn’t give him a satisfying answer. God doesn’t provide a chart of the divine blueprint. God basically says, *“The righteous will live by faith.”* Which is… cryptic? Helpful, but not in the way Habakkuk probably wanted.

But then Habakkuk writes one of the most beautiful poems in the Bible. He says: *“Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior.”*

Notice what he’s saying. He’s not saying, “Now I understand everything and it all makes sense.” He’s saying, “I still don’t see the fruit. I still don’t have the evidence I asked for. The questions are still there. But I’m choosing to stay. I’m choosing to rejoice—not because the doubt is gone, but because the dialogue continues.”

This isn’t just an Old Testament thing. Jesus himself, on the cross, quotes a psalm that starts as a scream: *“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”* The question doesn’t get answered there either. But it gets asked.

**Excavation, Not Demolition**

We often think doubt works like a wrecking ball. One question swings in, and the whole building of faith collapses. But what if it’s more like archaeology?

When archaeologists find an ancient city, they don’t just accept the topsoil. They dig. They remove layers of dirt and debris—later additions that don’t belong to the original structure. Sometimes the digging is uncomfortable. Sometimes they hit bedrock and realize some of what they thought was ancient was actually just garbage someone dumped there last century.

Doubt works like that. When you ask, “Do I actually believe this?” or “Is this consistent with a loving God?” you’re not destroying your faith. You’re excavating it. You’re finding out what’s bedrock and what was just cultural topsoil—things you inherited from your parents, or from a youth group culture, or from a fear of hell, rather than from your own encounter with whatever is true.

The faith that survives honest questioning is different from the faith that never asks. It’s thinner in some places—yes, you lose some certainties—but it’s denser. It has texture. It’s connected to your actual brain, your actual experience, not just a script you’re performing.

And here’s something nobody tells you: the people you admire most in the Christian tradition—the writers, the saints, the theologians—nearly all of them have journals where they’re screaming into the void like Habakkuk. C.S. Lewis—the guy who gave us Aslan—wrote after his wife died that he felt God was an “unscrupulous dentist.” Mother Teresa’s private letters reveal decades of feeling nothing but silence from God. They didn’t publish these doubts to be edgy. They wrote them because faith that can’t accommodate darkness isn’t faith—it’s denial.

**What to Do With the Questions**

So what do you do when you’re in it? When the 3 AM questions show up and won’t leave?

I’m not going to tell you to “just pray more” or “read your Bible until you feel better.” That’s like telling someone with a broken leg to just run faster. Instead, I want to give you three specific options, depending on what fits you right now.

**Option One: The Habakkuk Journal**

Get a notebook or open a notes app that no one else has access to—not because it’s shameful, but because it needs to be private enough that you won’t censor yourself. Once this week, set a timer for ten minutes and write a letter to God that begins exactly like Habakkuk’s: *“How long, LORD…”* or *“I don’t understand why…”* or even *“I’m angry at you because…”*

Write the thing you’re most afraid to say out loud. Like: *“I’m angry at you for letting my friend get depressed.”* Or: *“What if prayer is just me talking to myself?”* Or: *“I don’t know if I can trust the Bible when it seems to contradict science.”*

Then—and this is the hard part—don’t try to resolve it. Don’t end the entry with “but I know God has a plan.” Just let it sit there. Close the notebook. Come back to it in three days. Read what you wrote. And then write a second entry—not an answer, not a theological correction, just an update on where you are now. Is the question sharper? Has it shifted? Are you still in the dark?

Do this for a month. You’re not looking for the moment when the doubt disappears. You’re looking for the moment when you realize you’re still showing up to the conversation—even angry, even confused, even silent. That’s the Habakkuk moment. That’s faith with calluses on its hands.

**Option Two: The Adult Who Doesn’t Panic**

If you’re not a journal person, find one adult—maybe not even your pastor, maybe a teacher, a counselor, an older cousin—who has eyes that don’t panic when you ask scary questions. Look for someone who pauses before they answer, whose voice gets quieter not louder when you ask hard things. Ask them: *“Did you ever think about leaving? What kept you here?”* Listen for the hesitation in their voice. The real answer is usually in the pause before they speak.

**Option Three: The Two-Person Doubt Club**

Or find one friend in this room, text them tonight, and say, *“Hey, do you ever have the 3 AM thing?”* Start a two-person doubt club. Meet at a coffee shop or on FaceTime and agree that you won’t try to fix each other. You’ll just witness. Sometimes knowing you’re not the only one staring at the ceiling makes the dark room feel less empty.

**The Permission to Be Unfinished**

I’ll close with this: you are allowed to be unfinished. You are allowed to sit in the back row during worship because the lyrics feel too heavy to sing right now. You are allowed to tell your parents, “I need to figure out what I actually believe before I keep going through the motions.” You are allowed to read the Bible with a pen in your hand, underlining the parts that trouble you instead of the parts that comfort you. You are allowed to say, “I don’t know,” when someone at school asks what you believe.

The goal was never to achieve a state of perfect certainty. The goal is to become someone who can hold complexity without letting go of hope. Habakkuk never got his explanation. But he got something better: he got to keep talking. He got to keep wrestling. And in the wrestling, he found that God could handle the weight of his raw, uncensored honesty.

Your questions are not a detour from the path of faith. Right now, they *are* the path. Keep walking. Keep asking. The dark room at 3 AM is not empty. You’re just learning to see in the dark.

**The 3 AM Question**

Picture this: It’s 2:47 on a Tuesday morning. You’re not awake because you’re having fun. You’re awake because your brain has decided to run a background check on everything you believe, and the results are not looking good. You’re staring at the ceiling, and suddenly the questions arrive—not polite, theoretical questions, but the kind that feel like they’re physically sitting on your chest.

*What if this is all just a story we tell ourselves to feel better?*

*If God is good, why does the news look like that?*

*Am I only a Christian because my parents are?*

If you’ve been there, you’re not alone. In fact, if you *haven’t* been there yet, you probably will be. And here’s what I need you to hear first: that moment, that 3 AM panic, doesn’t make you a bad Christian. It makes you a thinking human being.

We don’t talk about this enough in church, so let me say it clearly: doubt is not the opposite of faith. It’s often the *texture* of it. You’re at an age where your brain is literally rewiring itself to handle abstract thought, to question authority, to test what’s real against what’s just inherited. That’s not spiritual failure. That’s development. If your faith can’t withstand your honest questions, it wasn’t really yours to begin with—it was just a costume you were wearing.

So let’s stop pretending. Let’s look at someone who doubted out loud, in writing, and somehow got it included in the Bible.

**Habakkuk: The Prophet Who Wouldn’t Shut Up**

Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah, probably around the time when everything was falling apart—corruption in the government, violence in the streets, the rich exploiting the poor while religious leaders looked the other way. And Habakkuk looks at God and says, essentially, *What gives?*

His book opens with zero preamble. No “Dear God, praise Your holy name.” Just: *“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save?”* He accuses God of being silent, of being idle, of watching wrongdoing and doing nothing.

It’s angry. It’s raw. It’s the kind of prayer you’d be afraid to say out loud in youth group because you’re worried someone would hand you a pamphlet afterward.

But here’s the thing: God doesn’t strike him down. God doesn’t say, “How dare you question me?” Instead, God says, *“Look at the nations and watch—and be utterly amazed. For I am going to do something in your days that you would not believe, even if you were told.”*

That’s not a satisfying answer. It’s not an explanation. It’s basically God saying, “I’m working, but you won’t understand it yet.”

So Habakkuk does what most of us do when we don’t get answers: he doubles down. “Okay, but *why* do you tolerate the treacherous? Why are you silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?” He’s not letting it go. He’s wrestling.

And then comes the strange part. God tells him to write the vision down, to wait for it, that it will come at the appointed time. So Habakkuk waits. We don’t know how long—days, months, years. The text is silent about the waiting, which is accurate, because that’s what waiting feels like: silence.

But the book ends with one of the most honest statements in Scripture. Habakkuk writes a poem saying that even if the fig tree doesn’t bud, even if there are no grapes on the vines, even if the fields produce no food and the stalls are empty—*“yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.”*

Notice what didn’t happen. God didn’t explain the suffering. He didn’t give Habakkuk a theological diagram that made everything make sense. The violence was still there. The questions were still valid. But Habakkuk had moved from accusation to trust—not because he got answers, but because he stayed in the conversation long enough to remember who he was talking to.

**Excavation, Not Demolition**

There’s a difference between doubt that destroys and doubt that excavates. Demolition doubt says, “This is broken, so I’m walking away.” Excavation doubt says, “Something here doesn’t make sense, so I’m going to dig until I find what’s real.”

When you ask hard questions—about suffering, about science and faith, about why some prayers seem to bounce off the ceiling—you’re not breaking your faith. You’re stress-testing it. Anyone can believe something when it’s easy, when the worship music is loud and the youth retreat high is still wearing off. But faith that holds up at 3 AM, when you’re alone with your thoughts—that’s architecture. That’s steel.

The danger isn’t your questions. The danger is pretending you don’t have them, stuffing them down until they calcify into cynicism or explode into sudden abandonment of everything you once valued. The most fragile faith I’ve seen belongs to people who never allowed themselves to doubt out loud, who performed certainty until they couldn’t perform it anymore, and then left in a single night because they had no practice in holding tension.

But when you bring your doubt into the light—when you say to a friend, “I’m not sure I believe this,” or write in a journal, “God, where are you?”—something shifts. You’re no longer alone with it. You’ve turned doubt into dialogue. And dialogue is where relationship lives.

**The Habakkuk Challenge**

So here’s what I want you to try this week. Not a commitment to believe harder. Not a promise to stop asking questions. Just this:

**Write one honest complaint.**

Find a piece of paper, your notes app, whatever. Write a sentence that starts with “How long, Lord…” or “I don’t understand why…” or “It seems like…” Make it specific. Not “Why is there suffering?” but “Why did my friend get hurt when they were trying to do the right thing?” Not “Is the Bible true?” but “I read that story about the conquest of Canaan and it doesn’t match the God I thought I knew—what do I do with that?”

Write it as if God is actually listening, because the story of Habakkuk suggests that He is—even to the angry ones, especially to the honest ones.

Then, wait. Don’t demand an answer by Friday. Just let it sit. See if anything shifts. See if someone crosses your path who knows something about that question. See if a verse hits differently. See if the question itself changes shape.

And if you’re feeling brave: tell one person. Not the whole group. Just one person you trust—maybe a mentor, maybe a friend who gets it—and say, “I’ve been wrestling with this.” You might be surprised to hear them say, “Me too.”

**The Invitation**

I can’t promise you that all your questions will resolve into neat answers. I’m not going to stand here and tell you that faith is easy if you just try hard enough. That would be a lie, and you’re old enough to know a lie when you hear one.

But I can tell you that the God who listened to Habakkuk’s rage, who let Thomas touch the wounds, who sat with Job in the ash heap without explaining Himself—that God can handle your 3 AM questions. He’s not fragile. Your doubt won’t break Him.

And the faith that emerges from honest wrestling? It’s different than the faith you inherited. It’s quieter, maybe. Less defensive. But it’s yours. It’s held through the night. And when the morning comes—whether that’s next week or next year—you’ll find that the questions didn’t destroy your faith. They just cleared away everything else that was pretending to be it.

So write the question. Ask it out loud. Stay in the conversation. The silence won’t last forever.

You’re awake because your brain has decided to run a background check on everything you believe, and the results are not looking good. You’re staring at the ceiling, and suddenly the questions arrive—not polite, theoretical questions, but the kind that feel like they’re physically sitting on your chest.

*What if this is all just a story we tell ourselves to feel better?*

*If God is good, why does the news look like that?*

*Am I only a Christian because my parents are?*

And then, right underneath those, the ones that feel even more urgent: *What if I fail this test? What if I never figure out what I’m supposed to do with my life? And underneath all of that, the big one: What if God isn't listening to any of it?*

If you’ve been there, you’re not alone. In fact, if you *haven’t* been there yet, you probably will be. And here’s what I need you to hear first: that moment, that 3 AM panic, doesn’t make you a bad Christian. It makes you a thinking human being.

We don’t talk about this enough in church, so let me say it clearly: doubt is not the opposite of faith. It’s often the *texture* of it. You’re at an age where your brain is literally rewiring itself to handle abstract thought, to question authority, to test what’s real against what’s just inherited. That’s not spiritual failure. That’s development. If your faith can’t withstand your honest questions, it wasn’t really yours to begin with—it was just a costume you were wearing.

So let’s stop pretending. Let’s look at someone who doubted out loud, in writing, and somehow got it included in the Bible.

**Habakkuk: The Prophet Who Wouldn’t Shut Up**

Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah, probably around the time when everything was falling apart—corruption in the government, violence in the streets, the rich exploiting the poor while religious leaders looked the other way. And Habakkuk looks at God and says, essentially, *What gives?*

His book opens with zero preamble. No “Dear God, praise Your holy name.” Just: *“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save?”* He accuses God of being silent, of being idle, of watching wrongdoing and doing nothing.

It’s angry. It’s raw. It’s the kind of prayer that comes from a place of deep betrayal—the feeling that you’ve been holding up your end of the bargain, and God has gone quiet. It’s the prayer you’d be afraid to say out loud in youth group because you’re worried someone would hand you a pamphlet afterward, or because saying the words might make the silence feel permanent.

But here’s the thing: God doesn’t strike him down. God doesn’t say, “How dare you question me?” Instead, God says, *“Look at the nations and watch—and be utterly amazed. For I am going to do something in your days that you would not believe, even if you were told.”*

That’s not a satisfying answer. It’s not an explanation. It’s basically God saying, “I’m working, but you won’t understand it yet.”

So Habakkuk does what most of us do when we don’t get answers: he doubles down. “Okay, but *why* do you tolerate the treacherous? Why are you silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?” He’s not letting it go. He’s wrestling.

And then comes the strange part. God tells him to write the vision down, to wait for it, that it will come at the appointed time. So Habakkuk waits. We don’t know how long—days, months, years. The text is silent about the waiting, which is accurate, because that’s what waiting feels like: silence.

**The 3 AM Question**

Picture this: It’s 2:47 on a Tuesday morning. You’re not awake because you’re having fun. You’re awake because your brain has decided to run a background check on everything you believe, and the results are not looking good. You’re staring at the ceiling, and suddenly the questions arrive—not polite, theoretical questions, but the kind that feel like they’re physically sitting on your chest.

*What if this is all just a story we tell ourselves to feel better?*

*If God is good, why does the news look like that?*

*Am I only a Christian because my parents are?*

*What if I'm only doing this to avoid disappointing the people who love me?*

If you’ve been there, you’re not alone. In fact, if you *haven’t* been there yet, you probably will be. And here’s what I need you to hear first: that moment, that 3 AM panic, doesn’t make you a bad Christian. It makes you a thinking human being.

We don’t talk about this enough in church, so let me say it clearly: doubt is not the opposite of faith. It’s often the *texture* of it. You’re at an age where your brain is literally rewiring itself to handle abstract thought, to question authority, to test what’s real against what’s just inherited. That’s not spiritual failure. That’s development. If your faith can’t withstand your honest questions, it wasn’t really yours to begin with—it was just something you borrowed, not something you built.

So let’s stop pretending. Let’s look at someone who doubted out loud, in writing, and somehow got it included in the Bible.

**Habakkuk: The Prophet Who Wouldn’t Shut Up**

Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah, probably around the time when everything was falling apart—corruption in the government, violence in the streets, the rich exploiting the poor while religious leaders looked the other way. And Habakkuk looks at God and says, essentially, *What gives?*

His book opens with zero preamble. No “Dear God, praise Your holy name.” Just: *“How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen? Or cry out to you, ‘Violence!’ but you do not save?”* He accuses God of being silent, of being idle, of watching wrongdoing and doing nothing.

It’s angry. It’s raw. It’s the kind of prayer you’d be afraid to say out loud in youth group because you’re worried someone would hand you a pamphlet afterward.

But here’s the thing: God doesn’t strike him down. God doesn’t say, “How dare you question me?” Instead, God says, *“Look at the nations and watch—and be utterly amazed. For I am going to do something in your days that you would not believe, even if you were told.”*

That’s not a satisfying answer. It’s not an explanation. It’s basically God saying, “I’m working, but you won’t understand it yet.”

So Habakkuk does what most of us do when we don’t get answers: he doubles down. “Okay, but *why* do you tolerate the treacherous? Why are you silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?” He’s not letting it go. He’s wrestling.

And then comes the strange part. God tells him to write the vision down, to wait for it, that it will come at the appointed time. So Habakkuk waits. We don’t know how long—days, months, years. The text is silent about the waiting, which is accurate, because that’s what waiting feels like: silence.

But the book ends with one of the most honest statements in Scripture. Habakkuk writes a poem saying that even if the fig tree doesn’t bud, even if there are no grapes on the vines, even if the fields produce no food and the stalls are empty—*“yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.”*

Notice what didn’t happen. God didn’t explain the suffering. He didn’t give Habakkuk a theological diagram that made everything make sense. The violence was still there. The questions were still valid. But Habakkuk had moved from accusation to trust—not because he got answers, but because he stayed in the conversation long enough to remember who he was talking to.

This kind of doubt—staying in the conversation when nothing makes sense—is what I call excavation, not demolition.

**Excavation, Not Demolition**

There’s a difference between doubt that destroys and doubt that digs. Demolition doubt says, “This is broken, so I’m walking away.” Excavation doubt says, “Something here doesn’t make sense, so I’m going to dig until I find what’s real.”

When you ask hard questions—about suffering, about science and faith, about why some prayers seem to bounce off the ceiling—you’re not breaking your faith. You’re stress-testing it. Anyone can believe something when it’s easy, when the worship music is loud and the youth retreat high is still wearing off. But faith that holds up at 3 AM, when you’re alone with your thoughts—that’s architecture. That’s steel.

The danger isn’t your questions. The danger is pretending you don’t have them, stuffing them down until they calcify into cynicism or explode into sudden abandonment of everything you once valued. I’ve watched this happen to people who never allowed themselves to doubt out loud, who performed certainty until they couldn’t perform it anymore, and then left in a single night because they had no practice in holding tension. They never learned that you can stay in the conversation even when you’re furious.

But when you bring your doubt into the light—when you say to a friend, “I’m not sure I believe this,” or write in a journal, “God, where are you?”—something shifts. You’re no longer alone with it. You’ve turned doubt into dialogue. And dialogue is where relationship lives.

**The Habakkuk Challenge**

So here’s what I want you to try this week. Not a commitment to believe harder. Not a promise to stop asking questions. Just this:

**Write one honest complaint.**

Find a piece of paper, your notes app, whatever. Write a sentence that starts with “How long, Lord…” or “I don’t understand why…” or “It seems like…” Make it specific. Not “Why is there suffering?” but “Why did my friend get hurt when they were trying to do the right thing?” Not “Is the Bible true?” but “I read that story about the conquest of Canaan and it doesn’t match the God I thought I knew—what do I do with that?”

Write it as if God is actually listening, because the story of Habakkuk suggests that He is—even to the angry ones, especially to the honest ones.

Then, wait. Don’t demand an answer by Friday. Just let it sit. See if anything shifts. See if someone crosses your path who knows something about that question. See if a verse hits differently. See if the question itself changes shape—you might find that the question you start with isn’t the question you end with, and that’s okay too.

And if you’re feeling brave: tell one person. Not the whole group. Just one person you trust—maybe a mentor, maybe a friend who gets it—and say, “I’ve been wrestling with this.” You might be surprised to hear them say, “Me too.”

**So Here’s the Thing**

I can’t promise you that all your questions will resolve into neat answers. I’m not going to stand here and tell you that faith is easy if you just try hard enough. That would be a lie, and you’re old enough to know a lie when you hear one.

But I can tell you that the God who listened to Habakkuk’s rage, who let Thomas touch the wounds, who sat with Job in the ash heap without explaining Himself—that God can handle your 3 AM questions. He’s not fragile. Your doubt won’t break Him.

And the faith that emerges from honest wrestling? It’s different than the faith you inherited. It’s quieter, maybe. Less defensive. But it’s yours. It’s held through the night. And when the morning comes—whether that’s next week or next year—you’ll find that the questions didn’t destroy your faith. They just cleared away everything else that was pretending to be it.

So write the question. Ask it out loud. Stay in the conversation. 

The silence won’t last forever.

You’re stress-testing it. Anyone can believe something when it’s easy, when the worship music is loud and the youth retreat high is still wearing off. But faith that holds up at 3 AM, when you’re alone with your thoughts—that’s architecture. That’s steel.

The danger isn’t your questions. The danger is pretending you don’t have them, stuffing them down until they calcify into cynicism or explode into sudden abandonment of everything you once valued. The most fragile faith I’ve seen belongs to people who never allowed themselves to doubt out loud, who performed certainty until they couldn’t perform it anymore, and then left in a single night because they had no practice in holding tension.

But when you bring your doubt into the light—when you say to a friend, “I’m not sure I believe this,” or write in a journal, “God, where are you?”—something shifts. You’re no longer alone with it. You’ve turned doubt into dialogue. And dialogue is where relationship lives.

**The Habakkuk Challenge**

So here’s what I want you to try this week. Not a commitment to believe harder. Not a promise to stop asking questions. Just this:

**Write one honest complaint.**

Find a piece of paper, your notes app, whatever. Write a sentence that starts with “How long, Lord…” or “I don’t understand why…” or “It seems like…” Make it specific. Not “Why is there suffering?” but “Why did my friend get hurt when they were trying to do the right thing?” Not “Is the Bible true?” but “I read that story about the conquest of Canaan and it doesn’t match the God I thought I knew—what do I do with that?”

Write it as if God is actually listening, because the story of Habakkuk suggests that He is—even to the angry ones, especially to the honest ones.

Then, wait. Don’t demand an answer by Friday. Just let it sit. See if anything shifts. See if someone crosses your path who knows something about that question. See if a verse hits differently. See if the question itself changes shape.

And if the silence lasts longer—months, even years—that doesn’t mean you failed at the exercise. Some questions are slow work. The point isn’t to get an answer. It’s to stop pretending you don’t have the question.

If you’re feeling brave: tell one person. Not the whole group. Just one person you trust—maybe a mentor, maybe a friend who gets it—and say, “I’ve been wrestling with this.” You might be surprised to hear them say, “Me too.” If the first person doesn’t get it, try a second. Not everyone knows how to hold someone else’s doubt. That’s about them, not about the validity of your question.

**The Invitation**

I can’t promise you that all your questions will resolve into neat answers. I’m not going to stand here and tell you that faith is easy if you just try hard enough, or that the morning always comes quickly. That would be a lie, and you’re old enough to know a lie when you hear one. Some nights last a long time.

But I can tell you that the God who listened to Habakkuk’s rage about the Babylonians, who let Thomas touch the wounds, who sat with Job in the ash heap without explaining Himself—that God can handle your 3 AM questions. He’s not fragile. Your doubt won’t break Him.

And the faith that emerges from honest wrestling? It’s different than the faith you inherited. It’s quieter, maybe. Less defensive. But it’s yours. It’s held through the night. And when the morning comes—whether that’s next week or next year—you’ll find that the questions didn’t destroy your faith. They just cleared away everything else that was pretending to be it.

So write the question. Ask it out loud. Stay in the conversation. The silence won’t last forever—but even while it does, you’re allowed to be there, fully honest, fully heard.

**The Questions We Don't Say Out Loud**

---

I want to tell you about a Tuesday night last October. I was sitting in my car in the parking lot of a twenty-four-hour grocery store, engine off, phone in my lap, staring at the steering wheel like it might start talking to me. I'd just come from a hospital room. A friend from my early twenties—someone I'd prayed with, laughed with, believed with—was dying of something that shouldn't have killed someone our age. And I couldn't pray. I mean, I physically could not form the words. Everything I'd said about God for fifteen years suddenly felt like language I'd learned for a test I no longer believed was coming.

I sat there for almost an hour. Not crying, not praying, just... stuck. The fluorescent lights from the store kept flickering, and I remember thinking, *Even the electricity here is uncertain.*

I tell you this because I think we need to start with the real thing, not the cleaned-up version. If you're sitting here tonight thinking *I have questions I'm not supposed to ask*, or *Everyone else seems fine and I'm falling apart*, or *What if this whole thing is wrong and I'm the only one who noticed*—you're not broken. You're not failing some spiritual test. You're being human in a world that makes believing genuinely difficult.

---

Here's what nobody told me when I was your age: doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Certainty is. I know that sounds backwards. We grow up thinking faith means *being sure*—saying the right words, feeling the right feelings, never wavering. But look at the actual people in the actual Bible, and you find something messier.

Take Habakkuk. Most people skip him because he's only three chapters, tucked between Nahum and Zephaniah—names that sound like medications. But Habakkuk is maybe the most honest book in the whole Bible. It starts with the prophet looking around at violence and injustice and saying, essentially, *God, what are you doing?* Not politely. Not with his hands folded. He's shouting. "How long, LORD, must I call for help, but you do not listen?" That's verse one. No introduction, no flattery. Just raw frustration.

And here's the wild part: God answers. Not with a rebuke. Not with *how dare you question me.* God says, essentially, *I hear you. Keep watching. It's worse than you think, and better than you can imagine, and both things are true at once.* The conversation continues—Habakkuk pushes back again, God responds again—and by the end, Habakkuk hasn't gotten the answers he wanted. The injustice hasn't disappeared. But something has shifted in him. He ends with this extraordinary statement: "Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food... yet I will rejoice in the LORD."

Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say *I understand now.* He doesn't say *The problem is solved.* He says: *I don't have what I need, and I will still sing.* That's not certainty. That's something stranger and stronger—faith that has walked through doubt and found it wasn't fatal.

Or consider Thomas. We call him "Doubting Thomas" like it's his full name, like he was born skeptical and died that way. But read the story again. Thomas missed the resurrection appearance. His friends came to him breathless, saying *We've seen the Lord!* And Thomas said, *Unless I see the nail marks, I won't believe.* We hear that as stubbornness, but I think it was grief. Thomas had already watched Jesus die. Hope hurts when you've been disappointed. He was protecting himself.

A week later, Jesus shows up specifically for him. Not with condemnation—*with his wounds still visible.* "Put your finger here," Jesus says. "See my hands." The wounds are part of the proof. And Thomas, touching the broken places, becomes the first person in John's gospel to call Jesus "God." Not Peter, who was so eager. Not John, who was so close. Thomas, who needed to see before he could speak.

I used to think that story was about Jesus satisfying doubt with evidence. Now I think it's about Jesus meeting Thomas in his doubt with presence. The scars remained. The questions didn't disappear. But Thomas found that the one he doubted was still there, still reaching toward him.

---

I want to be careful here, because I know how these talks can go. Someone says *doubt is normal* and you think *okay, but what if my doubt is the real kind?* Like there's a safe doubt and a dangerous doubt, and you have to figure out which one you have before anyone finds out.

I don't think it works that way. I've had doubts that dissolved like morning fog—questions I asked, answers I found, peace that followed. I've had other doubts that stayed for years, that changed shape, that I'm still carrying. Both have been part of my faith. Both have taught me something.

What I've learned is that the danger isn't doubt itself. The danger is pretending. When we perform certainty we don't feel, we cut ourselves off from the very people who could walk with us. When we silence our own questions, we often silence our capacity for wonder too. Real faith isn't the absence of uncertainty; it's the courage to keep showing up while uncertain.

There's research from the Fuller Youth Institute that tracked young people who stayed in faith communities through college. The ones who lasted weren't the ones with the most answers. They were the ones who had *permission to ask*—adults who said *I don't know either* instead of *just believe harder*, communities where questions were welcomed rather than managed. That matches what I see. The people I know with the deepest faith are often the ones who've walked through the most honest doubt.

---

So what do we do with this? I don't want to leave you with *just keep asking questions* and no road forward. Here's what I want to suggest.

**Find one person you can be honest with.** Not the whole youth group, not Instagram, not even your parents if that's not safe right now. One person—a friend, a mentor, a teacher, a counselor—who has earned the right to hear your real questions. Someone who won't panic, who won't try to fix you in three sentences, who can sit with you in the not-knowing. Vulnerability is risky, but isolation is worse. Your doubts will grow in the dark. They shrink, strangely, when spoken.

And here's a practice: for the next month, keep a question journal. Not answers—a journal of questions. When something bothers you about faith, write it down. When you hear something in a sermon that doesn't sit right, note it. When you pray and feel nothing, record that too. Date each entry. Then, every few weeks, read back through. You'll start to see patterns. Some questions will resolve. Others will deepen. A few might become the questions that shape your whole life. But you'll have evidence that you didn't ignore your own mind—that you took yourself seriously, which is part of taking God seriously.

The goal isn't to get to certainty. The goal is to become people who can hold complexity without collapsing, who can say *I don't fully understand this, and I'm still here.* That's the faith Habakkuk found. That's the faith Thomas found, touching wounds. That's the faith available to you—not despite your questions, but through them.

---

I'll end where I started. I did eventually pray that night in the parking lot, but it wasn't impressive. It was something like *I'm here and I don't know what I believe and I'm angry and I need you to be real because I can't pretend anymore.* Not exactly the Lord's Prayer. But it was true. And I've come to think that true is better than correct. That God meets us not in our polished performances but in our actual lives, with their actual mess.

Your questions are not a detour from faith. For many of you, they will be the path into something real and lasting. Don't apologize for needing to see. Don't rush to answers that don't satisfy. Keep walking. Keep asking. The one you're looking for has scars, and patience, and time for you.

---

*What's one question you've been afraid to say out loud? Who might you trust with it this week?*

# When You're Not Sure

Let me tell you something that might sound familiar.

You're sitting in youth group, or maybe church, or maybe just in a conversation with some friends who seem to know what they believe. Everyone's talking about faith like it's simple. Like they have it figured out. And you're sitting there thinking, *Wait, you actually feel that? You actually experience that?*

Or maybe it's 2 a.m. and you can't sleep because you've been thinking about something you can't quite name. Something about God. Something about whether any of this is real. And you don't tell anyone because you're afraid of what they'd think. You're afraid they might say you don't have enough faith. You're afraid they might be right.

Here's the first thing I want you to know: you're not alone. And more than that, you're not broken.

---

I think we get this idea that faith is supposed to feel certain all the time. Like if you really believe, you should never question anything. You should never feel lost. You should never sit in the dark and wonder if anyone's there.

But that's not what the Bible actually shows us. Not even close.

Look at the people in Scripture. These aren't perfect saints who never doubted. These are real people who wrestled with God, who argued with him, who screamed into the void and demanded answers.

David, the guy after God's own heart, wrote psalms about feeling abandoned. About God being far away. About crying out and hearing nothing back. This is in the Bible. These are prayers God preserved for thousands of years.

Job lost everything—his family, his health, his wealth—and then had to sit through his friends telling him he must have done something wrong. And what does Job do? He argues with God. He demands an explanation. He's not quiet about his confusion.

And then there's Thomas. You know the one. "Doubting Thomas." The guy who wouldn't believe Jesus was alive until he could touch the wounds himself.

Here's what I love about Thomas: he's honest. Everyone else is saying they've seen the risen Lord, and Thomas says, *Nope. Not convinced. I need to see it for myself.* He's not pretending. He's not performing faith he doesn't feel.

And here's what happens: Jesus shows up. And he doesn't rebuke Thomas for doubting. He doesn't say, "You should have just believed." He says, "Go ahead. Touch my hands. Touch my side. Stop doubting and believe."

That's not a condemnation. That's an invitation.

---

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't want to give you a cheap answer. I don't want to say, "Just have faith like Thomas and everything will be fine." That's not honest, and you know it.

The reality is, sometimes you do the asking and the seeking and the reaching, and you still don't get the answer you wanted. Sometimes you touch the wounds and you're still confused. Sometimes the 2 a.m. questions don't resolve by morning.

But here's what I think Thomas shows us: doubt can be a way of taking faith seriously. It's not the opposite of faith. It's actually a form of it. It's saying, *This matters too much to pretend about.* It's refusing to settle for something that doesn't feel true.

When Thomas demanded evidence, he wasn't rejecting Jesus. He was seeking him. And Jesus met him there.

That's what I want you to hear: you can bring your questions to God. You can bring your uncertainty. You don't have to pretend to be further along than you are.

---

Now, I'm not going to stand here and tell you that doubt is always comfortable or easy. It's not. It hurts to not know. It hurts to feel like everyone else has it figured out and you're still back at the beginning.

But I think there's a difference between the kind of doubt that says, "I don't care anymore" and the kind that says, "I care too much to pretend." And I think most of you in this room—the fact that you're here, the fact that you're thinking about this at all—that's the second kind. That's the kind that still has some hope in it.

Faith isn't the absence of questions. It's what you do while you're still asking.

---

So here's your next step. I'm not going to give you a three-point plan to fix everything. I'm going to give you one thing to sit with.

This week, I want you to do something that might feel scary: find one person you trust—could be a youth leader, a parent, a friend, someone at school—and tell them about one thing you're actually uncertain about. Not something you perform. Something real.

I know that sounds terrifying. And I also know that staying silent is what's killing a lot of you. You're walking around carrying these huge questions alone, pretending you don't have them, and it's exhausting.

You don't have to have it figured out. But you don't have to carry it by yourself either.

And if you can't find someone to talk to—if you look around and you don't see a safe person—then here's what I want you to do: take that question, that doubt, that thing keeping you up at night, and bring it to God. Not as a polished prayer. Just as it is. Even if it's just: *I don't know if you're there. But I'm looking.*

That's what Thomas did. He didn't pretend. He reached out. And he found something.

You might too.

*"Here's what I wish I could feel…"*

*"Here's what I don't want anyone else to know…"*

*"If you're real, show me something small this week."*

*"I'm still here. That's all I've got."*

And if nothing happens this week, that's not failure; it's just the next place to keep showing up.

And you don't tell anyone because you're afraid of what they'd think. You're afraid they might say you don't have enough faith. You're afraid they might be right.

Here's the first thing I want you to know: you're not alone. And more than that, you're not broken.

---

I think we get this idea that faith is supposed to feel certain all the time. Like if you really believe, you should never question anything. You should never feel lost. You should never sit in the dark and wonder if anyone's there.

But that's not what the Bible actually shows us. Not even close.

Look at the people in Scripture. These aren't perfect saints who never doubted. These are real people who wrestled with God, who argued with him, who screamed into the void and demanded answers.

And what does Job do? He argues with God. He demands an explanation. He says, "Let me speak to you. I have questions. I have objections."

And here's what I love about Job's story: God doesn't strike him down for questioning. God doesn't say, "How dare you challenge me?" Instead, God shows up. And Job gets to argue with the Creator of the universe face to face. Not because God has all the answers Job wanted—but because Job's wrestling itself was faithful. Because bringing your confusion to God, even in anger, is a kind of trust.

That's not a story we talk about enough. It's not a neat Sunday school lesson. But it's in the Bible for a reason.

---

And then there's Thomas. You know the one. "Doubting Thomas." The guy who wouldn't believe Jesus was alive until he could touch the wounds himself.

The reality is, sometimes you do the asking and the seeking and the reaching, and you still don't get the answer you wanted. Sometimes you touch the wounds and you're still confused. Sometimes the 2 a.m. questions don't resolve by morning.

But here's what I think Thomas shows us: doubt can be a way of taking faith seriously. It's not the opposite of faith. It's actually a form of it. It's saying, *This matters too much to pretend about.* It's refusing to settle for something that doesn't feel true.

When Thomas demanded evidence, he wasn't rejecting Jesus. He was seeking him. And Jesus met him there.

That's what I want you to hear: you can bring your questions to God. You can bring your uncertainty. You don't have to pretend to be further along than you are.

---

Now, I'm not going to stand here and tell you that doubt is always comfortable or easy. It's not. It hurts to not know. It hurts to feel like everyone else has it figured out and you're still back at the beginning.

And here's the thing—I know what it's like to hear other people talk about their faith and sound so sure. To sit in a room full of people who seem confident, and wonder what's wrong with you that you can't feel that way. That loneliness is real. It's one thing to have questions; it's another thing to feel like you're the only one with them.

But I want to suggest something: maybe some of those people aren't as certain as they sound either. Maybe some of them are doing the same thing you're doing—sitting in the dark, wondering, hoping no one notices. And maybe the reason no one talks about it is because nobody goes first.

---

So here's your next step. I'm not going to give you a three-point plan to fix everything. I'm going to give you one thing to sit with.

This week, I want you to do something that might feel scary: find one person you trust—could be a youth leader, a parent, a friend, a counselor at school—and tell them about one thing you're actually uncertain about. Not something you perform. Something real.

I know that sounds terrifying. And I also know that staying silent is what's killing a lot of you. You're walking around carrying these huge questions alone, pretending you don't have them, and it's exhausting.

You don't have to have it figured out. But you don't have to carry it by yourself either.

And if you look around and you don't see a safe person—if you don't know who you could trust with this—then here's what I want you to do: take that question, that doubt, that thing keeping you up at night, and bring it to God. Not as a polished prayer. Just as it is. Even if it's just: *I don't know if you're there. But I'm looking.*

That's what Thomas did. He didn't pretend. He reached out. And he found something.

You might too.

Alright, can I start with a question? How many of you have ever been in a situation where you were supposed to be feeling one thing, and you were actually feeling something completely different?

Here's the scenario. It's a Wednesday night. You're sitting in youth group, maybe not even at this youth group specifically, but somewhere like it. The worship band's playing, everyone's singing, lights are dimmed, and someone next to you has their hands raised and eyes closed and looks genuinely moved. And you're just standing there. Not because you're angry or rebellious — you actually want to feel something. You want it to be real. But mostly you're thinking about the math test tomorrow, or whether that text you sent three hours ago was a mistake, or whether anyone actually believes the stuff being sung. And underneath all of that, there's a quiet thought you don't say out loud: *What if I'm doing this wrong? What if something's broken in me?*

If that was you — or if it's you right now — I want you to know something: you are not alone, and you are not broken.

I think we need to start here because I don't think we talk about this enough. We talk about faith like it's a light switch. Either you have it or you don't, either you're "in" or you're "out." But if you're honest, most of you here probably live somewhere in the messy middle. You care about this. You want it to be true. But sometimes it feels blurry, and sometimes it feels far away, and sometimes you're not even sure what you believe anymore. And when you're in that place, the last thing you need is someone telling you to just have more faith. Because that feels like being told to be less honest. And I think honesty matters to God. I think it always has.

Now, I want to say something that might sound surprising at first: doubt is not the opposite of faith. In fact, I think doubt can be part of how faith grows. And I'm not just saying that to make you feel better. I think it's actually true, and I think the Bible is more honest about this than we sometimes give it credit for.

Let me take you to one of the most famous stories in the New Testament. You've probably heard it — Thomas. Sometimes called "Doubting Thomas." The story goes that after Jesus is resurrected, he appears to his disciples, but Thomas isn't there. And when the others tell him they've seen the Lord, Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe."

Now, we have usually treated Thomas as the example of bad faith. The guy who doubted. The one who didn't have enough trust. But read the story again. There's something else going on here. Thomas wasn't saying he didn't want it to be true. He was saying he needed it to be *really* true. He wasn't being faithless — he was being rigorous. He wanted to believe something that could survive honest examination. And a week later, when Jesus appears again and invites Thomas to touch his wounds, Jesus doesn't rebuke him. He says, "Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." That's not a slap on the wrist. That's Jesus saying: *Thomas, your honesty matters to me. And there's a kind of faith that's actually deeper than what you just had — the kind that believes without needing to touch the wounds.*

Here's what I think that story is doing. It's not telling us that doubt is great and we should all be cynical. It's telling us that God can handle our honest questions. And that sometimes the people who wrestle hardest with belief end up with a faith that's more solid, not less.

But let's be real — that's not the only example. David, in the Psalms, over and over again, is crying out, "Where are you, God? Why have you forgotten me? How long?" That's not the prayer of someone with neat, tidy faith. That's someone in the middle of honest struggle. And Job — wow. Job loses everything, and his friends show up and give him terrible advice about why he deserves it, and Job looks at God and says, "I know that my Redeemer lives. But I want to argue my case before God." That's borderline audacious. And God doesn't strike him down. God shows up in a whirlwind and says, "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" — and then, somehow, Job ends up more restored than before. Not because he got the right answers, but because he brought his real questions to a God big enough to handle them.

So here's what I want to offer you. I don't think the problem is your doubt. I think the problem is sometimes we treat faith like it's supposed to feel a certain way, or look a certain way, and when it doesn't, we assume we've failed. But what if faith is more like a relationship than a performance? Think about the relationships that matter most to you. Are they the ones where everything's polished and perfect? Or are they the ones where you can be honest — even when it's messy, even when you're confused, even when you're angry?

I think God wants that kind of relationship with you. Not a relationship where you have everything figured out, but one where you keep showing up and asking real questions. Not the kind of questions you ask just to argue, but the kind you ask because you actually care about the answer. Because you want it to be true. That's not rebellion. That's intimacy.
