Let me tell you about something that happened to a kid I know. Actually, it's about me. A few years back, I was sitting in a church service, and the pastor said something that didn't sit right with me. I don't even remember exactly what it was anymore—something about faith being simple, about just believing. And I remember thinking, *But it's not simple. It's actually really complicated.* And then, almost immediately, I felt guilty for thinking that. Like maybe there was something wrong with me.

For a while, I just buried that. I figured everyone else seemed fine with their faith, so I must be the problem. I must be doing faith wrong.

Does any of that sound familiar? Maybe not exactly, but maybe you've had a moment like it. You're sitting in youth group, or at church, or even just praying alone at night, and something feels off. A question you can't shake. A doubt that keeps creeping in. And your first instinct is to hide it, because it feels like admitting doubt means you're failing at this whole faith thing.

I want to say something to you today that I wish someone had said to me: you don't have to pretend.

**Doubt isn't the opposite of faith**

Here's the thing that took me years to understand: doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Fear is the opposite of faith. Apathy is the opposite of faith. Doubt is actually part of the package—it's what happens when you're taking this stuff seriously enough to wrestle with it.

When you're a kid, you just believe what you're told. That's not bad—it's how you survive childhood. But at some point, you start to think for yourself. You start asking why. You start noticing things that don't add up, or questions that don't have easy answers. And if you're paying attention, some of that stuff is going to make you uncomfortable.

That discomfort? That's not a sign you're losing your faith. It might actually be a sign that your faith is growing up.

**The guy who needed to touch the wounds**

Let me tell you about someone in the Bible who had serious doubts. You probably know him: Thomas.

Thomas is famous for being the one who didn't believe Jesus had risen. The other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord," and Thomas said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I won't believe."

Now, a lot of preachers use this as an example of bad faith—like Thomas was failing at being a good Christian. But I think that's a misread. Thomas wasn't abandoning his faith. He was asking for the same thing he'd always asked for: evidence. Proof. He wasn't trying to be difficult. He was trying to be honest.

And here's what I love about Jesus's response. He doesn't shame Thomas. He doesn't say "You should have just trusted me." Instead, Jesus says, "Put your finger here. Look at my hands. Believe."

Thomas's answer is one of the most beautiful statements of faith in the entire Bible. He says, "My Lord and my God."

But notice—he got there through his doubt. His honest, stubborn, "I need to see it for myself" doubt. And Jesus met him there. Not in spite of his doubt, but through it.

**The Psalms are full of complaints**

If Thomas is the guy who needed proof, David is the guy who just needed to vent. Go read the Psalms sometime—there are so many of them where David is basically complaining to God. He's angry. He's confused. He's asking "Where are you?" He's crying out about injustice and pain and why bad things happen to him.

These aren't polished prayers. They're raw. David is essentially saying, "God, I don't understand what's happening, and I'm not happy about it."

And those prayers are in the Bible. All of them. Which tells me that God can handle your honest questions. He can handle your confusion. He can handle when you're angry at him or confused by him. That's not the same as rejecting him. That's actually talking to him—really talking, not just performing.

**What if questions made faith bigger?**

Here's something I've been thinking about a lot: what if your doubts aren't holes in your faith, but actually openings? What if the things you're questioning are things that, if you keep wrestling with them, will make your faith deeper and more real than it would be if you just never asked?

There's a difference between "I don't believe any of this" and "I believe this, but I don't understand part of it, and that bothers me." The second statement assumes there's something worth believing in the first place. The doubt is actually pointing you toward something you care about.

When I was younger, I thought faith was supposed to feel certain all the time, like a light switch. Either you're "in" or you're "out." But now I think it's more like a muscle. You grow it by using it—even by questioning it. Not by ignoring the hard parts, but by bringing them into the light.

**So what do you do with it?**

Okay, here's where I want to get practical. Because talks like this are easy to listen to and then forget. So let me give you something to actually do.

First, here's your assignment this week: find one question you've been hiding. Something you've wondered about faith, about God, about the Bible, about why things are the way they are. And instead of pushing it away, write it down. Just write the question. Don't try to answer it yet.

Then, here's the harder part: talk to someone about it. Not someone who will just tell you to stop asking questions. Find someone who will take your question seriously. Maybe it's a youth leader. Maybe it's a parent. Maybe it's a friend who's also trying to figure this stuff out.

And if you can't find anyone who feels safe, come talk to me. I mean that. I'd rather have an honest conversation with you about your doubts than watch you pretend everything's fine.

Here's the thing: the faith that survives isn't the faith that never doubts. It's the faith that doubts and keeps asking anyway. It's the faith that says, "I don't understand everything, but I'm still here. I'm still reaching. I'm still following."

That's the kind of faith I want. And I think that's the kind of faith worth having.

So welcome your questions. Bring them with you. And trust that the God who made your mind isn't afraid of how you use it.

# When Doubt Shows Up

A few years back, I was sitting in a church service, and the pastor said something that broke something in me. He'd just finished praying with a family who'd lost their dad to cancer—way too young, brutal and unfair—and then in his sermon, he said, "Everything happens for a reason."

I remember sitting there thinking, *What reason? What possible reason makes that okay?*

And then I felt guilty. Because everyone around me seemed to nod along, and I was sitting there with this knot of anger and confusion, and I thought: *There must be something wrong with me. A good Christian wouldn't feel this way.*

For a long time, I buried that. I figured everyone else had it figured out, and I was just broken somehow. I must be doing faith wrong.

Does any of that sound familiar? Maybe not exactly. Maybe your moment was different. Maybe it was watching a TikTok that "debunked" Christianity and you couldn't unsee the arguments. Maybe it was a friend who came out and you couldn't square what you'd been taught with the love you know they deserve. Maybe it was praying for something—really praying—and getting only silence.

Whatever it is, I want you to know: you don't have to pretend. And you don't have to hide.

**The different kinds of doubt**

Here's something that took me years to understand: doubt isn't all the same thing. Sometimes it's in your head—*Can I actually believe this? Is this true?* That's intellectual doubt. Sometimes it's in your heart—*Does God actually care about me? Is he really good?* That's emotional doubt. Sometimes it's deeper than both—*Why is there so much suffering? How do I hold this whole thing together?* That's existential doubt.

All of those are real. All of them belong in prayer. And none of them make you a bad Christian.

**The guy who needed to touch the wounds**

Let me tell you about Thomas. You probably know him as "Doubting Thomas," which is unfair, because he's actually one of the most honest people in the Bible.

When the other disciples told Thomas, "We have seen the Lord," Thomas didn't just shrug and go along. He said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I won't believe."

Now, a lot of preachers use this as an example of weak faith—like Thomas was failing at being a good Christian. But I think they miss the whole story. Thomas wasn't just being stubborn or difficult. He'd watched his best friend be executed. He'd seen Jesus die. And when the others said "We saw him," Thomas was protecting his heart. He'd already lost everything once. He couldn't afford false hope.

That's not bad faith. That's honest grief. That's what happens when you've been hurt and you're not going to pretend it didn't happen.

And here's what I love about Jesus's response. He doesn't shame Thomas. He doesn't say, "You should have just trusted me." Instead, he says, "Put your finger here. Look at my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe."

The Greek word there is interesting. It's better translated as "stop being faithless"—not "stop asking questions," but "stop letting doubt become disbelief." Jesus meets Thomas in his doubt. He doesn't avoid it. He walks right into it.

And Thomas's answer? "My Lord and my God." That's one of the strongest declarations of faith in the entire Bible. He got there *through* his doubt. Not around it.

**The Psalms are full of complaints**

If Thomas is the guy who needed proof, David is the guy who just needed to vent. Go read the Psalms sometime—there are so many of them where David is essentially complaining to God.

Here's Psalm 13: "How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" That's not a polished prayer. That's raw honesty.

Or Psalm 22, which Jesus actually quoted on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" David wrote that hundreds of years before Jesus. It's in the Bible. All of it. Which tells me God can handle your confusion. He can handle your anger. He can handle when you're yelling at him.

And then notice what David does. He doesn't just complain and stop. Look at how Psalm 13 ends: "But I trust in your unfailing love; my heart rejoices in your salvation. I will sing the Lord's praise." He brings his complaint to God, and then he reminds himself of what he knows to be true. That's the pattern of biblical lament: bring everything—your anger, your grief, your confusion—and then make room for what you know.

That's not weak faith. That's the most biblical faith there is.

Or look at Habakkuk, who looked at the violence and injustice in his world and said, "How long, Lord, must I call for help but you do not listen?" He wasn't fired as a prophet. God didn't say "You have bad faith." Instead, God said, "Write this down. Make it plain." Your questions matter enough to be recorded.

**The difference between fear and doubt**

Let me give you something to hold onto theologically. I said earlier that doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Here's what I think fear is: fear says "I can't trust God with this question." Doubt says "I trust God enough to ask it."

That's a huge difference. Fear keeps you silent and hiding. Doubt keeps you reaching and wrestling. The one that destroys faith isn't asking questions—it's being too afraid to ask them.

And I want to be honest with you: even now, I don't have it all figured out. I'm still wrestling with why God seems silent sometimes. I'm still confused about suffering. But I've learned that those questions don't mean I'm outside of faith—they mean I'm inside it, still reaching, still following.

**So let's do something**

I want to pause here for ten seconds. Don't write anything down yet. Just think: what's the question you've been carrying? The one you've been hiding. The one that makes you feel guilty or ashamed. Just hold it in your mind. That's your question. That's the one God wants to hear.

Okay. Here's your assignment this week. I've got three options, because I know we're all at different places.

**Level one (just starting):** Write your question on a note card. Put it in your Bible. Let it sit there. That's it. You're not solving it today—you're just not hiding it anymore.

**Level two (ready to engage):** Find one person who's earned your trust. Not someone who will just tell you to stop asking questions. Someone who will take your question seriously. Ask them: "What's a question about faith you wrestle with?" Let them go first. Then share yours.

**Level three (ready to go deeper):** Pick a Psalm of lament—13, 22, or 73. Rewrite it in your own words, with your specific doubt. Read it out loud as a prayer. Don't perform it. Just say it to God.

And if you don't know who to talk to, come find me. Seriously. Grab me after. Text me. I'll have coffee with you and we won't fix it—we'll just sit with it. That's okay too.

Here's what I know: the faith that survives isn't the faith that never doubts. It's the faith that doubts and keeps asking anyway. It's the faith that says, "I don't understand everything, but I'm still here. I'm still reaching. I'm still following."

That's the kind of faith I want. And I think it's the kind worth having.

So don't let your doubts drive you into hiding. Let them drive you deeper. The God who made your mind is not afraid of your questions.

In fact, he's waiting in them.

That shows me that doubt and trust can exist in the same sentence. That you can be furious at God and still reach for him at the same time.

**What if questions made faith bigger?**

Here's something I've been thinking about a lot: what if your doubts aren't holes in your faith, but actually openings? What if the things you're questioning are things that, if you keep wrestling with them, will make your faith deeper and more real than it would be if you just never asked?

Think about a muscle. If you never lift anything heavy, the muscle stays weak. It never has to struggle, so it never gets stronger. Faith is the same way. If you never ask the hard questions, your faith stays weak—it's just a habit you inherited from your parents. But when you wrestle with a question, when you stare at it and refuse to look away until you find an answer, you are building a faith that is actually yours. A faith that can hold weight when life gets hard. A faith that won't collapse the first time something doesn't make sense.

**So what do you do with it?**

Okay, here's where I want to get practical. Because talks like this are easy to listen to and then forget. So let me give you something to actually do.

First, here's your assignment this week: find one question you've been hiding. Something you've wondered about faith, about God, about the Bible, about why things are the way they are. And instead of pushing it away, write it down. Just write the question. Don't try to answer it yet. Just get it out of your head and onto paper.

Look for someone who won't just tell you to stop asking, but who will actually sit with you in the question. And if you're worried about what that conversation might look like, practice on me first. Come talk to me. I promise not to give you a three-point answer. I'll just listen.

Here's the thing: the faith that survives isn't the faith that never doubts. It's the faith that doubts and keeps asking anyway. It's the faith that says, "I don't understand everything, but I'm still here. I'm still reaching. I'm still following."

That's the kind of faith I want. And I think that's the kind of faith worth having.

So welcome your questions. Bring them with you. And trust that the God who made your mind isn't afraid of how you use it.

And if you can't find anyone who feels safe, come talk to me. I mean that. I'd rather have an honest conversation with you about your doubts than watch you pretend everything's fine.

One more thing. Tonight when you brush your teeth, stare at yourself in the mirror and say one doubt out loud. Give it a name. It's harder than writing it down, but naming turns the monster into a roommate you can examine.

**The faith worth having**

Here's the thing: the faith that survives isn't the faith that never doubts. It's the faith that doubts and keeps asking anyway. It's the faith that says, "I don't understand everything, but I'm still here. I'm still reaching. I'm still following."

That's the kind of faith I want. And I think that's the kind of faith worth having.

So welcome your questions. Bring them with you. And trust that the God who made your mind isn't afraid of how you use it.

# When You're Not Sure

I want to start by asking you something, and I want you to be honest with yourself—even if you've never admitted this out loud.

Have you ever been in youth group, or a church service, or even just sitting in your room, and looked around at everyone else and thought: *Everyone here seems to get it. Why don't I? What's wrong with me?*

Maybe it's when everyone else seems to feel something in worship and you're just standing there. Maybe it's when the pastor says something and everyone nods like it makes perfect sense and you're lost. Maybe it's when you're praying and it feels like you're talking to the ceiling.

I want you to know something: you are not alone. And you are not broken.

I don't think I've ever led a youth group session—ever—without someone coming up to me afterward and saying, almost in a whisper, "Can I tell you something? I don't actually believe most of this. I just don't want to say anything."

If that's you, I'm glad you're here. I'm glad you came. And I want to tell you: doubt is not the opposite of faith. Sometimes, doubt is what faith looks like when it's honest.

---

Here's something the church doesn't always talk about: half the Bible is people arguing with God.

Turn to the Psalms. Half of them are complaints. David, the man after God's own heart, writes things like "How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That's not a Sunday school answer. That's a person who is angry and confused and bringing those feelings directly to God.

Then there's Job. Job loses everything—his family, his health, his wealth—and what does he do? He argues with his friends for forty chapters. He tells God exactly how unfair this all seems. And you know what God says at the end? He doesn't give Job the answer. He shows up in the storm and says, basically, "Where were you when I made all this? Do you really think you could run things better?"

That's not a satisfying answer. But it's an answer. And Job responds by worshipping.

And then there's Thomas. You know his story—Thomas wasn't there when Jesus appeared to the other disciples after the resurrection. They told him, "We saw the Lord!" And Thomas said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe."

For centuries, Thomas has been called "Doubting Thomas." Like doubt is his defining flaw. But let me ask you something: isn't it also kind of brave? Thomas is saying, "I'm not going to pretend. I'm not going to go along with this just because everyone else says it's true. I need to know for myself."

A week later, Jesus shows up. And what does he do? Does he rebuke Thomas for doubting? Does he say, "Your faith is too small"?

No. He says, "Put your finger here. See my hands. Stop doubting and believe."

And Thomas's response? "My Lord and my God."

Here's what I think about Thomas: his doubt wasn't the end of his story. It was the doorway. He needed to bring his honesty to the table, and when he did, he encountered something that changed him.

---

Now, I want to be real with you: I'm not here to tell you that if you just doubt hard enough, you'll automatically land on the other side with stronger faith. Sometimes doubt is painful. Sometimes you don't get the answer you want. Sometimes faith feels like groping in the dark, and you're not sure if you're holding onto anything at all.

That's okay. That's human. That's also biblical.

What I am saying is this: the questions you carry—the ones you're afraid to ask out loud, the ones that keep you up at night—those questions are not evidence that something is wrong with you. They're evidence that you're taking this seriously. You're not just repeating what you've been told. You're thinking. You're wrestling. You're engaging.

And that engagement? That's not the opposite of faith. That's what faith looks like when it's trying to grow.

---

So here's my question for you: what would it look like to stop pretending?

What would it look like to bring your actual questions—not the safe ones, not the ones you think you're supposed to ask but the real ones,—to whatever space you use to think about this stuff?

Maybe that's a journal. Maybe it's a conversation with someone you trust. Maybe it's just giving yourself permission to sit with uncertainty for a while instead of trying to resolve it immediately.

Here's your next step. I want you to think about one question—one honest, maybe even uncomfortable question—about faith, about God, about yourself. And I want you to do something with it.

Don't just let it sit in your chest and weigh you down. Write it down. Ask someone. Argue with it. Bring it to whatever you understand as sacred.

Because here's what I've learned: the things we bury don't go away. They just go underground. But the things we bring into the light—even the hard things, especially the hard things—those are the things that can actually grow.

You don't have to have it figured out. You're not supposed to have it figured out. But you can be honest about where you are.

And that honesty might just be the beginning of something real.

# When You're Not Sure

Let me tell you something that happened to me.

When I was seventeen, my friend Tyler died in a car accident. sudden, senseless, no warning. And I remember sitting in my room after the funeral, trying to pray like I'd always prayed, and nothing came out. Not because I didn't want to talk to God—I did. But because every word felt like a lie. Like I was performing something I didn't feel.

So I stopped. I stopped praying, stopped going to youth group, stopped pretending I had any idea what I believed. And honestly? That was the most honest I'd ever been.

I tell you this because I want you to know: I'm not up here pretending I have it figured out. I've sat in the dark too. And I think that's actually where we need to start.

---

So here's the question I want to ask you—and I want you to be honest with yourself, even if you've never admitted it out loud:

Have you ever been in youth group, or a church service, or just sitting in your room, and looked around at everyone else and thought: *Everyone here seems to get it. Why don't I? What's wrong with me?*

Maybe it's when everyone else seems to feel something in worship and you're just standing there. Maybe it's when the pastor says something and everyone nods like it makes perfect sense and you're lost. Maybe it's when you're praying and it feels like you're talking to the ceiling.

Maybe it's when your science teacher explains evolution and you wonder if Genesis is just a fairy tale. Maybe it's when you realize you're gay and every sermon feels like it's about you. Maybe it's when you see church leaders posting racist stuff online and you think: *If this is what faith produces, I'm out.* Maybe it's when you prayed and prayed and someone you loved still died, and you're supposed to call that "God's plan."

If that's you—if any of that's you—you're in good company. Literally. David, Job, and Thomas were all standing where you're standing.

---

Here's something the church doesn't always talk about: half the Bible is people arguing with God.

Turn to the Psalms. David, the man after God's own heart, writes things like this in Psalm 13:

> *How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I wrestle with my thoughts and day after day have sorrow in my heart?*

That's not a Sunday school answer. That's a person who is angry and confused and terrified—and bringing those feelings directly to God. That's not in the "doubt" section of the Bible. That's Scripture. God put David's panic attack in His book.

Then there's Job. Job loses everything—his family, his health, his wealth—and what does he do? He argues with his friends for forty chapters. He tells God exactly how unfair this all seems.

And then God shows up. Not with an explanation. Not with a reason. He gives Job a tour of the universe. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation? Can you bind the chains of the Seven Stars? Do you give the horse its strength?"

That's not a mic drop. It's an invitation into mystery. God isn't saying "shut up." He's saying, "You're asking a question bigger than any answer you could understand right now. But I'm here, in the storm, with you."

And Job responds by worshipping. Not because he got his answer. Because he got God.

---

And then there's Thomas. You know his story—Thomas wasn't there when Jesus appeared to the other disciples after the resurrection. They told him, "We saw the Lord!" And Thomas said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe."

For centuries, Thomas has been called "Doubting Thomas." Like doubt is his defining flaw. But let me ask you something: isn't it also kind of brave? Thomas is saying, "I'm not going to pretend. I'm not going to go along with this just because everyone else says it's true. I need to know for myself."

A week later, Jesus shows up. And what does he do? He says, "Put your finger here. See my hands. Stop doubting and believe."

And Thomas's response? "My Lord and my God."

But here's what we often miss: then Jesus says something wild. "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed."

He's not dissing Thomas. He's saying there are two paths here: one with proof, one with trust. Both are welcome at this table. Some of you need to touch the wounds. Some of you are trying to believe without seeing. Neither way is wrong. Neither way is faith failing.

---

Now, I want to be real with you: I'm not here to tell you that if you just doubt hard enough, you'll automatically land on the other side with stronger faith. Sometimes doubt is painful. Sometimes you don't get the answer you want. Sometimes faith feels like groping in the dark, and you're not sure if you're holding onto anything at all.

That's okay. That's human. That's also biblical.

What I am saying is this: the questions you carry—the ones you're afraid to ask out loud, the ones that keep you up at night—those questions are not evidence that something is wrong with you. They're evidence that you're taking this seriously. You're not just repeating what you've been told. You're thinking. You're wrestling. You're engaging.

Doubt is faith stretching, not faith snapping. Doubt is faith trying to grow.

---

So here's my question for you: What would happen if you stopped performing the "good Christian" script?

What would you lose? Who might you actually find?

You don't have to have it figured out. You're not supposed to have it figured out. But you can be honest about where you are.

Here's your next step—pick one that fits where you are right now:

**Solo:** Write your question at the top of a journal page. Below it, write a letter to God that you don't edit. Ugly, angry, confused—send it. Don't worry about sounding holy. Just be honest.

**Pair:** Find one person—a youth leader, a friend, a parent, anyone—and text them: "Can I ask you a real question about faith that I'm scared to say out loud?" If they say yes, ask it. If they shut you down, find someone else. There are people who can handle your honesty. Go find them.

**Practice:** For one week, replace one "churchy" prayer with a prayer of complaint. Use David's words if you need to: "How long, Lord?" See what happens when you stop performing and start actually talking.

And if you don't have someone to ask, find me after. Not so I can give you the answer—because honestly, I probably don't have it. But so we can sit in the question together. Because that's what church is supposed to be: a place where we don't have to pretend.

Doubt isn't the opposite of faith. It's the engine. It's faith trying to figure out what it actually believes.

And that honesty? That's where faith actually begins.

qV8s9St37sUpG0xI6xhZY.text:
Alright, can I ask you something? Have you ever been in a situation where you didn't know what you believed anymore — or maybe you did know, but you weren't sure you believed it? Not in a dramatic, movie-moment kind of way. Just like, sitting in class, or lying in bed at night, or sitting in the back row on a Sunday morning, and something just… didn't add up.

Let me tell you about a week I had a couple years ago. I was leading a small group, and one night a kid — I'll call him Marcus — stayed after. And he said, "I don't think I believe any of this anymore." He said it quietly, not like he was trying to shock me. He said it like he was tired. He'd been coming to youth group for a while. He was involved. He prayed before meals when people were watching. And underneath all of that, he'd been carrying this question for months: *What if none of it's real?*

Now, here's the thing. My first instinct — and I'm not proud of this — was to fix it. I wanted to open my Bible and show him a verse that would make it better. But the look on his face told me he didn't need a verse. He needed someone to hear him. So I just said, "Tell me more." And he did. And for about twenty minutes, he laid out questions that honestly, I didn't have great answers for. Questions about suffering. Questions about why his parents' divorce didn't seem to fit with a loving God. Questions about whether he'd just been going along with something because everyone else was.

That conversation changed how I think about faith. Because Marcus wasn't betraying his faith. He was being honest about what was actually going on inside his head. And that's rare. That's actually really hard to do when you're fourteen, fifteen, sixteen — when you're surrounded by people who seem like they've got it figured out, or at least are performing that way.

So here's what I want to say to you, and I mean it: **doubt is not the opposite of faith. Doubt is often what faith looks like when it's getting serious.**

When you stop casually believing and start actually wrestling — that's not a spiritual failure. That is, in a lot of ways, the most faithful thing you can do. Because it means you care enough to ask whether any of this is true.

And I know that might feel like a weird thing to hear from someone up here. I know some of you have been told — maybe from a church, maybe from a youth leader, maybe from your own family — that you're supposed to have it all together. That faith means never questioning. That if you doubt, something is wrong with you.

I don't believe that. And more importantly, the Bible doesn't back that up. Not even a little.

Let's look at some people in Scripture who disagreed with the "never question" approach. Because there are a lot of them.

Thomas. You know the story — the disciple who wasn't there when Jesus showed up after the resurrection. Everyone else said they'd seen the Lord. And Thomas said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe." (John 20:25) Most sermons I've heard paint Thomas as the bad example. The skeptic. The one who got called out. But read that passage more carefully. Jesus doesn't shame him out of his doubt. He invites Thomas to touch his wounds. He meets Thomas in his skepticism. And Thomas's response isn't just belief — it's one of the most powerful confessions in the entire New Testament: "My Lord and my God." (John 20:28) Thomas's doubt, when it was finally resolved, produced one of the clearest declarations of who Jesus is. Doubt didn't destroy his faith. It deepened it into something unshakable.

Then there's David. You know David as the shepherd-turned-king, the man after God's own heart. But read the Psalms. Half of them are David screaming at God. "Why have you forgotten me?" "Why do you hide your face?" These aren't polite prayers. These are the prayers of a man who is furious and terrified and confused. And God never once tells David to stop asking questions. The Psalms are literally a collection of honest doubt wrapped in worship.

And honestly, I'd point you to Habakkuk — one of the shortest books in the Bible, but maybe the most honest. Habakkuk looks at the world, at injustice and violence, and he basically says to God, "This is wrong. How can you stand it?" He's arguing with God. And God's answer isn't a neat explanation — it's a promise that eventually, "the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea." (Habakkuk 2:14) Habakkuk doesn't get all his questions answered. But he ends the book in a completely different place than he started. Listen to how he finishes: "Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior." (Habakkuk 3:17-18) That's not blind faith. That's faith that has looked at the worst and chosen to trust anyway. That's faith that has been refined through doubt, not around it.

So here's what I think is happening, and I want you to sit with this: **your doubt might actually be the most spiritual thing you're doing right now.** Not because doubt itself is holy, but because it means you're not pretending. You're not just copying what everyone else says. You're taking this — your life, your eternity, your understanding of God — seriously enough to ask real questions. And that is incredibly valuable.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying doubt is comfortable. It's not. It's lonely. It can feel like standing in fog with no map. And I'm not saying you should go looking for doubt or manufacturing questions you don't actually have. That's its own kind of performance.

But what I am saying is this: when the questions come — and they will — don't run from them immediately. Don't feel like you have to stuff them down and pretend they're not there. The faith that survives isn't the faith that never questions. It's the faith that learns to carry the questions honestly and keep walking.

And this is where it gets practical, because I think you deserve something real to do with what I'm saying.

Here's a thought: **the next time you have a question about faith that scares you, don't hide it.** Find one person — a parent, a youth leader, a friend who can handle it — and say it out loud. Not to get fixed. Just to say it. Because questions that stay buried don't get answered. They just get heavier.

Or maybe your next step is quieter. Maybe it's sitting with one question this week. Just one. Not trying to solve it. Just noticing it. Where is it coming from? What would it mean if it were true? What would it mean if it weren't? You don't have to resolve it. But you can stop running from it.

And here's the thing I'll leave you with. The God we talk about — the one revealed in Jesus — is not scared of your questions. He didn't run from doubters. He walked toward them. He invited Thomas to touch his wounds. He sat with the woman at the well who had five husbands and was currently living with a man who wasn't her husband — that's a whole conversation about complicated faith. He didn't wait for people to have it all figured out. He met them where they were.

You don't have to have it figured out to be worth meeting. That's the whole point.

eLf4sUajDLvgkFAdZdiUy.text:
# When You're Not Sure

Let me start with something that might sound familiar. Imagine you're at a youth group night, or maybe just sitting in your room, and someone says something about God — something that sounds simple and certain — and you feel... nothing. Or worse, you feel a quiet pull inside that says, "I don't know if I buy this." And immediately, a voice in your head says, *What's wrong with me? Everyone else seems fine.*

Here's the thing. You're not alone. And more than that, you're not broken.

I want to talk to you tonight about something that most people in this room — maybe most people in this building — have felt but almost no one talks about openly. I want to talk about doubt.

---

Let's be honest for a second. You are fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen. You are in the middle of one of the most disorienting seasons of life. Your body is changing. Your brain is literally reorganizing itself. You're starting to see the world in shades of gray instead of black and white, and everyone around you seems to want simple answers. Your parents want you to figure out what you believe. Your youth leader wants you to have it together. And somewhere in the middle of all that, you're trying to hear your own voice.

So when someone tells you to just "have faith," and you're sitting there with a list of questions longer than your arm, of course you feel stuck. Of course you feel alone. But what if I told you that the doubt you're carrying might actually be one of the most honest things about you right now?

Here's what I want you to hear first and clearly: doubt is not a failure of faith. It's often the place where faith gets real.

---

Now, I'm not saying this just to make you feel better. I want to show you that this is not a new problem. This is ancient. The Bible is full of people who wrestled with God, who argued with God, who straight-up told God they didn't understand what He was doing.

Let's look at Thomas. You know the story — Thomas wasn't there when Jesus showed up after the resurrection. The other disciples said, "We saw the Lord." And Thomas said, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe." (John 20:25)

That's not a small thing. That's Thomas looking at the most important people in his life and saying, essentially, "I wasn't there. I don't believe you. I need more."

And what does Jesus do when He shows up later? He doesn't rebuke Thomas. He doesn't say, "Your faith is too weak." He says, "Put your finger here. See my hands. Stop doubting and believe." (John 20:27)

Here's what I find so striking. Jesus meets Thomas in his doubt. He doesn't shame him out of it. He invites him deeper. And Thomas's response isn't some hesitant, second-tier faith. It's one of the most powerful confessions in the entire New Testament: "My Lord and my God." (John 20:28)

Thomas doubted. And then he believed more deeply than most.

But Thomas isn't the only one. Turn the clock back a few thousand years and you find someone like Habakkuk — a prophet who looked at the world and said to God, "This is chaos. How long? You're telling me the righteous will live by faith, but I don't see it. Where is it?" (Habakkuk 1–2)

That's not a quiet prayer. That's an argument. That's a person standing in front of the God of the universe and saying, "I don't understand, and I'm not going to pretend I do."

And God didn't strike him down. God answered. Not with a neat explanation, but with a promise: "The righteous will live by their faithfulness." (Habakkuk 2:4)

Habakkuk didn't get everything he wanted to know. But he got something he needed — a bigger vision of who God is. And in the last chapter of that book, Habakkuk closes with this extraordinary statement: "Though the fig tree does not bud... yet I will rejoice in the Lord." (Habakkuk 3:17–19)

That is not blind optimism. That is someone who has argued with God, who has not gotten all the answers, and who has decided to trust anyway — not because everything makes sense, but because God is still God.

---

Now, I want to be careful here, because I'm not trying to sell you a version of faith that pretends doubt is no big deal. Sometimes doubt is painful. Sometimes it's heavy. Sometimes you feel like you're losing something. And I'm not here to tell you to just get over it.

But I do want to offer something, and I think it's true.

Your questions are not the problem. The problem is when your questions become the only conversation you're having — when you stop listening for an answer. Faith is not the absence of questions. Faith is what happens when you keep the conversation going, even when the answer doesn't come in the form you wanted.

Here's what I've noticed. A lot of the time, the reason doubt feels so exhausting is because we think we have to resolve it all at once. We think we have to either believe everything or walk away. But that's a false choice. You can hold a question in one hand and still reach toward God with the other. You can say, "I don't understand this, but I'm not done seeking." That's not weakness. That is, honestly, what it looks like to take faith seriously.

The faith that survives isn't the faith that never doubted. It's the faith that wrestled and stayed in the ring.

---

So here's my invitation to you. And I mean this practically, not just as something to think about later and forget.

I want you to pick one thing. One thing you genuinely don't understand — about God, about the Bible, about why things are the way they are — and I want you to stop pushing it down. I want you to stop pretending you have it figured out. I want you to take that question and sit with it honestly.

Maybe you talk to someone about it. Maybe you bring it to youth group. Maybe you write it down in a journal. But here's what I'd really encourage you to do: ask it in prayer. Not as a challenge. Not as a trap. But as a real conversation. Say, "God, I don't understand this. Show me."

And then wait. And pay attention. Not for a thunderbolt — maybe it won't come that way. Pay attention for something smaller. A conversation that happens. A thought that won't leave you. A person who says exactly what you needed to hear. A passage you read that suddenly hits different. God is not limited to one way of answering.

I'm not promising you that every question will be resolved. I'm not promising you clarity by Thursday. But I am telling you this: the people who have found the deepest faith are not the people who never questioned. They're the people who brought their questions to God and refused to let go.

---

So here's your question to sit with this week. And I want you to actually think about it, not just hear it and move on.

What is the one thing I keep avoiding? The one question I've been pushing down because I'm afraid of what it means if I actually look at it?

That's the thing I want you to bring into the light. Not to solve. Just to bring.

And then find one person — a friend, a leader, a parent, someone you trust — and tell them where you're actually at. Not the version of yourself that has it all figured out. The real one. The one with the questions.

You might be surprised. You might find that the room is fuller of doubters than you thought. And you might find that faith, real faith, is big enough to hold everything you're carrying.

# When Faith Gets Complicated

Let me tell you about something that happened a few years ago. There was a kid at a youth group—just like this one—who had been coming to church since they were in elementary school. Served in the kids' ministry, went on mission trips, prayed before meals, the whole thing. Then around sophomore year, something shifted. They started reading news articles about suffering around the world. They learned about historical stuff that never came up in their Sunday school lessons. And they started thinking: "Wait. Does any of this actually add up?"

So they did what maybe some of you have done—they kept showing up to youth group, kept smiling, kept saying the right things, because they didn't know how to say, "Hey, I'm not sure I believe this anymore." They thought they were the only one. They thought something was wrong with them.

If that story sounds familiar—maybe not exactly, but the feeling of it—I want you to know something right away: you are not broken. You are not failing. You are doing exactly what growing up looks like.

---

Here's the thing about being a teenager. You're at this point in life where you're starting to think for yourself. You're realizing that the answers you got when you were ten might not be enough anymore. And that's not a crisis—that's actually progress. You're developing the capacity to wrestle with big questions, and that's a gift, even when it feels confusing.

The same thing happens with faith. Faith isn't supposed to be a thing you have or don't have, like a light switch. It's supposed to be a relationship—a living, breathing conversation with something infinite. And if you've ever had a real relationship, you know it gets complicated. It gets messy. You don't always agree with the other person. You have hard conversations. You question things. You say, "I need more than that."

That's not the opposite of faith. That's faith growing up.

---

Now, here's where it gets interesting. This whole thing—doubt, questioning, wrestling—it's not new. It's not unique to your generation. The Bible is full of people who argued with God, who demanded answers, who couldn't make sense of what was happening to them.

Take Thomas. You know him as "Doubting Thomas," which is honestly an unfair nickname. Here's the story: Jesus has died, the other disciples tell Thomas they've seen him resurrected, and Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe." That's what he said. Out loud. To the other disciples.

And here's what I love about Thomas: he didn't fake it. He didn't pretend to believe when he didn't. He said, "I need more." He was honest about where he was.

A week later, Jesus shows up. And what does he do? He doesn't rebuke Thomas for doubting. He says, "Put your finger here; see my hands." He invites Thomas to touch the wounds. To investigate. To be satisfied.

And Thomas's response? He says, "My Lord and my God."

That's the thing about honest doubt. When Thomas finally got what he needed—when he encountered the real Jesus—his doubt didn't just disappear. It transformed into worship. His question became a doorway to something deeper.

---

Here's what I think happens when we pretend we don't have questions: we stay on the surface. We develop a faith that's fragile, because it's built on things we can't actually defend. But when we bring our real questions—when we stop performing and start actually wrestling—we build something that can last. Not because we'll get perfect answers to everything, but because we'll have encountered the person behind the answers.

That's what happened to Thomas. That's what can happen to you.

---

Now, I'm not going to stand here and tell you that all your questions will be answered. That would be dishonest, and you deserve better than that. Some of the things you're wondering about might not get resolved in a way that feels satisfying. That's part of being human. That's part of having a faith that's real.

But I will tell you this: the questions themselves can become a gift. They can push you deeper. They can force you to figure out what you actually believe and why, rather than just repeating what you were taught. And that's the kind of faith that actually matters—the kind that survives college, hard times, and everything else life throws at you.

So here's my invitation to you.

---

This week, I want you to do something. I want you to take one question—one real, honest question you have about faith, about God, about why the world is the way it is—and instead of pushing it down, I want you to sit with it. Not to solve it. Just to sit with it.

Maybe you write it down. Maybe you bring it to a conversation with someone you trust—a parent, a youth leader, a friend who's willing to wrestle with the same stuff. Maybe you read a Psalm where someone is yelling at God, like Psalm 88 or Psalm 13, and you realize it's okay to talk to God like that.

And then I want you to pay attention. Not for a lightning bolt of certainty, but for something smaller. A sense that maybe this faith thing isn't about having it all figured out. Maybe it's about trusting that the search itself is worthwhile. That the wrestling is part of the relationship. That you don't have to be finished to be faithful.

Your doubts might be the most faithful thing about you right now. Because they mean you're taking this seriously. You're not just going through the motions. You're actually in it.

That's worth something. That might actually be where faith starts.

KXYhi_stDzXDCJVLwdEG_.text:
Hey. Can I ask you something? Have you ever sat in a church service, or a youth group, or maybe just in your room at night, and felt like something didn't add up? Not in a dramatic, movie-moment kind of way — more like a quiet, nagging sense that the things you've been told don't quite match the way the world actually looks. You hear something about faith being simple, about trusting God no matter what, and inside you're thinking, *well, it's a little more complicated than that.*

If that's you — if that's even a little bit you — I want to start by saying: you're not broken. You're not less of a Christian. You're not on some slippery slope away from God. You're probably right where a lot of honest, thoughtful people have stood. Including some people in the Bible.

I want to be honest with you about something. I used to think doubt was the enemy of faith. Like if you really had faith, you wouldn't doubt. And if you did doubt, you had to fix it as fast as possible, like it was some kind of spiritual malfunction. But that never felt right to me. And the more I've read the Bible — not just the warm fuzzy parts, but all of it — the more I think I had it backwards. I think doubt, handled honestly, can actually be a doorway into a deeper, more real faith. Not a faith that's naive or pretend, but a faith that's been tested and chosen.

Let's talk about Thomas. You know the story — Jesus appears to the disciples after the resurrection, and Thomas isn't there. The others tell him, "We have seen the Lord." And Thomas says, "Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I will not believe." He's not being stubborn. He's being honest. He's saying, *I can't pretend to believe something this big just because you told me to.* And honestly, that's a reasonable response to a claim that a dead man came back to life.

A week later, Jesus shows up and says to Thomas, "Put your finger here. Stop doubting and believe." And Thomas's response is one of the most honest declarations in the whole Bible: "My Lord and my God." But here's what I find so interesting — Jesus doesn't rebuke Thomas for doubting. He meets him where he is. He offers the evidence. And then he says something that gets overlooked: "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." That's not a condemnation of Thomas. It's a recognition that faith looks different for different people, and that the kind of faith Thomas ends up with — the kind that has wrestled with the hardest question and come through — is deeply valuable.

Now, Thomas isn't the only one. David, in the Psalms, cries out things like "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" He doesn't whisper that. He shouts it. He writes it down. He lets thousands of years of people read his confusion and his pain. That's not a man pretending everything is fine. That's a man bringing his real questions to God and trusting that God can handle them.

Or take Habakkuk — this tiny book in the Old Testament where the prophet basically argues with God. He says, "How long do I have to cry out to you about violence and injustice before you do something?" He's frustrated. He's confused. He lays out some of the hardest questions a person can ask — Why do bad things happen? Why does injustice persist? Why don't you act? And God's answer isn't a simple explanation. It's almost cryptic. But Habakkuk ends the book not with all his questions answered, but with a posture shift. He says, "Even if the fig tree doesn't blossom and there is no fruit on the vines, even if the olive crop fails, I will rejoice in the Lord." That's not blind optimism. That's someone who has brought their doubt all the way to God and found that the relationship survives the questions. In fact, the relationship deepens because of them.

Here's what I think happens when we treat doubt as something to be ashamed of. We end up with a faith that's fragile — a faith that falls apart the moment something hard happens, because we've built it on the idea that faith means never asking hard questions. And that's not a faith that will last. That's a faith that collapses the moment real life shows up and doesn't match the Sunday school answers.

But when we bring our doubt to God honestly — when we say, "I don't understand this, and I'm not going to pretend I do" — something shifts. We're no longer pretending. We're no longer performing faith. We're actually living in a relationship with someone we believe is big enough to handle our questions. And that kind of faith is a lot harder to shake.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying doubt is the goal. I'm not saying you should go looking for things to question just for the sake of it. I'm also not saying there's no value in trusting what you've been taught or in sometimes simply showing up and worshipping even when you don't feel like it. There is deep value in that. But I'm saying that if you *are* doubting — if you *are* confused — you don't have to hide that. You don't have to pretend. God can handle it. And honestly, the church should be a place where you can bring those questions.

So here's my invitation. Not a formula. Not a three-step plan to fix your doubt. Just an invitation to do something honest this week.

Here's what I want you to sit with. Not answer — sit with. There's a difference. I want you to pick one question you actually have about faith, about God, about Christianity, about yourself — one question that feels real to you — and instead of pushing it away or trying to immediately solve it, I want you to just sit with it. Bring it to God, even if it feels awkward. Say, "I don't understand this. But I'm still here." And then pay attention to what happens inside you over the next few days. Not some dramatic lightning bolt. Maybe just a quiet sense that the question doesn't have to be the end of your faith. Maybe it can be the beginning of a more honest version of it.

And if you have a friend in this room — or outside this room — who you trust, maybe start there. Maybe say, "Hey, I've been wrestling with something. Can I talk to you about it?" Not so they can give you the right answer. Just so you don't have to carry it alone. Some of the best faith conversations I've ever had started with someone saying, "I don't know what I believe anymore." That can be the most faithful thing you do all week.

Doubt isn't the problem. Pretending is. So let's stop pretending. Let's bring our real, messy, complicated questions to a God who can take it — and see what grows.

# When Faith Gets Complicated

So here's a scenario. You're at youth group, and someone's sharing something vulnerable—maybe about struggling with prayer, or feeling distant from God. And everyone else seems to nod along, to relate, and you're sitting there thinking, *I feel that too*, but you don't say anything. Because what if you're the only one? What if you speak up and people look at you like you don't belong?

Or maybe it's like this: you go to church, and everyone seems so certain. So sure. And you want that. You want to feel that peace everyone talks about. But mostly you just feel confused. You prayed for something and it didn't happen. You read something in the Bible and it didn't make sense. Someone hurt you and you don't know where God was in that. Or you look at the news—really look at it—and you think, *how could a good God exist alongside all this?*

And you don't say any of that out loud. Because maybe you're afraid it makes you a bad Christian. Or not a Christian at all.

I want to start by saying: I don't have all the answers. I'm not going to stand up here and solve your doubt like it's a math problem. But I want to tell you something I wish someone had told me: what you're feeling isn't weird. It isn't wrong. And you're definitely not alone.

Doubt isn't new to faith. It's always been part of it.

---

Here's what I used to think: doubt means you don't have enough faith. Like doubt is the opposite of faith, and if you just tried harder, read more, prayed more, you wouldn't feel this way anymore.

But that's not what the Bible shows us. Not even close.

Look at the Psalms. Half of them are complaints. David writes over and over: *Where are you, God? Why have you forgotten me? Why do the wicked prosper?* He's not performing faith. He's bringing his real questions to the only place he knows to bring them.

Or look at Job. The guy loses everything—kids, wealth, health—and his friends show up with all the answers. And Job looks at them and says, *You don't know what you're talking about.* Then he turns to God and says, *I have questions.* And God doesn't smite him. God shows up. And what does God say? He doesn't explain the suffering. He shows up in the whirlwind and says, *I'm God. You aren't. Let's talk.*

Or look at Habakkuk—one of the shortest books in the Bible. It's basically one guy saying, *How long, Lord? The evil people are winning. The righteous are suffering. Do something.* And God's answer is strange and unsettling. And Habakkuk doesn't get everything resolved. But at the end, he says something beautiful: *Even if the fig tree doesn't bloom and the fields are empty, I will rejoice in the Lord.* That's not blind faith. That's someone who decided to keep wrestling.

---

Now, I know the most famous doubt story: Thomas.

You know Thomas. Called "Doubting Thomas." The guy who wouldn't believe Jesus was alive unless he could touch the wounds.

But here's what I love about Thomas. He's not faithless. He's *honest*. When the other disciples say they've seen the risen Lord, Thomas says, *Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, I won't believe.*

He's not rejecting faith. He's saying: *I need something real. I need to see for myself.*

And then Jesus shows up. And what does he say to Thomas? He doesn't rebuke him. He doesn't say, *You should have just believed.* He says, *Put your finger here. See my hands. Stop doubting and believe.*

And then Jesus says this: *Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.*

Thomas gets remembered for doubt. But his doubt led him to something deeper. He demanded honesty—and he got it. And then he believed in a way that was his own. Not inherited. Not performed. *His.*

---

Here's what I want you to take away: your doubt might not be the problem. It might actually be the door.

The things you're questioning—the hard stuff, the stuff that keeps you up at night—those are the questions faithful people have asked for thousands of years. You're not breaking new ground. You're walking a road that's been walked before. And that road doesn't end in losing faith. Sometimes it ends in faith that's harder to shake. Because it's been tested. It's been wrestled with. It's yours.

There's a difference between doubt that runs from God and doubt that runs toward God. The first one is disconnection. The second one is actually a form of trust. You're saying: *I need to know. I need you to be real enough to handle my questions.*

And here's the thing: God can handle it.

---

Now, here's your next step. Not a formula. Not a prayer to pray that will make everything okay. Something real.

I want you to take one question—one you've been holding onto, maybe one you're afraid to say out loud—and bring it to someone. Not to fix it. Just to say it.

It could be a youth leader. A parent. A friend who doesn't roll their eyes when things get heavy. Someone who will listen without trying to shut you down.

Or if you're not ready to say it out loud, write it down. Put it somewhere. Sit with it.

The point isn't to find the answer immediately. The point is to stop pretending you don't have the question.

And here's something else: read the Gospel of John. Not to find proof. Just notice the people who come to Jesus. The blind man. The woman at the well. Nicodemus at night. The disciples after the resurrection. Notice how Jesus meets them where they are. In their confusion. In their need. In their doubt.

Maybe that's who he is. Maybe that's who he's been all along.

You don't have to have it figured out. You just have to stay in the conversation.

# Detailed Feedback on "Doubt and Faith" Youth Group Talk

## Overall Impression

This is a strong, thoughtful piece of writing that takes its audience seriously and handles a sensitive topic with genuine care. It does many things well. But it also has structural and tonal patterns that, over its length, work against some of its best instincts. Below I'll walk through each of your five criteria with specific observations.

---

## 1. Authenticity

**Strengths:**
The Maya scenario is well-drawn and specific. "Trying to look fine, trying to pretend the questions don't exist" — that's a line that will land because it describes a behavior, not a feeling. It trusts the audience to recognize themselves in the action rather than being told how to feel. The hallway setting is grounded and sensory (fluorescent lights, hot chocolate), which earns credibility.

The line "doubt doesn't disqualify you from being part of this community" is direct and important. It does the actual pastoral work of making the room safe, rather than just gesturing toward safety.

**Areas for Improvement:**
The talk *tells* the audience it won't offer clichés, but then occasionally drifts toward polished, aphoristic language that functions like a cliché in a nicer outfit. For example:

> "Faith isn't a full inventory checked off in a single afternoon; it's a relationship you're learning to live with."

> "Doubt isn't a malfunction in your spiritual life; it's a signal that you're alive to truth, longing for integrity, and willing to grow."

These are well-constructed sentences. They're also the kind of sentences that sound great from a stage and evaporate thirty seconds later. A teenager who is genuinely struggling will hear the rhythm and think, *that's a line*, not *that's true*. The talk is at its most authentic when it's specific and slightly awkward — the Maya paragraph, the Habakkuk cry — and at its least authentic when it reaches for polished summation.

**Suggestion:** In revision, identify every sentence that could be pulled out and printed on a coffee mug. Then ask: does this earn its place through specificity, or is it doing the work of sounding wise? Cut or rewrite at least half of them. Replace them with something rougher, more concrete, or more honestly uncertain. For instance, instead of "doubt is a signal that you're alive to truth," you might say something like: "The fact that you're bothered by the question probably means you care about the answer. That's not weakness. That's the starting point."

---

## 2. Theological Depth Without Being Academic

**Strengths:**
The handling of Thomas is genuinely good. You push past the "Doubting Thomas" caricature and offer a reading that's textually grounded without being exegetical in a dry sense. The observation that Jesus *meets* Thomas rather than *shaming* him is theologically rich and pastorally important. The move from "God does not shame honest questions" to "God meets honest questions with presence" is the strongest theological claim in the talk, and it's stated plainly enough to stick.

The inclusion of Habakkuk is a smart choice — it's less familiar than Thomas, which gives the talk range and avoids the predictability of only using the "obvious" doubt passage.

**Areas for Improvement:**
The Habakkuk section, while promising, stays somewhat surface-level compared to the Thomas section. You quote the opening cry and then jump to "the righteous shall live by faith" without spending much time in the middle — which is where the real theological tension lives. Habakkuk 1:13 ("Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?") and God's bewildering answer in chapter 1:5-11 (essentially, "I'm sending the Babylonians, and it's going to be worse than you think") are where the book gets genuinely uncomfortable. The prophet doesn't just doubt; he's *angry at God's answer*. That's a level of honesty most youth talks never reach, and it would strengthen yours considerably.

Also, the phrase "the righteous shall live by faith" is introduced and then glossed quickly. You say it's "not a neat slogan," but the gloss you offer — "a practice of living through uncertainty with trust that endures" — is itself somewhat sloganistic. What does that actually look like for Habakkuk? He climbs a watchtower and waits. He writes what he sees. He ends with a hymn that's half defiance and half surrender. Those concrete details would give the theological claim texture.

**Suggestion:** Spend 3-4 more sentences inside Habakkuk's actual argument with God. Let the audience feel how unsatisfying God's initial answer is. Then the pivot to "yet I will rejoice" carries real weight because they've felt the cost of that "yet." You might even say something like: "Habakkuk doesn't get the answer he wants. He gets a God who says, 'Keep watching.' And somehow that's enough — not because it feels good, but because the relationship holds."

---

## 3. Age-Appropriate Engagement

**Strengths:**
The talk generally respects its audience's intelligence. You don't condescend, you don't use slang that would feel forced, and you don't simplify the biblical material into a children's lesson. The Maya scenario is age-appropriate without being patronizing — the questions you give her (suffering, science and faith, permission to doubt) are real questions teenagers actually ask.

The three-step practical framework (name, bring into relationship, do one small thing) is well-scaled for this age group. It's concrete without being prescriptive.

**Areas for Improvement:**
The talk runs long, and its second half becomes increasingly repetitive. The summary paragraph near the end ("To sum up: doubt isn't a malfunction…") essentially restates the entire talk. A 16-year-old's attention will flag here. You've already made these points; making them again, even with slightly different language, signals that you don't trust the audience to have absorbed them the first time.

There's also a density issue. The talk is almost entirely abstract reflection with one concrete scenario (Maya) at the top. After Maya, the audience doesn't get another story, image, or moment of concrete human experience until the very end. For teenagers — who are concrete thinkers even when they're capable of abstraction — this is a long stretch without a handhold. The Habakkuk and Thomas sections are *about* stories but don't *tell* them with much narrative energy.

**Suggestion:** Cut the summary paragraph entirely. Trust your ending. Also, consider adding one brief, concrete moment in the middle of the talk — maybe a sentence or two about what it actually felt like for Thomas to be in that room, or what Habakkuk's watchtower might have looked like. Even a line like "Imagine standing on a wall at night, watching for something you're not sure is coming" would give the audience's imagination something to grip.

Additionally, the current word count pushes past 1,800 words — well beyond the 1,500-word ceiling. Cutting the repetitive summary and tightening the practical section (which currently offers multiple options where one confident recommendation would be stronger) would bring it into range and improve pacing.

---

## 4. Faithful Handling of Biblical Material

**Strengths:**
The John 20 passage is handled with care. You quote Jesus directly, you don't distort the text, and your interpretation — that Jesus meets doubt with invitation rather than condemnation — is well-supported by the passage. You also rightly note that "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" is often cherry-picked, and you resist the easy reading. That's good biblical literacy modeled for the audience.

The Habakkuk 3:17-18 allusion at the end ("Though the fig tree does not blossom…") is accurate and well-placed.

**Areas for Improvement:**
One claim needs more care. You write:

> "In the weeks after that encounter, Thomas isn't erased from the story; he becomes a man who teaches others what it means to follow [a] kind of Messiah who is present even in the room when we're scared or unsure."

This is a reasonable inference from church tradition (Thomas is traditionally credited with missionary work in India), but the biblical text itself doesn't tell us much about Thomas after John 20. You should either flag that this is tradition rather than text, or soften the claim. As written, a sharp teenager — or a sharp youth leader — might push back and ask, "Where does it say that?" and you'd be on thin ground.

There's also a small typo: "follow kind of Messiah" should be "follow a kind of Messiah" or "follow the kind of Messiah."

**Suggestion:** Revise the Thomas post-encounter claim to something like: "Thomas doesn't disappear from the story. Tradition tells us he went on to carry the gospel further than almost any other disciple. His doubt didn't disqualify him; it prepared him." This is honest about the source and still makes your point.

---

## 5. Practical and Actionable Conclusion

**Strengths:**
The three-step framework (name, bring into relationship, act) is genuinely useful. It's simple without being simplistic, and it respects the reality that not every teenager will be ready for the same step. The suggestion to write a lament as an alternative to conversation is a particularly thoughtful inclusion — it gives introverts and those who aren't ready to talk aloud a real entry point.

The starter questions ("What would I need to believe about God to feel okay with the things I don't understand yet?") are strong. They're open-ended, non-leading, and genuinely interesting.

**Areas for Improvement:**
The practical section is too long and offers too many options. You give the three-step framework, then two starter questions, then the lament alternative, then a final "your move this week" restatement. By the time you reach the end, the audience has been given roughly five different practical suggestions, which paradoxically makes it *less* likely they'll do any of them. Choice overload is real, especially for teenagers.

The final paragraph also circles back to Thomas one more time ("remember Thomas isn't the enemy here; he's the road map"), which, while a nice callback, adds length without adding substance. The talk has already made this point effectively.

**Suggestion:** Pick *one* clear next step and commit to it. I'd recommend the journal-and-conversation challenge: write down one question, find one person, have one conversation this week. That's clean, memorable, and actionable. Move the lament suggestion into the body of the talk (perhaps after Habakkuk, where it fits naturally) rather than leaving it as an alternative in the conclusion. Cut the final Thomas callback. End on something short and direct — the "you're allowed to doubt, you're allowed to question, you're allowed to say to God, 'I don't get it, and I still want to know you'" line is your real ending. Stop there or very close to there.

---

## Summary of Key Revisions

1. **Cut polished aphorisms** that function as dressed-up clichés. Replace with rougher, more specific language.
2. **Deepen the Habakkuk section** — spend time inside the discomfort of God's answer, not just the resolution.
3. **Add one concrete, sensory moment** in the middle of the talk to re-anchor the audience's attention.
4. **Cut the summary paragraph and the final Thomas callback.** Trust your audience to have listened.
5. **Streamline the practical section** to one clear, confident ask. Move alternatives into the body.
6. **Flag the Thomas tradition claim** as tradition, not text.
7. **Bring the word count down** to the 1,000-1,500 range by eliminating repetition.

This is a talk with a genuine heart and real theological substance. The core message — that God meets honest questions with presence, not shame — is exactly right, and it's delivered with warmth. The revision work is mostly about trusting your best instincts more fully: being specific where you're currently polished, being brief where you're currently repetitive, and letting the rough edges stay rough, because that's where teenagers will feel the honesty you're aiming for.
